type:LABEL: collection
name: The five great court epics (pañca-mahākāvya)
summary: The conventional canon of five Sanskrit mahākāvyas — Kālidāsa’s Raghuvaṃśa and Kumārasambhava, Bhāravi’s Kirātārjunīya, Māgha’s Śiśupālavadha and Śrīharṣa’s Naiṣadhīyacarita. Four of the five rework episodes of the epics.

type:LABEL: text
name: Raghuvaṃśa
summary: Kālidāsa’s mahākāvya in nineteen cantos on the kings of the solar line, from Dilīpa and Raghu through Aja and Daśaratha to Rāma (cantos 10–15), his descendants and the dissolute Agnivarṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Indumatī
summary: Princess of Vidarbha, sister of king Bhoja, who chooses Aja at her svayaṃvara (Raghuvaṃśa 6) and dies when a celestial garland falls on her breast (canto 8).
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: character
name: Sudakṣiṇā
summary: Queen of Dilīpa and mother of Raghu in the Raghuvaṃśa; with Dilīpa she serves the cow Nandinī to obtain a son.
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: character
name: Nandinī (Vasiṣṭha’s cow)
summary: The wish-granting cow of Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage, daughter of Surabhi, whom Dilīpa tends and protects from a lion in Raghuvaṃśa 1–2.
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: character
name: Agnivarṇa
summary: The last king of the Raghuvaṃśa, a pleasure-loving ruler who dies of consumption; his pregnant queen rules as regent at the poem’s end (canto 19).
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Dilīpa and the cow Nandinī
summary: The childless king Dilīpa and queen Sudakṣiṇā tend Vasiṣṭha’s cow Nandinī; when a lion (Śiva’s servant) seizes her, Dilīpa offers his own body, and the cow grants him a son, Raghu (Raghuvaṃśa 1–2).
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Aja and Indumatī
summary: Aja wins Indumatī at her svayaṃvara among many kings (Raghuvaṃśa 6–7); years later she dies when a celestial garland falls on her, and Aja’s grief (8) leads to his death.
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Daśaratha kills the ascetic’s son
summary: Hunting by night, the young Daśaratha shoots at the sound of a pitcher being filled, thinking it an elephant, and kills the only son of a blind ascetic couple; the dying father curses him to die of grief for a son (later tradition names the boy Śravaṇa).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kumārasambhava
summary: Kālidāsa’s mahākāvya on the courtship and marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī — Pārvatī’s birth to Himālaya, the gods’ plight under the demon Tāraka, Kāma’s incineration by Śiva’s third eye, Pārvatī’s penance and the wedding; cantos 9–17 (Kumāra’s birth and Tāraka’s death) are usually held to be a later continuation.

type:LABEL: text
name: Abhijñānaśākuntalam
summary: Kālidāsa’s seven-act nāṭaka on king Duḥṣanta (Duṣyanta) and Śakuntalā. It reworks the Mahābhārata’s Śakuntalopākhyāna (MBh 1.62–69) by adding the sage Durvāsas’s curse, which makes the king forget her, and the recognition-ring (abhijñāna) whose loss and recovery drive the plot.

type:LABEL: character
name: Durvāsas
summary: An irascible sage, son of Atri, whose curses and boons drive several stories: in the Mahābhārata he gives Kuntī the mantra by which she summons gods; in Kālidāsa’s Śākuntala his curse makes Duḥṣanta forget Śakuntalā; in Purāṇic tellings his curse on Indra leads to the churning of the ocean.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Durvāsas’s curse and Śakuntalā’s ring
summary: Kālidāsa’s addition to the Śakuntalā story: lost in thought of the king, Śakuntalā fails to greet Durvāsas, who curses her to be forgotten until her lover sees a token; the king’s signet ring, lost while bathing, is found by a fisherman and restores his memory.
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: text
name: Meghadūta
summary: Kālidāsa’s lyric “messenger poem”: an exiled yakṣa at Rāmagiri sends a monsoon cloud with a message to his wife in Alakā. The opening places him among hermitages “whose waters are hallowed by the bathing of Janaka’s daughter”, and the wife is to greet the cloud as Maithilī greeted the son of the Wind.

type:LABEL: character
name: The yakṣa of the Meghadūta
summary: The unnamed yakṣa, a servant of Kubera exiled for a year for neglecting his duty, who speaks the Meghadūta’s message to the cloud.
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: character
name: Āyus (son of Purūravas)
summary: Son of Purūravas and Urvaśī; in Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīya the boy, brought up secretly in a hermitage, is revealed to his father in the last act. In the Purāṇic genealogies he continues the Lunar line through his son Nahuṣa.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhāsa
summary: A Sanskrit dramatist praised by Bāṇa (Harṣacarita, introductory verse 15) for plays “begun by the sūtradhāra”. Thirteen anonymous plays found in Kerala and published by T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī from 1912 are attributed to him — an attribution that remains disputed.

type:LABEL: collection
name: The Trivandrum plays (“Bhāsa-nāṭaka-cakra”)
summary: Thirteen anonymous Sanskrit plays preserved in Kerala manuscripts and the Kūṭiyāṭṭam performance tradition, published by T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series (1912–15) as the works of Bhāsa. Seven retell the Mahābhārata or the Kṛṣṇa story, two the Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Trivandrum plays are the works of Bhāsa
summary: T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī’s thesis (1912) that the thirteen Kerala plays are the lost dramas of Bhāsa praised by Kālidāsa and Bāṇa. Many scholars accept a common origin for the corpus but doubt or deny that it is Bhāsa’s; a widely held alternative treats the plays as Kerala acting versions (perhaps abridged) prepared for Cākyār performance.

type:LABEL: text
name: Pratimānāṭaka
summary: A seven-act Rāma play attributed to Bhāsa, from Rāma’s exile to his coronation after Rāvaṇa’s death. Its eponymous invention is the statue-house (pratimā-gṛha) of the Ikṣvāku kings, where the returning Bharata learns of his father’s death by seeing Daśaratha’s statue.

type:LABEL: text
name: Abhiṣekanāṭaka
summary: A six-act Rāma play attributed to Bhāsa, from the killing of Vālin to Rāma’s consecration (abhiṣeka) after the war.

type:LABEL: text
name: Dūtavākya
summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa on Kṛṣṇa’s embassy to Duryodhana: Duryodhana insults him and tries to bind him; Kṛṣṇa reveals his cosmic form and summons his personified weapons, led by the discus Sudarśana.

type:LABEL: text
name: Dūtaghaṭotkaca
summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa set after Abhimanyu’s death: Ghaṭotkaca comes to the Kauravas as Kṛṣṇa’s envoy with a warning of Arjuna’s vengeance.

type:LABEL: text
name: Karṇabhāra
summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa: on the battlefield, with Śalya as his charioteer, Karṇa gives his natural armour and earrings to Indra disguised as a brahmin, and is sent the spear Vimalā in return.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ūrubhaṅga
summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa on Duryodhana’s death after Bhīma breaks his thighs. Unusually for Sanskrit drama, the hero dies on stage — repentant, reconciled, forbidding vengeance — while Balarāma rages and Aśvatthāman vows the night massacre.

type:LABEL: text
name: Madhyamavyāyoga
summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa: Ghaṭotkaca, sent by Hiḍimbā to find her a human meal, seizes the “middle” son of a brahmin family; Bhīma, the middle Pāṇḍava, offers himself instead, and father and son recognise each other.

type:LABEL: text
name: Pañcarātra (Bhāsa)
summary: A three-act play attributed to Bhāsa: as his sacrificial fee Droṇa asks Duryodhana to give the Pāṇḍavas half the kingdom; Duryodhana agrees if they are found within five nights (pañcarātra), and the Virāṭa cattle-raid reveals them — an invented happy ending to the quarrel.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bālacarita
summary: A five-act play attributed to Bhāsa on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood, from his birth in Kaṃsa’s prison through the exploits in the cowherd settlement to the killing of Kaṃsa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Svapnavāsavadatta
summary: The best-known of the Trivandrum plays, on king Udayana of Vatsa and his queen Vāsavadattā, who is thought dead; a play of this name is ascribed to Bhāsa by later critics, which anchors the attribution of the whole corpus.

type:LABEL: character
name: Durjaya (son of Duryodhana, in the Ūrubhaṅga)
summary: Duryodhana’s young son in Bhāsa’s Ūrubhaṅga, who wants to sit on his dying father’s lap; Duryodhana tells him to serve the Pāṇḍavas, obey Kuntī and honour Draupadī and Subhadrā as mothers.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bharata in the statue-house (Pratimānāṭaka)
summary: Bhāsa’s invention in the Pratimānāṭaka: returning from his uncle’s house, Bharata enters the shrine where statues of the dead Ikṣvāku kings stand, sees a new statue of Daśaratha, and so learns of his father’s death.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhīma meets Ghaṭotkaca (Madhyamavyāyoga)
summary: The plot of the Madhyamavyāyoga: Ghaṭotkaca, hunting a human for his mother Hiḍimbā, demands the “middle” son of a brahmin; Bhīma, the middle Pāṇḍava, goes in his place, fights him, and the two recognise each other as father and son.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Karṇa gives away his armour and earrings
summary: Indra, disguised as a brahmin, begs Karṇa for the armour and earrings he was born with; Karṇa, warned beforehand by the Sun, cuts them from his body and in the Mahābhārata obtains in exchange Indra’s unfailing spear, good for one kill.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhavabhūti
summary: Sanskrit dramatist of the early 8th century, author of the Mahāvīracarita and Uttararāmacarita (Rāma plays) and the Mālatīmādhava. Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (4.144) places him with Vākpatirāja at the court of Yaśovarman of Kānyakubja.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mahāvīracarita
summary: Bhavabhūti’s seven-act play on Rāma’s early career, from Viśvāmitra’s hermitage and the breaking of Śiva’s bow to the war and coronation. Its chief innovation is to make Rāvaṇa’s minister Mālyavat the schemer behind events Vālmīki leaves to chance or to Kaikeyī, such as Śūrpaṇakhā’s disguise as Mantharā.

type:LABEL: text
name: Uttararāmacarita
summary: Bhavabhūti’s seven-act play on “Rāma’s later life”: the banishment of the pregnant Sītā, Rāma’s grief on revisiting Pañcavaṭī where the invisible Sītā watches him (act 3), the meeting with his sons, and a final play-within-a-play staged by Vālmīki after which Sītā is restored and reunited with Rāma — reversing Vālmīki’s ending.

type:LABEL: character
name: Candraketu (son of Lakṣmaṇa)
summary: Son of Lakṣmaṇa and Ūrmilā; in the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (CE 7.92) Rāma installs him and his brother Aṅgada as kings in the west and north. In Bhavabhūti’s Uttararāmacarita he guards the sacrificial horse and fights his cousin Lava.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mālyavat (rākṣasa)
summary: Eldest son of the rākṣasa Sukeśa and brother of Sumālin, Rāvaṇa’s maternal grandfather (VR (CE) 7.5–6). Bhavabhūti’s Mahāvīracarita makes him Rāvaṇa’s scheming minister who engineers the plot against Rāma.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kirātārjunīya
summary: Bhāravi’s mahākāvya in eighteen cantos expanding a short episode of the Āraṇyakaparvan: urged by Draupadī and Bhīma and advised by Vyāsa, Arjuna performs austerities on Mount Indrakīla, resists the apsarases sent to test him, fights Śiva disguised as a mountain hunter over a boar, and receives the Pāśupata weapon.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mūka (the boar-demon)
summary: A son of Diti who takes the form of a boar to kill Arjuna at his austerities and is shot simultaneously by Arjuna and Śiva-as-kirāta, setting off their quarrel (MBh (CE) 3.40.7–16).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: person
name: Māgha
summary: Sanskrit poet of western India, author of the Śiśupālavadha. In the poem’s closing verses on his family (not in the GRETIL text) he names his grandfather Suprabhadeva as minister of a king Varmalāta, who is usually identified with the Varmalāta of a Vasantgaḍh inscription of 625 CE, placing Māgha in the later 7th or 8th century.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śiśupālavadha
summary: Māgha’s mahākāvya in twenty cantos: Nārada asks Kṛṣṇa to kill Śiśupāla; Kṛṣṇa, torn between that duty and Yudhiṣṭhira’s invitation to the rājasūya, takes counsel with Balarāma and Uddhava, journeys to Indraprastha, and at the sacrifice beheads the insulting king of Cedi, whose radiance enters Kṛṣṇa’s body.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhaṭṭi
summary: Author of the Rāvaṇavadha (Bhaṭṭikāvya), a Rāma poem that doubles as a textbook of Pāṇini’s grammar. Its last verse says it was composed at Valabhī in the realm of king Śrīdharasena, one of the Maitraka kings of that name (6th–7th c.).

type:LABEL: person
name: Śrīharṣa
summary: Twelfth-century poet and philosopher, author of the Naiṣadhīyacarita and of the Advaita dialectical treatise Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya. The colophon verses of his poem name his parents Śrīhīra and Māmalladevī; tradition places him at the Gāhaḍavāla court of Kānyakubja.

type:LABEL: text
name: Naiṣadhīyacarita
summary: Śrīharṣa’s mahākāvya in twenty-two cantos on Nala and Damayantī, the last and most elaborate of the five classical mahākāvyas. It expands the first part of the Mahābhārata’s Nala story — the golden goose as go-between, the gods’ courtship, the svayaṃvara at which four gods take Nala’s form, and the marriage — and ends before Nala’s fall.

type:LABEL: person
name: Murāri
summary: Sanskrit dramatist, author of the Anargharāghava; he names his parents as Vardhamānaka and Tantumatī and is placed in the 9th–10th centuries (before the 12th-century Maṅkha, who praises him).

type:LABEL: text
name: Anargharāghava
summary: Murāri’s seven-act Rāma play, from Viśvāmitra’s request for Rāma to the return to Ayodhyā; celebrated by later critics for its learned, ornate style rather than its stagecraft.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rājaśekhara
summary: Sanskrit and Prakrit poet-critic (c. 880–920), teacher of the Gurjara-Pratihāra king Mahendrapāla I and poet at the court of Mahīpāla; author of the Bālarāmāyaṇa, Bālabhārata, the Prakrit Karpūramañjarī, the Viddhaśālabhañjikā and the Kāvyamīmāṃsā.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bālarāmāyaṇa (Rājaśekhara)
summary: Rājaśekhara’s ten-act Rāma play — among the longest Sanskrit dramas — in which Rāvaṇa appears as a rejected suitor at Sītā’s svayaṃvara, giving the war a romantic motive.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bālabhārata (Pracaṇḍapāṇḍava)
summary: Rājaśekhara’s unfinished Mahābhārata play, of which two acts survive (Draupadī’s svayaṃvara and the dice game).

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṣemendra
summary: Kashmiri polymath of the 11th century, son of Prakāśendra and pupil of Abhinavagupta, who abridged the great narrative works into “mañjarīs” (Rāmāyaṇamañjarī, Bhāratamañjarī, Bṛhatkathāmañjarī) and wrote the Daśāvatāracarita, satires and works on poetics. His Bhāratamañjarī colophon calls him “Vyāsadāsa”.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhāratamañjarī
summary: Kṣemendra’s verse abridgement of the whole Mahābhārata, parvan by parvan, ending with the Harivaṃśa section and a hymn to Vyāsa; about 10,000 verses.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rāmāyaṇamañjarī
summary: Kṣemendra’s verse abridgement of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, including the Uttarakāṇḍa; like the Bhāratamañjarī it reflects the Kashmiri (north-western) version of its source.

type:LABEL: text
name: Daśāvatāracarita
summary: Kṣemendra’s poem on the ten avatāras of Viṣṇu, one of the earliest datable literary lists to include the Buddha among them; its colophon dates it to 1066 CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa (author of the Veṇīsaṃhāra)
summary: Dramatist named in the prologue of the Veṇīsaṃhāra (“the work of the poet Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa, whose emblem is the lion”). Bengali genealogical tradition makes him one of five brahmins brought from Kānyakubja by king Ādiśūra; he is generally placed before c. 800 CE.

type:LABEL: text
name: Veṇīsaṃhāra
summary: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s six-act play on the Mahābhārata war, built on Bhīma’s vow to bind Draupadī’s braid — loosened when Duḥśāsana dragged her by the hair — with hands wet with Duryodhana’s blood; the play ends with Bhīma binding the braid.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhānumatī (wife of Duryodhana)
summary: Duryodhana’s queen as named in Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s Veṇīsaṃhāra, where in act 2 she has an ill-omened dream and performs rites for her husband’s safety. The Mahābhārata critical text does not name Duryodhana’s wife.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The binding of Draupadī’s braid
summary: Draupadī leaves her hair unbound after Duḥśāsana drags her by it in the assembly; Bhīma vows to bind it again with hands red with Duryodhana’s blood, and does so after the war — the plot-frame of the Veṇīsaṃhāra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kumāradāsa
summary: Author of the Sanskrit mahākāvya Jānakīharaṇa. Sri Lankan tradition identifies him with King Kumāradhātusena of Anurādhapura (6th c.), an identification many scholars treat with caution; he is usually placed in the 6th–8th centuries.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jānakīharaṇa
summary: Kumāradāsa’s mahākāvya on the Rāma story in the manner of Kālidāsa’s Raghuvaṃśa. For long known chiefly through a Sinhalese word-by-word gloss (sannaya) and anthology citations, its Sanskrit text was later recovered from South Indian manuscripts.

type:LABEL: person
name: Hāla
summary: A Sātavāhana king to whom the Prakrit anthology Gāhā Sattasaī is traditionally attributed as compiler; the Purāṇic king-lists of the Āndhras include a Hāla.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yogavāsiṣṭha
summary: A vast philosophical dialogue (about 29,000 verses in the vulgate) in which the sage Vasiṣṭha instructs the despondent young Rāma in a non-dualist teaching through many illustrative tales; framed as part of the Rāmāyaṇa and traditionally attributed to Vālmīki.

type:LABEL: text
name: Hanumannāṭaka (Mahānāṭaka)
summary: A loosely dramatic Rāma play in verse, transmitted in two recensions — a western one of 14 acts arranged by Dāmodaramiśra and an eastern one of 9–10 acts by Madhusūdana. Legend says Hanumān himself composed it on rocks and threw it into the sea so as not to eclipse Vālmīki.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jayadeva (author of the Prasannarāghava)
summary: Dramatist and rhetorician, author of the Prasannarāghava and the Candrāloka (poetics), usually placed in the 12th–13th centuries; distinct from Jayadeva of the Gītagovinda.

type:LABEL: text
name: Prasannarāghava
summary: Jayadeva’s seven-act Rāma play, known for its lyrical verses (including river-personifications); later borrowed into vernacular Rāma literature, notably by Tulsīdās.

type:LABEL: person
name: Dhīranāga (Diṅnāga)
summary: Author of the Kundamālā, a play on Sītā’s banishment; manuscripts name him Dhīranāga or Diṅnāga (not the Buddhist logician). His date is uncertain (proposals from the 5th to the 10th c.).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kundamālā
summary: A six-act play on Rāma’s later life: the abandoned Sītā gives birth in Vālmīki’s hermitage; Rāma recognises her garland of kunda flowers floating on the river; the twins recite the Rāmāyaṇa; and, as in Bhavabhūti, the play ends with Sītā’s vindication and reunion.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śaktibhadra
summary: Kerala dramatist, author of the Āścaryacūḍāmaṇi; tradition makes him a pupil of Śaṅkara, and he is usually placed in the 9th century.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āścaryacūḍāmaṇi
summary: Śaktibhadra’s seven-act Rāma play from Kerala, from Śūrpaṇakhā’s mutilation to Sītā’s vindication; named after the “wonderful crest-jewel” and ring that protect the couple. Its acts are staple pieces of Kūṭiyāṭṭam (Śūrpaṇakhāṅkam, Aṅgulīyāṅkam).

type:LABEL: text
name: Campū Rāmāyaṇa (Rāmāyaṇa Campū)
summary: A Rāma story in mixed prose and verse (campū), the first five kāṇḍas attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja and the Yuddhakāṇḍa supplied later by Lakṣmaṇasūri.

type:LABEL: person
name: Trivikramabhaṭṭa
summary: Poet of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa court, author of the Nalacampū (Damayantīkathā), the earliest surviving Sanskrit campū; he composed the eulogy of the Bagumra (Nausari) copper plates of Indra III dated 915 CE.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nalacampū (Damayantīkathā)
summary: Trivikramabhaṭṭa’s campū on Nala and Damayantī, in seven ucchvāsas, unfinished — it breaks off before Nala’s misfortunes.

type:LABEL: person
name: Villiputtūrār
summary: Tamil poet, author of the Villi Pāratam, a Tamil Mahābhārata in about 4,350 viruttam verses; usually dated to the 14th century, under the patronage of a chief Varapati Āṭkoṇṭāṉ.

type:LABEL: text
name: Villi Pāratam
summary: Villiputtūrār’s Tamil Mahābhārata, which ends with the eighteenth day of the war; it became the standard Tamil Bhāratam and a source for Terukkūttu and the Draupadī cult of Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kāśīrāma Dāsa
summary: Bengali poet of the 16th–17th century whose Bengali Mahābhārata (the “Kāśīdāsī Mahābhārata”) became the standard Bengali version; by tradition he completed only the first parvans and relatives or successors completed the rest.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kāśīdāsī Mahābhārata
summary: The Bengali verse Mahābhārata associated with Kāśīrāma Dāsa (16th–17th c.), widely read and recited in Bengal; often printed together with Kṛttibās’s Rāmāyaṇa as the two Bengali epics.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Anukramaṇīparvan (MBh 1.1)
summary: The table of contents: Ugraśravas arrives at Naimiṣa and outlines the epic, including Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s lament “yadāśrauṣam …”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Parvasaṃgrahaparvan (MBh 1.2)
summary: The summary of the parvans, which names the hundred upaparvans (1.2.34–70) and outlines the eighteen books.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Pauṣyaparvan (MBh 1.3)
summary: Janamejaya and the dog’s curse; the stories of Āruṇi, Upamanyu, Veda and Uttaṅka, whose quest for the queen’s earrings motivates the snake sacrifice.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Paulomaparvan (MBh 1.4–12)
summary: Ugraśravas at Śaunaka’s sacrifice; the Bhārgava stories of Pulomā, Cyavana and Ruru.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ādivaṃśāvataraṇaparvan (MBh 1.54–58)
summary: Vyāsa comes to Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice and Vaiśaṃpāyana begins the Bhārata with its summary and the origins of the dynasties.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Saṃbhavaparvan (MBh 1.59–123)
summary: The births: creation and partial incarnations of gods and demons (1.61), Śakuntalā (1.62–69), the Lunar dynasty, Śantanu and Bhīṣma, Vyāsa’s niyoga, the births of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas and their training under Droṇa.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Jatugṛhaparvan (MBh 1.124–138)
summary: The tournament of the princes, Karṇa’s challenge and the plot to burn the Pāṇḍavas in the house of lac at Vāraṇāvata, and their escape.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Haiḍimbaparvan (MBh 1.139–144)
summary: Bhīma kills the rākṣasa Hiḍimba, unites with Hiḍimbā and fathers Ghaṭotkaca.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bakavadhaparvan (MBh 1.145–152)
summary: At Ekacakrā Bhīma takes the brahmin family’s turn to feed the man-eater Baka and kills him.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Caitrarathaparvan (MBh 1.153–173)
summary: On the way to Pañcāla Arjuna defeats the gandharva Citraratha, who tells the stories of Tapatī, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra and urges them to take a priest.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Svayaṃvaraparvan (MBh 1.174–184)
summary: Draupadī’s svayaṃvara: Arjuna, disguised as a brahmin, strings the bow and hits the target, and the Pāṇḍavas fight off the angry kings.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Vaivāhikaparvan (MBh 1.185–191)
summary: The debate over Draupadī’s marriage to five husbands, Vyāsa’s justifications (including the Five Indras, 1.189) and the wedding.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viduragamanaparvan (MBh 1.192–199)
summary: The Kauravas learn the Pāṇḍavas survived; Vidura is sent to bring them back to Hāstinapura.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Rājyalambhaparvan (MBh 1.200–204)
summary: The Pāṇḍavas receive half the kingdom at Khāṇḍavaprastha; Nārada tells the story of Sunda and Upasunda to warn them about sharing Draupadī.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Arjunavanavāsaparvan (MBh 1.205–210)
summary: Arjuna breaks the agreement about Draupadī and goes into exile, marrying Ulūpī and Citrāṅgadā on his travels.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Subhadrāharaṇaparvan (MBh 1.211–212)
summary: At the Raivataka festival Arjuna falls in love with Kṛṣṇa’s sister Subhadrā and carries her off with Kṛṣṇa’s consent.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Haraṇāharikaparvan (MBh 1.213)
summary: Kṛṣṇa pacifies the angry Vṛṣṇis; the wedding gifts; birth of Abhimanyu and of the five sons of Draupadī.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Khāṇḍavadāhaparvan (with Mayadarśana) (MBh 1.214–225)
summary: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna help Agni burn the Khāṇḍava forest, fighting off Indra; Maya the Dānava is spared.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sabhāparvan (the building of the hall) (MBh 2.1–4)
summary: Maya builds Yudhiṣṭhira’s assembly hall at Indraprastha.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mantraparvan (MBh 2.5–17)
summary: Nārada describes the halls of the world-guardians and urges the rājasūya; Kṛṣṇa advises that Jarāsaṃdha must first be removed.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Jarāsaṃdhavadhaparvan (MBh 2.18–22)
summary: Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma and Arjuna enter Girivraja disguised as brahmins; Bhīma kills Jarāsaṃdha in a wrestling match.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Digvijayaparvan (MBh 2.23–29)
summary: Arjuna, Bhīma, Sahadeva and Nakula conquer the four quarters for the rājasūya.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Rājasūyikaparvan (MBh 2.30–32)
summary: The rājasūya is prepared and the kings assemble.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Arghābhiharaṇaparvan (MBh 2.33–36)
summary: On Bhīṣma’s advice the first guest-gift goes to Kṛṣṇa; Śiśupāla protests.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śiśupālavadhaparvan (MBh 2.37–42)
summary: Bhīṣma tells of Śiśupāla’s birth; Śiśupāla insults Kṛṣṇa, who beheads him with his discus (2.42.21).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Anudyūtaparvan (MBh 2.66–72)
summary: The second dice game, which sends the Pāṇḍavas into twelve years of forest exile and a thirteenth incognito.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āraṇyakaparvan (the exile begins) (MBh 3.1–11)
summary: The Pāṇḍavas go to the forest followed by brahmins; Yudhiṣṭhira receives the inexhaustible vessel from the Sun; Vidura’s banishment and Maitreya’s curse on Duryodhana.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kirmīravadhaparvan (MBh 3.12)
summary: Vidura tells Dhṛtarāṣṭra how Bhīma killed the rākṣasa Kirmīra, Baka’s brother.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kairātaparvan (MBh 3.13–41)
summary: Kṛṣṇa visits the exiles; debates of Draupadī, Bhīma and Yudhiṣṭhira; Arjuna goes to Indrakīla, is tested by Indra (3.38), fights Śiva as a kirāta and receives the Pāśupata (3.40–41).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Indralokābhigamanaparvan (MBh 3.42–79)
summary: The world-guardians give Arjuna weapons and he is taken to Indra’s heaven; meanwhile Bṛhadaśva tells Yudhiṣṭhira the story of Nala (3.50–78).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Tīrthayātrāparvan (MBh 3.80–153)
summary: The Pāṇḍavas’ pilgrimage to the sacred fords with Lomaśa, with many embedded stories (Agastya, Ṛśyaśṛṅga, Paraśurāma, Bhīma’s meeting with Hanumān).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Jaṭāsuravadhaparvan (MBh 3.154)
summary: The rākṣasa Jaṭāsura, disguised as a brahmin, abducts Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins and Draupadī and is killed by Bhīma.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Yakṣayuddhaparvan (MBh 3.155–172)
summary: In Kubera’s realm Bhīma fights the yakṣas; Arjuna returns from heaven and tells of the Nivātakavacas.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ājagaraparvan (MBh 3.173–178)
summary: The python that seizes Bhīma is king Nahuṣa under a curse; Yudhiṣṭhira frees him by answering his questions.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mārkaṇḍeyasamasyāparvan (MBh 3.179–221)
summary: At Kāmyaka the sage Mārkaṇḍeya tells many stories: the flood, the yugas, Dhundhumāra, the faithful wife and the hunter, and the birth of Skanda.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Draupadīsatyabhāmāsaṃvādaparvan (MBh 3.222–224)
summary: Draupadī explains to Satyabhāmā how she keeps her husbands devoted.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ghoṣayātrāparvan (MBh 3.225–243)
summary: Duryodhana’s cattle-inspection expedition to gloat over the exiles; captured by the gandharva Citrasena, he is freed by the Pāṇḍavas, and in shame resolves to fast to death.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mṛgasvapnabhayaparvan (MBh 3.244)
summary: The deer of Dvaitavana appear to Yudhiṣṭhira in a dream and he moves the camp to Kāmyaka.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Vrīhidrauṇikaparvan (MBh 3.245–247)
summary: Vyāsa tells the story of the gleaner Mudgala, who declines heaven.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Draupadīharaṇaparvan (MBh 3.248–283)
summary: Jayadratha abducts Draupadī and is caught and humiliated; Mārkaṇḍeya consoles Yudhiṣṭhira with the Rāmopākhyāna (3.257–275) and the story of Sāvitrī (3.277–283).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āraṇeyaparvan (MBh 3.295–299)
summary: The brahmin’s fire-drill carried off by a deer; the brothers die at the yakṣa’s lake and Yudhiṣṭhira revives them by answering the yakṣa’s (Dharma’s) questions (3.297–298).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Vairāṭaparvan (Pāṇḍavapraveśa) (MBh 4.1–12)
summary: The Pāṇḍavas enter Virāṭa’s service in disguise for the year of concealment.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kīcakavadhaparvan (MBh 4.13–23)
summary: Kīcaka, the queen’s brother, harasses Draupadī (Sairandhrī); Bhīma kills him in the dance-hall and then his brothers.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Gograhaṇaparvan (MBh 4.24–62)
summary: The Kauravas and Trigartas raid Virāṭa’s cattle; Arjuna, as the eunuch Bṛhannaḍā, drives prince Uttara’s chariot and routs the Kuru army.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Vaivāhikaparvan (Virāṭa) (MBh 4.63–67)
summary: The Pāṇḍavas reveal themselves; Virāṭa’s daughter Uttarā is married to Abhimanyu.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Udyogaparvan (the war council) (MBh 5.1–21)
summary: The allies meet at Upaplavya; Duryodhana and Arjuna both ask Kṛṣṇa’s help; Drupada’s priest goes as envoy.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Saṃjayayānaparvan (MBh 5.22–32)
summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra sends Saṃjaya to the Pāṇḍavas; the exchange of messages.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Yānasaṃdhiparvan (MBh 5.46–69)
summary: Saṃjaya reports to the Kuru assembly; debates about peace and war.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ulūkadūtāgamanaparvan (MBh 5.157–161)
summary: Duryodhana sends Śakuni’s son Ulūka with insulting messages to the Pāṇḍavas.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Rathātirathasaṃkhyāparvan (MBh 5.162–169)
summary: Bhīṣma, appointed commander, rates the warriors of both sides as rathas and atirathas.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Jambūkhaṇḍavinirmāṇaparvan (MBh 6.1–11)
summary: Vyāsa grants Saṃjaya divine sight; Saṃjaya describes the continent Jambūdvīpa and Bhāratavarṣa.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhūmiparvan (MBh 6.12–13)
summary: Saṃjaya describes the other continents (dvīpas).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhagavadgītāparvan (MBh 6.14–40)
summary: Saṃjaya returns to announce Bhīṣma’s fall and narrates from the first day: the armies, and Kṛṣṇa’s teaching to Arjuna (the Gītā, 6.23–40).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhīṣmavadhaparvan (MBh 6.41–117)
summary: The ten days of Bhīṣma’s command, ending with his fall, pierced by Arjuna’s arrows with Śikhaṇḍin in front.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Droṇābhiṣekaparvan (MBh 7.1–15)
summary: Droṇa is consecrated commander and vows to capture Yudhiṣṭhira.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Saṃśaptakavadhaparvan (MBh 7.16–32)
summary: The Trigarta “sworn warriors” draw Arjuna away; the battle with Bhagadatta.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Abhimanyuvadhaparvan (MBh 7.33–51)
summary: Abhimanyu breaks into Droṇa’s circular array and is killed; Arjuna returns to the news.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Pratijñāparvan (MBh 7.52–59)
summary: Arjuna’s vow to kill Jayadratha before sunset or enter the fire, and the preparations of both sides.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Jayadrathavadhaparvan (MBh 7.60–121)
summary: The fourteenth day: Arjuna fights through to Jayadratha and beheads him at sunset (7.121).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ghaṭotkacavadhaparvan (MBh 7.122–154)
summary: The night battle, in which Karṇa spends Indra’s spear on Ghaṭotkaca.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Droṇavadhaparvan (MBh 7.155–165)
summary: The false report of Aśvatthāman’s death; Droṇa lays down his arms and is beheaded by Dhṛṣṭadyumna (7.165.47).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nārāyaṇāstramokṣaparvan (MBh 7.166–173)
summary: Aśvatthāman looses the Nārāyaṇa weapon, neutralised when the Pāṇḍavas lay down their arms on Kṛṣṇa’s advice.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śalyaparvan (Śalya’s command) (MBh 9.1–28)
summary: Śalya commands the Kauravas on the eighteenth day and is killed by Yudhiṣṭhira (9.16); Sahadeva kills Śakuni.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Hradapraveśanaparvan (MBh 9.29–30)
summary: Duryodhana hides in a lake; the Pāṇḍavas find him and goad him out.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Gadāyuddhaparvan (MBh 9.31–64)
summary: The mace duel of Bhīma and Duryodhana (enclosing the Sārasvata section, 9.34–53), Balarāma’s anger and Duryodhana’s lament.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sārasvataparvan (MBh 9.34–53)
summary: Balarāma’s pilgrimage along the Sarasvatī, told as he arrives for the duel.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sauptikaparvan (the night raid) (MBh 10.1–9)
summary: Aśvatthāman, inspired by an owl killing crows, attacks the sleeping camp; Duryodhana dies on hearing the news (10.9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Aiṣīkaparvan (MBh 10.10–18)
summary: The pursuit of Aśvatthāman; his brahmaśiras weapon is diverted into Uttarā’s womb; Kṛṣṇa curses him and he gives up his crest-jewel.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Jalapradānikaparvan (MBh 11.1–8)
summary: Vidura and Vyāsa console Dhṛtarāṣṭra in his grief.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Strīparvan (the laments) (MBh 11.9–25)
summary: The women go to the battlefield; Dhṛtarāṣṭra crushes the iron Bhīma; Gāndhārī’s lament over the dead (11.16–25) ends in her curse on Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śrāddhaparvan (MBh 11.26–27)
summary: The funeral rites; Kuntī reveals that Karṇa was her son.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āśramavāsaparvan (MBh 15.1–35)
summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, Kuntī, Vidura and Saṃjaya retire to the forest; Vidura’s death.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Putradarśanaparvan (MBh 15.36–44)
summary: Vyāsa makes the dead warriors rise from the Gaṅgā for one night (15.40).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nāradāgamanaparvan (MBh 15.45–47)
summary: Nārada reports that Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī and Kuntī died in a forest fire.

type:LABEL: character
name: Baka (rākṣasa of Ekacakrā)
summary: A man-eating rākṣasa who exacts a daily tribute of food and a human from the town of Ekacakrā until Bhīma, taking the brahmin family’s turn, kills him (MBh (CE) 1.145–152).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kirmīra
summary: A rākṣasa, brother of Baka, who bars the exiled Pāṇḍavas’ way into the Kāmyaka forest and is killed by Bhīma (MBh (CE) 3.12).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Jaṭāsura
summary: A rākṣasa who, disguised as a brahmin, carries off Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins and Draupadī, and is killed by Bhīma (MBh (CE) 3.154).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Citrasena (gandharva king)
summary: King of the gandharvas, friend of Arjuna (who learnt music and dance from him in Indra’s heaven); in the Ghoṣayātrā he captures Duryodhana and releases him at the Pāṇḍavas’ request.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Uttara (son of Virāṭa)
summary: Prince of the Matsyas, son of Virāṭa and brother of Uttarā. In the cattle raid he boasts, panics at the sight of the Kuru army and is made charioteer by Bṛhannaḍā (Arjuna), who routs the Kurus; he dies in the war.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Mudgala (the gleaner)
summary: A sage who lives by gleaning a measure of rice (vrīhidroṇa) every fortnight, feeds even Durvāsas without anger, and declines heaven when he learns its limits (MBh (CE) 3.245–247).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Baka
summary: At Ekacakrā, where the Pāṇḍavas live disguised as brahmins, Bhīma takes the place of their host’s family as the rākṣasa Baka’s victim and kills him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Arjuna carries off Subhadrā
summary: During his exile Arjuna sees Kṛṣṇa’s sister Subhadrā at the Raivataka festival and, with Kṛṣṇa’s connivance, carries her off in his chariot; Kṛṣṇa then reconciles the angry Vṛṣṇis.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Kirmīra
summary: As the exiles enter the Kāmyaka forest the rākṣasa Kirmīra, Baka’s brother, blocks their way; Bhīma kills him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Arjuna in Indra’s heaven
summary: After the Kirāta encounter the world-guardians give Arjuna their weapons and Indra’s charioteer Mātali takes him to Indra’s heaven, where he lives for five years learning weapons and, from Citrasena, music and dance.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Jaṭāsura
summary: A rākṣasa disguised as a brahmin carries off Yudhiṣṭhira, Nakula, Sahadeva and Draupadī while Bhīma is away hunting; Bhīma overtakes and kills him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Nahuṣa the python
summary: A huge python seizes Bhīma in the Himālaya; it is king Nahuṣa, cursed by Agastya for his arrogance as Indra. Yudhiṣṭhira frees Bhīma, and Nahuṣa from the curse, by answering his questions about brahminhood and conduct.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Duryodhana’s cattle expedition (Ghoṣayātrā)
summary: Duryodhana goes to Dvaitavana on the pretext of inspecting his cattle in order to flaunt his wealth before the exiles; the gandharva king Citrasena captures him, the Pāṇḍavas free him at Yudhiṣṭhira’s order, and the humiliated Duryodhana resolves to fast to death until the dānavas dissuade him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Jayadratha abducts Draupadī
summary: While the Pāṇḍavas are out hunting, Jayadratha king of Sindhu carries Draupadī off from the Kāmyaka hermitage; the brothers overtake him, Bhīma spares his life at Yudhiṣṭhira’s word, and Jayadratha is shaved and released in humiliation.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Mudgala and the measure of rice
summary: Vyāsa consoles Yudhiṣṭhira with the story of Mudgala, who lives on gleanings, feeds the testing Durvāsas, and refuses the heaven offered him because merit there is exhausted.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The cattle raid on Virāṭa (Gograhaṇa)
summary: At the end of the year of concealment the Trigartas and then the Kurus raid Virāṭa’s cattle; Arjuna, disguised as the eunuch dance-teacher Bṛhannaḍā, takes his weapons from the śamī tree, makes prince Uttara his charioteer and routs Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa and Duryodhana.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The marriage of Abhimanyu and Uttarā
summary: When the Pāṇḍavas reveal themselves, Virāṭa offers his daughter Uttarā to Arjuna, who accepts her as daughter-in-law for his son Abhimanyu, since he had been her teacher.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The vision of the cosmic form (Viśvarūpa-darśana)
summary: At Arjuna’s request Kṛṣṇa reveals his “sovereign form” (aiśvaraṃ rūpam), many-armed and many-faced, containing all beings and devouring the warriors of both armies; Arjuna, terrified, begs him to resume his familiar form (Bhagavad Gītā 11).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Arjuna’s vow and the killing of Jayadratha
summary: Blaming Jayadratha for blocking the Pāṇḍavas at the array where Abhimanyu died, Arjuna vows to kill him before the next sunset or enter the fire; after a day of fighting through the Kaurava host he beheads Jayadratha as the sun sets.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Aśvatthāman’s Nārāyaṇa weapon
summary: Enraged at his father’s killing, Aśvatthāman looses the Nārāyaṇa weapon on the Pāṇḍava army; on Kṛṣṇa’s advice the warriors lay down their arms and dismount, and the weapon subsides — Bhīma, who resists, is dragged from his chariot by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhīma drinks Duḥśāsana’s blood
summary: On the seventeenth day Bhīma kills Duḥśāsana and drinks his blood, fulfilling the vow he made when Duḥśāsana dragged Draupadī into the assembly; onlookers flee crying that he is not human.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Śalya
summary: On the eighteenth day the Kaurava commander Śalya, king of the Madras, is killed by Yudhiṣṭhira with a spear.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Balarāma’s pilgrimage on the Sarasvatī
summary: Unwilling to fight his kin, Balarāma spends the war on a pilgrimage up the Sarasvatī from the sea; the tīrthas he visits are described as he arrives at Kurukṣetra for the mace duel.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Aśvatthāman’s brahmaśiras and Kṛṣṇa’s curse (Aiṣīka)
summary: Pursued after the night massacre, Aśvatthāman looses the brahmaśiras weapon from a blade of grass; Arjuna counters, and when Aśvatthāman cannot recall his weapon he turns it into the wombs of the Pāṇḍava women. Kṛṣṇa curses him to wander for three thousand years and promises to revive Uttarā’s child.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The lament of the women (Strīvilāpa)
summary: After the war Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī and the Kuru women go to the battlefield; given divine sight, Gāndhārī describes to Kṛṣṇa the dead sons, husbands and brothers and the grieving widows, and ends by cursing him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The revival of Parikṣit
summary: Uttarā’s son is born dead, killed in the womb by Aśvatthāman’s weapon; Kṛṣṇa, keeping his promise, restores him to life, and the child is named Parikṣit.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Yudhiṣṭhira’s horse sacrifice
summary: To expiate the war Yudhiṣṭhira performs the aśvamedha: the horse wanders for a year guarded by Arjuna, who fights the Trigartas, Babhruvāhana and others; the sacrifice is completed at Hāstinapura, after which a half-golden mongoose belittles it.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s retirement and death in the forest fire
summary: Fifteen years after the war Dhṛtarāṣṭra retires to the forest with Gāndhārī, Kuntī, Vidura and Saṃjaya; two years later Nārada reports that the three elders died in a forest fire, which their own sacred fires had kindled.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The night of the risen dead (Putradarśana)
summary: At the elders’ forest hermitage Vyāsa, at Gāndhārī’s and Kuntī’s plea, makes the dead warriors of both sides rise from the Gaṅgā for one night, free of enmity, before returning to their worlds.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Arjuna fails against the Ābhīras
summary: After the destruction of the Yādavas Arjuna escorts the Vṛṣṇi women from Dvārakā, which the sea engulfs; on the way Ābhīra herdsmen attack, his weapons and strength fail him, and many women are carried off.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Yudhiṣṭhira in heaven and hell (Svargārohaṇa)
summary: Arriving in heaven Yudhiṣṭhira finds Duryodhana enthroned and his brothers absent; led to a hell where he hears their cries, he chooses to stay with them — and the hell vanishes, an illusion devised by Indra. Bathing in the heavenly Gaṅgā he takes a divine body, and the heroes return to their divine origins.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Hanumān meets Sītā in the Aśoka grove
summary: Searching Laṅkā, Hanumān finds Sītā guarded by rākṣasīs in Rāvaṇa’s aśoka grove, witnesses Rāvaṇa’s threats, then reveals himself, gives her Rāma’s signet ring and receives her crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) as a token for Rāma.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Hanumān burns Laṅkā
summary: Captured and brought before Rāvaṇa, Hanumān has his tail set on fire as punishment; he escapes his bonds and leaps from roof to roof setting the city ablaze, then checks that Sītā is unharmed.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Hanumān brings the mountain of herbs
summary: When Indrajit’s weapon fells Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and the vānara host, Jāmbavat sends Hanumān to the Himālaya for four healing herbs; unable to identify them, Hanumān uproots the whole peak and carries it to Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma kills Rāvaṇa
summary: In the final duel Rāma, on Mātali’s advice, looses the Brahmā weapon given by Agastya, which pierces Rāvaṇa’s heart; the rākṣasa women come out lamenting.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma’s horse sacrifice at Naimiṣa
summary: Rāma performs the aśvamedha in the Naimiṣa forest with a golden image of Sītā as his ritual wife; it is there that Vālmīki’s pupils Kuśa and Lava sing the Rāmāyaṇa before him.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Itihāsa (the epics)
summary: The Sanskrit category itihāsa (“thus indeed it was”) designates the two great epics, the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, which present themselves as accounts of the past and as authoritative teaching on dharma.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
summary: The Sanskrit epic of Rāma attributed to the sage Vālmīki, in seven books (kāṇḍas); in the Baroda Critical Edition 606 sargas and c. 18,760 verses. Most scholars regard Books 2–6 as the older core and the Bālakāṇḍa and Uttarakāṇḍa as later.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mahābhārata
summary: The Sanskrit epic of the Bhārata war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa; in the Pune Critical Edition 18 parvans, 1,995 adhyāyas and c. 74,000 verses, with the Harivaṃśa as its supplement (khila).

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhagavad Gītā
subtype: philosophical dialogue embedded in the epic
summary: Kṛṣṇa’s 700-verse teaching to Arjuna on the eve of battle, embedded in the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata: MBh (CE) 6.23–40 (= chapters 25–42 of the Bhīṣmaparvan in the vulgate numbering).

type:LABEL: text
name: Harivaṃśa
summary: The “Genealogy of Hari”, transmitted as the khila (supplement) of the Mahābhārata, narrating the Yādava genealogy and Kṛṣṇa’s life from birth among the cowherds to his rule in Dvārakā. Critical Edition by P. L. Vaidya (BORI 1969–71): 118 adhyāyas, c. 6,000 verses — about a third of the vulgate.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rāmopākhyāna (Mahābhārata)
summary: The Mahābhārata’s own telling of the Rāma story, narrated by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya to Yudhiṣṭhira after Jayadratha’s attempt to abduct Draupadī: MBh (CE) 3.257–275, Āraṇyakaparvan.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bālakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 1)
summary: The “Book of Youth”: the frame (Nārada’s summary to Vālmīki, the krauñca curse and the invention of the śloka, the teaching of Lava and Kuśa), the sacrifice for sons, Viṣṇu’s decision to be born, the births of the four princes, Viśvāmitra’s expedition, Ahalyā, the breaking of Śiva’s bow and the marriages, and the encounter with Paraśurāma.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ayodhyākāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 2)
summary: The “Book of Ayodhyā”: the planned consecration, Kaikeyī’s two boons, Rāma’s exile with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, Daśaratha’s death, Bharata’s refusal and the sandals.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Araṇyakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 3)
summary: The “Book of the Forest”: life among the sages of the Daṇḍaka, Śūrpaṇakhā’s mutilation, the war with Khara, the golden deer, Sītā’s abduction, Jaṭāyu’s death, Kabandha and Śabarī.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 4)
summary: The “Book of Kiṣkindhā”: Hanumān’s meeting with Rāma, the alliance with Sugrīva, the killing of Vālin and the search for Sītā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sundarakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 5)
summary: The “Beautiful Book”: Hanumān’s leap to Laṅkā, his search, his meeting with Sītā in the aśoka grove, the token ring, and the burning of the city.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Yuddhakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 6)
summary: The “Book of the War”: Vibhīṣaṇa’s defection, the causeway built by Nala, the war, the deaths of Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit and Rāvaṇa, Sītā’s fire ordeal and Brahmā’s hymn, and the return and consecration in Ayodhyā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Uttarakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 7)
summary: The “Last Book”: Rāvaṇa’s origins and earlier conquests, Hanumān’s childhood, the banishment of Sītā, the birth of Lava and Kuśa in Vālmīki’s hermitage, the Śambūka episode, the recitation of the poem by the twins, Sītā’s return into the earth and Rāma’s return to Viṣṇu’s form.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ādiparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 1)
summary: The “First Book”: the frame narratives, the snake sacrifice, the origins of the Bhārata line (Śakuntalā, Śantanu, Bhīṣma’s vow), the births and youth of the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas, the house of lac, Draupadī’s svayaṃvara and marriage, Indraprastha and the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sabhāparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 2)
summary: The “Book of the Assembly Hall”: the hall built by Maya, the killing of Jarāsandha, the rājasūya and the killing of Śiśupāla, the dice game, Draupadī’s humiliation and the second game that sends the Pāṇḍavas into exile.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āraṇyakaparvan (Vanaparvan) (Mahābhārata, Book 3)
summary: The “Book of the Forest”: twelve years of exile, Arjuna’s acquisition of weapons (Kirāta), pilgrimages, and many embedded tales — Nala and Damayantī, the Rāmopākhyāna, Sāvitrī — ending with the theft of Karṇa’s earrings and the Yakṣa’s questions.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Virāṭaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 4)
summary: The “Book of Virāṭa”: the thirteenth year in disguise at the Matsya court, the killing of Kīcaka, the cattle raid and Uttarā’s marriage to Abhimanyu.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Udyogaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 5)
summary: The “Book of the Effort”: embassies and preparations for war, Vidura’s and Sanatsujāta’s counsels, Kṛṣṇa’s embassy and theophany at the Kaurava court, Kṛṣṇa’s and Kuntī’s approaches to Karṇa, and the story of Ambā/Śikhaṇḍin.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhīṣmaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 6)
summary: The “Book of Bhīṣma”: the first ten days of battle under Bhīṣma’s command, containing the Bhagavad Gītā (6.23–40), ending with Bhīṣma’s fall onto a bed of arrows (6.114).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Droṇaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 7)
summary: The “Book of Droṇa”: the battle under Droṇa, the deaths of Abhimanyu, Jayadratha and Ghaṭotkaca, and Droṇa’s death after the report of “Aśvatthāman’s” death.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Karṇaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 8)
summary: The “Book of Karṇa”: Karṇa’s command, Śalya as his charioteer, Bhīma’s killing of Duḥśāsana, and Arjuna’s killing of Karṇa (8.67).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śalyaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 9)
summary: The “Book of Śalya”: Śalya’s command and death, Balarāma’s pilgrimage along the Sarasvatī, and the mace duel in which Bhīma breaks Duryodhana’s thighs (9.57).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sauptikaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 10)
summary: The “Book of the Sleepers”: Aśvatthāman’s night massacre of the Pāñcālas and Draupadī’s sons, and Kṛṣṇa’s curse on Aśvatthāman.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Strīparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 11)
summary: The “Book of the Women”: lament on the battlefield, Gāndhārī’s curse on Kṛṣṇa, and Kuntī’s revelation that Karṇa was her son.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śāntiparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 12)
summary: The “Book of Peace”: Bhīṣma’s instruction of Yudhiṣṭhira from the bed of arrows — Rājadharma (12.1–128), Āpaddharma (129–167) and Mokṣadharma (168–353), including the Nārāyaṇīya (321–339).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Anuśāsanaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 13)
summary: The “Book of Instruction”: further teaching by Bhīṣma (including the Viṣṇusahasranāma, 13.135) and his death at the winter solstice (13.154).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āśvamedhikaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 14)
summary: The “Book of the Horse Sacrifice”: the Anugītā (14.16–50), the revival of the still-born Parīkṣit by Kṛṣṇa, and Yudhiṣṭhira’s horse sacrifice.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āśramavāsikaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 15)
summary: The “Book of the Hermitage”: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, Kuntī and Vidura retire to the forest; Vyāsa shows the dead warriors to the living; the elders die in a forest fire.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mausalaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 16)
summary: The “Book of the Clubs”: the self-destruction of the Yādavas at Prabhāsa, Balarāma’s and Kṛṣṇa’s deaths, and the submergence of Dvārakā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mahāprasthānikaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 17)
summary: The “Book of the Great Departure”: the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī walk towards the Himālaya; all fall except Yudhiṣṭhira, who refuses to abandon the dog that follows him.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Svargārohaṇaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 18)
summary: The “Book of the Ascent to Heaven”: Yudhiṣṭhira’s vision of hell and heaven, the final state of the heroes, and the close of the recitation.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Harivaṃśaparvan (Harivaṃśa)
summary: Book 1 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): cosmogony, the solar and lunar dynasties and the genealogy of the Yādavas down to Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇuparvan (Harivaṃśa)
summary: Book 2 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): the life of Kṛṣṇa from the gods’ plan and his birth to Devakī (HV 48) through his childhood in Vraja, the killing of Kaṃsa (76), the move to Dvārakā (85–86) and later wars and marriages.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhaviṣyaparvan (Harivaṃśa)
summary: Book 3 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): a short concluding section on the future and the close of Janamejaya’s line.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nalopākhyāna (MBh 3.50–78)
summary: The story of Nala and Damayantī, told by the sage Bṛhadaśva to Yudhiṣṭhira during the forest exile (MBh (CE) 3.49 frame; 3.50–78 story).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Pativratāmāhātmya / Sāvitrī-upākhyāna (MBh 3.277–283)
summary: The story of Sāvitrī, who wins back her husband Satyavān from Yama, told by Mārkaṇḍeya to Yudhiṣṭhira (MBh (CE) 3.277–283).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śakuntalopākhyāna (MBh 1.62–69)
summary: The story of King Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā and the birth of Bharata, eponym of the Bhāratas (MBh (CE) 1.62–69).

type:LABEL: passage
name: The churning of the ocean (MBh 1.15–17)
summary: The Mahābhārata’s account of the churning of the ocean for amṛta, told by Ugraśravas to explain the horse Uccaiḥśravas (MBh (CE) 1.15–17; 1.18.1 closes “thus I have told you how the amṛta was churned”).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Aṃśāvataraṇa: the partial incarnations (MBh 1.61)
summary: The catalogue of which gods, demons and others were born as the epic’s characters — e.g. Kṛṣṇa as a portion of Nārāyaṇa, Balarāma of Śeṣa, Karṇa of the Sun, Draupadī of Śrī, Duryodhana of Kali (MBh (CE) 1.61.63–99).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Pañcendropākhyāna: the five Indras (MBh 1.189)
summary: Vyāsa’s account to Drupada of five former Indras born as the Pāṇḍavas with Śrī as their common wife, followed by the tale of the sage’s daughter who asked Śiva five times for a husband (MBh (CE) 1.189.1–49).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Dyūtaparvan: the dice game (MBh 2.43–65)
summary: The sub-book of the first dice game, from Duryodhana’s envy at Indraprastha to Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s boons to Draupadī and the Pāṇḍavas’ release (MBh (CE) 2.43–65); the return match follows in 2.66–72.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ambopākhyāna (MBh 5.170–193)
summary: Bhīṣma’s narration of Ambā’s abduction, her rejection, his duel with Paraśurāma, her rebirth as Śikhaṇḍinī and the sex-exchange with the yakṣa Sthūṇa (MBh (CE) 5.170–193).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kuṇḍalāharaṇa: the theft of Karṇa’s earrings (MBh 3.284–294)
summary: Sūrya warns Karṇa that Indra will beg his armour and earrings; the narrative of Kuntī’s boon, Karṇa’s birth and abandonment in a basket on the Aśvanadī, and his rescue by Adhiratha and Rādhā; Indra receives the armour and gives the spear (MBh (CE) 3.284–294).

type:LABEL: passage
name: The Yakṣa’s questions (MBh 3.297–298)
summary: At the poisoned lake the yakṣa — the god Dharma — questions Yudhiṣṭhira and restores his brothers (MBh (CE) 3.297–298).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viduranīti / Prajāgara (MBh 5.33–40)
summary: Vidura’s night-long counsel on policy and conduct to the sleepless Dhṛtarāṣṭra (MBh (CE) 5.33–40).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sanatsujātīya (MBh 5.42–45)
summary: The sage Sanatsujāta’s teaching to Dhṛtarāṣṭra on death and liberation (MBh (CE) 5.42–45).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhagavadyāna: Kṛṣṇa’s embassy (MBh 5.70–137)
summary: Kṛṣṇa’s peace mission to Hāstinapura, including his theophany when the Kauravas plan to seize him (5.129) (MBh (CE) 5.70–137).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Rājadharma (MBh 12.1–128)
summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on the duties of kings (MBh (CE) 12.1–128).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āpaddharma (MBh 12.129–167)
summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on conduct in emergencies (MBh (CE) 12.129–167).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mokṣadharma (MBh 12.168–353)
summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on liberation, incorporating Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Nārāyaṇa theology (MBh (CE) 12.168–353).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nārāyaṇīya (MBh 12.321–339)
summary: The Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mokṣadharma, an early Pāñcarātra-related account of Nārāyaṇa worship, Nārada’s visit to Śvetadvīpa and the vyūha doctrine (MBh (CE) 12.321–339).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇusahasranāma (MBh 13.135)
summary: The thousand names of Viṣṇu, taught by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira (MBh (CE) 13.135).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Anugītā (MBh 14.16–50)
summary: After the war Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to repeat the Gītā; Kṛṣṇa says he cannot and teaches anew (MBh (CE) 14.16–50).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Āstīkaparvan (MBh 1.13–53)
summary: The story of Jaratkāru, Āstīka and Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice, which forms the outer frame of Vaiśampāyana’s recitation (MBh (CE) 1.13–53).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Saṃkṣepa Rāmāyaṇa: Nārada’s summary (VR 1.1)
summary: The opening sarga in which Vālmīki asks Nārada who is the most virtuous man living and Nārada summarises Rāma’s story (VR (CE) 1.1).

type:LABEL: passage
name: The krauñca episode and the first śloka (VR 1.2)
summary: Vālmīki’s grief at a hunter killing one of a pair of krauñca birds turns into the first śloka, “mā niṣāda …” (VR (CE) 1.2.14).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Brahmā’s hymn to Rāma (VR 6.105)
summary: After Sītā’s fire ordeal Brahmā tells Rāma that he is Nārāyaṇa and that Sītā is Lakṣmī (VR (CE) 6.105.12, 25).

type:LABEL: character
name: Rāma
summary: Prince of Ayodhyā, eldest son of Daśaratha and Kausalyā and hero of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; exiled for fourteen years, he recovers his wife Sītā from Rāvaṇa and rules as the model righteous king. Vaiṣṇava tradition regards him as an avatāra of Viṣṇu.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Sītā
summary: Daughter of King Janaka of Videha — found in a ploughed furrow — and wife of Rāma; abducted by Rāvaṇa, she is vindicated by an ordeal of fire but later banished, and finally returns into the earth. Brahmā’s hymn in the Yuddhakāṇḍa identifies her with Lakṣmī.
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Lakṣmaṇa
summary: Son of Daśaratha and Sumitrā, twin of Śatrughna, who accompanies Rāma and Sītā into exile and fights beside Rāma; he mutilates Śūrpaṇakhā, kills Indrajit, and in the Uttarakāṇḍa leaves Sītā in the forest at Rāma’s command.
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Bharata (brother of Rāma)
summary: Son of Daśaratha and Kaikeyī, for whom Kaikeyī demands the throne; he refuses it, seeks Rāma in the forest, and rules from Nandigrāma as regent with Rāma’s sandals on the throne.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śatrughna
summary: Youngest son of Daśaratha, Lakṣmaṇa’s twin by Sumitrā and companion of Bharata; in the Uttarakāṇḍa he kills the demon Lavaṇa and founds Madhurā (Mathurā).

type:LABEL: character
name: Hanumān
summary: Vānara minister of Sugrīva, son of the wind god Vāyu and Añjanā (wife of the vānara Kesarin), who leaps the ocean to find Sītā in Laṅkā and becomes Rāma’s loyal servant and messenger; later devotional traditions make him the model devotee (bhakta).

type:LABEL: character
name: Rāvaṇa
summary: Ten-headed rākṣasa king of Laṅkā, son of the sage Viśravas and the rākṣasī Kaikasī, made invulnerable to gods and demons by Brahmā’s boon; he abducts Sītā and is killed by Rāma.
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Vibhīṣaṇa
summary: Righteous younger brother of Rāvaṇa who urges him to return Sītā, defects to Rāma, and is installed as king of Laṅkā after the war.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sugrīva
summary: Vānara prince of Kiṣkindhā, son of the Sun, exiled by his brother Vālin; he allies with Rāma, who kills Vālin and restores him, and in return sends the vānara armies in search of Sītā.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Vālin
summary: Vānara king of Kiṣkindhā, son of Indra and elder brother of Sugrīva, whom he had driven out; he is killed by Rāma’s arrow during his duel with Sugrīva and is succeeded by his son Aṅgada as heir.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)
earliest_material: second half of the 5th century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Jaṭāyu
summary: King of the vultures and friend of Daśaratha, who tries to stop Rāvaṇa carrying off Sītā, is mortally wounded, and tells Rāma what happened before dying.

type:LABEL: character
name: Daśaratha
summary: Ikṣvāku king of Ayodhyā, father of Rāma, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna; bound by two boons promised to Kaikeyī, he exiles Rāma and dies of grief.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaikeyī
summary: Princess of Kekaya, wife of Daśaratha and mother of Bharata, who, prompted by the servant Mantharā, claims her two boons: Bharata’s consecration and Rāma’s fourteen-year exile.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kausalyā
summary: Chief queen of Daśaratha and mother of Rāma.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Janaka (father of Sītā)
summary: King of Videha at Mithilā (Sīradhvaja Janaka in the Rāmāyaṇa) who found Sītā in a furrow while ploughing and set the stringing of Śiva’s bow as the condition for her marriage.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vālmīki
summary: Sage to whom the Rāmāyaṇa is attributed: he hears the story from Nārada, invents the śloka metre in grief at a krauñca bird’s death, composes the poem and teaches it to Rāma’s sons Lava and Kuśa, at whose hermitage Sītā lives after her banishment.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kumbhakarṇa
summary: Gigantic brother of Rāvaṇa who sleeps for long periods; roused for the war, he devastates the vānara army before Rāma kills him.

type:LABEL: character
name: Indrajit
summary: Son of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, born as Meghanāda and called Indrajit (“conqueror of Indra”) after capturing Indra; a master of illusion who twice binds Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with serpent-arrows and is finally killed by Lakṣmaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śūrpaṇakhā
summary: Sister of Rāvaṇa who propositions Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in the Pañcavaṭī forest; Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears, provoking the war with Khara and then Rāvaṇa’s abduction of Sītā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ahalyā
summary: Wife of the sage Gautama, seduced by Indra and cursed by her husband to do penance unseen in the hermitage until Rāma’s arrival restores her.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śabarī
summary: Female ascetic of the Śabara community living at the Pampā lake, who receives Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa and then ascends to heaven.

type:LABEL: character
name: Lava
summary: One of the twin sons of Rāma and Sītā (the younger), born in Vālmīki’s hermitage, named by Vālmīki and taught by him to sing the Rāmāyaṇa, which they perform before Rāma.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kuśa
summary: One of the twin sons of Rāma and Sītā (the elder), born in Vālmīki’s hermitage, named by Vālmīki and taught by him to sing the Rāmāyaṇa, which they perform before Rāma.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sumitrā
summary: Wife of Daśaratha and mother of the twins Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ūrmilā
summary: Daughter of Janaka and younger sister of Sītā, married to Lakṣmaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Māṇḍavī
summary: Daughter of Kuśadhvaja (Janaka’s brother) married to Bharata.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śrutakīrti
summary: Daughter of Kuśadhvaja married to Śatrughna.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mandodarī
summary: Chief queen of Rāvaṇa, daughter of the dānava architect Maya and the apsaras Hemā, and mother of Indrajit.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aṅgada
summary: Son of Vālin and Tārā, made heir-apparent of Kiṣkindhā under Sugrīva; leads the southern search party and serves as Rāma’s envoy to Rāvaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tārā
summary: Wife of Vālin and mother of Aṅgada, whose lament over Vālin and counsel to Sugrīva are prominent in the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mantharā
summary: Hunchbacked servant of Kaikeyī who persuades her to claim her boons; in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna she is the gandharvī Dundubhī born on earth at Brahmā’s command.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mārīca
summary: Rākṣasa, son of Tāṭakā, who at Rāvaṇa’s command takes the form of a golden deer to lure Rāma away from Sītā and is killed by him.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tāṭakā
summary: Yakṣī turned demoness who ravages the forest near the Gaṅgā; Rāma kills her at Viśvāmitra’s instruction.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kabandha
summary: Headless monster of the forest, freed from a curse when Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa cut off his arms and cremate him; he directs them to Sugrīva.

type:LABEL: character
name: Saṃpāti
summary: Elder brother of Jaṭāyu, a vulture with burnt wings who tells the searching vānaras that Sītā is in Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Trijaṭā
summary: Rākṣasī guard of Sītā in the aśoka grove who dreams of Rāvaṇa’s ruin and befriends Sītā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kesarin
summary: Vānara chief, husband of Añjanā, in whose “field” Hanumān is born; Hanumān is thus his kṣetraja son while being Vāyu’s own son.

type:LABEL: character
name: Añjanā
summary: Apsaras Puñjikasthalā living as a vānarī, wife of Kesarin and mother of Hanumān by the wind god.

type:LABEL: character
name: Viśravas
summary: Sage, son of Pulastya, father of Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) and, by Kaikasī, of Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaikasī
summary: Daughter of the rākṣasa Sumālin, who at her father’s bidding chooses the sage Viśravas and becomes the mother of Rāvaṇa and his siblings.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa)
summary: Son of Viśravas, lord of wealth and guardian of a direction, first ruler of Laṅkā, who is driven out by his half-brother Rāvaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vedavatī
summary: Daughter of the sage Kuśadhvaja (son of Bṛhaspati) who, molested by Rāvaṇa, enters the fire vowing to be reborn for his destruction; the Uttarakāṇḍa identifies her with Sītā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śambūka
summary: Śūdra ascetic performing austerities, whom Rāma beheads in the Uttarakāṇḍa after a brahmin’s son dies prematurely; the episode is a focus of modern criticism.

type:LABEL: character
name: Gautama (husband of Ahalyā)
summary: Sage of Mithilā’s forest whose wife Ahalyā is seduced by Indra; he curses both and later receives her back purified.

type:LABEL: character
name: Guha
summary: Niṣāda chief of Śṛṅgaverapura on the Gaṅgā, Rāma’s friend, who hosts the exiles and ferries them across the river.

type:LABEL: character
name: Jāmbavān
summary: King of the bears (ṛkṣas) in Rāma’s army, eldest counsellor of the search party, who reminds Hanumān of his parentage and powers before the leap.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nala (vānara engineer)
summary: Vānara son of Viśvakarman who builds the causeway (setu) across the ocean to Laṅkā — distinct from King Nala of Niṣadha (char:nala).

type:LABEL: character
name: Ṛśyaśṛṅga
summary: Sage, son of Vibhāṇḍaka, brought to Daśaratha’s court on Sumantra’s advice to perform the sacrifice that produces the four princes; married to Śāntā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bharadvāja
summary: Sage whose hermitage at Prayāga hosts Rāma and later Bharata in the Rāmāyaṇa; in the Mahābhārata he is the father of Droṇa.
earliest_material: 8th century CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796)

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛṣṇa
summary: Vṛṣṇi prince, son of Vasudeva and Devakī, cousin and ally of the Pāṇḍavas, Arjuna’s charioteer and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā; the Mahābhārata calls him a portion of Nārāyaṇa, the Harivaṃśa and Purāṇas narrate his cowherd childhood, and Vaiṣṇava traditions worship him as Viṣṇu’s avatāra or, for some schools, the supreme Lord himself.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Vyāsa
summary: Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, the island-born son of the sage Parāśara and Satyavatī, credited with arranging the Vedas and composing the Mahābhārata; he fathers Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura by niyoga and repeatedly intervenes in the story he authors.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhīṣma
summary: Devavrata, son of King Śantanu and the river goddess Gaṅgā, who renounces the throne and marriage so that his father may marry Satyavatī; grand-uncle of both Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, he commands the Kaurava army for ten days, falls to Arjuna and Śikhaṇḍin, and instructs Yudhiṣṭhira from his bed of arrows.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Yudhiṣṭhira
summary: Eldest Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by the god Dharma and legal son of Pāṇḍu; the “Dharma king” who loses his kingdom, brothers and wife at dice, endures exile, wins the war and rules, and is tested to the end by Dharma himself.
earliest_textual: within the epic’s growth, c. 3rd century BCE – 3rd century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhīma
summary: Second Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by the wind god Vāyu, of enormous strength and appetite; he kills Hiḍimba, Baka, Jarāsandha, Kīcaka, Duḥśāsana and the Kaurava brothers, and breaks Duryodhana’s thighs.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Arjuna
summary: Third Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by Indra, the supreme archer who wins Draupadī, marries Ulūpī, Citrāṅgadā and Subhadrā, obtains divine weapons from Śiva and Indra, and receives the Bhagavad Gītā from Kṛṣṇa, his charioteer and friend.
earliest_textual: c. mid-4th c. BCE or later (terminus post quem c. 350 BCE)

type:LABEL: character
name: Nakula
summary: One of the twin Pāṇḍavas (with Sahadeva), sons of Mādrī by the Aśvins and legal sons of Pāṇḍu.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Sahadeva
summary: One of the twin Pāṇḍavas (with Nakula), sons of Mādrī by the Aśvins and legal sons of Pāṇḍu.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Draupadī
summary: Daughter of King Drupada, born from the sacrificial altar, won by Arjuna at her svayaṃvara and married to all five Pāṇḍavas; staked and dragged into the assembly hall at the dice game, her question whether Yudhiṣṭhira could stake her after losing himself and her humiliation drive the epic’s conflict.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Karṇa
summary: Son of Kuntī by the Sun god, born before her marriage with innate armour and earrings, set adrift and raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā; made king of Aṅga by Duryodhana, he remains loyal to the Kauravas even after learning he is the eldest Pāṇḍava, and is killed by Arjuna.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Duryodhana
summary: Eldest of the hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, rival of the Pāṇḍavas, who contrives the house of lac and the dice game, refuses any settlement and dies after Bhīma breaks his thighs.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Duḥśāsana
summary: Second Kaurava, who drags Draupadī into the assembly hall and pulls at her garment; Bhīma kills him in battle and drinks his blood, fulfilling a vow.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Droṇa
summary: Brahmin teacher of arms to the Kuru princes, son of the sage Bharadvāja born from a vessel (droṇa), who demands Ekalavya’s thumb, takes half of Drupada’s kingdom, commands the Kaurava army after Bhīṣma, and is killed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna after being told that “Aśvatthāman” is dead.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)
earliest_material: 8th century CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796)

type:LABEL: character
name: Aśvatthāman
summary: Son of Droṇa and Kṛpī, born of the combined portions of Mahādeva, Antaka, Kāma and Krodha; after the war he massacres the sleeping Pāñcālas and Draupadī’s sons and is cursed by Kṛṣṇa to wander for three thousand years.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)
earliest_material: 8th century CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796)

type:LABEL: character
name: Vidura
summary: Son of Vyāsa by a servant woman of Ambikā, wise counsellor of the Kurus and uncle of the Pāṇḍavas, an incarnation of Dharma owing to the sage Māṇḍavya’s curse.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kuntī
summary: Pṛthā, daughter of the Yādava Śūra and sister of Vasudeva, given in adoption to King Kuntibhoja; with Durvāsas’s mantra she bears Karṇa by the Sun before marriage and, as Pāṇḍu’s wife, Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna by Dharma, Vāyu and Indra.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Gāndhārī
summary: Princess of Gandhāra, daughter of Subala and sister of Śakuni, who blindfolds herself on marrying the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, bears the hundred Kauravas and a daughter, and after the war curses Kṛṣṇa with the destruction of his clan.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra
summary: Blind king of the Kurus, son of Vyāsa and Ambikā by niyoga, husband of Gāndhārī and father of the hundred Kauravas; his indulgence of Duryodhana allows the dice game and the war, which Sañjaya narrates to him.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Pāṇḍu
summary: King of the Kurus, son of Vyāsa and Ambālikā by niyoga, cursed to die if he approaches a woman; he authorises Kuntī and Mādrī to bear sons by gods and is the legal father of the five Pāṇḍavas.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Mādrī
summary: Princess of Madra, second wife of Pāṇḍu, who bears the twins Nakula and Sahadeva by the Aśvins and joins Pāṇḍu on his funeral pyre.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Śakuni
summary: Prince of Gandhāra, son of Subala and brother of Gāndhārī, the expert dicer who wins for Duryodhana against Yudhiṣṭhira; an incarnation of the Dvāpara age.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Balarāma
summary: Elder brother of Kṛṣṇa, son of Vasudeva and Rohiṇī, wielder of the plough and club, teacher of Duryodhana and Bhīma in mace fighting, who stays neutral in the war; the Mahābhārata calls him a portion of the serpent Śeṣa.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Abhimanyu
summary: Son of Arjuna and Subhadrā, married to Uttarā, who breaks into Droṇa’s circular array on the thirteenth day and is killed after being surrounded; father of the posthumously born Parīkṣit.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Subhadrā
summary: Sister of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, abducted with Kṛṣṇa’s approval by Arjuna and married to him; mother of Abhimanyu.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era
earliest_material: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

type:LABEL: character
name: Śantanu
summary: Kuru king, husband of Gaṅgā (mother of Bhīṣma) and then of Satyavatī (mother of Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya).
