earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyavatī
summary: Fisherman’s daughter (born from a fish, raised by the chief of fishermen) who bears Vyāsa to Parāśara and then marries Śantanu on condition that her son inherit, prompting Bhīṣma’s vow; matriarch of the Kuru line.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Drupada
summary: King of Pañcāla, Droṇa’s estranged boyhood friend, who sacrifices for a son to kill Droṇa and receives Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Draupadī from the fire; father also of Śikhaṇḍin.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Śikhaṇḍin
summary: Child of Drupada born female (Śikhaṇḍinī), the reborn Ambā, who becomes male through an exchange with the yakṣa Sthūṇa; Bhīṣma refuses to fight him, and Arjuna shoots Bhīṣma from behind him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Ekalavya
summary: Niṣāda prince, son of Hiraṇyadhanus, who learns archery before a clay image of Droṇa after being refused as a pupil; when his skill surpasses Arjuna’s, Droṇa demands his right thumb as teacher’s fee, and Ekalavya gives it.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Jarāsandha
summary: King of Magadha, born in two halves joined by the demoness Jarā, enemy of Kṛṣṇa and the Yādavas, killed by Bhīma in a wrestling match before the rājasūya.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Śiśupāla
summary: King of Cedi and cousin of Kṛṣṇa who objects to Kṛṣṇa’s receiving the first honour at Yudhiṣṭhira’s rājasūya and is beheaded by Kṛṣṇa’s discus.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Sañjaya
summary: Charioteer and minister of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, given divine sight by Vyāsa to narrate the battle — including the Bhagavad Gītā — to the blind king.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ghaṭotkaca
summary: Son of Bhīma and the rākṣasī Hiḍimbā, who fights for the Pāṇḍavas and is killed at night by Karṇa with the spear Indra had given him — the weapon Karṇa had reserved for Arjuna.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Parīkṣit
summary: Son of Abhimanyu and Uttarā, born still-born after Aśvatthāman’s weapon and revived by Kṛṣṇa; he succeeds Yudhiṣṭhira and dies of the bite of the serpent Takṣaka, which prompts his son Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.

type:LABEL: character
name: Janamejaya
summary: Kuru king, son of Parīkṣit, at whose snake sacrifice Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata; his questions punctuate the narrative.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Vaiśampāyana
summary: Disciple of Vyāsa who, at his teacher’s instruction, recites the Mahābhārata to King Janamejaya during the snake sacrifice.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Devakī
summary: Wife of Vasudeva and mother of Kṛṣṇa, whose earlier children are killed by her cousin Kaṃsa; Kṛṣṇa is born to her in captivity and exchanged with Yaśodā’s daughter.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Vasudeva (father of Kṛṣṇa)
summary: Yādava (Vṛṣṇi) noble, son of Śūra, brother of Kuntī and husband of Devakī and Rohiṇī; father of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Kept distinct from the deity Vāsudeva.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Nanda
summary: Chief of the cowherds of Vraja who, with his wife Yaśodā, fosters Kṛṣṇa (and Balarāma) after Vasudeva brings the infant from Mathurā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yaśodā
summary: Wife of Nanda and foster mother of Kṛṣṇa; she gives birth to a daughter at the same time as Devakī bears Kṛṣṇa, and the children are exchanged.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaṃsa
summary: King of Mathurā, son of Ugrasena and cousin of Devakī, who kills her children fearing a prophecy and is killed by Kṛṣṇa in the wrestling arena.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Rukmiṇī
summary: Princess of Vidarbha, daughter of Bhīṣmaka, abducted by Kṛṣṇa before her intended marriage to Śiśupāla; Kṛṣṇa’s chief queen and mother of Pradyumna. Later tradition identifies her with Lakṣmī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Pradyumna
summary: Son of Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, carried off as an infant by the demon Śambara and later kills him; the Mahābhārata calls him an incarnation of Sanatkumāra.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nala
summary: King of Niṣadha, son of Vīrasena, whose love for Damayantī, loss of his kingdom at dice under the influence of Kali, and eventual restoration form the Nalopākhyāna (MBh 3.50–78) — distinct from the vānara engineer Nala (char:nala-vanara).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Damayantī
summary: Princess of Vidarbha who chooses Nala over the gods at her svayaṃvara, is abandoned by him in the forest, and through her resourcefulness recovers him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Sāvitrī
summary: Daughter of King Aśvapati of Madra who chooses the exiled prince Satyavān knowing he will die within a year, follows Yama when he takes Satyavān’s life, and wins back her husband by her eloquence and boons.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Śakuntalā
summary: Daughter of the sage Viśvāmitra and the apsaras Menakā, raised by the sage Kaṇva, who marries King Duḥṣanta by gāndharva rite and, when he later disowns her, compels his recognition of their son Bharata.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Rohiṇī (wife of Vasudeva)
summary: Wife of Vasudeva and mother of Balarāma; in Vyāsa’s account Nārāyaṇa’s white hair enters her womb, while in the Harivaṃśa Devakī’s seventh embryo is transferred to her.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambā
summary: Eldest princess of Kāśī, abducted by Bhīṣma for Vicitravīrya, rejected by her chosen suitor Śālva and by Bhīṣma; she does austerities for Bhīṣma’s death and is reborn as Śikhaṇḍinī, daughter of Drupada.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambikā
summary: Second princess of Kāśī, wife of Vicitravīrya, who by niyoga with Vyāsa bears the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambālikā
summary: Youngest princess of Kāśī, wife of Vicitravīrya, who by niyoga with Vyāsa bears Pāṇḍu.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Parāśara
summary: Sage, grandson of Vasiṣṭha, who fathers Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa on Satyavatī during a pilgrimage and restores her virginity.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Vicitravīrya
summary: Younger son of Śantanu and Satyavatī, married to Ambikā and Ambālikā, who dies childless, occasioning the niyoga with Vyāsa.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Citrāṅgada (son of Śantanu)
summary: Elder son of Śantanu and Satyavatī, installed by Bhīṣma and killed young by a gandharva of the same name — distinct from Citrāṅgadā of Maṇipūra.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Uttarā
summary: Daughter of King Virāṭa of Matsya, taught dance by the disguised Arjuna, whom Arjuna accepts as daughter-in-law for Abhimanyu; mother of Parīkṣit.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Ulūpī
summary: Nāga princess who takes Arjuna beneath the Gaṅgā during his exile and becomes his wife; mother of Irāvat.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Citrāṅgadā (of Maṇipūra)
summary: Daughter of King Citravāhana of Maṇipūra, married to Arjuna on condition that their son continue her father’s line; mother of Babhruvāhana.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Babhruvāhana
summary: Son of Arjuna and Citrāṅgadā, king of Maṇipūra, who fights and kills his father during the horse-sacrifice campaign; Arjuna is revived by Ulūpī’s jewel.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Irāvat
summary: Son of Arjuna and the nāga Ulūpī, killed in the war; in South Indian traditions worshipped as Aravāṉ.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Adhiratha
summary: Charioteer (sūta) of the Kurus, husband of Rādhā, who finds the infant Karṇa in a basket on the river and raises him as his son.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Rādhā (foster mother of Karṇa)
summary: Wife of the charioteer Adhiratha, childless until she takes in the infant Karṇa found floating in a basket; Karṇa is called Rādheya after her. Distinct from Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa’s beloved (char:radha).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Hiḍimbā
summary: Rākṣasī of the forest who falls in love with Bhīma after he kills her brother Hiḍimba; with Kuntī’s leave she lives with him and bears Ghaṭotkaca.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛpa
summary: Brahmin teacher of arms to the Kuru princes before Droṇa, son of the sage Śaradvat, adopted with his twin sister Kṛpī by Śantanu; one of the three Kaurava survivors.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛpī
summary: Twin sister of Kṛpa, wife of Droṇa and mother of Aśvatthāman.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Śalya
summary: King of Madra and brother of Mādrī, maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva, tricked by Duryodhana into fighting for the Kauravas; Karṇa’s charioteer and the last Kaurava commander, killed by Yudhiṣṭhira.
earliest_textual: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

type:LABEL: character
name: Virāṭa
summary: King of the Matsyas at whose court the Pāṇḍavas spend the thirteenth year of exile in disguise; father of Uttarā and Uttara, ally of the Pāṇḍavas in the war.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kīcaka
summary: Commander of Virāṭa’s army and brother of Queen Sudeṣṇā, who harasses the disguised Draupadī and is killed at night by Bhīma.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhīṣmaka
summary: King of Vidarbha (Kuṇḍina), father of Rukmiṇī and Rukmin, a vassal-ally of Jarāsandha.

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyabhāmā
summary: Beloved wife of Kṛṣṇa, daughter of Satrājit, who in the Āraṇyakaparvan asks Draupadī how she keeps five husbands devoted.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Ugrasena
summary: King of the Vṛṣṇis/Andhakas at Mathurā, father of Kaṃsa, deposed by his son and restored by Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sāmba
summary: Son of Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavatī whom the Yādava youths dress as a pregnant woman to mock visiting sages; the sages’ curse that he will bear an iron club brings about the Yādavas’ destruction.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Jarā (the hunter)
summary: Hunter whose arrow, mistaking Kṛṣṇa’s foot for a deer, strikes the sole of Kṛṣṇa’s foot as he lies in yoga, causing his death.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Dhṛṣṭadyumna
summary: Son of Drupada born from the sacrificial fire with Draupadī, destined to kill Droṇa; commander of the Pāṇḍava army, he beheads Droṇa and is killed in his sleep by Aśvatthāman.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Sātyaki
summary: Vṛṣṇi warrior, pupil of Arjuna and loyal ally of the Pāṇḍavas; an incarnation of the Maruts.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛtavarman
summary: Vṛṣṇi/Bhoja warrior who fights for the Kauravas, one of the three survivors who join Aśvatthāman’s night raid.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Jayadratha
summary: King of the Sindhus, husband of Duḥśalā, who tries to abduct Draupadī during the exile and is killed by Arjuna on the fourteenth day.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Duḥśalā
summary: The only daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, married to Jayadratha.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Yuyutsu
summary: Son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra by a vaiśya woman, who crosses over to the Pāṇḍavas before the battle and survives it.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kuntibhoja
summary: Childless king, friend of Śūra, who receives Śūra’s first daughter Pṛthā in adoption; she is therefore called Kuntī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śūra (Yādava)
summary: Yādava chief, father of Vasudeva and of Pṛthā (Kuntī), whom he gives in adoption to Kuntibhoja.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Subala
summary: King of Gandhāra, father of Gāndhārī and Śakuni.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Duḥṣanta
summary: Paurava king who meets Śakuntalā while hunting, marries her by gāndharva rite and later acknowledges their son Bharata.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Bharata (son of Śakuntalā)
summary: Son of Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā, universal sovereign from whom the Bhārata lineage and the epic take their name — distinct from Rāma’s brother Bharata.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaṇva
summary: Sage of the Kāśyapa line who raises Śakuntalā in his hermitage.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Menakā
summary: Apsaras sent by Indra to distract Viśvāmitra; mother of Śakuntalā.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyavān
summary: Son of the blind, exiled king Dyumatsena, chosen by Sāvitrī as husband though fated to die within a year.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Aśvapati
summary: King of Madra, father of Sāvitrī, who obtains her by worshipping the goddess Sāvitrī.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Dyumatsena
summary: Exiled, later blind king of the Śālvas, father of Satyavān, whose sight and kingdom are restored by Sāvitrī’s boons.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Bṛhadaśva
summary: Sage who visits the exiled Pāṇḍavas and tells Yudhiṣṭhira the story of Nala and Damayantī.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Māṇḍavya
summary: Sage (Aṇī-Māṇḍavya) wrongly impaled as a thief, who curses Dharma for punishing a childhood fault too severely; Dharma is therefore born as Vidura.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Ugraśravas
summary: Bard (sūta, paurāṇika), son of Lomaharṣaṇa, who comes to Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest and recites the Mahābhārata as he heard it from Vaiśampāyana.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Lomaharṣaṇa
summary: Bard (sūta), father of Ugraśravas, regarded in Purāṇic tradition as a disciple of Vyāsa who received the Purāṇas.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Śaunaka
summary: Kulapati (head of a family of sages) of the Naimiṣa forest, at whose twelve-year sacrifice Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Takṣaka
summary: Serpent king whose bite kills Parīkṣit, provoking Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Āstīka
summary: Son of the sage Jaratkāru and the nāga woman Jaratkāru who halts Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice and saves Takṣaka.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Maya (dānava architect)
summary: Dānava architect who builds the Pāṇḍavas’ assembly hall in gratitude for being spared in the Khāṇḍava fire; in the Rāmāyaṇa’s Uttarakāṇḍa he is the father of Mandodarī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kāliya
summary: Many-headed serpent poisoning a pool of the Yamunā in Vraja, subdued by the boy Kṛṣṇa, who dances on his heads and banishes him to the ocean.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Dharma (the god)
summary: Dharma personified as a god in the Mahābhārata: the divine father of Yudhiṣṭhira, born as Vidura through Māṇḍavya’s curse, the yakṣa who questions Yudhiṣṭhira at the lake and the dog who follows him to heaven. The epic at times identifies him with Yama.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: concept
name: Dharma
summary: The central normative concept of the epics — right order, duty, law and virtue — whose subtlety (sūkṣmatā) the Mahābhārata repeatedly stresses, notably in Draupadī’s question, Yudhiṣṭhira’s dilemmas and Bhīṣma’s teachings.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma’s exile
summary: Rāma’s fourteen-year banishment to the forest with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, imposed through Kaikeyī’s boons and accepted by Rāma to keep his father’s word.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The breaking of Śiva’s bow and Sītā’s marriage
summary: At Mithilā Rāma lifts and breaks the great bow of Śiva that Janaka had set as the test for Sītā’s hand; the four brothers are then married to Sītā, Ūrmilā, Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The abduction of Sītā
summary: Rāvaṇa, having sent Mārīca as a golden deer to draw Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa away, carries Sītā off from the Pañcavaṭī hermitage through the sky to Laṅkā, mortally wounding Jaṭāyu who tries to stop him.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Hanumān’s leap and search in Laṅkā
summary: Hanumān leaps the ocean from the southern shore, searches Laṅkā by night, finds Sītā in the aśoka grove, gives her Rāma’s ring, is captured and has his tail set on fire, and burns the city before returning.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The building of the bridge to Laṅkā
summary: At the Ocean’s suggestion the vānara Nala, son of Viśvakarman, directs the vānaras in building a causeway across the sea to Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The war in Laṅkā and the death of Rāvaṇa
summary: The war between Rāma’s vānara army and Rāvaṇa’s rākṣasas, culminating in the deaths of Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit and Rāvaṇa, whom Rāma kills with the Brahmā weapon given by Agastya.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Sītā’s ordeal by fire
summary: After Rāvaṇa’s death Rāma publicly refuses Sītā; she has Lakṣmaṇa build a pyre and enters the fire calling Agni to witness her fidelity; Agni returns her unharmed and the gods proclaim Rāma’s divinity.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The banishment of Sītā and her return to the earth
summary: Hearing that his subjects gossip about Sītā’s stay in Rāvaṇa’s house, Rāma has Lakṣmaṇa abandon the pregnant Sītā near Vālmīki’s hermitage; years later, asked to prove her purity again at the horse sacrifice, she calls upon the Earth, who receives her.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The krauñca bird and the first śloka
summary: Vālmīki sees a hunter kill one of a pair of mating krauñca birds; his grief (śoka) issues spontaneously as the first verse (śloka), and Brahmā bids him compose Rāma’s story in that metre.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The sacrifice for sons and the birth of the four princes
summary: Daśaratha’s sacrifice performed by Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the gods’ request that Viṣṇu be born as a man to kill Rāvaṇa, and the births of Rāma, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna as portions of Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma kills Tāṭakā
summary: On Viśvāmitra’s instruction the young Rāma kills the demoness Tāṭakā, his first deed against the rākṣasas.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The release of Ahalyā
summary: Passing Gautama’s hermitage, Rāma ends the curse on Ahalyā, who had been seduced by Indra.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma and Paraśurāma
summary: On the way back from Mithilā, Jāmadagnya Rāma (Paraśurāma) challenges Dāśarathi Rāma to string Viṣṇu’s bow; Rāma does so and Paraśurāma yields.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kaikeyī’s two boons
summary: Incited by Mantharā, Kaikeyī reminds Daśaratha of the two boons he granted when she saved him in battle and demands Bharata’s consecration and Rāma’s exile.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Daśaratha
summary: Grieving for Rāma, Daśaratha recalls how he once killed an ascetic’s son and was cursed to die lamenting a son, and dies in the night.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bharata and the sandals
summary: Bharata seeks Rāma at Citrakūṭa and begs him to return; Rāma refuses, and Bharata takes his gold-adorned sandals to rule in his name.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā
summary: Rāvaṇa’s sister Śūrpaṇakhā propositions Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa at Pañcavaṭī and attacks Sītā; Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears, setting the war with the rākṣasas in motion.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The golden deer
summary: At Rāvaṇa’s command Mārīca takes the form of a jewelled golden deer near the hermitage; Sītā asks Rāma to catch it, and Mārīca, dying, cries out in Rāma’s voice to draw Lakṣmaṇa away.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Jaṭāyu’s fight with Rāvaṇa
summary: The vulture king Jaṭāyu attacks Rāvaṇa to free Sītā, is mortally wounded, and lives long enough to tell Rāma what happened.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The alliance of Rāma and Sugrīva
summary: Hanumān brings Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to Sugrīva on Ṛśyamūka; they swear friendship before fire, Rāma promising to kill Vālin and Sugrīva to search for Sītā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Vālin
summary: During Sugrīva’s second duel with Vālin, Rāma shoots Vālin from concealment; the dying Vālin reproaches him and Rāma defends the act.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Vibhīṣaṇa joins Rāma
summary: Rebuked by Rāvaṇa for urging Sītā’s return, Vibhīṣaṇa flies to Rāma’s camp; despite Sugrīva’s suspicion Rāma accepts him and promises him Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Kumbhakarṇa
summary: Roused from sleep for the war, Kumbhakarṇa devastates the vānaras until he is killed — by Rāma in Vālmīki’s Yuddhakāṇḍa, by Lakṣmaṇa with the Brahmā weapon in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Indrajit
summary: Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa’s son Indrajit after a long duel.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The return to Ayodhyā and Rāma’s consecration
summary: Rāma returns to Ayodhyā with Sītā and is consecrated king, as the gods consecrated Indra.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāvaṇa’s boon from Brahmā
summary: Through austerities Rāvaṇa obtains from Brahmā invulnerability to gods, demons, nāgas, yakṣas and other beings — but not to humans; Vibhīṣaṇa asks only for steadfastness in dharma.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Vedavatī’s curse
summary: The ascetic Vedavatī, molested by Rāvaṇa, enters the fire vowing to be reborn for his destruction; the Uttarakāṇḍa says she is reborn as Sītā.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Hanumān’s childhood leap at the sun
summary: The infant Hanumān leaps at the rising sun thinking it a fruit, is struck down by Indra’s thunderbolt; the wind god withdraws in grief until the gods restore the child and grant him boons.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Śambūka
summary: When a brahmin’s son dies prematurely, Rāma finds the śūdra Śambūka performing austerities and beheads him, after which the boy revives.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Lava and Kuśa sing the Rāmāyaṇa
summary: At Vālmīki’s instruction the twins sing the whole poem in Rāma’s presence during his horse sacrifice, leading to their recognition as his sons.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Rāma’s return to Viṣṇu’s form
summary: At the end of his reign Rāma, with his brothers, enters the Sarayū and, at Brahmā’s invitation, the radiance of Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The dice game
summary: Duryodhana, envious of the Pāṇḍavas’ wealth, has Śakuni challenge Yudhiṣṭhira to dice in the new hall at Hāstinapura; Yudhiṣṭhira loses his wealth, kingdom, brothers, himself and Draupadī, and in the return match the Pāṇḍavas are condemned to twelve years’ exile and a thirteenth incognito.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The humiliation of Draupadī in the assembly hall
summary: Draupadī, staked and lost, is dragged by her hair into the hall in a single garment; she asks whether Yudhiṣṭhira lost himself before staking her; Duḥśāsana tries to strip her and her garment is miraculously renewed; Dhṛtarāṣṭra finally grants her boons.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Draupadī’s svayaṃvara
summary: At Drupada’s city the disguised Arjuna strings the great bow and hits the target to win Draupadī; Kuntī’s unwitting instruction to share leads to her marriage to all five Pāṇḍavas, justified in several ways in the text.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The house of lac
summary: Duryodhana has a house of lac built at Vāraṇāvata to burn the Pāṇḍavas and Kuntī; warned by Vidura, they escape through a tunnel and are thought dead.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Kurukṣetra war
summary: The eighteen-day war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas at Kurukṣetra, narrated in the Bhīṣma-, Droṇa-, Karṇa- and Śalyaparvans, which ends in the death of almost all the warriors on both sides.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa’s discourse to Arjuna (the Gītā)
summary: On the battlefield, Arjuna, seeing his kinsmen and teachers arrayed against him, lays down his bow; Kṛṣṇa teaches him on duty, action without attachment, knowledge and devotion, and reveals his universal form.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The destruction of the Yādavas and Kṛṣṇa’s death
summary: Thirty-six years after the war, the Yādavas, cursed through Sāmba and fulfilling Gāndhārī’s curse, kill one another at Prabhāsa with clubs grown from erakā grass; Balarāma departs in yoga and Kṛṣṇa is shot in the foot by the hunter Jarā.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The birth of Kṛṣṇa
summary: Kṛṣṇa is born to Devakī and Vasudeva in Kaṃsa’s prison at Mathurā, after Kaṃsa has killed her earlier children; he is carried to Vraja and exchanged with the daughter born to Yaśodā at the same time.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa lifts Mount Govardhana
summary: Kṛṣṇa persuades the cowherds to honour the mountain instead of Indra; when Indra sends a deluge he uproots Govardhana and holds it up for seven days to shelter Vraja, and Indra comes to honour him.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa subdues the serpent Kāliya
summary: The boy Kṛṣṇa plunges into the pool of the Yamunā poisoned by Kāliya, subdues the serpent by dancing on its heads and sends it away to the ocean.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Kaṃsa
summary: Summoned to Mathurā for a wrestling festival, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma kill the wrestlers, and Kṛṣṇa drags Kaṃsa down by the hair and kills him, restoring Ugrasena.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Nala and Damayantī
summary: Damayantī chooses Nala over the gods; possessed by Kali, Nala loses his kingdom at dice to his brother Puṣkara and abandons her in the forest; after many trials, disguised as a charioteer, he is recognised and regains his kingdom.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Sāvitrī and Satyavān
summary: Sāvitrī marries Satyavān knowing he will die in a year; when Yama takes his life she follows and, winning boon after boon by her words, obtains his life back.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ugraśravas’ recitation at Naimiṣa
summary: The outer frame of the Mahābhārata: the bard Ugraśravas arrives at Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest and recites the epic he heard at Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice
summary: To avenge his father Parīkṣit, killed by Takṣaka, Janamejaya performs a sacrifice that draws the serpents into the fire; Āstīka stops it. During its intervals Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhīṣma’s vow
summary: To let his father Śantanu marry Satyavatī, whose father demands that her son inherit, Devavrata renounces the throne and vows lifelong celibacy, and is thenceforth called Bhīṣma.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Vyāsa’s niyoga: the births of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura
summary: After Vicitravīrya dies childless, Satyavatī asks her son Vyāsa to raise offspring on his widows; Ambikā bears the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Ambālikā the pale Pāṇḍu, and a servant woman Vidura.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The birth and abandonment of Karṇa
summary: The unmarried Kuntī tests Durvāsas’s mantra on the Sun and bears Karṇa with armour and earrings; fearing disgrace she sets him adrift, and the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā raise him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The births of the Pāṇḍavas
summary: Cursed never to approach his wives, Pāṇḍu asks Kuntī to use her mantra: she bears Yudhiṣṭhira by Dharma, Bhīma by Vāyu and Arjuna by Indra; Mādrī bears the twins by the Aśvins.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ekalavya’s thumb
summary: The niṣāda Ekalavya, refused by Droṇa, teaches himself archery before a clay image of him; when Arjuna sees his skill, Droṇa demands Ekalavya’s right thumb as fee, and Ekalavya cuts it off.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The tournament of the Kuru princes
summary: At the public display of the princes’ skill Karṇa enters and matches Arjuna; challenged on his birth, he is made king of Aṅga by Duryodhana, and Adhiratha’s arrival exposes him to Bhīma’s scorn as a sūta’s son.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhīma and Hiḍimbā
summary: After escaping the house of lac Bhīma kills the man-eater Hiḍimba and, with Kuntī’s consent, lives with his sister Hiḍimbā, who bears Ghaṭotkaca.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The burning of the Khāṇḍava forest
summary: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna help the fire god Agni consume the Khāṇḍava forest against Indra’s rains; Agni gives Arjuna the bow Gāṇḍīva and Kṛṣṇa the discus, and the spared Maya later builds the Pāṇḍavas’ hall.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Jarāsandha
summary: Before the rājasūya, Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma and Arjuna enter Magadha disguised as brahmins and Bhīma kills Jarāsandha in a wrestling match.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The rājasūya and the killing of Śiśupāla
summary: At Yudhiṣṭhira’s royal consecration Bhīṣma proposes Kṛṣṇa for the first honour; Śiśupāla protests and insults Kṛṣṇa, who beheads him with his discus.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Arjuna and the Kirāta
summary: Seeking divine weapons in the Himālaya, Arjuna fights a hunter (kirāta) over a boar; the hunter is Śiva, who, pleased, gives him the Pāśupata weapon.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Yakṣa’s questions
summary: At a lake whose water kills his brothers, Yudhiṣṭhira answers the questions of a yakṣa — the god Dharma — and wins back their lives.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The killing of Kīcaka
summary: At Virāṭa’s court the general Kīcaka harasses Draupadī (disguised as Sairandhrī); Bhīma meets him at night in the dancing hall and kills him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa’s embassy to the Kauravas
summary: Kṛṣṇa goes to Hāstinapura to seek peace; when Duryodhana plots to seize him he reveals his cosmic form, then leaves, taking Karṇa aside to reveal his birth.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ambā’s revenge and Śikhaṇḍin
summary: Ambā, rejected after Bhīṣma’s abduction, seeks his death, is reborn as Drupada’s daughter Śikhaṇḍinī and becomes the man Śikhaṇḍin through an exchange of sex with the yakṣa Sthūṇa.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kuntī meets Karṇa
summary: Before the war Kuntī goes to Karṇa on the bank of the Gaṅgā and asks him to join his brothers; he refuses but promises to spare all but Arjuna, so that she will still have five sons.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The fall of Bhīṣma
summary: On the tenth day, with Śikhaṇḍin before him, Arjuna pierces Bhīṣma with arrows; Bhīṣma falls and lies on a bed of arrows awaiting the winter solstice.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Abhimanyu
summary: On the thirteenth day Abhimanyu breaks into Droṇa’s circular array, is surrounded by several warriors and killed by Duḥśāsana’s son with a mace.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Ghaṭotkaca
summary: In the night battle Karṇa uses Indra’s infallible spear, reserved for Arjuna, to kill Ghaṭotkaca.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Droṇa
summary: Told that “Aśvatthāman” is dead — an elephant of that name killed by Bhīma, confirmed by Yudhiṣṭhira — Droṇa lays down his weapons and is beheaded by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The death of Karṇa
summary: On the seventeenth day Karṇa’s chariot wheel sinks into the earth; while he struggles to free it, Arjuna, urged by Kṛṣṇa, kills him.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The mace duel and the breaking of Duryodhana’s thighs
summary: In the final mace duel, prompted by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, Bhīma strikes Duryodhana below the navel, breaking his thighs as he had vowed, to Balarāma’s anger.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The night massacre
summary: Aśvatthāman, with Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, enters the Pāṇḍava camp by night and kills Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Draupadeyas and the sleeping warriors.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Gāndhārī curses Kṛṣṇa
summary: Lamenting on the battlefield, Gāndhārī blames Kṛṣṇa for not preventing the slaughter and curses him and his clan to perish in thirty-six years.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhīṣma’s instruction from the bed of arrows
summary: At Kṛṣṇa’s urging, the dying Bhīṣma instructs Yudhiṣṭhira at length on kingship, emergencies, liberation and many other topics before dying at the winter solstice.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The great departure of the Pāṇḍavas
summary: Renouncing the kingdom, the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī walk towards Mount Meru; one by one they fall, and only Yudhiṣṭhira, followed by a dog that proves to be Dharma, reaches Indra’s chariot.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śakuntalā and Duḥṣanta
summary: King Duḥṣanta meets Śakuntalā in Kaṇva’s hermitage and marries her by gāndharva rite; when she later brings their son to court he denies her until a heavenly voice confirms her, and the boy Bharata becomes heir.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa carries off Rukmiṇī
summary: Kṛṣṇa takes Rukmiṇī, daughter of Bhīṣmaka of Vidarbha, away from her intended marriage to Śiśupāla and defeats her brother Rukmin.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ayodhyā
summary: Capital of Kosala and of the Ikṣvāku kings in the Rāmāyaṇa, Rāma’s birthplace and royal seat; traditionally identified with Ayodhya on the Sarayū (Ghaghara) in Uttar Pradesh, and with ancient Sāketa.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mithilā
summary: Capital of Videha ruled by Janaka, where Rāma breaks Śiva’s bow and marries Sītā; traditionally identified with Janakpur in the Nepal Terai, within the wider Mithilā region of north Bihar and Nepal.

type:LABEL: place
name: Laṅkā (in the Rāmāyaṇa)
summary: Rāvaṇa’s island fortress-city beyond the southern ocean, earlier the seat of Kubera; widely identified in tradition with the island of Sri Lanka, though some scholars have proposed locations in central India.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kiṣkindhā
summary: Cave-city of the vānara kings Vālin and Sugrīva near the Pampā lake and Ṛśyamūka hill; traditionally identified with the Hampi–Anegundi area on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka.

type:LABEL: place
name: Citrakūṭa
summary: Hill in the forest south of the Yamunā where Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa first settle in exile on Bharadvāja’s advice, and where Bharata finds them; identified with Chitrakoot on the Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh border.

type:LABEL: place
name: Pañcavaṭī
summary: Forest spot on the Godāvarī recommended by Agastya, where Rāma builds his hermitage and from which Sītā is abducted; traditionally identified with Panchavati in Nashik, Maharashtra.

type:LABEL: place
name: Daṇḍaka forest
summary: The vast forest of the exile, peopled by sages and harassed by rākṣasas, stretching (in later understanding) between the Narmadā and the Godāvarī/Kṛṣṇā; the modern Dandakaranya region of central-eastern India takes its name from it.

type:LABEL: place
name: Hastināpura
summary: Capital of the Kuru kings and seat of the Kauravas; identified with Hastinapur in Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, where B. B. Lal excavated Painted Grey Ware levels (1950–52).

type:LABEL: place
name: Indraprastha
summary: City founded by the Pāṇḍavas on the Yamunā after clearing the Khāṇḍava forest, seat of Yudhiṣṭhira’s rājasūya; traditionally identified with the area of the Purana Qila in Delhi.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kurukṣetra
summary: The “field of the Kurus” where the eighteen-day war is fought, also called Samantapañcaka and dharmakṣetra; identified with the Kurukshetra region in Haryana, an important pilgrimage area.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: place
name: Dvārakā
summary: Kṛṣṇa’s city by the western sea, to which the Yādavas move from Mathurā, and which the sea submerges after Kṛṣṇa’s death; identified with Dwarka in Gujarat (with Bet Dwarka island also associated).

type:LABEL: place
name: Mathurā
summary: City of the Śūrasenas on the Yamunā, ruled by Kaṃsa, where Kṛṣṇa is born and kills Kaṃsa; the modern city in Uttar Pradesh, an important early centre of Vāsudeva–Kṛṣṇa worship.

type:LABEL: place
name: Vṛndāvana
summary: Forest near the Yamunā to which the cowherds move from their first settlement and where Kṛṣṇa’s childhood feats and sports with the gopīs take place; identified with Vrindavan near Mathura.

type:LABEL: place
name: Naimiṣa forest
summary: Forest where Śaunaka holds his twelve-year sacrifice and Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata (and, in Purāṇic frames, the Purāṇas); identified with Nimsar (Neemsar) on the Gomatī in Sitapur district, Uttar Pradesh.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kāmpilya
summary: Capital of southern Pañcāla left to Drupada after Droṇa’s victory, the setting of Draupadī’s svayaṃvara in tradition; identified with Kampil in Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh.

type:LABEL: place
name: Takṣaśilā
summary: City in Gandhāra from which Janamejaya returns to Hāstinapura after his snake sacrifice (MBh 18.5.29); identified with Taxila in Punjab, Pakistan.

type:LABEL: place
name: Virāṭanagara
summary: Capital of King Virāṭa of the Matsyas, where the Pāṇḍavas spend the thirteenth year in disguise; traditionally identified with Viratnagar (Bairat) in Jaipur district, Rajasthan.

type:LABEL: place
name: Prabhāsa
summary: Coastal tīrtha where the Yādavas gather and destroy one another in drunken strife; identified with Prabhas Patan (Somnath) in Gujarat.

type:LABEL: place
name: Pampā lake
summary: Lake near Ṛśyamūka on whose western shore Śabarī lives and near which Rāma meets Hanumān and Sugrīva; identified with Pampa Sarovar near Hampi, Karnataka.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śṛṅgaverapura
summary: Town of the niṣāda chief Guha on the Gaṅgā, where Rāma crosses the river at the start of the exile; identified with Shringverpur near Prayagraj.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Kuru lineage
summary: The royal line descended from Kuru in the lunar dynasty, ruling from Hāstinapura, to which Śantanu, Bhīṣma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and both the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas belong.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Pāṇḍavas
summary: The five legal sons of Pāṇḍu — Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna (by Kuntī) and Nakula and Sahadeva (by Mādrī), each fathered by a god — with their shared wife Draupadī and their descendants down to Parīkṣit and Janamejaya.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Kauravas
summary: The hundred sons (and one daughter) of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, led by Duryodhana; also, more broadly, the Kuru side in the war.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Yādavas / Vṛṣṇis
summary: The descendants of Yadu, including the Vṛṣṇi, Andhaka and Bhoja clans of Mathurā and Dvārakā, to which Śūra, Vasudeva, Kuntī, Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Subhadrā belong; their genealogy fills the Harivaṃśa.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Paulastyas (line of Pulastya)
summary: The descendants of the sage Pulastya through Viśravas: Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) and the rākṣasa siblings Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The vānaras of Kiṣkindhā
summary: The monkey people of Kiṣkindhā ruled by Vālin and Sugrīva, among them Hanumān, Aṅgada, Nala and Nīla, born — in the Rāmāyaṇa and Rāmopākhyāna — of gods to aid Viṣṇu’s descent.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Pāñcālas (line of Drupada)
summary: The ruling house of Pañcāla: Drupada and his children Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin and Draupadī, allies of the Pāṇḍavas.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: The Bhāratas (line of Bharata Dauḥṣanti)
summary: The lineage named after Bharata, son of Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā, from which the Kurus descend and after which the epic (Bhārata, Mahābhārata) is named.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The identification of the Rāmāyaṇa’s Laṅkā with Sri Lanka
summary: The traditional and widely held view that Rāvaṇa’s island-city Laṅkā is the island of Sri Lanka, set against scholarly proposals that the epic’s Laṅkā lay elsewhere (notably in central India) or is a purely literary geography.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā of Varāhamihira
summary: Varāhamihira’s sixth-century Sanskrit compendium of natural astrology and omens, which also contains the earliest surviving systematic chapters on temple types, image proportions and the iconography of the gods.

type:LABEL: person
name: Varāhamihira
summary: Astronomer and astrologer of Avanti (Ujjain), author of the Pañcasiddhāntikā, Bṛhajjātaka and Bṛhat Saṃhitā, active in the sixth century CE.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 52: Vāstuvidyā (the science of sites)
summary: Chapter on house and site planning, with the myth of the Vāstupuruṣa pressed down by the gods (52.2–3) and the 81-square diagram of 45 deities with Brahmā at the centre (52.42–49).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 55: Prāsādalakṣaṇa (characteristics of temples)
summary: Chapter on temples: siting near water and gardens, a 64-square plan, proportions of sanctum and door, door guardians and auspicious couples, and a list of twenty named temple types.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 57: Pratimālakṣaṇa (characteristics of images)
summary: Chapter on images: the aṅgula scale, the proportions of a standard figure, and the distinguishing marks of Viṣṇu, Baladeva, Ekānaṃśā, Brahmā, Skanda, Indra, Śiva, the Buddha, the Jina, Sūrya, the liṅga, the Mothers, Revanta, Yama, Varuṇa and Kubera.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 59: Pratimāpratiṣṭhāpana (installation of images)
summary: Chapter on consecrating an image, ending with the rule that each god is installed by priests of his own cult (59.19).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 42–43: temple construction and the deities of the temple
summary: Hayagrīva’s instruction on the general temple (a 16-part square plan, wall and spire proportions; 42) and on placing deities on the building (43).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 44–47: images of Vāsudeva, pedestals and śālagrāma stones
summary: Proportions of the Vāsudeva image (44), the pedestal (piṇḍikā, 45) and the marks and worship of śālagrāma stones (46–47).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 48: Caturviṃśatimūrti-stotra (the twenty-four forms of Viṣṇu)
summary: A hymn naming twenty-four forms of Viṣṇu (Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava … Hari), each distinguished by how the conch, discus, mace and lotus are distributed among the four hands.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 49: images of the ten avatāras and other Vaiṣṇava forms
summary: Prescriptions for Matsya, Kūrma, Bhū-Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Balarāma, Buddha and Kalki, the Vāsudeva group of nine, Brahmā, eight-armed Viṣṇu on Garuḍa, Trailokyamohana, a twenty-armed four-faced Viśvarūpa, Hayagrīva and Dattātreya.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 50: images of the Goddess and her circle
summary: Prescriptions for Caṇḍī slaying the buffalo demon, the nine Durgās, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā on the makara and Yamunā on the tortoise, the Mothers, Cāmuṇḍā, Vināyaka, Skanda, and attendants such as Nandīśa.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 51: images of Sūrya, the planets, nāgas and lokapālas
summary: Sūrya on a one-wheeled chariot of seven horses holding two lotuses, with Daṇḍa and Piṅgala (51.1–3); the twelve Ādityas; the planets with their attributes (51.10–12); eight nāgas (51.13); and the two-armed guardians of the directions with their mounts (51.14–16).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 52: the sixty-four yoginīs and the retinue of the Mothers
summary: A list of sixty-four yoginīs (52.1–8), described as eight- or four-armed (52.9), followed by Vīrabhadra on a bull before the Mothers and Caṇḍikā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 53–55: proportions, materials and pedestals of the liṅga
summary: The liṅga divided into Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva portions (square, octagonal and round, 53), the ranking of liṅgas by material (54) and the pedestal (55).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa III.35–43: the Citrasūtra (treatise on painting)
summary: The section of the third book of the Viṣṇudharmottara that teaches painting: proportions, the five male types, postures, colours, and the expression of sentiments (rasa).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa III.44–85: image-making (pratimālakṣaṇa)
summary: The chapters of the third book of the Viṣṇudharmottara that describe how to make images of the gods, including Vaiṣṇava forms, Śiva as Gaurīśvara (Ardhanārīśvara), the planets and the guardians of the directions.

type:LABEL: text
name: Citralakṣaṇa of Nagnajit
summary: An early treatise on painting and the proportions of figures attributed to Nagnajit, lost in Sanskrit but preserved in a Tibetan translation in the Tanjur and reconstructed in Sanskrit.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mayamata
summary: A South Indian Sanskrit treatise on architecture, settlements, houses, temples and iconography attributed to Maya, one of the two most complete surviving Drāviḍa-tradition vāstu texts (with the Mānasāra).

type:LABEL: text
name: Mānasāra
summary: A large Sanskrit treatise on architecture and sculpture in 70 chapters from South India, edited and translated by P. K. Acharya, whose name he rendered as “essence of measurement”.

type:LABEL: text
name: Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra
summary: An eleventh-century Sanskrit treatise on architecture attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja of Dhārā, the fullest surviving description of North Indian temple types, including the Bhūmija.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aparājitapṛcchā
summary: A Sanskrit treatise of western India attributed to Bhuvanadeva, framed as answers to Aparājita’s questions, important for Nāgara and Māru-Gurjara temple architecture and iconography.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śilpa Prakāśa
summary: A medieval Odishan Sanskrit text on temple architecture by Rāmacandra Kaulācāra, which describes Kaliṅga temple forms, their sculpture and tantric yantras placed in the foundations.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rūpamaṇḍana
summary: A fifteenth-century Sanskrit manual of iconography by Maṇḍana, sūtradhāra at the Mewar court of Rāṇā Kumbhā, a companion to his Prāsādamaṇḍana on temples.

type:LABEL: text
name: Prāsādamaṇḍana
summary: Maṇḍana’s fifteenth-century Sanskrit manual on temple building in the western Indian (Māru-Gurjara) tradition, still used by hereditary Sompura architects.

type:LABEL: person
name: Maṇḍana (sūtradhāra)
summary: Master builder (sūtradhāra) at the court of Rāṇā Kumbhā of Mewar in the fifteenth century, author of the Prāsādamaṇḍana, Rūpamaṇḍana and other manuals.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śilparatna
summary: A sixteenth-century Sanskrit compendium of architecture and iconography by Śrīkumāra of Kerala, cited by Gopinatha Rao for many iconographic forms.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tantrasamuccaya
summary: A fifteenth-century Kerala manual of temple ritual by Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan Nampūtiri that also governs temple planning and image installation in Kerala.

type:LABEL: text
name: Toḍala Tantra
summary: A Śākta tantra in ten chapters, a dialogue of Śiva and the Goddess, whose tenth chapter equates the ten Mahāvidyās with Viṣṇu’s ten avatāras.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vāstuśāstra (science of building)
summary: The Sanskrit tradition of texts and practice on siting, planning and proportioning settlements, houses and temples; its earliest surviving systematic statement is in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śilpaśāstra (science of the arts)
summary: The texts on making images, painting and other crafts, often overlapping with vāstuśāstra; they prescribe proportions (tālamāna), attributes and gestures for each deity.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vāstupuruṣa-maṇḍala
summary: The square grid on which a site or temple is laid out, imagined as the body of the Vāstupuruṣa pressed face down by the gods, with Brahmā in the centre and other deities in the surrounding squares.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Tālamāna (iconometry)
summary: The system of proportional measurement for images, expressing a figure’s height in tālas (face-lengths) and aṅgulas (digits) of its own body; different classes of beings are given different tāla canons.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Ardhanārīśvara
summary: Śiva as “the lord who is half woman”: a single figure whose right half is Śiva and left half Pārvatī, expressing the inseparability of god and his śakti.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Harihara
summary: A composite image whose right half is Śiva (Hara) and left half Viṣṇu (Hari), expressing the identity of the two gods; it is common in sixth- to eighth-century India and in pre-Angkorian Cambodia.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Dakṣiṇāmūrti
summary: Śiva as the south-facing teacher: a youthful ascetic seated under a banyan tree, teaching sages by gesture and silence, his right foot on the dwarf of ignorance.
earliest_material: c. 700 CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha, c. 690–728)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Somāskanda
summary: A Pallava-born family group in which Śiva sits with Umā and the child Skanda between them (sa-umā-skanda); it became the central processional icon of Tamil Śaiva temples.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Liṅgodbhavamūrti
summary: Śiva emerging from a fiery pillar of light, with Brahmā flying upward as a goose and Viṣṇu digging downward as a boar, the iconic form of the Liṅgodbhava myth of Śiva’s supremacy.
earliest_material: c. 700 CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha, c. 690–728)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bhikṣāṭana
summary: Śiva as a naked, beautiful mendicant wandering with a skull-bowl, followed by a deer and a dwarf attendant, who enchants the wives of the sages of the Pine Forest.
earliest_material: c. 700 CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha, c. 690–728)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kalyāṇasundara
summary: The marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī (pāṇigrahaṇa), with Śiva taking the bride’s hand, Brahmā as officiating priest and, in southern versions, Viṣṇu giving the bride away.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Gajāsurasaṃhāra
summary: Śiva destroying the elephant demon and dancing within its flayed hide, which he holds stretched above him like an arch; a fierce form favoured by Cōḻa and Hoysaḷa sculptors.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Tripurāntaka
summary: Śiva as the archer who destroys with a single arrow the three flying cities of the asuras, riding a chariot made of the gods with Brahmā as charioteer.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era
earliest_material: c. 756–773 CE (main excavation, reign of Kṛṣṇa I), with later elements

type:LABEL: deity
name: Gaṅgādhara
summary: Śiva receiving the descending river Gaṅgā in a lock of his hair to break her fall, often with Pārvatī turning away and Bhagīratha in worship.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bhairava
summary: The terrifying form of Śiva: naked, fanged, garlanded with skulls and accompanied by a dog, who in Purāṇic myth cuts off Brahmā’s fifth head and wanders until freed of the skull at Vārāṇasī.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Andhakāsuravadhamūrti
summary: Śiva as a fierce form impaling the blind demon Andhaka on his trident while catching the demon’s multiplying blood in a skull-bowl, sometimes helped by the Mothers.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Caṇḍeśānugrahamūrti
summary: Śiva, with Umā, blessing his devotee Caṇḍeśa by binding a flower garland on his head, rewarding the boy who struck his own father for disrupting his worship of the liṅga.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Rāvaṇānugrahamūrti
summary: Śiva and Pārvatī seated on Mount Kailāsa while Rāvaṇa, trapped beneath, tries to shake the mountain; Śiva presses it down with his toe and later grants Rāvaṇa grace and a sword.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kirātamūrti (Kirātārjunamūrti)
summary: Śiva disguised as a Kirāta hunter, with Pārvatī as a huntress, who fights Arjuna over a boar and then grants him the Pāśupata weapon.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Sadāśiva
summary: Śiva as the five-faced, ten-armed supreme form of Śaiva Siddhānta, whose faces Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna embody five aspects and five mantras.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Liṅga (aniconic form of Śiva)
summary: The cylindrical, usually aniconic emblem in which Śiva is principally worshipped; textual canons divide it into a square Brahmā part, an octagonal Viṣṇu part and a round Rudra part that alone is visible.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Mukhaliṅga
summary: A liṅga carved with one or more faces of Śiva projecting from the shaft; one-faced (ekamukha), four-faced (caturmukha) and five-faced (pañcamukha) types are distinguished.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Ekamukhaliṅga
summary: A liṅga with a single face of Śiva on its front, the commonest mukhaliṅga of Gupta-period north India.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: deity
name: Caturmukhaliṅga
summary: A liṅga with four faces of Śiva looking in the four directions, sometimes with a fifth implied on top (pañcamukha).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Pañcamukhaliṅga
summary: A liṅga with five faces, four around the shaft and one on top, corresponding to Sadāśiva’s five faces.
earliest_material: 10th c. (early 10th c. for the main temple)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Umā-Maheśvara
summary: Śiva seated with Umā (Pārvatī) on his left knee in an embrace (āliṅgana), a conjugal image very popular in Pāla Bengal, Kashmir and Nepal.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kālāntaka (Kālāri)
summary: Śiva bursting out of the liṅga to kick Yama, the god of death, who has come to take the boy-devotee Mārkaṇḍeya clinging to the liṅga.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Lakulīśa
summary: The founder-teacher of the Pāśupata Śaivas, venerated as an avatāra of Śiva and shown as a seated ascetic with an erect phallus (ūrdhvaliṅga) holding a club (lakuṭa) and a citron.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Anantaśayana (Śeṣaśāyī Viṣṇu)
summary: Viṣṇu reclining in cosmic sleep on the serpent Ananta (Śeṣa) on the ocean between creations, with Lakṣmī at his feet and Brahmā born on a lotus from his navel.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: deity
name: Trivikrama
summary: Viṣṇu in the act of taking his three strides across the worlds after the dwarf Vāmana has won from Bali the land he can cover in three steps; one leg is raised high toward the sky.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vaikuṇṭha Caturmūrti
summary: A four-faced Viṣṇu with a human face in front, a lion face and a boar face at the sides and a fierce face (Kapila) at the back, developed above all in Kashmir between the 8th and 10th centuries.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Viśvarūpa
summary: Viṣṇu (or Kṛṣṇa) in his universal form, with many heads and arms and the whole cosmos, gods and beings emerging from or contained in his body, as revealed to Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gītā.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa
summary: Viṣṇu seated with Lakṣmī on his left thigh, embracing her, a conjugal image popular in medieval north and central India and in Hoysaḷa Karnataka.
earliest_material: 10th c. (main temple, attributed to Sāhila Varman)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Yoga-Narasiṃha
summary: Narasiṃha seated in yogic posture with his knees bound by a band (yogapaṭṭa), calm rather than in the act of killing Hiraṇyakaśipu; worshipped at many South Indian hill shrines.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bhū-Varāha (Nṛvarāha)
summary: Varāha as a boar-headed man lifting the Earth goddess (Bhū) out of the ocean on his tusk or arm, one foot on the serpent king; the dominant anthropomorphic form of the boar avatāra.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Yajña-Varāha (zoomorphic boar)
summary: Varāha as a colossal boar whose body is covered with rows of small figures of gods and sages, representing the boar as the embodiment of the sacrifice and of the cosmos.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Veṇugopāla
summary: Kṛṣṇa as the cowherd playing the flute, standing cross-legged with cows and cowherds around him; a favourite image of Hoysaḷa, Vijayanagara and later Vaiṣṇava art.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kāliyamardana Kṛṣṇa
summary: The child Kṛṣṇa dancing on the hoods of the serpent Kāliya in the Yamunā, holding its tail; one of the most popular Cōḻa bronze subjects.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Govardhanadhara Kṛṣṇa
summary: Kṛṣṇa lifting Mount Govardhana on one hand as an umbrella to shelter the cowherds from Indra’s storm; one of the earliest Kṛṣṇa scenes to be made as a cult image.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Caturviṃśatimūrti (the twenty-four forms of Viṣṇu)
summary: Twenty-four named standing forms of four-armed Viṣṇu (Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda … Hari, Kṛṣṇa) that look identical except for the order in which the conch, discus, mace and lotus are held in the four hands.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Sudarśana (personified discus)
summary: Viṣṇu’s discus as a deity in its own right: the Cakrapuruṣa of Gupta art, the many-armed Sudarśana (Cakrattāḻvār) of South Indian temples, and the wooden post worshipped beside Jagannātha at Puri.
earliest_material: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

type:LABEL: concept
name: Āyudhapuruṣa (personified weapons)
summary: The convention of showing a deity’s weapons as small human attendants, such as the male Cakrapuruṣa (discus) and the female Gadādevī (mace) beside Gupta images of Viṣṇu.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: deity
name: Mahiṣāsuramardinī
summary: The Goddess (Durgā, Caṇḍikā) slaying the buffalo demon Mahiṣa, the most widespread warrior image of the Goddess, attested from Kuṣāṇa Mathurā to Pāla Bengal, Java and Cambodia.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: deity
name: Gaja-Lakṣmī
summary: Lakṣmī (Śrī) standing or seated on a lotus while two elephants pour water over her from pots held in their trunks; one of the oldest goddess images in Indian art.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Lajjā Gaurī
summary: A fertility goddess shown squatting with legs drawn up and open, often with a lotus in place of a head, worshipped across the Deccan from about the 1st to the 8th century; her identity and name are reconstructions.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Catuḥṣaṣṭi Yoginī (the sixty-four yoginīs)
summary: A circle of sixty-four powerful female deities of tantric cults, worshipped from about the 9th to the 12th century in circular, roofless temples in Odisha and central India.
earliest_material: 9th–10th c. CE (traditionally c. 864 under Queen Hīrādevī)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Daśa Mahāvidyās (the ten Great Wisdoms)
summary: A group of ten tantric goddesses — Kālī, Tārā, Tripurasundarī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī and Kamalā — understood as forms of the one Goddess.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Tārā (Mahāvidyā)
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: dark blue goddess standing on a corpse, with sword, severed head, lotus and skull-cup; the Hindu Tārā shares her name with the Buddhist saviour goddess.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Tripurasundarī (Ṣoḍaśī, Lalitā)
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: beautiful sixteen-year-old seated on a couch whose legs are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara, holding noose, goad, sugarcane bow and flower arrows; the goddess of the Śrīvidyā tradition.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bhuvaneśvarī
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: mistress of the worlds, golden or red, holding noose and goad and showing varada and abhaya.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bhairavī (Mahāvidyā)
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: fierce red goddess with rosary, book, abhaya and varada, garlanded with skulls.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Chinnamastā
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: self-decapitated goddess holding her own head, three streams of blood feeding the head and two attendants, standing on a copulating couple (Kāma and Rati).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Dhūmāvatī
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: old widow in a crow-bannered chariot or on a crow, holding a winnowing basket, the inauspicious smoke goddess.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bagalāmukhī
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: yellow goddess pulling the tongue of a demon and raising a club, the power to paralyse an enemy.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Mātaṅgī
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: dark-green goddess of speech and music, often playing a vīṇā, associated with pollution and leftovers (ucchiṣṭa).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kamalā (Kamalātmikā)
summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: Lakṣmī seated on a lotus and bathed by elephants, the gaja-lakṣmī image incorporated into the Mahāvidyā group.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Annapūrṇā
summary: The Goddess as giver of food, holding a ladle and a bowl of rice, from whom Śiva as a mendicant receives alms; her principal temple is at Vārāṇasī.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Sarasvatī (Jain Śrutadevatā)
summary: Sarasvatī as worshipped by Jains, the goddess of the scriptures (Śrutadevatā); the earliest dated image of Sarasvatī in any tradition is a Jain one from Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā, Mathurā, of the Kuṣāṇa period.
earliest_material: year 54 of the Kaniṣka era = c. 132 CE (if the era began in 78 CE)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Gaṅgā and Yamunā as door guardians
summary: The placing of the river goddesses Gaṅgā (on a makara) and Yamunā (on a tortoise) on either side of a temple doorway, a Gupta-period innovation that became standard in North Indian temples.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Tortoise (Yamunā’s vāhana)
summary: The tortoise on which the river goddess Yamunā stands in temple-door iconography, as the makara carries Gaṅgā.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Gaṇeśa verse of the Bṛhat Saṃhitā is a later addition
summary: Kern’s edition of the Bṛhat Saṃhitā includes a verse describing Vināyaka (his 58.58) that is absent from Tripathi’s text and Utpala’s commentary; if it is an interpolation, the sixth-century text did not describe Gaṇeśa.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Heramba Gaṇapati
summary: A five-headed, ten-armed Gaṇeśa riding a lion, popular in Nepal and Bengal, often shown with his consort.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Ucchiṣṭa Gaṇapati
summary: A tantric form of Gaṇeśa worshipped by the Ucchiṣṭa sect of Gāṇapatyas, shown with a female consort on his lap in an erotic embrace; worship in a state of ritual impurity (ucchiṣṭa) is part of the rite.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Nṛtta Gaṇapati (dancing Gaṇeśa)
summary: Gaṇeśa dancing, usually with eight arms, one leg raised; a favourite of Pāla Bengal, Hoysaḷa Karnataka and Nepal.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Ṣaṇmukha (six-faced Skanda)
summary: Skanda with six heads and usually twelve arms, the form explained by his being nursed by the six Kṛttikās; in Tamil, Āṟumukam.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Devasenāpati (Subrahmaṇya with Vaḷḷi and Devasenā)
summary: Murukaṉ–Subrahmaṇya standing or seated on his peacock between his two consorts, the celestial Devasenā (Teyvāṉai) and the hunter-girl Vaḷḷi; the standard form in Tamil temples.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi
summary: Murukaṉ as a shaven-headed renunciant boy holding a staff, wearing only a loincloth, the form worshipped on the hill at Palani.
earliest_material: medieval to modern fabric (dating not established in this pass)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Svāminātha
summary: Murukaṉ as the child teacher who explained the meaning of the syllable Om to his father Śiva, worshipped at Swamimalai.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Udīcyaveṣa Sūrya (Sūrya in northern dress)
summary: The standard North Indian image of the Sun god, dressed in the “northern” fashion of Central Asia — a long coat (kañcuka), belt and boots that cover him from feet to chest — and holding a lotus in each hand.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Revanta
summary: A son of Sūrya, lord of horses and of the hunt, shown riding a horse with attendants, dogs and hunting gear; his images are mostly of the 6th–12th centuries in north and east India.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Navagraha (the nine planets)
summary: The nine “seizers” of Indian astral religion — Sūrya, Candra (Soma), Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu and Ketu — carved as a row on temple door lintels from the post-Gupta period and worshipped in their own shrines in South India.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Maṅgala (Mars)
summary: The planet Mars as a deity, red-complexioned, holding a spear and rosary in the Agni Purāṇa; also called Aṅgāraka and Bhauma (son of the Earth).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bṛhaspati (Jupiter)
summary: Bṛhaspati, preceptor of the gods, as the planet Jupiter, holding a water-pot and rosary in the Agni Purāṇa.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Śani (Saturn)
summary: The planet Saturn as a slow, dark and feared deity, son of Sūrya and Chāyā, shown with a girdle of bells in the Agni Purāṇa and later with a crow or vulture as mount.
earliest_material: Cōḻa foundation with later additions (not dated in the reference)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Ketu (the descending node)
summary: The ninth graha, the headless body (or tail) of the eclipse demon, shown with a sword and a lamp in the Agni Purāṇa; often half-serpent in sculpture.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Aṣṭa-dikpāla (guardians of the eight directions)
summary: The eight guardians of the directions — Indra (east), Agni (south-east), Yama (south), Nirṛti (south-west), Varuṇa (west), Vāyu (north-west), Kubera (north) and Īśāna (north-east) — carved on the corners of temple walls and ceilings.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Nirṛti (guardian of the south-west)
summary: Nirṛti, a Vedic power of decay and misfortune (female in the Veda), who in temple iconography becomes the male guardian of the south-west, holding a sword and riding a man or a corpse.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Īśāna (guardian of the north-east)
summary: Īśāna, a name of Śiva/Rudra, as guardian of the north-east, shown like Śiva with trident and bull.

type:LABEL: character
name: Airāvata
summary: Indra’s white elephant, said to have emerged at the churning of the ocean; the Bṛhat Saṃhitā gives him four tusks.

type:LABEL: character
name: Buffalo (Yama’s vāhana)
summary: The male water buffalo on which Yama, god of death and guardian of the south, rides.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ram / goat (Agni’s vāhana)
summary: The ram or he-goat (chāga) on which Agni, guardian of the south-east, rides in temple iconography.

type:LABEL: character
name: Deer (Vāyu’s vāhana)
summary: The deer or antelope on which Vāyu, the wind god and guardian of the north-west, rides.

type:LABEL: character
name: Parrot (Kāmadeva’s vāhana)
summary: The parrot (śuka) on which Kāmadeva, god of love, rides in later iconography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Pañcamukha Hanumān
summary: Hanumān with five faces — his own (east), Narasiṃha, Garuḍa, Varāha and Hayagrīva — and ten arms, a protective tantric form popular in South India from the late medieval period.
earliest_material: present building (19th–21st c., not dated in the reference)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vīra Hanumān
summary: The heroic, striding or flying Hanumān, often carrying the mountain of healing herbs and raising a mace or his hand in protection; the form at many village shrines and on banners.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Dāsa Hanumān
summary: Hanumān as the humble servant of Rāma, standing or kneeling with joined palms (añjali) before Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; the usual form in Rāma temples.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Nāga (serpent deities)
summary: Serpent deities shown as hooded cobras or as humans with a canopy of serpent hoods, worshipped since at least the Śuṅga–Kuṣāṇa period as guardians of water, fertility and treasure.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Yakṣa
summary: Nature and wealth spirits worshipped in monumental, pot-bellied standing images from the Maurya–Śuṅga period; Kubera is their king, and yakṣa imagery shaped later Hindu, Buddhist and Jain icons.
earliest_material: second half of the 1st century BCE (palaeography of the inscription)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Yakṣī
summary: Female nature spirits shown as voluptuous women grasping a tree branch (śālabhañjikā) or holding a fly-whisk, among the earliest monumental female figures of Indian art.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Hindu temple architecture (prāsāda)
summary: The architecture of the Hindu temple as a house and body of the god: a sanctum (garbhagṛha) beneath a tower, reached through halls and enclosed by walls, designed on a square grid and grown from aedicular parts.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Nāgara (northern temple style)
summary: The North Indian temple tradition, whose sanctum is crowned by a curvilinear tower (śikhara) topped by a ribbed āmalaka and a pot finial; its plan is a square made complex by projecting offsets (rathas).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Latina (single-spired Nāgara)
summary: The earliest and basic Nāgara tower, a single curvilinear spire whose faces carry vertical bands of interlaced arch motifs (latā, “creeper”), crowned by an āmalaka.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śekharī (clustered-spire Nāgara)
summary: The composite Nāgara tower in which half-spires (urūśṛṅgas) and miniature spires (śṛṅgas) are clustered against the central Latina spire, building up a mountain-like silhouette from the 10th century.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Bhūmija (storeyed-spire Nāgara)
summary: A Nāgara tower whose four faces carry central bands of interlaced arches separated by quarters filled with horizontal rows of miniature spires (kūṭastambhas) stacked in storeys (bhūmi), developed in Mālava under the Paramāras in the 11th century.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Drāviḍa (southern temple style)
summary: The South Indian temple tradition, whose sanctum tower (vimāna) rises in storeys (tala) of miniature pavilions — square kūṭas, oblong śālās and horseshoe-arched pañjaras — to a domed crowning member called the śikhara.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vesara
summary: A term of the southern texts for a temple whose crowning member is circular (or apsidal), now used loosely for the hybrid temple architecture of Karnataka that combines Nāgara and Drāviḍa features.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Karṇāṭa Drāviḍa
summary: Adam Hardy’s term for the Drāviḍa tradition of the Karnataka region from the early Cālukyas (7th c.) through the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, Later Cālukyas and Hoysaḷas (13th c.), marked by increasingly projected, staggered and finally stellate plans.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kaliṅga (Odishan) temple style
summary: The temple architecture of Odisha, a regional Nāgara tradition with its own terms: the curvilinear rekhā deuḷa over the sanctum, the pyramidal pīḍhā deuḷa over the hall (jagamohana) and the barrel-roofed khākharā deuḷa.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Rekhā deuḷa
summary: The Odishan curvilinear tower over the sanctum, a regional form of the Latina śikhara.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pīḍhā deuḷa
summary: The Odishan stepped pyramidal roof of horizontal tiers (pīḍhā), used over the jagamohana and other halls.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Khākharā deuḷa
summary: The Odishan rectangular shrine with a barrel-vaulted roof (named after a gourd), used chiefly for goddess shrines such as the Vaitāl Deuḷ in Bhubaneswar.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kerala temple style
summary: The temple architecture of Kerala: square, circular or apsidal sanctums (śrīkōvil) of laterite and timber under steep conical or pyramidal roofs of tiles or copper, set within a cloistered rectangular court (nālambalam) with a lamp-gallery (vilakkumāṭam).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kashmiri temple style
summary: The stone temple architecture of Kashmir (8th–11th c.), with steep double-pitched pyramidal roofs, trefoil arches set in triangular pediments, fluted columns and colonnaded courtyards.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Khmer temple architecture
summary: The temple architecture of Cambodia and its empire (6th–13th c.), culminating in the “temple-mountain”: towers (prasat) on stepped terraces, often in a quincunx, surrounded by concentric galleries and moats, built in brick, laterite and sandstone with corbelled vaults.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Central Javanese temple architecture
summary: The stone candi architecture of Central Java (c. 7th–10th c.): a square cella on a high base, a doorway framed by kāla-makara ornament, and a stepped roof crowned with miniature shrines or ratnas.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Cham temple architecture
summary: The brick tower-sanctuaries (kalan) of Champa in central Vietnam (7th–13th c.), with finely carved brick and sandstone decoration, mostly dedicated to Śiva as Bhadreśvara.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Bengal temple style (cālā and ratna)
summary: The brick and terracotta temples of Bengal (16th–19th c.), whose curved roofs imitate thatched huts (cālā types) or carry pinnacles (ratna types), their façades covered in terracotta plaques of epic and Kṛṣṇa scenes.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Cālā temple (Bengal)
summary: Bengali temple type whose curved roof imitates the thatched village hut: do-cālā (two slopes), cār-cālā (four) and āṭ-cālā (four with a smaller four-sloped storey above).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Ratna temple (Bengal)
summary: Bengali temple type with a flat or curved roof carrying one, five (pañcaratna) or nine (navaratna) towers.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Māru-Gurjara (Solaṅkī) style
summary: The western Indian Nāgara tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan (c. 10th–13th c. and revived since), with richly carved Śekharī towers, ornate pillared halls and stepped tanks; the term was coined by M. A. Dhaky.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Hemāḍpanthī style
summary: A name used in Maharashtra for medieval temples of dry-laid, mortarless stone masonry, traditionally credited to Hemādri (Hemāḍpant), minister of the Yādava kings in the 13th century.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Newar pagoda style
summary: The multi-roofed temple architecture of the Kathmandu Valley, with tiered roofs of tile or gilt copper on brick cores, supported by carved wooden struts (tunāla) depicting deities.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Rock-cut temple
summary: A temple excavated into living rock, either as a cave (guhā) behind a pillared façade or as a monolith carved free from the hillside; the dominant form for Brahmanical temples in the Deccan and Tamil country from the 5th to the 8th century.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Gupta flat-roofed shrine
summary: The earliest type of free-standing stone temple in north India (early 5th c.): a small square sanctum with a flat slab roof and a pillared porch.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pañcāyatana plan
summary: A temple layout with the main shrine at the centre of a platform and four subsidiary shrines at its corners.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Sāndhāra (temple with ambulatory)
summary: A temple whose sanctum is enclosed by an inner ambulatory passage within the outer walls, as opposed to a nirandhāra temple without one.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Gajapṛṣṭha (apsidal) plan
summary: A temple plan with a rounded (apsidal) back, “like an elephant’s back”, derived from early Buddhist caitya halls and used for some Hindu shrines in the Deccan and Tamil country.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Balinese temple (pura)
summary: The open-air walled temple compound of Bali, with courtyards and multi-roofed meru towers whose number of roofs marks the rank of the deity.

type:LABEL: claim
name: “Vesara” names the hybrid temple style of Karnataka
summary: A modern art-historical use of the textual term vesara for the Later Cālukya and Hoysaḷa temples of Karnataka; in the Mayamata and Mānasāra the word only denotes a temple with a circular crowning member.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Garbhagṛha (sanctum)
summary: The dark, usually square inner sanctum (“womb-chamber”) housing the principal image or liṅga, at the centre of the temple’s axis.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vimāna
summary: In South Indian usage the whole sanctum building with its storeyed tower; in some northern texts a name for particular temple types.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śikhara (tower / crowning member)
