summary: In the north, the curvilinear tower rising above the sanctum; in Drāviḍa usage, the domed or polygonal crowning member at the top of the vimāna.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Gopura (gateway tower)
summary: The monumental gateway tower in the enclosure walls of South Indian temples, growing from the 12th century to dwarf the sanctum tower (Chidambaram, Śrīraṅgam, Madurai).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Maṇḍapa (pillared hall)
summary: A pillared hall in front of or around the sanctum, used for gathering, dance, music or ritual; temples may have several in sequence.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Āmalaka
summary: The ribbed, cushion-shaped stone disc (named after the āmalaka fruit) that crowns a Nāgara tower beneath the finial; smaller āmalakas mark the storeys of the tower’s corners.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kalaśa (pot finial)
summary: The pot-shaped finial at the summit of a temple tower or gateway, the point where the vertical axis meets the sky.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Prākāra (enclosure wall)
summary: An enclosure wall around a temple; large South Indian temples have up to seven concentric prākāras with gopuras on their axes.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Antarāla (vestibule)
summary: The vestibule linking the sanctum to the hall in front of it.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Jagamohana
summary: The Odishan assembly hall in front of the sanctum, roofed with a pīḍhā pyramid; at Konark it is the main surviving structure.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Gavākṣa (candraśālā / kuḍu)
summary: The horseshoe-shaped arch motif, derived from the window of wooden buildings, that is multiplied into the mesh of Nāgara towers and the kuḍu arches of Drāviḍa cornices.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pradakṣiṇāpatha (ambulatory)
summary: The path for clockwise circumambulation of the sanctum, either inside the walls (sāndhāra temples) or around the building.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Dvārapāla (door guardian)
summary: Guardian figures flanking the sanctum doorway, often fierce, armed with clubs, and in Śaiva temples sometimes identified with Nandin and Mahākāla.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Mithuna (auspicious couple)
summary: Amorous couples carved on doorways and walls as auspicious, protective images; the Bṛhat Saṃhitā already lists them among the door decorations.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Mathurā school of sculpture (Śaka–Kuṣāṇa period)
summary: The red-sandstone sculpture of Mathurā from the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE, which produced the earliest anthropomorphic images of many Hindu deities — Vṛṣṇi heroes, Ardhanārīśvara, Mahiṣāsuramardinī, the Mothers, Sūrya, Kārttikeya and nāgas — alongside Buddhist and Jain images.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Gupta-period sculpture
summary: Sculpture of north and central India in the Gupta and immediately post-Gupta period (c. 320–550), in which most of the standard Hindu iconographic forms first appear in mature, often dated, examples.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pāla–Sena sculpture
summary: The sculpture of Bihar and Bengal under the Pāla and Sena dynasties (8th–12th c.), mostly finely carved black stone steles with elaborate back-slabs, crowded attendants and fully codified multi-armed iconography, Buddhist and Hindu alike.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Cōḻa bronzes
summary: The lost-wax copper-alloy processional images (utsava-mūrti) of the Tamil country made under the Cōḻas (c. 850–1280), designed to be dressed and carried in festivals; they include the classic Naṭarāja, Somāskanda, Bhikṣāṭana and Kāliyamardana types.

type:LABEL: concept
name: The 108 karaṇas
summary: The 108 units of dance movement defined in the fourth chapter of Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra, carved as series of dance panels on Cōḻa and later Tamil temples, where Śiva is understood as their originator.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Abhaya-mudrā (gesture of fearlessness)
summary: The right hand raised, palm outward, granting protection; the Bṛhat Saṃhitā calls Viṣṇu’s empty hand “peace-giving” (śāntida).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Varada-mudrā (boon-giving gesture)
summary: The hand lowered, palm outward, bestowing boons.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vyākhyāna- / cin-mudrā (teaching gesture)
summary: Thumb and index finger joined in a circle, the other fingers extended, signifying exposition or knowledge; characteristic of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Tribhaṅga (thrice-bent posture)
summary: A standing pose in which the body bends at neck, waist and knee in alternating directions, used for graceful deities, consorts and Kṛṣṇa as flute-player.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Utkuṭikāsana with yogapaṭṭa
summary: A squatting yogic posture with the knees raised and bound by a cloth band (yogapaṭṭa).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Triśūla (trident)
summary: Śiva’s three-pronged spear, also carried by Durgā, Māheśvarī and Īśāna.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śaṅkha (conch)
summary: Viṣṇu’s conch (Pāñcajanya in the epic), held in a left hand; with discus, mace and lotus it defines his twenty-four forms.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Gadā (mace)
summary: Viṣṇu’s mace (Kaumodakī), often personified as the female Gadādevī; also carried by Balarāma, Hanumān and Bhīma.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Paraśu (axe)
summary: The battle-axe held by Śiva in several forms, by Gaṇeśa and by Paraśurāma.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pāśa (noose)
summary: The noose, weapon of Varuṇa, Yama and of the Goddess, binding enemies and the bound soul.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Aṅkuśa (elephant goad)
summary: The elephant goad, held by Gaṇeśa, Indra and the Goddess as Tripurasundarī.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vajra (thunderbolt)
summary: Indra’s thunderbolt, carried also by Aindrī and many tantric deities.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Ḍamaru (hourglass drum)
summary: The small two-headed drum held by Śiva (above all as Naṭarāja), Bhairava and fierce goddesses.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Akṣamālā (rosary)
summary: The rosary of beads held by ascetic and teaching deities such as Brahmā, Sarasvatī, Dakṣiṇāmūrti and the planets.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kamaṇḍalu (water-pot)
summary: The ascetic’s water-pot, the mark of Brahmā and of sages.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śrīvatsa
summary: An auspicious mark on the chest of Viṣṇu (and in Jain images of the Jina), the seat of Śrī; the Bṛhat Saṃhitā prescribes it for both.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śakti / vel (spear)
summary: The lance of Skanda (the Tamil vel) and of Kaumārī.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Western Himalayan timber temple
summary: The wooden and timber-laced stone temples of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, built in the kāṭh-kuṇi technique of alternating timber and stone courses, with tiered pent or pagoda roofs and carved wooden façades.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 258–263: images, pedestals and the liṅga
summary: The block of Matsya Purāṇa chapters on making images of Viṣṇu and Śiva and their forms (Bhairava, Ardhanārīśvara, Umā-Maheśvara and others), on pedestals and on the liṅga, among the oldest Purāṇic iconographic chapters.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Western Kṣatrapas (Kārdamaka line of Caṣṭana)
summary: Śaka rulers of western and central India (Gujarat, Malwa) from the 1st to the 4th century CE, whose dated records use the Śaka era. Rudradāman I of this line issued the Junagadh rock inscription of year 72.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rudradāman I
summary: Mahākṣatrapa of the Western Kṣatrapa (Kārdamaka) line, grandson of Caṣṭana. His Junagadh rock inscription of (Śaka) year 72 = c. 150 CE is the earliest long royal praśasti in Sanskrit.

type:LABEL: person
name: Aśoka (Maurya)
summary: Mauryan emperor (r. c. 268–232 BCE) whose rock edicts at Girnar share a boulder with the inscriptions of Rudradāman and Skandagupta; the Junagadh inscription names him as the king for whom the Yavana Tuṣāspha built conduits on the Sudarśana lake.

type:LABEL: person
name: Samudragupta
summary: Gupta emperor (r. c. 335/350–375 CE), son of Candragupta I and the Licchavi princess Kumāradevī. His conquests are recorded in Hariṣeṇa's praśasti on the Allahabad pillar; his coins include the Garuḍa-standard and aśvamedha types.

type:LABEL: person
name: Hariṣeṇa
summary: Gupta minister (sāndhivigrahika, kumārāmātya, mahādaṇḍanāyaka), son of Dhruvabhūti, who composed the praśasti of Samudragupta inscribed on the Allahabad pillar.

type:LABEL: person
name: Skandagupta
summary: Gupta emperor (r. c. 455–467 CE), son of Kumāragupta I. His Bhitari pillar records the installation of an image of Viṣṇu (Śārṅgin) and battles with the Hūṇas; his Junagadh rock inscription records the repair of the Sudarśana lake (Gupta years 136–138).

type:LABEL: person
name: Parṇadatta
summary: Governor of Surāṣṭra appointed by Skandagupta, named in the Junagadh rock inscription; father of Cakrapālita.

type:LABEL: person
name: Cakrapālita
summary: Son of Parṇadatta and officer at Girinagara (Junagadh) who repaired the Sudarśana lake embankment after it burst in Gupta year 136 and, according to Fleet's reading, built a temple of Viṣṇu (Cakrabhṛt) in year 138.

type:LABEL: person
name: Uditācārya
summary: Māheśvara (Pāśupata) teacher who in Gupta year 61 (380 CE) installed two liṅgas named after his teachers, Upamiteśvara and Kapileśvara, at Mathurā. The record counts him tenth in descent from Kuśika.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kadamba dynasty (Banavāsi)
summary: Dynasty of the western Deccan (4th–6th century CE) with its capital at Vaijayantī (Banavāsi); its founding legend, the brahmin Mayūraśarman turning warrior after a quarrel at the Pallava capital, is told in the Tāḷagunda inscription.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mayūraśarman
summary: Founder of the Kadamba dynasty as the Tāḷagunda inscription tells it: a brahmin of the Kadamba family who went to the Pallava capital to study, was humiliated in a quarrel with a Pallava horseman and took up arms.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śāntivarman (Kadamba)
summary: Kadamba king in whose reign the poet Kubja engraved the Tāḷagunda pillar praśasti; grandson of Kākusthavarman.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kubja (poet of Tāḷagunda)
summary: Poet who composed and engraved ("lilekha") the Tāḷagunda praśasti of the Kadambas under Śāntivarman.

type:LABEL: person
name: Parameśvaravarman I (Pallava)
summary: Pallava king (r. c. 670–695 CE) in whose time the Kūram copper plates were issued for a Śiva temple at Kūram; the grant provides for recitation of the Bhārata.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sundara Cōḻa (Parāntaka II)
summary: Cōḻa king (r. c. 957–970 CE), father of Rājarāja I; the Anbil copper plates were issued in his fourth regnal year.

type:LABEL: site
name: Girnar rock (Junagadh) — Aśokan rock with Rudradāman and Skandagupta inscriptions
summary: Granite boulder at the foot of Girnar near Junagadh, Gujarat, carrying Aśoka's fourteen rock edicts, the Sanskrit praśasti of Rudradāman (c. 150 CE) and the record of Skandagupta (455–458 CE), all three linked to the Sudarśana reservoir.

type:LABEL: site
name: Bhitari (Ghazipur district)
summary: Village in Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh, with Skandagupta's inscribed pillar and Gupta-period brick remains; a seal of Kumāragupta II was also found here.

type:LABEL: site
name: Bilsad (Etah district)
summary: Village in Etah district, Uttar Pradesh, where two inscribed pillars of Gupta year 96 record works at a temple of Svāmi-Mahāsena (Kārttikeya).

type:LABEL: site
name: Tāḷagunda (Sthānakuṇḍūra)
summary: Village in Shikaripura taluk, Shivamogga district, Karnataka, ancient Sthānakuṇḍūra, with the Praṇaveśvara temple and the 5th-century Kadamba pillar inscription.

type:LABEL: site
name: Uttaramērūr
summary: Brahmin village (caturvedimaṅgalam) in Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, whose temple walls carry Pallava and Cōḻa inscriptions, including the assembly (sabhā) regulations of Parāntaka I's 12th and 14th years.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradāman I (year 72)
aliases: Girnar inscription of Rudradaman|Junagarh rock inscription
summary: Sanskrit prose praśasti cut on the Girnar rock in (Śaka) year 72, c. 150 CE, recording the repair of the Sudarśana lake after a storm. It recalls that the lake was made by Puṣyagupta, provincial governor of Candragupta Maurya, and given conduits by the Yavana Tuṣāspha for Aśoka. It is the earliest long royal record composed in Sanskrit.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Allahabad pillar praśasti of Samudragupta
summary: Sanskrit praśasti in verse and prose by Hariṣeṇa, cut on an Aśokan pillar now in the Allahabad Fort, listing Samudragupta's conquests in Āryāvarta, the Deccan and the frontiers. It compares the king to Dhanada (Kubera), Varuṇa, Indra and Antaka (Yama) and likens his fame to the Gaṅgā released from Paśupati's matted locks.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Bhitari pillar inscription of Skandagupta
summary: Sanskrit inscription on a sandstone pillar at Bhitari recording that Skandagupta installed an image of Śārṅgin (Viṣṇu bearing the bow Śārṅga) and granted the village to it. It also alludes to his fight with the Hūṇas and gives the Gupta genealogy, calling Kumāragupta I a parama-bhāgavata.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Junagadh rock inscription of Skandagupta (Gupta years 136–138)
summary: Sanskrit verse inscription on the Girnar rock recording that the Sudarśana lake burst in Gupta year 136 (455/456 CE) and was repaired by Cakrapālita, son of the governor Parṇadatta, under Skandagupta. It opens by praising Viṣṇu, who took back Śrī from Bali for the sake of Indra — the Vāmana story.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Mathurā pilaster inscription of Candragupta II (Gupta year 61)
aliases: Mathura Lakulisha pilaster inscription|Mathura pillar inscription of Chandragupta II
summary: Inscription dated Gupta year 61 (380 CE), in the fifth regnal year of Candragupta II, son of Samudragupta. It records that the Māheśvara teacher Uditācārya, tenth in descent from Kuśika, installed liṅgas named Upamiteśvara and Kapileśvara in a shrine of his teachers. The earliest dated epigraphic evidence of the Pāśupata teacher lineage.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Bilsad pillar inscription of Kumāragupta I (Gupta year 96)
summary: Inscription of Gupta year 96 (415/416 CE), in the reign of Kumāragupta I, recording works by Dhruvaśarman at the temple (āyatana) of Svāmi-Mahāsena, called brahmaṇya-deva — the god Kārttikeya/Skanda. One of the earliest dated records of a Skanda temple.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Tāḷagunda pillar inscription of the time of Śāntivarman (Kadamba)
aliases: Talagunda inscription|Talgunda pillar inscription of Kakusthavarman
summary: Sanskrit verse praśasti composed and engraved by Kubja under the Kadamba king Śāntivarman, at the Śiva shrine of Sthānakuṇḍūra. It tells how the brahmin Mayūraśarman went with his teacher Vīraśarman to the Pallava capital to study, was angered by a quarrel with a Pallava horseman, and took up the warrior's life in this Kali age.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Kūram copper plates of Parameśvaravarman I
summary: Pallava copper-plate grant of Parameśvaravarman I for a Śiva temple (Vidyāvinīta-Pallava-Parameśvara-gṛha) at Kūram near Kanchipuram. It is often cited because the grant also provides for the recitation (vācana) of the Bhārata at the temple.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Kasakudi copper plates of Nandivarman II Pallavamalla
summary: Pallava copper-plate grant of Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, edited by Hultzsch as SII II no. 73. Its Sanskrit portion traces the Pallava line back through Aśvatthāman, Droṇa and Bharadvāja to Bṛhaspati, Aṅgiras and Brahmā — an epic genealogy claimed by a historical dynasty.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Velurpalaiyam copper plates of Nandivarman III
summary: Pallava grant of Nandivarman III (9th century), SII II no. 98. Its genealogy attributes to the ancestor Vīrakūrca a marriage with a Nāga princess; the editor notes that the Rāyakōṭa plates tell the same of Aśvatthāman himself and compares Arjuna's Nāga marriage in the Mahābhārata.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Tiruvālaṅkāṭu copper plates of Rājendra I (regnal year 6)
summary: Cōḻa copper-plate charter of Rājendra I, issued in his sixth regnal year (c. 1018 CE). Its long Sanskrit praśasti traces the Cōḻa line back through solar kings — Manu, Ikṣvāku, Śibi and others — to the Sun: a mythic genealogy placed in a royal title deed.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Anbil copper plates of Sundara Cōḻa (regnal year 4)
summary: Copper-plate grant of the Cōḻa king Sundara Cōḻa (Parāntaka II) of his fourth regnal year (c. 961 CE), edited by T. A. Gopinatha Rao in EI XV. Like the later Tiruvālaṅkāṭu plates, its Sanskrit praśasti gives the Cōḻas a Purāṇic solar ancestry.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Uttaramērūr assembly (sabhā) inscriptions of Parāntaka I (regnal years 12 and 14)
summary: Tamil inscriptions on the Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple at Uttaramērūr recording the rules by which the brahmin assembly chose its committees by lot (kuḍavōlai, the "pot-ticket" system), with qualifications and disqualifications of members, in the 12th and 14th years of Parāntaka I (c. 919 and 921 CE).

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Lakṣmaṇa temple inscription of Yaśovarman, Khajuraho (Vikrama 1011)
summary: Sanskrit inscription on a slab in the porch of the Lakṣmaṇa temple, Khajuraho, dated Vikrama 1011 (953/954 CE). It records that the Candela Yaśovarman built a temple of Vaikuṇṭha (Viṣṇu) whose image had come from the Bhoṭa (Tibetan) region via the Śāhi king of Kīra and the Pratīhāra Herambapāla.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Belur consecration inscription of Viṣṇuvardhana (Śaka 1039 = 1117 CE)
summary: Hoysaḷa record at the Cennakeśava temple, Belur, which dates the consecration of the god Vijayanārāyaṇa (Cennakeśava) by Viṣṇuvardhana to 1117 CE. It is the anchor for dating the temple.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Mahākūṭa pillar inscription of Maṅgaleśa
summary: Sanskrit inscription on a pillar from the Mahākūṭa temple complex near Bādāmi, recording Maṅgaleśa's grant to the god Makuṭeśvaranātha (Śiva) and the conquests of the early Cālukyas. Usually dated c. 595–602 CE. The pillar was removed to the Bijapur museum.

type:LABEL: institution
name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
summary: Encyclopaedic art museum in New York whose Department of Asian Art holds South and Southeast Asian sculpture, bronzes and paintings; its Open Access programme releases public-domain object images under CC0.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Art Institute of Chicago
summary: Art museum in Chicago with a major collection of Indian, Himalayan and Southeast Asian sculpture and painting; collection data and public-domain images are released under CC0 through its public API.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Victoria and Albert Museum, London
summary: Museum of art and design in London whose South Asian collection includes folios from Akbar's Persian Mahābhārata (Razmnāma) and Harivaṃśa, Pahari paintings and Hoysaḷa sculpture.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Government Museum, Chennai
summary: State museum of Tamil Nadu (founded 1851), holding Pallava and Cōḻa copper-plate charters and one of the largest collections of Cōḻa bronzes.

type:LABEL: institution
name: National Museum of Cambodia, Phnom Penh
summary: Cambodia's national museum of Khmer art (opened 1920), holding the Phnom Da sculptures (Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa Govardhana, Balarāma, Rāma) and the Harihara of Prasat Andet.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Bangkok National Museum
summary: Thailand's principal museum of art and archaeology, holding the Sdok Kak Thom stele (K. 235), moved to Bangkok in the 1920s and damaged in a 1960 fire.

type:LABEL: institution
name: National Museum of Vietnamese History, Hanoi
summary: Vietnam's national history museum, holding the Võ Cạnh stele (a national treasure since 2013) and Cham sculpture.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Museum of Islamic Art, Doha
summary: Qatar's museum of Islamic art, which holds the illustrated Persian Rāmāyaṇa made for Akbar's mother Ḥamīda Bānū Begum.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II Museum, City Palace, Jaipur
summary: Museum of the former Jaipur royal collection, holding Akbar's imperial copies of the Razmnāma (c. 1584–86) and the Persian Rāmāyaṇa (1588–91).

type:LABEL: institution
name: Freer Gallery of Art (National Museum of Asian Art), Washington
summary: Smithsonian museum of Asian art holding the "Freer Rāmāyaṇa", the Persian Rāmāyaṇa illustrated for ʿAbd al-Raḥīm Khān-i Khānān (c. 1597–1605).

type:LABEL: institution
name: Allahabad Museum (Prayagraj)
summary: Museum in Prayagraj holding terracottas and sculpture from Kauśāmbī and the surrounding region, and a Gupta and Kuṣāṇa collection.

type:LABEL: institution
name: University of Allahabad, Department of Ancient History, Culture and Archaeology
summary: University department that excavated Kauśāmbī (1949–1960s) under G. R. Sharma.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Museum für Asiatische Kunst, Berlin (formerly Museum für Indische Kunst)
summary: Berlin state museum of Asian art whose predecessor, the Museum für Indische Kunst, excavated Sonkh near Mathurā (1966–74) under Herbert Härtel.

type:LABEL: institution
name: École française d'Extrême-Orient (EFEO)
summary: French research institute (founded 1900) responsible for most early epigraphic and archaeological work in Cambodia, Vietnam and Laos, including the K- and C-number inventories of Khmer and Cham inscriptions and the excavation of Oc Eo.

type:LABEL: institution
name: DHARMA project (ERC) / Dharmalekha
summary: European Research Council project "The Domestication of Hindu Asceticism and the Religious Making of South and Southeast Asia" (2019–2025), which publishes digital critical editions of South and Southeast Asian inscriptions as Dharmalekha, incorporating the SIDDHAM Gupta-period corpus.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kutai (Mūlavarman's kingdom), East Borneo
summary: Early kingdom on the Mahakam river in East Kalimantan known only from the yūpa inscriptions of Mūlavarman (c. 400 CE), the earliest Sanskrit inscriptions of the Indonesian archipelago. The name "Kutai Martadipura" is a later convention.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mūlavarman
summary: King in East Borneo, son of Aśvavarman and grandson of Kuṇḍuṅga, whose sacrifices and gifts to brahmins are commemorated on stone sacrificial posts (yūpa) found at Muara Kaman.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kuṇḍuṅga
summary: Grandfather of Mūlavarman named in the Kutai yūpa inscriptions; his non-Sanskrit name, beside the Sanskrit names of his son Aśvavarman and grandson, is often read as a sign of local adoption of Indic court culture.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Tārumānagara (West Java)
summary: Kingdom of West Java known from the Sanskrit rock and boulder inscriptions of Pūrṇavarman (Ciaruteun, Tugu, Kebon Kopi, Jambu and others), dated by palaeography to the 5th century CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Pūrṇavarman
summary: King of Tārumānagara in West Java (5th century CE) whose inscriptions compare his footprints to Viṣṇu's and record the digging of the Candrabhāgā and Gomatī channels in his 22nd regnal year.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sañjaya (king of Mataram, Java)
summary: King of Central Java who in Śaka 654 (732 CE) established a liṅga on the hill Sthirāṃśa, according to the Canggal (Gunung Wukir) inscription; later Javanese charters count an era from him.

type:LABEL: person
name: Gajayāna (Limva) of Kāñjuruhan
summary: King of Kāñjuruhan in East Java, son of Devasiṃha, who in Śaka 682 (760 CE) had a black-stone image of the sage Agastya made to replace an ancestral image of cedar wood, according to the Dinoyo (Kanjuruhan) charter.

type:LABEL: person
name: Udayādityavarman II
summary: Khmer king (r. 1050–1066) in whose reign the Sdok Kak Thom stele (Śaka 974) was set up; builder of the Baphuon.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jayavarman II (Khmer)
summary: Khmer king (c. 770/790–835) presented by the Sdok Kak Thom stele as the founder of royal sovereignty independent of "Java", consecrated on Mahendraparvata (Phnom Kulen) with the devarāja ritual of the brahmin Hiraṇyadāma.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śivakaivalya
summary: Chaplain (purohita) of Jayavarman II and first member of the priestly family whose nine generations of service to the devarāja the Sdok Kak Thom stele records.

type:LABEL: person
name: Devānīka
summary: King ("supreme king of kings") of the Vat Phu region named in the 5th-century stele of Vat Luang Kau (K. 365), who founded a tīrtha called the "new Kurukṣetra" with sacrifices and gifts of cows.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhadravarman I (Champa)
summary: Early king of Champa who founded the god Bhadreśvara (a Śiva named after himself) at Mỹ Sơn and endowed it with land, according to his Sanskrit stele.

type:LABEL: person
name: Satyavarman (Champa)
summary: King of Champa (Kauṭhāra region) who, according to his stele at Po Nagar, restored the temple and its mukhaliṅga after seaborne raiders damaged it in the 770s.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Funan
summary: Chinese name for an early polity of the lower Mekong (c. 1st–6th century CE), associated archaeologically with the port of Oc Eo and the sculpture of Phnom Da. Its own name and extent are uncertain.

type:LABEL: site
name: Muara Kaman (Kutai), East Kalimantan
summary: Riverside site on the Mahakam in Kutai Kartanegara regency, East Kalimantan, where the yūpa inscriptions of Mūlavarman were found.

type:LABEL: site
name: Ciaruteun (Bogor), West Java
summary: Inscribed boulder site at the confluence of the Cisadane, Cianten and Ciaruteun rivers near Bogor, where Pūrṇavarman's footprint inscription stands in situ.

type:LABEL: site
name: Tugu (Koja, North Jakarta)
summary: Findspot of Pūrṇavarman's Tugu boulder inscription in the Batutumbuh hamlet of Tugu, North Jakarta.

type:LABEL: site
name: Gunung Wukir (Canggal), Central Java
summary: Hill in Magelang regency, Central Java, with the ruins of a Śaiva temple (Candi Gunung Wukir) where the Canggal inscription of Sañjaya (732 CE) was found.

type:LABEL: site
name: Dinoyo (Malang), East Java
summary: Findspot near Malang of the Kanjuruhan charter (760 CE), associated with the nearby Candi Badut.

type:LABEL: site
name: Prasat Sdok Kak Thom (Sa Kaeo, Thailand)
summary: Khmer temple ruin in Khok Sung district, Sa Kaeo province, Thailand, findspot of the Sdok Kak Thom stele (K. 235).

type:LABEL: site
name: Vat Luang Kau (Champasak), near Vat Phu
summary: Village site on the Mekong near Vat Phu in southern Laos, findspot of the 5th-century stele of Devānīka (K. 365) and an early walled settlement.

type:LABEL: site
name: Võ Cạnh (Nha Trang)
summary: Village about 4 km from Nha Trang, Khánh Hòa province, Vietnam, where the Võ Cạnh stele was discovered in 1885.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Yūpa inscriptions of Mūlavarman (Kutai, East Borneo)
summary: Seven stone posts in the form of Vedic sacrificial stakes (yūpa), inscribed in Sanskrit verse, commemorating King Mūlavarman's sacrifices and gifts to brahmins (including a gift of many thousands of cows) and naming his father Aśvavarman and grandfather Kuṇḍuṅga. They are the oldest Sanskrit inscriptions of the Indonesian archipelago.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Ciaruteun inscription of Pūrṇavarman
summary: Four-line Sanskrit verse (anuṣṭubh) on a boulder near Bogor beside a carved pair of footprints, declaring them the footprints of Pūrṇavarman, lord of Tārumā, like those of Viṣṇu — an image of the god's three strides applied to a king's claim to the land.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Tugu inscription of Pūrṇavarman
summary: Five-line Sanskrit verse inscription on an egg-shaped boulder from North Jakarta recording that in Pūrṇavarman's 22nd regnal year the Candrabhāgā and Gomatī channels were dug, and that brahmins received a gift of 1,000 cows. The river names echo rivers of the Indian Purāṇic geography.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Canggal (Gunung Wukir) inscription of Sañjaya (Śaka 654 = 732 CE)
summary: Sanskrit stele dated Monday, Kārttika śukla 13, Śaka 654 (732 CE), recording that King Sañjaya established a liṅga on the hill called Sthirāṃśa, with verses to Śiva (Bhava), whose crest bears the moon and the Gaṅgā. It is the earliest dated inscription of the Mataram kingdom of Central Java.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Dinoyo (Kanjuruhan) charter of Gajayāna (Śaka 682 = 760 CE)
summary: Sanskrit charter dated Śaka 682 (760 CE), the oldest dated inscription of East Java. King Gajayāna of Kāñjuruhan, devoted to the "pot-born" sage Agastya, replaced an ancestral cedar-wood image of Agastya with one of black stone and had a temple for it built.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Sdok Kak Thom stele (K. 235), Śaka 974
summary: Bilingual stele of Śaka 974 (1052/1053 CE) under Udayādityavarman II, tracing nine generations of the Śivakaivalya priestly family who served the devarāja (Old Khmer kamraten jagat ta rāja) from the time of Jayavarman II. It says the brahmin Hiraṇyadāma performed rites so that Kambuja would no longer depend on "Java", and that Jayavarman II was established on Mahendraparvata. It is the principal source for the devarāja cult and for Jayavarman II.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The devarāja was a cult of the deified Khmer king
summary: The older reading of the Sdok Kak Thom stele, associated with Cœdès, took the devarāja ("god-king") as a cult identifying the king with Śiva through a royal liṅga. Later scholars (e.g. Hermann Kulke; Kamaleswar Bhattacharya) read kamraten jagat ta rāja as a movable protective image — "the god who is king" — tended by one priestly family, not a deification of the ruler.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Vat Luang Kau stele of Devānīka (K. 365): the "new Kurukṣetra"
summary: Fifth-century Sanskrit stele from near Vat Phu, Laos, in which King Devānīka founds a great tīrtha named Kurukṣetra — "the new Kurukṣetra" — so that the merit of bathing at the Indian Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa and Puṣkara may be gained there. It compares the king to Yudhiṣṭhira in dharma, Dhanañjaya (Arjuna) in victory and Śibi in generosity, and quotes verses in praise of Kurukṣetra of the kind found in the Mahābhārata's tīrtha chapters.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Mỹ Sơn stele of Bhadravarman I (C. 72)
summary: Sanskrit stele from group A at Mỹ Sơn recording that King Bhadravarman, blessed by the feet of the Lord Bhadreśvara, gave a permanent endowment of land with its cultivators to the god Bhadreśvara, with boundaries given by mountains and the great river. It opens with homage to Maheśvara, Umā, Agni, Brahmā and Viṣṇu and the five elements. It is the founding record of the Mỹ Sơn sanctuary.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Po Nagar stele of Satyavarman (781/784 CE)
summary: Sanskrit record of King Satyavarman at Po Nagar, Nha Trang, reporting that seaborne raiders had damaged the temple and carried off and broken its mukhaliṅga, and that the king restored the temple and re-established the liṅga (781; restoration completed 784).

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Võ Cạnh stele
summary: Sanskrit stele found in 1885 near Nha Trang, naming a royal line descended from Śrī Māra. Often called the earliest Sanskrit inscription of Southeast Asia, it is dated by some to the 2nd–3rd century CE and by others (e.g. Sircar, Zakharov) to the 4th century or later.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Võ Cạnh stele is the earliest Sanskrit inscription in Southeast Asia (2nd–3rd century CE)
summary: Claim resting on an early palaeographic dating; disputed by scholars who date the text to the 4th century or later on grounds of metre and vocabulary.

type:LABEL: person
name: Candragupta I
summary: Gupta king (r. c. 319–335/350 CE), father of Samudragupta by the Licchavi princess Kumāradevī; the Gupta era of 319/320 CE is often associated with his accession.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kumāradevī
summary: Licchavi princess, queen of Candragupta I and mother of Samudragupta, who is called "Licchavi-dauhitra" (daughter's son of the Licchavis) in the Allahabad praśasti and on Gupta coins and seals.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Standard-type gold coins of Samudragupta (Garuḍa standard)
summary: The commonest gold type of Samudragupta: the king, haloed, sacrifices at an altar holding a standard, with a Garuḍa standard (garuḍadhvaja) beside him; the reverse goddess on a throne with cornucopia is copied from the late Kuṣāṇa Ardochsho type. Allan reads the Garuḍa standard as the emblem of Viṣṇu and the Gupta seal.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Aśvamedha-type gold coins of Samudragupta
summary: Rare gold coins commemorating Samudragupta's horse sacrifice: the obverse shows the sacrificial horse before a decorated sacrificial post (yūpa); the reverse a queen holding a fly-whisk, whom Allan identifies as the chief queen who took part in the rite.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Candragupta I–Kumāradevī type gold coins
aliases: King and Queen type|Candragupta I type
summary: Gold coins showing Candragupta I offering a ring or bracelet to Queen Kumāradevī, with the legend "Licchavayaḥ" on the reverse and a goddess seated on a lion. Allan thought they were struck by Samudragupta to commemorate his parents; he identified the goddess as probably Lakṣmī, or Mahādevī (Durgā), whose vehicle is the lion.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: King-and-Lakṣmī type gold coins of Skandagupta
summary: Gold type of Skandagupta, formerly called the "King and Queen" type: the king stands holding a bow, facing a female figure Allan identifies as Lakṣmī, with a Garuḍa standard between them.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Aśvamedha-type gold coins of Kumāragupta I
summary: Gold coins of Kumāragupta I modelled on Samudragupta's aśvamedha type, with a saddled horse and, on the reverse, a queen holding a fly-whisk and a ceremonial spear.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Huviṣka's gold coins with Skanda, Kumāra, Viśākha and Mahāsena
summary: Gold coins of the Kuṣāṇa king Huviṣka (c. 150–180/190 CE) naming in Bactrian Greek script the war gods Skando, Komaro, Bizago (Viśākha) and Maaseno (Mahāsena), sometimes together — the earliest coin images of the Skanda–Kārttikeya group, which replaced the Iranian war god Orlagno on his coinage.

type:LABEL: person
name: Huviṣka
summary: Kuṣāṇa emperor (c. 150–180/190 CE), successor of Kaniṣka I, whose gold coinage displays the widest range of deities of any Kuṣāṇa ruler, including Indian (Skanda, Viśākha, Mahāsena, Oesho, Ommo), Iranian and Greek gods.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gold coin of the Kuṣāṇa king Vāsudeva I (Cleveland 1999.226)
summary: Gold coin of Vāsudeva I, the last great Kuṣāṇa emperor, with the king's portrait on the obverse and a deity on the reverse; on Vāsudeva's coinage this is predominantly Oesho with the bull.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vāsudeva I (Kuṣāṇa)
summary: Kuṣāṇa emperor (c. 190–230 CE), successor of Huviṣka; the first Kuṣāṇa ruler with an Indian name, whose coins almost always show Oesho with the bull Nandi. Not to be confused with the deity Vāsudeva.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Yaudheyas
summary: Republican (gaṇa) people of the eastern Punjab and Haryana, known from Pāṇini, from coins proclaiming "victory to the Yaudheya gaṇa", from Rudradāman's Junagadh inscription (which boasts of defeating them) and from Samudragupta's Allahabad list. Their coins make Kārttikeya their tutelary god.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Yaudheya coins with Kārttikeya (Brahmaṇyadeva)
summary: Copper coins of the Yaudheya republic showing Kārttikeya standing with a spear, often with a peacock, including a six-headed (ṣaṇmukha) form of the 1st–2nd century CE; other issues carry the legend "yaudheya-gaṇasya jaya". Allan's British Museum catalogue (1936) records issues naming the god as Brahmaṇyadeva Kumāra.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Audumbaras
summary: People of the Pathankot–Kangra region of the Punjab hills who issued coins from about the 1st century BCE, including issues of the king Dharaghoṣa and issues in the name of Mahādeva (Śiva).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Audumbara coin of Dharaghoṣa with Viśvāmitra
summary: Silver coin of the Audumbara king Dharaghoṣa (c. 100 BCE) in Indo-Greek style: a standing ascetic figure labelled with the name of the sage Viśvāmitra, with a bilingual Kharoṣṭhī and Brāhmī legend; the reverse shows a trident-battle-axe and a tree in a railing.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Audumbara coins in the name of Mahādeva (Śiva)
summary: Audumbara coins of about the 1st century BCE issued in the name of Mahādeva (Śiva), with a bull on one side and an elephant with a trident on the other; a related Audumbara type shows a pillared shrine with a trident standard, often read as an early depiction of a Śiva temple.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Durgā slaying the buffalo demon, Kuṣāṇa terracotta from Mathurā (AIC 1985.1108)
summary: Small molded terracotta of the goddess killing the buffalo demon, attributed to Kuṣāṇa Mathurā in the 2nd century CE. It belongs to the earliest group of Mahiṣāsuramardinī images, in which the goddess presses or lifts the buffalo itself — centuries before the Devī Māhātmya gave the myth its classic form.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kārttikeya holding a spear, Kuṣāṇa Mathurā (AIC 1985.1037)
summary: Spotted red sandstone figure of the war god Kārttikeya (Skanda) holding a spear, carved at Mathurā in the 2nd century CE — contemporary with Huviṣka's coins naming Skanda, Kumāra, Viśākha and Mahāsena.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Two-armed Gaṇeśa holding a bowl of sweets, Mathurā (AIC 2021.245)
summary: Small two-armed elephant-headed god holding a bowl of sweets, from Mathurā, attributed to the 3rd–4th century CE. Images of this simple Mathurā type are among the earliest representations of Gaṇeśa, before he appears with Purāṇic narrative or a fixed name in inscriptions.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Liṅga with face of Śiva (ekamukhaliṅga), Gupta, Madhya Pradesh (Met 1987.142.323)
summary: Small sandstone liṅga carrying a single face of Śiva, of the type also seen at Udayagiri (Cave 4) in the early 5th century: an aniconic emblem and an anthropomorphic face combined.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Standing four-armed Viṣṇu, Gupta terracotta, Uttar Pradesh (Met 1987.142.293)
summary: Terracotta four-armed Viṣṇu of the Gupta period, an example of the small-scale, probably domestic or shrine images that accompanied the stone cult images of Udayagiri and Deogarh.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kṛṣṇa killing the horse demon Keśī, Gupta terracotta (Met 1991.300)
summary: Large Gupta terracotta relief, probably from a brick temple frieze, showing the youthful Kṛṣṇa thrusting his arm into the mouth of the horse demon Keśī — an episode of the Harivaṃśa and Bhāgavata cycles of Kṛṣṇa's youth.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Head of Viṣṇu from Vidiśā (Cleveland 1969.57)
summary: Near life-size head from a 4th-century image of Viṣṇu from the Vidiśā region, with a lion head at the centre of the crown — an emblem of royal authority that the museum relates to Gupta imagery of Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Viṣṇu, Gupta period (Cleveland 1976.75)
summary: Sandstone Viṣṇu of the late 5th century, once four-armed, in the restrained Gupta style of central India.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Standing Viṣṇu, late Gupta, Mathurā (Cleveland 1963.580)
summary: Red sandstone standing Viṣṇu from Mathurā of the late 6th century, at the end of the Gupta sculptural tradition of the city that produced the first Vaiṣṇava images.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: River goddess Gaṅgā, Mathurā (Cleveland 1966.119)
summary: Figure of the river goddess Gaṅgā of about 700 from Mathurā, of the kind placed with Yamunā on temple door-jambs from the Gupta period onward to purify those entering the sanctum.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kārttikeya, Kashmir (Cleveland 1974.75)
summary: Stone image of Kārttikeya attributed to 5th-century Kashmir, contemporary with the Bilsad record of a Mahāsena temple (415/416 CE) and Kumāragupta I's peacock coins.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Durgā slaying the buffalo demon, Madhya Pradesh (AIC 2006.187)
summary: Sixth-century central Indian Mahiṣāsuramardinī, from the period when the Devī Māhātmya was taking shape (a verse of it is quoted on stone in 608 CE).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Durgā slaying the buffalo demon, Pāla period, Bihar (Met 91.21)
summary: Black-schist Mahiṣāsuramardinī of the Pāla period from Bihar, in the developed iconography in which the demon emerges in human form from the decapitated buffalo.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Durgā Mahiṣāsuramardinī, Hoysaḷa period, southern Karnataka (V&A IS.77-1965)
summary: Eight-armed Durgā piercing the buffalo demon with her trident, carved in southern Karnataka in the mid-13th century in the ornate Hoysaḷa manner; the V&A identifies the weapons as arrow, discus, sword and trident on the right, bow, bell and shield on the left.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gaja-Lakṣmī, Kashmir (Met 1993.194)
summary: Sixth-century Kashmiri image of Lakṣmī lustrated by elephants (Gaja-Lakṣmī), a motif that goes back to the early Buddhist railings of Bharhut and Sanchi and to Gupta-period coin and seal imagery.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Standing Pārvatī, Cōḻa bronze (Met 57.51.3)
summary: Early Cōḻa processional bronze of Pārvatī (Umā), probably once the consort of a Śiva image, from the first quarter of the 10th century.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Śiva, Pārvatī and their son Skanda (Somāskandamūrti), Cōḻa bronze (Met 1982.220.10)
summary: Cōḻa bronze of the Somāskanda group — Śiva seated with Umā and the child Skanda — the family image that Pallava and Cōḻa temples placed behind the liṅga and carried in procession.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Śiva and Umā seated with Skanda (Somāskanda), Vijayanagara bronze (AIC 1966.334)
summary: Vijayanagara-period Somāskanda bronze of about 1400, showing the continuity of the Cōḻa family-image type into the later medieval Tamil country.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Hanumān conversing, Cōḻa bronze (Met 1982.220.9)
summary: Cōḻa bronze of Hanumān with his hand raised to his mouth in speech, a figure type that belonged with processional groups of Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa in Tamil temples.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kṛṣṇa dancing on the serpent Kāliya, Vijayanagara bronze (AIC 1995.62)
summary: South Indian bronze of the child Kṛṣṇa dancing on the hood of the serpent Kāliya (Kāliyadamana).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Varāha lifting the Earth goddess, Rajasthan (AIC 1997.707)
summary: Eleventh-century Rajasthani image of the boar-headed Varāha raising the Earth goddess, the iconographic type first monumentalised at Udayagiri (c. 401–415 CE) and Eran (c. 510).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Viṣṇu attended by Cakrapuruṣa and Śaṅkhapuruṣa, Pāla bronze (Cleveland 1964.453)
summary: Pāla-period bronze of Viṣṇu flanked by the personified discus and conch (Cakrapuruṣa and Śaṅkhapuruṣa), a Gupta-period convention continued in eastern India.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: One-faced liṅga, Pāla Bihar (Cleveland 1973.73)
summary: Chloritic schist ekamukhaliṅga from Bihar of the 7th–8th century.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Standing Viṣṇu as Keśava, Hoysaḷa (Met 18.41)
summary: Hoysaḷa image of Viṣṇu as Keśava, which the Met attributes probably to Belur in the first quarter of the 12th century — the period of Viṣṇuvardhana's Cennakeśava temple consecrated in 1117.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Harihara, pre-Angkorian Cambodia or Vietnam (Met 1977.241)
summary: Pre-Angkorian Harihara — Śiva and Viṣṇu combined in one body, Śiva's matted locks on one side of the head and Viṣṇu's mitre on the other — a form especially favoured in 7th-century Cambodia.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Standing Gaṇeśa, pre-Angkorian Cambodia (Met 1982.220.7)
summary: Pre-Angkorian standing Gaṇeśa of the later 7th century.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gaṇeśa, southern Cambodia or Vietnam (Cleveland 1987.147)
summary: Seventh-century sandstone Gaṇeśa, which the museum describes as among the first Hindu deities venerated in large-scale stone sculpture in Southeast Asia.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Durgā slaying the buffalo demon, Angkor period (AIC 1996.32)
summary: Angkor-period Mahiṣāsuramardinī, evidence of the Goddess's buffalo-slaying form in Khmer sculpture.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Eight-armed Viṣṇu from Phnom Da (National Museum of Cambodia)
summary: Colossal eight-armed standing Viṣṇu found at Phnom Da (Angkor Borei), the principal image of the Phnom Da group of the 6th–7th century, now in the National Museum of Cambodia, Phnom Penh. With the Kṛṣṇa Govardhana in Cleveland it is a key early Vaiṣṇava image of the Mekong delta.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Harihara of Prasat Andet (National Museum of Cambodia)
summary: Sandstone Harihara found at Prasat Andet (Kampong Thom province), regarded as one of the finest pre-Angkorian sculptures (late 7th century), now in the National Museum of Cambodia.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gaṅgā and Yamunā terracottas from Ahichchhatra (National Museum, New Delhi)
summary: Large terracotta figures of Gaṅgā on her makara and Yamunā on her tortoise, excavated in 1940–44 at the Śiva temple mound of Ahichchhatra and now in the National Museum, New Delhi; among the earliest monumental river-goddess figures, of the 5th century CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: G. R. Sharma
summary: Indian archaeologist (1919–1986) of the University of Allahabad who excavated Kauśāmbī from 1949 and published the 1957–59 seasons; his reading of a brick structure there as a Vedic "śyenaciti" fire altar is contested.

type:LABEL: person
name: J. P. Joshi
summary: Indian archaeologist (ASI; Director General 1987–1990) who excavated Bhagwanpura in Haryana in 1975–76, documenting an overlap of Late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware occupation.

type:LABEL: person
name: Herbert Härtel
summary: German Indologist and museum director (1921–2017) of the Museum für Indische Kunst, Berlin, who directed the excavation of Sonkh near Mathurā (1966–1974).

type:LABEL: person
name: Louis Malleret
summary: French archaeologist (1901–1970) of the EFEO who excavated Oc Eo in the Mekong delta in 1944 and published L'Archéologie du delta du Mékong.

type:LABEL: person
name: H. G. Quaritch Wales
summary: British scholar (1900–1981) who surveyed and excavated candi sites in the Bujang Valley, Kedah, in 1936–1940.

type:LABEL: person
name: K. N. Dikshit
summary: Indian archaeologist who co-directed the excavation of Śṛṅgaverapura with B. B. Lal (1977–86).

type:LABEL: person
name: B. R. Mani
summary: Indian archaeologist of the ASI who led the court-ordered excavation at the disputed site in Ayodhya in 2003; he was succeeded during the work by Hari Manjhi.

type:LABEL: site
name: Sonkh (Mathurā district)
summary: Mound c. 24 km south-west of Mathurā excavated by the Museum für Indische Kunst, Berlin, under Herbert Härtel (1966–74). Its occupation runs from Painted Grey Ware levels to the Kuṣāṇa period and includes two apsidal shrines associated with Nāga worship of the Kuṣāṇa period, one of the best-stratified sequences for the region that produced the first Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva images.

type:LABEL: site
name: Śṛṅgaverapura excavations (1977–86)
summary: Excavation by B. B. Lal and K. N. Dikshit at Singraur on the Gaṅgā above Prayagraj, the place traditionally identified with the Rāmāyaṇa's Śṛṅgaverapura where Rāma crossed the river with the help of Guha. The project, part of Lal's survey of "Rāmāyaṇa sites", found occupation from the late 2nd millennium BCE and a large brick tank of the early centuries CE.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Excavations at "Rāmāyaṇa sites" (Ayodhyā, Śṛṅgaverapura, Bharadvāja Āśrama, Nandigrāma, Citrakūṭa) date the epic's setting
summary: B. B. Lal's project "Archaeology of the Rāmāyaṇa Sites" (1975–86) excavated places named in the Rāmāyaṇa and found that their earliest occupation began around the early 1st millennium BCE (or slightly earlier); Lal argued this gives an upper limit for the epic's geography. Critics note that a place-name's age says nothing about the historicity of the narrative.

type:LABEL: site
name: Bhagwanpura (Kurukshetra district)
summary: Small site in Haryana excavated by J. P. Joshi in 1975–76, where Late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware levels overlap — one of the key sites for the transition from the Harappan to the Iron Age Gaṅgā–Yamunā cultures in the region later called Kurukṣetra.

type:LABEL: site
name: Ahichchhatra (Bareilly district)
summary: Large fortified city mound in Bareilly district, Uttar Pradesh, identified with Ahicchatrā, capital of northern Pañcāla in the Mahābhārata. Excavated by the ASI in 1940–44; it yielded Painted Grey Ware and a long early historic sequence, Pañcāla coins and the Gupta-period terracottas of Gaṅgā and Yamunā from a Śiva temple.

type:LABEL: site
name: Kauśāmbī (Kosam)
summary: Great walled city on the Yamunā south-west of Prayagraj, capital of the Vatsas in Buddhist and epic tradition, excavated by G. R. Sharma for the University of Allahabad from 1949. The finds include massive ramparts, the Ghositārāma monastery and a brick structure that Sharma interpreted as a Vedic "falcon" fire altar (śyenaciti) used for a puruṣamedha.

type:LABEL: claim
name: A brick structure at Kauśāmbī is a Vedic falcon altar (śyenaciti) used for a puruṣamedha
summary: G. R. Sharma interpreted a falcon-shaped brick structure by the Kauśāmbī rampart, with skulls and bones, as a śyenaciti altar of the Vedic agnicayana and as evidence of a human sacrifice (puruṣamedha). Most later archaeologists regard the identification and the sacrifice interpretation as unproven.

type:LABEL: site
name: Bujang Valley (Lembah Bujang), Kedah
summary: Archaeological landscape in Kedah, Malaysia, with dozens of brick and laterite shrine (candi) foundations, Hindu and Buddhist sculpture and inscriptions from about the 5th to 14th century, including Candi Bukit Batu Pahat with Śaiva finds. Surveyed by H. G. Quaritch Wales (1936–40) and later Malaysian projects; the Sungai Batu complex has much earlier iron-smelting and jetty remains.

type:LABEL: site
name: Oc Eo (An Giang)
summary: Large early historic port and canal network in the Mekong delta, excavated by Louis Malleret in 1944, associated with the polity the Chinese called Funan (c. 1st–7th century CE). Finds include Indian-style seals, Viṣṇu and Buddha images, gold foils and a Roman gold medallion of Antoninus Pius (dated 152 CE).

type:LABEL: site
name: Ayodhyā: ASI excavation at the disputed site (2003)
summary: Excavation carried out by the Archaeological Survey of India between March and August 2003 on the orders of the Allahabad High Court, beneath and around the site of the Babri Masjid (demolished in 1992). The report described a long occupation sequence and, below the mosque, a large structure with some 50 pillar bases, which it said had features of north Indian temples. The report was contested by other archaeologists and was among the evidence considered by the Supreme Court in its 2019 judgment.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The structure beneath the Babri Masjid excavated in 2003 was a Hindu temple
summary: The ASI's 2003 report concluded that a massive structure with pillar bases, beneath the mosque, had features of north Indian temples of the early medieval period. Critics — including archaeologists who observed the excavation for the Sunni Central Waqf Board and the Aligarh Historians Society — disputed the identification of the "pillar bases", the stratigraphic reading and the omission of animal bones and glazed ware. In 2019 the Supreme Court treated the excavation as showing an underlying structure that was not Islamic, while stating that the report did not establish that a temple had been demolished to build the mosque; it decided the title dispute on other evidence.

type:LABEL: person
name: Akbar (Mughal emperor)
summary: Mughal emperor (r. 1556–1605) who set up a translation bureau (maktab-khāna) and commissioned Persian translations of the Mahābhārata (the Razmnāma, 1584–86) and the Rāmāyaṇa, with imperial illustrated copies.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ḥamīda Bānū Begum
summary: Mother of Akbar (d. 1604) for whom an illustrated copy of the Persian Rāmāyaṇa was made, now in the Museum of Islamic Art, Doha.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jagat Singh I of Mewar
summary: Rāṇā of Mewar (r. 1628–1652) who commissioned the great illustrated Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa of Udaipur (1649–53), painted by Sahib Din, Manohar and an anonymous master.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sahib Din
summary: Mewar court painter (active c. 1628–1655) who led the illustration of several books of Jagat Singh's Rāmāyaṇa (e.g. the Ayodhyākāṇḍa and Yuddhakāṇḍa volumes in the British Library).

type:LABEL: person
name: Manaku
summary: Pahari painter of the Guler family of Pandit Seu (c. 1700–1760), elder brother of Nainsukh, who painted the Gīta Govinda series dated 1730 for a woman patron (Mālinī) in the Basohli style.

type:LABEL: person
name: Banwari the Younger (Banwari Khurd)
summary: Mughal painter credited with the Razmnāma folio of 1598 showing Vyāsa watching his son Śuka approach (V&A IS.121-1955).

type:LABEL: person
name: Kamal, son of Khem (Mughal painter)
summary: Mughal painter whose name is written on the border of the Razmnāma folio "Duryodhana visits Śalya" (V&A CIRC.243-1922) from the copy of c. 1598.

type:LABEL: text
name: Razmnāma (Persian Mahābhārata)
summary: Persian prose translation of the Mahābhārata made at Akbar's order in 1584–86: brahmin scholars explained the Sanskrit, Naqīb Khān drafted the Persian and Faiẓī and others revised it; Abū'l-Faẓl wrote the preface (dated 1588 in the imperial copy). Its illustrated copies are among the masterpieces of Mughal painting.

type:LABEL: text
name: Persian Harivaṃśa (appendix to the Razmnāma)
summary: Persian translation of the Harivaṃśa made at Akbar's court as an appendix to the Razmnāma; an illustrated copy of about 1590, probably made at Lahore, was later dispersed.

type:LABEL: text
name: Persian Rāmāyaṇa of Akbar's court
summary: Persian translation of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa made at Akbar's court in the 1580s (the historian Badāʾūnī was its principal translator). Illustrated copies were made for Akbar (Jaipur), for his mother Ḥamīda Bānū Begum (Doha) and for the courtier ʿAbd al-Raḥīm (the "Freer Rāmāyaṇa").

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Imperial Razmnāma of Akbar (City Palace Museum, Jaipur)
summary: Akbar's own illustrated copy of the Persian Mahābhārata, made c. 1584–86 (preface dated 1588) by imperial painters including Basāwan, Daswanth and Lāl, now in the Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II Museum, Jaipur. It has some 169–176 paintings (counts differ); 147 were reproduced by Hendley in 1883–84.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Razmnāma of 1598–99 (dispersed second copy)
summary: Second illustrated Razmnāma made at the Mughal court in 1598–99 with about 161 paintings, divided in 1921 and dispersed; its last five parts are British Library Or. 12076 and other leaves are in museums including the Victoria and Albert Museum.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Vyāsa watches Śuka approach, Razmnāma folio of 1598 (V&A IS.121-1955)
summary: Page from the 1598 Razmnāma showing the sage Vyāsa with three disciples in his hermitage, watching his son Śuka approach through the air like a ball of fire — an episode of the Śāntiparvan.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Duryodhana visits Śalya, Razmnāma folio (V&A CIRC.243-1922)
summary: Razmnāma page by Kamal showing Duryodhana, with his brothers, at the house of Śalya to ask him to serve as Karṇa's charioteer.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Illustrated Persian Harivaṃśa of c. 1590 (dispersed)
summary: Illustrated Mughal copy of the Persian Harivaṃśa, completed about 1590 (probably at Lahore) and later dispersed; some leaves were given ornate borders for an album, probably in 18th-century Lucknow. The V&A holds six folios.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: The infant Kṛṣṇa uproots the twin arjuna trees, Persian Harivaṃśa folio (V&A IS.2-1970)
summary: Folio from Akbar's Persian Harivaṃśa showing the infant Kṛṣṇa, tied to a mortar, uprooting a pair of giant arjuna trees.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Śiva destroys Andhaka, Persian Harivaṃśa folio (V&A IS.7-1970)
summary: Folio from the same Persian Harivaṃśa showing Śiva destroying the demon Andhaka, who had stolen a flowering creeper from a garden of the gods.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Akbar's imperial Persian Rāmāyaṇa (City Palace Museum, Jaipur)
summary: Imperial illustrated copy of the Persian Rāmāyaṇa made for Akbar (c. 1588–91), kept with the Razmnāma in the former Jaipur royal collection.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Rāmāyaṇa of Ḥamīda Bānū Begum (Museum of Islamic Art, Doha)
summary: Illustrated Persian Rāmāyaṇa made for Akbar's mother Ḥamīda Bānū Begum, completed in 1594, now in the Museum of Islamic Art, Doha (some folios dispersed).

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Freer Rāmāyaṇa of ʿAbd al-Raḥīm Khān-i Khānān
summary: Illustrated Persian Rāmāyaṇa made c. 1597–1605 for the Mughal general and poet ʿAbd al-Raḥīm Khān-i Khānān by painters of his own atelier, now in the Freer Gallery of Art, Washington.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Mewar Rāmāyaṇa of Jagat Singh I (1649–53)
summary: Complete illustrated Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa in seven books painted at Udaipur for Rāṇā Jagat Singh I between 1649 and 1653 in three styles — those of Sahib Din and of Manohar and their studios, and of an anonymous master in a mixed Mewar–Deccani style. Four volumes went to James Tod in 1820 and are now British Library Add MS 15295–15297; the others are in Mumbai (CSMVS) and elsewhere. Digitised by the British Library with CSMVS.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa search in vain for Sītā, Mewar Rāmāyaṇa folio (Met 1974.148)
summary: Folio from a later dispersed Mewar Rāmāyaṇa series (c. 1680–90) showing Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa searching the forest for Sītā after her abduction.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Gīta Govinda of 1730 painted by Manaku
summary: Series of paintings of Jayadeva's Gīta Govinda in the Basohli style, commissioned in 1730 for a lady patron probably named Mālinī and painted by Manaku of Guler; the leaves are dispersed (examples in the V&A).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rādhā's messenger describes Kṛṣṇa with the gopīs, Basohli Gīta Govinda (V&A IM.88-1930)
summary: Spring scene from the 1730 Gīta Govinda: Rādhā is told of Kṛṣṇa's dalliance with the gopīs; iridescent beetle-wing cases imitate emeralds.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs on the bank of the Yamunā, "Tehri Garhwal" Gīta Govinda (Met 2017.736)
summary: Folio from the "second" or "Tehri Garhwal" Gīta Govinda of c. 1775–80, the celebrated Kangra-style series associated with the workshop of Manaku and Nainsukh's sons.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rādhā awaiting reconciliation with Kṛṣṇa, Mewar Gīta Govinda (Cleveland 1990.41)
summary: Mewar Gīta Govinda page in which Rādhā is shown six times as she waits for Kṛṣṇa, preparing a bower and pleading with his picture.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Shangri Rāmāyaṇa (dispersed Pahari series)
summary: Large dispersed Rāmāyaṇa series of about 1690–1725 from the Punjab hills, named after the Shangri branch of the Kulu royal family that owned it; several distinct styles are distinguished (Style II leaves are attributed by the Met to Bahu/Jammu and Mankot). Leaves are in the Cleveland, Metropolitan and other museums.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: King Daśaratha confers with Kaikeyī, Shangri Rāmāyaṇa (Cleveland 1996.361)
summary: Daśaratha, preparing to name Rāma his successor, confers with Kaikeyī.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Ṛśyaśṛṅga addresses the courtesans, Shangri Rāmāyaṇa (Cleveland 2002.6)
summary: The ascetic boy Ṛśyaśṛṅga, who had never seen a woman, meets the courtesans sent to bring him to the drought-stricken kingdom (Bālakāṇḍa).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Śūrpaṇakhā demands vengeance, Shangri Rāmāyaṇa (Cleveland 2018.107)
summary: The mutilated Śūrpaṇakhā before her brother Rāvaṇa, shown with ten crowned heads and twenty arms.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Sītā asks Rāma to fetch the golden deer, Shangri Rāmāyaṇa (Cleveland 2025.7)
summary: Sītā, captivated by the jewelled deer (Mārīca in disguise), begs Rāma to catch it.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa on Mount Pavarasana (Pravarṣaṇa), Shangri Rāmāyaṇa (Met 1999.400)
summary: Style II leaf of the Shangri Rāmāyaṇa: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa waiting out the rains on the mountain while Sugrīva delays (Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Battle of Rāvaṇa and Jaṭāyu, "Burnt" Rāmāyaṇa (Cleveland 2013.306)
summary: Folio from the fire-damaged "Burnt" Rāmāyaṇa of Bundelkhand (c. 1605), illustrating Araṇyakāṇḍa chapters 50–51 of Vālmīki: the vulture Jaṭāyu fights Rāvaṇa to save Sītā.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa at the hermitage of Bharadvāja, Kangra Rāmāyaṇa (Met 1976.15)
summary: Kangra Rāmāyaṇa folio of about 1780: the exiles visit the sage Bharadvāja at Prayāga (Ayodhyākāṇḍa).

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: "Large Basohli" Bhāgavata Purāṇa (dispersed)
summary: Dispersed large-format Bhāgavata Purāṇa series from the Punjab hills of about 1760–65, with figures set against boldly contrasting coloured grounds.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Pradyumna and Śambara fight with maces, "Large Basohli" Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Cleveland 1960.184)
summary: Kṛṣṇa's son Pradyumna, kidnapped as an infant by the demon Śambara, confronts him in battle (Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 10).

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Early Rajput dispersed Bhāgavata Purāṇa (c. 1520–40)
summary: Early illustrated Bhāgavata Purāṇa from the Delhi–Agra region, c. 1520–40, in the pre-Mughal "Caurapañcāśikā" style, with Sanskrit text above horizontal paintings; leaves are now dispersed among the Cleveland, Metropolitan and Art Institute of Chicago museums and others.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Nanda and the elders, early Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Cleveland 1960.53)
summary: Kṛṣṇa's foster father Nanda confers with the elders about moving the cowherd community, harassed by demons sent by Kaṃsa.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: The infant Kṛṣṇa carried away by Vasudeva, early Bhāgavata Purāṇa (AIC 1998.182)
summary: Vasudeva carries the new-born Kṛṣṇa out of Kaṃsa's prison across the Yamunā to Gokula.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rāmāyaṇa murals of the Mattancherry Palace, Kochi
summary: Kerala-style tempera murals in the Mattancherry ("Dutch") Palace, built by the Portuguese c. 1545 for the Raja of Cochin; the bedchamber walls carry a long Rāmāyaṇa cycle and other rooms Purāṇic scenes, generally dated to the 16th–17th century.

type:LABEL: person
name: Eugen Hultzsch
summary: German Indologist (1857–1927), Government Epigraphist of Madras, who founded the South Indian Inscriptions series and edited the Kūram and Kasakudi plates (SII I–II).

type:LABEL: person
name: H. Krishna Sastri
summary: Indian epigraphist (1870–1945) who edited SII II part V (Velurpalaiyam plates) and SII III part III (Tiruvālaṅkāṭu plates) and later served as Government Epigraphist.

type:LABEL: person
name: T. A. Gopinatha Rao
summary: Indian archaeologist and epigraphist (1872–1919) of Travancore, author of Elements of Hindu Iconography, who edited the Anbil plates of Sundara Cōḻa in EI XV.

type:LABEL: person
name: J. Ph. Vogel
summary: Dutch Indologist (1871–1958) who catalogued the Mathurā museum (1910) and edited the earliest Sanskrit inscriptions of Borneo (Kutai yūpas, 1918) and Java (1925).

type:LABEL: person
name: George Cœdès
summary: French epigraphist and historian (1886–1969) of the EFEO, editor of the Inscriptions du Cambodge, who with Pierre Dupont published the Sdok Kak Thom stele (1943) and edited the Vat Luang Kau stele (1956).

type:LABEL: person
name: Louis Finot
summary: French Indologist (1864–1935), first director of the EFEO, who published the Mỹ Sơn stele of Bhadravarman I in 1902.

type:LABEL: person
name: D. C. Sircar
summary: Indian epigraphist and historian (1907–1985), Government Epigraphist for India, whose Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization (vol. I, 2nd edn 1965) is the standard reader of early Indian inscriptions.

type:LABEL: person
name: Naravarman (Aulikara)
summary: Early Aulikara king of Daśapura (Mandsaur), son of Siṃhavarman and grandson of Jayavarman, named in the Mandsaur inscription of Kṛta year 461 (404/405 CE); father of Viśvavarman of the Gangdhar inscription.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Mandsaur inscription of the time of Naravarman (Kṛta year 461)
summary: Sanskrit verse inscription dated in the Kṛta (Mālava) era year 461 (404/405 CE), in the reign of the Aulikara king Naravarman. It opens with homage to the thousand-headed Puruṣa of immeasurable self who sleeps on the waters of the four oceans — Viṣṇu in the Puruṣasūkta idiom and the Anantaśayana image.

type:LABEL: institution
name: The Schøyen Collection (Oslo and London)
summary: Private manuscript collection formed by Martin Schøyen, with an online catalogue that includes South Asian palm-leaf manuscripts.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Devīmāhātmya palm-leaf manuscript, Schøyen Collection MS 2174
summary: Palm-leaf manuscript of the Devīmāhātmya in 32 folios in early Bhujimol script, with one miniature and carved wooden covers painted with ten miniatures, attributed to Nepal or Bihar in the 11th century. The catalogue says it "seems to be the oldest surviving copy of the text".

type:LABEL: polity
name: Pāla dynasty (Bengal and Bihar)
summary: Dynasty ruling Bengal and Bihar from the mid-8th to the 12th century CE, founded by Gopāla and patrons of the Buddhist monasteries of Nālandā and Vikramaśīla. Brahmanical images of Viṣṇu, Śiva and the Goddess in black stone and bronze were also produced in great numbers in their territories.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Male fertility divinity, possibly Śiva, Kuṣāṇa terracotta (Cleveland 1986.71)
summary: Kuṣāṇa terracotta of an ithyphallic male god with long matted locks, a water pot and weapons. The museum suggests he may be a local fertility divinity but "could also be recognized as an early form of the Hindu god Shiva".

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Standing Viṣṇu, Mathurā, 3rd–4th century (V&A IM.75-1927)
summary: Standing Viṣṇu in Mathurā sandstone attributed to the 3rd–4th century, the transition from late Kuṣāṇa to early Gupta Vaiṣṇava imagery at the city where the Vṛṣṇi heroes had been worshipped in images since the 1st century CE.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Head of Viṣṇu, Mathurā, Gupta (Cleveland 1942.498)
summary: Fifth-century Mathurā head of Viṣṇu with the squarish crown and central lion-head medallion spouting strings of pearls, which the museum reads as conveying the god's solar and royal radiance.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Yakṣī, Kuṣāṇa Mathurā (AIC 1995.260)
summary: Red sandstone yakṣī of 2nd-century Mathurā, of the type carved on stūpa railings for Buddhist and Jain monuments.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Standing Balarāma or Nāgarāja, Gupta (Met 1991.83.2)
summary: Mid-5th-century red sandstone figure under a serpent hood which the Met titles "Balarāma or Nāgarāja (serpent king)": the overlap between the snake-hooded Saṅkarṣaṇa/Balarāma and the nāga kings worshipped at Mathurā is visible in a single image.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Indian Museum, Kolkata
summary: India's oldest museum (founded 1814), where the gateway and railings of the Bharhut stūpa were reassembled.

type:LABEL: site
name: Bharhut stūpa (Satna district)
summary: Buddhist stūpa in Satna district, Madhya Pradesh, visited by Alexander Cunningham in 1873 and excavated the following year. Its carved railings (c. 125–100 BCE) and gateway (c. 100–75 BCE, "during the rule of the Sugas") are among the earliest narrative sculpture in India; they were reassembled in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gaja-Lakṣmī relief, Bharhut stūpa railing (Indian Museum, Kolkata)
summary: Relief on the Bharhut railing of a woman standing on a lotus and lustrated by two elephants — the Gaja-Lakṣmī type. On this Buddhist monument the figure is read either as Śrī-Lakṣmī, the goddess of prosperity, or as the Buddha's mother Māyādevī.

type:LABEL: institution
name: State Museum, Lucknow
summary: State museum of Uttar Pradesh (formerly the Provincial Museum), holding the Jain sculptures excavated at Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā, Mathurā, catalogued with "J" numbers.

type:LABEL: site
name: Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā (Mathurā)
summary: Mound at Mathurā excavated in the 1870s–1890s (notably by A. Führer, 1888–91) which yielded the remains of a Jain stūpa and many dated Jain sculptures and inscriptions of the Kuṣāṇa period, now mostly in the State Museum, Lucknow.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Jain Sarasvatī from Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā, Mathurā (State Museum, Lucknow, J.24)
summary: Headless seated image of the goddess Sarasvatī holding a manuscript, from the Jain site of Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā, with a pedestal inscription dated in year 54 of the Kuṣāṇa (Kaniṣka) era recording its gift by a smith named Gova, son of Siṃha, at the instance of a preacher. Often cited as the earliest dated image of Sarasvatī in any tradition.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Parkham yakṣa (Maṇibhadra), Mathurā Museum
summary: Colossal standing yakṣa from Parkham near Mathurā, now in the Government Museum, Mathurā. Its Prakrit inscription in Brāhmī, which Sircar dates palaeographically to the second half of the 1st century BCE, names the figure as (the yakṣa) Maṇibhadra and says it was made by Gomitaka, pupil of Kunika. The older theory that it portrays the king Ajātaśatru (Kuṇika) is rejected.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vāsudeva (deity of early inscriptions)
subtype: deity attested in inscriptions and coins
summary: Vāsudeva is the deity named in the earliest Vaiṣṇava inscriptions of the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, such as the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, where he is called devadeva, “god of gods”. He was later identified with Kṛṣṇa and with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa. The material record shows his worship centuries before the Purāṇic synthesis.
earliest_textual: c. mid-4th c. BCE or later (terminus post quem c. 350 BCE)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Saṅkarṣaṇa (deity of early inscriptions)
subtype: deity attested in inscriptions and coins
summary: Saṅkarṣaṇa is the deity invoked together with Vāsudeva in inscriptions of the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, and is usually named first. He is identified with Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa's elder brother, and later became the first emanation (vyūha) of Vāsudeva in Pāñcarātra theology.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Heliodorus pillar inscription, Besnagar
aliases: Garuda pillar|Khamba Baba|Garuḍa pillar|Besnagar pillar inscription
summary: Two Brāhmī inscriptions in Prakrit on a stone pillar at Besnagar (ancient Vidiśā) record that Heliodorus of Taxila set up a Garuḍa-standard (garuḍadhvaja) for Vāsudeva, “god of gods”. Heliodorus, son of Dion, calls himself a bhāgavata and was a Greek envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas to king Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra. It is among the earliest dated pieces of evidence for Vāsudeva devotion.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions
summary: Three fragmentary Sanskrit inscriptions in Brāhmī script from Ghosuṇḍī and Hāthībāḍā near Nagari (ancient Madhyamikā), Rajasthan, dated to the 2nd–1st century BCE. They record that king Sarvatāta of the Gājāyana lineage, a devotee of Bhagavat and performer of an aśvamedha, built a stone enclosure for the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, called Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā. They are among the earliest Sanskrit (as opposed to Prakrit) inscriptions.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of Nāganikā
summary: A long Brāhmī cave inscription at the Nāṇeghāṭ pass (Maharashtra), commissioned by the Sātavāhana queen Nāganikā (Nāyanikā). It opens by invoking Dharma, Indra, Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, the lunar line and the four Lokapālas (Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava), and lists Vedic sacrifices, including two horse sacrifices, with the fees paid for them. Most scholars date it to the 1st century BCE.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Mora well inscription (Mathurā)
summary: A fragmentary Sanskrit inscription on a stone slab from the Mora well near Mathurā, from the time of the Mahākṣatrapa Śoḍāsa, son of Rājuvula (c. 15 CE). It records the installation of images (pratimā) of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes (pañcavīra), called bhagavat, in a stone shrine linked to a woman named Toṣā. It is the earliest epigraphic reference to cult images of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Torso of a Vṛṣṇi hero from Mora
summary: A stone male torso of c. 15 CE found at Mora near Mathurā together with the Mora well inscription and a carved doorjamb. It is now in the Government Museum, Mathurā, and is probably one of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes whose images the inscription records. It is among the earliest surviving cult images associated with the Vāsudeva–Saṅkarṣaṇa group.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Vasu doorjamb inscription (Mathurā)
aliases: Mathura inscription of Śoḍāsa's time|Vasu inscription
summary: A twelve-line Sanskrit inscription in Brāhmī on the back of a red sandstone doorjamb found in an old well at Mathurā. It dates from the time of the Mahākṣatrapa Śoḍāsa (early 1st century CE) and records that a donor named Vasu set up a gateway (toraṇa) and railing (vedikā) at the great shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva. It is held in the Government Museum, Mathurā (GMM 13.367).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Coins of Agathocles with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva
summary: Six Indian-standard silver drachms of the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles (c. 190–180 BCE), found in 1970 at Aï Khanoum (Afghanistan), each show two male deities. One holds a plough and a pestle or club, the other a conch and a wheel. They are usually identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma and Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, and are often called the earliest unambiguous images of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Megasthenes’ “Herakles” of the Sourasenoi as Kṛṣṇa
subtype: identification of a deity in a Greek ethnography
summary: Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE), as excerpted by Arrian, Diodorus and Strabo, reported that an Indian people called the Sourasenoi especially honoured “Herakles”. They had two great cities, Methora and Kleisobora, and the navigable river Iobares ran through their land. Many scholars identify this Herakles with (Hari-)Kṛṣṇa, the Sourasenoi with the Śūrasenas, Methora with Mathurā and the Iobares with the Yamunā. Others propose Indra, Śiva or Balarāma, or doubt that the Greek label maps onto a single Indian deity.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Chāndogya’s Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra as the epic Kṛṣṇa
summary: The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (CU 3.17.6) names a Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra, “son of Devakī”, as a pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa who learns a teaching that allegorises the sacrifice. Some scholars take him to be the epic and Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, which would be the earliest textual reference to Kṛṣṇa. Others regard the shared name and matronymic as a coincidence, or the verse as an unrelated figure.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Heliodorus inscription B echoes a Mahābhārata verse
subtype: textual parallel claimed for an inscription
summary: Inscription B on the Heliodorus pillar lists three immortal steps: self-restraint, generosity and attentiveness (dama, cāga, apramāda). Since Raychaudhuri, scholars have compared this triad with a verse in the Mahābhārata's Strīparvan (MBh book 11). Some treat it as evidence that the epic, or its ethical verse tradition, was known in Vidiśā in the late 2nd century BCE.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: “Paśupati” seal, Mohenjo-daro
summary: A steatite stamp seal (c. 3.56 × 3.53 cm) excavated at Mohenjo-daro in 1928–29. It shows a horned, seated figure, possibly three-faced, in a yoga-like posture, surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a water buffalo and a rhinoceros, with two deer or ibexes below and seven Indus signs above. John Marshall called it a “proto-Śiva” as Paśupati, lord of animals. The identification has been widely disputed since the 1960s. The seal is now in the National Museum, New Delhi.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The “proto-Śiva” interpretation of the Paśupati seal
subtype: identification of a prehistoric image with a later deity
summary: John Marshall (1928–29; Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, 1931) proposed that the seated horned figure on the Mohenjo-daro seal 420 is a prototype of Śiva as Paśupati (lord of animals) and Mahāyogin. His view was widely accepted for about two generations. Since the 1960s it has been contested on iconographic, methodological and chronological grounds. There is no scholarly consensus.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gudimallam liṅga
summary: A stone liṅga about 1.5 m high in the Paraśurāmeśvara temple at Gudimallam, near Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh). It carries a standing two-armed figure in high relief, holding a ram or antelope and a water pot, with an axe on the shoulder, standing on a crouching dwarf or yakṣa. It is widely regarded as one of the earliest surviving liṅgas with a figural Śiva. Dates proposed range from the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd–4th century CE.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Gudimallam liṅga dates to the 2nd–1st century BCE
summary: Several art historians (e.g. Harle) date the Gudimallam liṅga to the 2nd–1st century BCE on stylistic grounds. If correct, it is the earliest surviving figural liṅga in worship. Other scholars prefer dates in the early centuries CE, partly because of finds from the 1973–74 excavation.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Oesho (OHÞO), deity of Kuṣāṇa coins
summary: Oesho (Bactrian ΟΗϷΟ) is the name of a deity on Kuṣāṇa coins from Kaniṣka I onward. On some issues he is shown with a bull, a trident and, from Huviṣka, several heads and four arms. Many numismatists identify him with Śiva. Others, notably Katsumi Tanabe and Helmut Humbach, read the name as the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Wēš), whose image took on Śaiva features.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Oesho on Kuṣāṇa coins is Śiva
summary: The traditional numismatic view holds that the Kuṣāṇa coin deity Oesho is Śiva, as his trident, bull and multiple heads and arms suggest. The alternative view holds that Oesho is the Bactrian form of the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Wēš). On this view the Śaiva iconography was borrowed and full syncretism with Śiva came later, as seen in Sogdian Weshparkar.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gold coins of Wima Kadphises with a deity and bull
subtype: coin type (gold double stater, stater, quarter stater; copper)
summary: Gold and copper coins of the Kuṣāṇa king Wima (Vima) Kadphises show on the reverse a deity holding a long trident, sometimes with a bull and on some coppers ithyphallic, together with the triratna or nandipada symbol. The Kharoṣṭhī legend calls the king mahiśvara, read by many as “devotee of Maheśvara”. The deity is usually identified with Śiva. Wima was also the first Kuṣāṇa ruler to issue gold coins.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kuṣāṇa coins naming OHÞO (Oesho)
summary: Gold and copper coin types of Kaniṣka I, Huviṣka and Vāsudeva I bear the Bactrian legend ΟΗϷΟ (Oesho) beside a deity with a trident, vajra, water pot and sometimes a bull. Under Huviṣka the deity has three heads and four arms. The type is central to the debate over whether Oesho is Śiva or the Iranian Vāyu.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Varāha relief, Udayagiri Cave 5
summary: A monumental rock-cut relief in the shallow niche called Cave 5 at Udayagiri near Vidiśā. It shows Viṣṇu as the boar-headed Varāha lifting the Earth goddess, who clings to his tusk, out of the cosmic ocean, watched by rows of gods and sages. It dates from the reign of the Gupta king Candragupta II (c. 401–412 CE) and is among the most studied reliefs of the Gupta period.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Udayagiri Cave 6 inscription of the time of Candragupta II (year 82)
aliases: Udayagiri Cave Inscription of Chandragupta II, Year 82
summary: A short Sanskrit inscription at the entrance of Udayagiri Cave 6, dated year 82 (Gupta era, 401/402 CE), on the 11th day of the bright half of Āṣāḍha. It records the pious gift (deyadharma) of a Sanakānīka mahārāja, son of Viṣṇudāsa and grandson of Chagalaga, who calls himself a devotee of the feet of the paramabhaṭṭāraka mahārājādhirāja Candragupta.
