It is the earliest dated record of Candragupta II.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Udayagiri Cave 8 inscription of Vīrasena
summary: A five-line Sanskrit verse inscription in Udayagiri Cave 8 (the Tawa cave). It records that Vīrasena of the Kautsa gotra, surnamed Śāba, a minister of Candragupta II, made the cave as a temple of Śambhu (Śiva) when he came to the place with the king. It is undated but falls within Candragupta II's reign.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Iron pillar inscription of Candra (Delhi)
aliases: Meharauli pillar inscription of Candra|Iron pillar of Delhi
summary: A Sanskrit verse inscription on the wrought-iron pillar now in the Qutb complex, Mehrauli, Delhi. It records that a king named Candra, a devotee of Viṣṇu, set up a standard (dhvaja) of Viṣṇu on a hill called Viṣṇupada. By script and style it dates to the late 4th or early 5th century CE, and Candra is generally identified with Candragupta II.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Colossal Varāha of Eran
summary: A free-standing red sandstone image of Varāha in full boar form, about 4.2 m long and 3.4 m high, standing in the open at Eran (ancient Airikiṇa). Small figures of gods and sages cover its body and the Earth goddess hangs from its tusk. An eight-line Sanskrit inscription on its chest is dated in the first regnal year of the Hūṇa king Toramāṇa. It records that Dhanyaviṣṇu, younger brother of the late Mātṛviṣṇu, had a stone temple built for Nārāyaṇa in the form of a boar.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Eran boar inscription of Toramāṇa
summary: An eight-line Sanskrit inscription in Brāhmī on the chest of the colossal Varāha at Eran, dated the 10th day of Phālguna in the first year of the reign of the mahārājādhirāja Toramāṇa. It records that Dhanyaviṣṇu, younger brother of the deceased mahārāja Mātṛviṣṇu, built a stone temple of the boar-formed Nārāyaṇa at Airikiṇa (Eran).

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Eran pillar inscription of the time of Budhagupta (Gupta year 165)
summary: A Sanskrit inscription on a monolithic pillar at Eran topped by a double Garuḍa with a wheel behind. It is dated Gupta year 165 (484/485 CE) in the reign of Budhagupta and records the erection of the pillar as a standard in honour of Janārdana (Viṣṇu).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gajendramokṣa panel, Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
summary: A relief niche (about 3.25 × 5 ft) on the north wall of the Gupta-period Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh. It shows the elephant Gajendra, held in a lotus pond by a nāga and makara, raising a lotus in his trunk as Viṣṇu arrives on Garuḍa to free him. It is one of the earliest monumental depictions of the Gajendramokṣa story.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Nara-Nārāyaṇa panel, Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
summary: The east wall niche of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh shows the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa seated in penance with rosaries, with flying celestials above, a lion and a deer below, and four-headed Brahmā on a lotus.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Anantaśayana Viṣṇu panel, Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
summary: The south wall niche of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh shows Viṣṇu reclining on the seven-hooded serpent Śeṣa (Ananta), with Lakṣmī at his feet and a small four-headed Brahmā above. In a register below stand five male figures and a woman, read as the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī or as personified weapons (āyudhapuruṣas) confronting Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa plinth panels, Deogarh
summary: A series of relief panels from the plinth of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh, many now in the National Museum, New Delhi. Rāmāyaṇa scenes include Ahalyā's release, the departure into exile, Atri's hermitage, Śūrpaṇakhā, Sītā's abduction, Sugrīva's victory and Hanumān bringing the mountain of herbs. Kṛṣṇa scenes include the birth in prison, Nanda and Yaśodā with Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, the fight with Kaṃsa and the theft of the bathers' clothes. They are among the earliest narrative cycles of both epics in stone.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rāmāyaṇa panels, Nachna
summary: Stone relief panels at the Gupta-period temples of Nachna (Nachna-Kuthara), Madhya Pradesh, show episodes of the Rāmāyaṇa. They include Rāvaṇa disguised as a mendicant asking Sītā for alms, Sītā rebuking Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma hesitating to shoot Vālin, and the monkey leaders including Hanumān paying respect to Rāma. They are counted among the earliest known Rāmāyaṇa friezes, though older single Rāmāyaṇa-related scenes are claimed at Bharhut and Sanchi.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Gold archer-type coin of Candragupta II with Śrī (Cleveland 1977.62)
summary: A gold coin (dīnāra) of Candragupta II, c. 400 CE, in the Cleveland Museum of Art (accession 1977.62). The obverse shows the king as an archer with bow and arrow. The reverse shows Śrī, the goddess of good fortune (Lakṣmī), seated on a lotus. The archer type is the commonest Gupta gold coinage.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kārttikeya (peacock) type gold coins of Kumāragupta I
summary: A gold coin type of the Gupta king Kumāragupta I (c. 415–455 CE). The obverse shows the king feeding a peacock, with the legend Śrī-Mahendra Kumāraḥ. The reverse shows the god Kārttikeya (Kumāra, Skanda) seated on his peacock. The king's name, Kumāra, puns on the god's.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kṛṣṇa Govardhanadhara from Varanasi (Bharat Kala Bhavan)
summary: A Gupta-period stone sculpture of Kṛṣṇa lifting Mount Govardhana, recovered from Varanasi and held in the Bharat Kala Bhavan museum, Banaras Hindu University. It is dated to the 4th–6th century CE, with some records giving the 5th century. It is one of the earliest monumental images of the Govardhana episode.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Gangdhar stone inscription of the time of Viśvavarman (423/424 CE)
aliases: Gangadhar inscription|Gangdhar stela of the time of Visvavarman
summary: A Sanskrit stone inscription from Gangdhar (Jhalawar district, Rajasthan), dated year 480 of the Mālava (Kṛta) era, the 13th of the bright half of Kārttika (423/424 CE), in the reign of the Aulikara king Viśvavarman. It records that his minister Mayūrākṣaka built a temple of Viṣṇu, a “terrifying abode of the divine Mothers” (Mātṛkās), and a well.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Mandasor inscription of the silk-weavers' guild (Mālava years 493 and 529)
aliases: Mandsaur stone inscription of Kumaragupta and Bandhuvarman
summary: A Sanskrit verse inscription from Mandasor (ancient Daśapura), composed by Vatsabhaṭṭi. It records that a guild of silk weavers who had migrated from Lāṭa (south Gujarat) built a temple of the Sun in Mālava year 493 (436/437 CE), while Kumāragupta ruled the earth and Bandhuvarman was lord of Daśapura. It also records that the same guild repaired the temple in year 529 (472/473 CE).

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Dadhimatī Mātā inscription of Dhruhlaṇa (Gupta year 289 = 608 CE)
summary: A Sanskrit inscription found in the ancient temple of the goddess Dadhimatī between Goth and Mānglod (Nagaur district, Rajasthan). It is dated Gupta year 289, 13th of the dark half of Śrāvaṇa (608 CE). Its lines 11–12 contain a verse that the editor identified as a quotation from the Devī Māhātmya, beginning sarva-maṅgala-māṅgalye. This gives a firm terminus ante quem for that text.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Eighteen-armed dancing Śiva, Bādāmi Cave 1
summary: A rock-cut relief about 1.5 m high, to the right of the entrance of Bādāmi Cave 1, showing Śiva dancing with eighteen arms. Some hands hold a drum, a flame, a serpent, a trident and an axe, and Gaṇeśa and Nandi are beside him. It belongs to the late 6th-century Cālukya cave series and is one of the earliest monumental images of the dancing Śiva.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Bādāmi Cave 3 inscription of Maṅgaleśa (Śaka 500 = 578 CE)
summary: An inscription in Cave 3 at Bādāmi, dated Kārttika full moon of Śaka 500 (31 October or 1 November 578 CE) in the reign of the Cālukya king Kīrtivarman I. It records that his younger brother Maṅgaleśa made the Viṣṇu cave temple, called Mahāviṣṇugṛha or Lañjīśvara, “well-proportioned and of wonderful workmanship”, and gave land to the temple's garland-makers. It is the only dated cave at Bādāmi.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Sadāśiva / Maheśamūrti (“Trimūrti”), Elephanta Cave 1
summary: A colossal three-headed bust, about 6–7 m high, carved on the south wall of the main cave at Elephanta near Mumbai. It shows Śiva with three faces: a fierce moustached face (Aghora-Bhairava), a calm central face (Tatpuruṣa) and a gentle face holding a lotus (Vāmadeva/Umā). Older literature called it a Trimūrti of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva; most modern scholars read it as Sadāśiva or Maheśamūrti. It dates to about the 6th century CE.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Mahiṣāsuramardinī relief, Mamallapuram
summary: A large relief on the north wall of the rock-cut Mahiṣāsuramardinī maṇḍapa at Mamallapuram (Pallava, 7th century). It shows the eight-armed goddess Durgā riding a lion into battle against the buffalo-headed Mahiṣāsura, with attendants, one of whom holds a parasol over her. The opposite wall shows Viṣṇu reclining on Ādiśeṣa, with the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha. It is considered one of the finest Pallava sculptures.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Great relief of Mamallapuram (“Arjuna's Penance” / “Descent of the Gaṅgā”)
aliases: Arjuna's Penance|Descent of the Ganges|Bhagiratha's Penance
summary: An open-air relief about 29 × 13 m carved across two granite boulders at Mamallapuram (Pallava, 7th century). A natural cleft between them, filled with nāgas, may once have carried water. Gods, celestials, sages, hunters and animals converge on the cleft. A figure standing on one leg in austerity before Śiva is read either as Arjuna seeking the Pāśupata weapon (the Kirātārjunīya episode) or as Bhagīratha bringing the Gaṅgā to earth. Which reading is right is debated (claim:mamallapuram-relief-identity).

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Mamallapuram great relief depicts the Descent of the Gaṅgā (not Arjuna's penance)
summary: Scholars disagree over whether the central ascetic of the great relief at Mamallapuram is Bhagīratha, whose penance brought the Gaṅgā to earth, or Arjuna performing austerities to obtain the Pāśupata weapon from Śiva. Some argue the ambiguity is intentional. This claim records the Descent-of-the-Gaṅgā reading and the evidence for and against it.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa (Rāvaṇānugraha), Kailāsa temple, Ellora
summary: A deep-cut relief at the monolithic Kailāsa temple (Ellora Cave 16). It shows the ten-headed Rāvaṇa trapped beneath Mount Kailāsa, trying to shake it, while Śiva and Pārvatī sit above and Śiva steadies the mountain with his foot. It is often described as one of the finest pieces of Indian sculpture. It dates to the 8th century under the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, or a few decades later according to some authors.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Aihole inscription of Pulakeśin II (Ravikīrti)
summary: A 19-line Sanskrit verse praśasti on the Meguti Jain temple at Aihole, composed by the Jain poet Ravikīrti for the Cālukya king Pulakeśin II. It is dated both Śaka 556 and 3735 years after the Bhārata war, equivalent to 634/635 CE. Ravikīrti claims to have reached the fame of Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, which makes the inscription a terminus ante quem for both poets. It also gives the Cālukya account of Pulakeśin's defeat of Harṣa.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Changu Narayan pillar inscription of Mānadeva
summary: A Sanskrit inscription on a stone pillar at the Changu Narayan temple near Bhaktapur (Kathmandu Valley), issued by the Licchavi king Mānadeva. It is dated Saṃvat 386, conventionally equated with 464 CE, and is often called the earliest dated inscription of Nepal. It was first published by Bhagvanlal Indraji and Georg Bühler (1885) and later by Sylvain Lévi.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Śivagṛha inscription (856 CE)
summary: An Old Javanese inscription on andesite, dated Śaka 778 (856 CE) by the chronogram wwalung gunung sang wiku. It was issued by Dyah Lokapāla (Rakai Kayuwangi) after the abdication of Rakai Pikatan (Jatiningrat). It describes the consecration of a great Śiva temple compound called Śivagṛha and the diversion of a river along its wall. J. G. de Casparis identified the compound with Prambanan (Candi Loro Jonggrang). The stone is in the National Museum of Indonesia, Jakarta (D.28).

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Chola bronze Naṭarāja (Cleveland Museum of Art 1930.331)
aliases: Cleveland Nataraja|Shiva as Lord of Dance
summary: A Cōḻa-period bronze of Śiva as Naṭarāja, lord of the dance, from Tamil Nadu, dated to the 11th century. It is 113 cm high and is in the Cleveland Museum of Art (accession 1930.331), bought in 1930 from the dealer C. T. Loo. It represents the classic ānanda-tāṇḍava form: Śiva dancing within a ring of flames on the dwarf of ignorance (Apasmāra), holding the drum and the flame.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Shiva Nataraja, Rijksmuseum (AK-MAK-187)
summary: A Cōḻa bronze Naṭarāja from Tamil Nadu, dated c. 1100–1200, about 153 cm high, displayed at the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, as object AK-MAK-187. It is on loan from the Royal Asian Art Society in the Netherlands, which bought it from C. T. Loo, Paris, in 1935 with support from the Vereniging Rembrandt.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Pathur Naṭarāja (the “London Nataraja”)
summary: A Cōḻa-style bronze Naṭarāja reportedly found in 1976 by a labourer near a ruined Śiva temple at Pathur, Tamil Nadu, and later sold abroad. Bought by the Bumper Development Corporation, it was seized by the Metropolitan Police in London. In Bumper Development Corp. v. Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis the English courts held that the London bronze was the Pathur image. They allowed the Pathur temple itself to sue as a party, and on 12 February 1991 the Court of Appeal ruled that it should return to Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Sivapuram Naṭarāja
summary: A 10th-century Cōḻa bronze Naṭarāja from the Śiva temple at Sivapuram (Thanjavur district, Tamil Nadu). A replica was substituted for it in the temple, and the substitution was uncovered in 1969. The original was bought by the Norton Simon Foundation in 1973 for about one million dollars. After Indian legal action, a 1976 settlement let the Foundation keep it for ten years before its return to India, reported as 1986 or 1987. It is now reportedly kept at the Kapaleeswarar temple, Chennai.

type:LABEL: artifact
name: Kṛṣṇa lifting Mount Govardhana, Phnom Da (Cleveland 1973.106)
summary: A monumental sandstone statue of Kṛṣṇa holding up Mount Govardhana, about 2 m high, from Phnom Da (Takeo province, Cambodia), dated c. 600 CE. It is in the Cleveland Museum of Art (1973.106), one of eight colossal figures from the mountain sanctuary near Angkor Borei. It is among the earliest images of the Govardhana episode outside South Asia. In 2020–21 Cleveland and the National Museum of Cambodia exchanged fragments to reconstruct two Phnom Da Kṛṣṇa statues.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Spitzer manuscript
summary: A palm-leaf Sanskrit manuscript of more than 1,000 fragments, found in 1906 by the Third German Turfan Expedition (led by Albert Grünwedel) at Ming-öi near the Kizil caves, Xinjiang. It is radiocarbon-dated to c. 130 CE (80–230 CE) and written in Kuṣāṇa-period Brāhmī. Probably the oldest surviving philosophical manuscript in Sanskrit, it contains, among Buddhist and Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika material, a list of the parvans of the Mahābhārata. Dieter Schlingloff (1969) showed that the list lacks the Anuśāsana and Virāṭa parvans.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Skandapurāṇa manuscript dated 810 CE (Kathmandu)
summary: A palm-leaf manuscript of the early Skandapurāṇa in a transitional Gupta script, in the National Archives, Kathmandu (NAK 2-229; NGMCP microfilm B 11/4). The editors Adriaensen, Bakker and Isaacson date it 810 CE, possibly copied on 10 March 811. It is one of the oldest dated Purāṇa manuscripts and the basis of the Groningen critical edition, which showed that the original Skandapurāṇa differs greatly from the later printed Skanda Purāṇa.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Rigveda manuscripts at BORI (Memory of the World)
summary: A collection of 30 manuscripts of the Rigveda at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007. It contains Saṃhitā, Padapāṭha and Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya manuscripts: one on birch bark in Śāradā script and 29 on paper in Devanāgarī. The oldest dated is No. 5/1882-83 of 1464 CE. The manuscripts were collected for the Bombay government from 1868 by Georg Bühler, F. Kielhorn and others.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Rigveda manuscript BORI No. 5/1882-83 (1464 CE)
summary: The oldest dated manuscript in BORI's UNESCO-inscribed Rigveda collection, dated 1464 CE according to the nomination file. It is on paper in Devanāgarī script.

type:LABEL: manuscript
name: Birch-bark Śāradā Rigveda manuscript, BORI No. 5/1875-76
summary: The only birch-bark manuscript in BORI's Rigveda collection, written in Kashmiri Śāradā script. The nomination file says Max Müller used it for his edition of the Rigveda with Sāyaṇa's commentary, and stresses its importance given the losses of Kashmiri manuscripts.

type:LABEL: site
name: Mohenjo-daro
summary: A major city of the Indus (Harappan) civilisation in Sindh, Pakistan, built c. 2500 BCE and abandoned c. 1700 BCE. It was visited by R. D. Banerji in 1919–20 and excavated from 1924 by K. N. Dikshit, John Marshall, Ernest Mackay and later Mortimer Wheeler and George Dales. It was the first UNESCO World Heritage Site in South Asia (1980). The 'Paśupati' seal was found here.

type:LABEL: site
name: Besnagar (Vidiśā)
summary: The archaeological site of ancient Vidiśā, about 3 km from modern Vidisha on the west bank of the Betwa, Madhya Pradesh. It was an important trade centre from the 6th–5th century BCE under the Śuṅgas, Nāgas, Sātavāhanas and Guptas. It is the site of the Heliodorus pillar and of an excavated elliptical Vāsudeva temple of the 2nd century BCE.

type:LABEL: site
name: Hastinapur excavations (1950–52)
summary: Excavations by B. B. Lal (ASI) in 1950–52 at Hastinapur, Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, a site traditionally identified with the Kuru capital Hastināpura of the Mahābhārata. Lal's main aim was to fix the stratigraphic position of Painted Grey Ware (PGW). He found Period I (Ochre Coloured Pottery), Period II (PGW, c. 1100–800 BCE in his dating), a flood-erosion break, Period III (NBPW, early 6th – early 3rd century BCE), Period IV (2nd century BCE – 3rd century CE) and Period V (from c. 11th century CE).

type:LABEL: site
name: Aï Khanoum
summary: A Hellenistic city at the confluence of the Oxus (Amu Darya) and Kokcha rivers in northern Afghanistan. It was probably founded c. 300–285 BCE under Seleucus I or Antiochus I, and captured by nomads c. 145 BCE. The French archaeological mission (DAFA) under Daniel Schlumberger and then Paul Bernard excavated it from 1964 to 1978. In 1970 the palace yielded the Agathocles drachms with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva.

type:LABEL: site
name: Dwarka offshore explorations
summary: Underwater and intertidal explorations off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka (Gujarat) by the Marine Archaeology Centre of the National Institute of Oceanography, Goa, led by S. R. Rao from the 1980s, and later by the ASI. They recorded stone blocks, walls and many stone anchors. Rao identified the remains with Kṛṣṇa's Dvārakā. Later NIO researchers (Gaur, Sundaresh, Tripati 2004) argue from anchor typology that the harbour belongs to the historical period.

type:LABEL: site
name: Mora (near Mathurā)
summary: A village about 11 km from Mathurā, Uttar Pradesh, whose well and mound yielded the Mora well inscription of the Vṛṣṇi heroes (c. 15 CE), a carved doorjamb and torsos probably of the heroes. The mound was excavated in 1911–12.

type:LABEL: site
name: Nagari (ancient Madhyamikā)
subtype: early historic site with cult enclosure
summary: An early historic site about 13 km north of Chittorgarh, Rajasthan, identified with ancient Madhyamikā. The Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions recording a stone enclosure for Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva come from here and from nearby Ghosuṇḍī. The Hāthībāḍā enclosure is one of the earliest known structures linked to Vāsudeva worship.

type:LABEL: site
name: Nāṇeghāṭ pass
subtype: rock-cut cave on a trade route
summary: A mountain pass in the Western Ghats (Pune district, Maharashtra) on an ancient trade route between the Konkan coast and the Deccan plateau. A rock-cut cave at its head carries the 1st-century BCE Sātavāhana inscriptions of queen Nāganikā and once held relief portraits of the royal family, now lost apart from their labels.

type:LABEL: site
name: Eran (ancient Airikiṇa)
summary: An archaeological site on the Bina river, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh. Its group of Gupta-period temples and monuments includes the colossal Varāha, the Garuḍa pillar of Budhagupta (484/85 CE), an inscription of Samudragupta (now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata), and the Goparāja memorial inscription of Gupta year 191 (510 CE), often cited as an early record of sati.

type:LABEL: site
name: Purana Qila (Old Fort), Delhi
subtype: multi-period settlement mound under a fort
summary: A 16th-century fort in Delhi whose mound has been excavated by B. B. Lal (1954–55 and 1969–72/73) and by Vasant Kumar Swarnkar (2013–14, 2017–18), with a further ASI season in 2023. The excavations found Painted Grey Ware sherds (c. 1000 BCE) and a sequence of Mauryan, Śuṅga, Kuṣāṇa, Gupta, Rajput, Sultanate and Mughal levels. Local tradition, Cunningham and India's Ministry of Culture identify the site with the Pāṇḍavas' Indraprastha.

type:LABEL: site
name: Kizil caves (Ming-öi)
summary: A Buddhist cave complex on the north bank of the Muzat river, about 65 km west of Kucha in Baicheng county, Xinjiang, China. The Third German Turfan Expedition (December 1905 – July 1907) worked here under Albert Grünwedel and found the Spitzer manuscript in the Ming-öi area.

type:LABEL: site
name: Gangdhar
summary: A town on the Kali Sindh river in Jhalawar district, Rajasthan, findspot of the 423/424 CE inscription of the Aulikara king Viśvavarman's minister Mayūrākṣaka, who built temples of Viṣṇu and of the Mothers there.

type:LABEL: site
name: Mandasor (ancient Daśapura)
summary: The town of Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh, identified with ancient Daśapura, seat of the Aulikara rulers. It is the findspot of the silk-weavers' Sun-temple inscription (436/437 and 472/473 CE). The Sondani victory pillars of Yaśodharman, who claims a victory over the Hūṇa Mihirakula, stand about 4 km away.

type:LABEL: site
name: Phnom Da
summary: A hill sanctuary about 3 km south-east of Angkor Borei, Takeo province, Cambodia. It is the findspot of colossal pre-Angkorian sandstone images, among them an eight-armed Viṣṇu and figures of Kṛṣṇa lifting Govardhana, attributed to the reign of Rudravarman (514–539). Its oldest standing temple dates to the 6th century.

type:LABEL: site
name: Goth–Mānglod (Dadhimatī Mātā temple site)
subtype: temple site (findspot of a dated inscription)
summary: The site of the Dadhimatī Mātā temple between the villages of Goth and Mānglod, Nagaur district, Rajasthan. A slab dated 608 CE found there quotes the Devī Māhātmya.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The claim that offshore remains at Dwarka are Kṛṣṇa’s city
subtype: identification of archaeological remains with a narrative place
summary: S. R. Rao and others hold that the submerged walls, blocks and anchors off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka are remains of Kṛṣṇa's Dvārakā, which the Mahābhārata says the sea swallowed after the Yādavas destroyed one another. Most archaeologists, including later NIO researchers, date the recorded structures and anchors to the historical period. They see no archaeological basis for identifying them with an epic city.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The claim that Adam’s Bridge is a man-made structure
subtype: claim about the origin of a natural feature
summary: Some people hold that Adam's Bridge (Rāma Setu), the 48 km chain of shoals between Pamban island (India) and Mannar island (Sri Lanka), is the remnant of the causeway built by Rāma's vānara army in the Rāmāyaṇa's Yuddhakāṇḍa. Geological and remote-sensing studies describe it as a natural formation of limestone shoals, sandbars and patch reefs. The question became politically salient in the controversy over the Sethusamudram Shipping Canal Project, approved in 2005.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Painted Grey Ware sites as the archaeological horizon of the Mahābhārata
subtype: correlation of an archaeological culture with an epic
summary: B. B. Lal argued from his Hastinapur excavation (1950–52) and later surveys that the Painted Grey Ware culture (c. 1200–600 BCE) is found at many sites bearing Mahābhārata place names, such as Hastināpura, Indraprastha (Purana Qila), Kurukṣetra and Mathurā. He proposed it as the material horizon of the epic's core events. Critics stress that pottery cannot be tied to a text without inscriptions, that PGW material culture differs from the epic's descriptions, and that PGW dates are being revised.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Hastinapur flood as the Purāṇic flood of Nicakṣu's reign
subtype: correlation of a stratigraphic event with a textual tradition
summary: B. B. Lal suggested that a flood-erosion break at the end of Period II (PGW, c. 800 BCE in his dating) at Hastinapur corresponds to the Purāṇic account. In that account the Gaṅgā carried away Hastināpura in the reign of Nicakṣu, a descendant of Parīkṣit, and the Kuru capital moved to Kauśāmbī.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Purana Qila is the site of the Pāṇḍavas' Indraprastha
subtype: identification of a site with a narrative place
summary: Local tradition, Alexander Cunningham and India's Ministry of Culture identify the Purana Qila mound in Delhi with Indraprastha, the Pāṇḍava capital of the Mahābhārata. Excavations have found PGW sherds of c. 1000 BCE and continuous later habitation, but nothing that names the site or ties it specifically to the epic.

type:LABEL: person
name: Heliodorus (Heliodoros), son of Dion
summary: A Greek (Yavana) envoy from Taxila, sent by the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas to king Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra at Vidiśā. On the Besnagar pillar he calls himself a bhāgavata and records setting up a Garuḍa-standard for Vāsudeva, “god of gods”. He is one of the earliest named foreign devotees in Indian epigraphy.

type:LABEL: person
name: Antialkidas (Antialcidas)
summary: An Indo-Greek king who ruled from Taxila and sent Heliodorus as envoy to Vidiśā. His reign is dated c. 115–95 BCE (Bopearachchi) or c. 130–120 BCE (Senior), and that choice affects the date of the Heliodorus pillar.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra
summary: A king at Vidiśā in whose 14th regnal year Heliodorus set up the Besnagar pillar. Early scholars identified him with a Śuṅga king of the Purāṇic lists. Later scholars, partly because of excavations at Sonkh near Mathurā, consider him more probably a local ruler.

type:LABEL: person
name: Agathocles of Bactria
summary: A Greco-Bactrian king (c. 190–180 BCE) who issued Indian-standard square and round drachms with Indian imagery. They include the Aï Khanoum drachms showing two deities identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, and a type with Lakṣmī.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nāganikā (Nāyanikā)
summary: A Sātavāhana queen, probably the widow of Sātakarṇi, who commissioned the Nāṇeghāṭ cave inscription recording Vedic sacrifices and invoking Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sarvatāta (Gājāyana)
summary: A king of the Gājāyana lineage, son of a Pārāśarī mother, performer of an aśvamedha and devotee of Bhagavat. The Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions record that he built a stone enclosure for Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva near Nagari (Madhyamikā).

type:LABEL: person
name: Śoḍāsa
summary: An Indo-Scythian (Śaka) Great Satrap (Mahākṣatrapa) of Mathurā, son of Rājuvula, in the early 1st century CE. Dedicatory inscriptions of his time include the Mora well inscription of the Vṛṣṇi heroes and the Vasu doorjamb inscription recording a gateway at the shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva.

type:LABEL: person
name: Wima (Vima) Kadphises
summary: A Kuṣāṇa emperor, father of Kaniṣka I according to the Rabatak inscription, and the first Kuṣāṇa to issue gold coins. His coins show a deity with trident and bull, generally identified as Śiva, and call him mahiśvara.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kaniṣka I
summary: A Kuṣāṇa emperor (c. 127–150 CE in Harry Falk's chronology) whose coins show a mixed Iranian, Greek, Indian and Buddhist pantheon, including Oesho (ΟΗϷΟ). His Rabatak inscription gives his genealogy and records the use of Bactrian.

type:LABEL: person
name: Candragupta II
summary: A Gupta emperor (c. 380–415 CE), also called Vikramāditya. His reign is attested by the Udayagiri inscriptions of Gupta year 82 (401/402 CE) and by Vīrasena's cave. He is generally identified with the king Candra of the Delhi iron pillar, and he issued the archer-type gold coins with Śrī-Lakṣmī. Gupta coins and inscriptions call him paramabhāgavata.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kumāragupta I
summary: A Gupta emperor (c. 415–455 CE), son of Candragupta II, known for his Kārttikeya-type gold coins. The Mandasor silk-weavers' inscription (436/437 CE) is dated in his reign.

type:LABEL: person
name: Budhagupta
summary: A later Gupta emperor whose reign is attested by the Eran Garuḍa pillar inscription of Gupta year 165 (484/485 CE).

type:LABEL: person
name: Vīrasena Śāba
summary: A minister of Candragupta II of the Kautsa gotra. His inscription in Udayagiri Cave 8 records that he made the cave as a temple of Śambhu (Śiva) when he came there with the king.

type:LABEL: person
name: Toramāṇa
summary: A king of the Alchon Huns (c. 493–515 CE) who conquered the Punjab and parts of central India. The Eran boar inscription is dated in the first year of his reign. He was succeeded by his son Mihirakula.

type:LABEL: person
name: Dhanyaviṣṇu
summary: A local Vaiṣṇava ruler at Eran, younger brother of the late mahārāja Mātṛviṣṇu. In the first year of Toramāṇa he built the stone temple of Nārāyaṇa in boar form, to which the colossal Eran Varāha belongs.

type:LABEL: person
name: Viśvavarman (Aulikara)
summary: An Aulikara king of western Mālwa, son of Naravarman. His minister Mayūrākṣaka's Gangdhar inscription of 423/424 CE records temples of Viṣṇu and the Mothers.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bandhuvarman
summary: An Aulikara ruler of Daśapura (Mandasor), son of Viśvavarman. The silk-weavers' inscription says the Sun temple was built in 436/437 CE while Kumāragupta ruled the earth and Bandhuvarman was lord of Daśapura.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vatsabhaṭṭi
summary: A Sanskrit poet who composed the Mandasor praśasti of the silk-weavers' guild (436/437 CE). He names himself in its closing verse.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kīrtivarman I (Cālukya)
summary: A Cālukya king of Bādāmi, father of Pulakeśin II and elder (probably half-) brother of Maṅgaleśa. The Bādāmi Cave 3 inscription of Śaka 500 (578 CE) is dated in his reign.

type:LABEL: person
name: Maṅgaleśa
summary: A Cālukya king of Bādāmi (c. 592–610 CE) who, as prince under his brother Kīrtivarman I, dedicated the Viṣṇu cave (Cave 3) at Bādāmi in 578 CE. His Mahākūṭa pillar inscription dates to his 5th regnal year (601 CE). His nephew Pulakeśin II overthrew him in a succession war, as the Aihole inscription relates.

type:LABEL: person
name: Pulakeśin II
summary: A Cālukya king of Bādāmi (c. 610–642 CE), son of Kīrtivarman I. His court poet Ravikīrti's Aihole inscription (634/635 CE) praises his victories, including one over Harṣa, which Xuanzang's account calls into question.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ravikīrti
summary: A Jain poet at the court of Pulakeśin II who composed the Aihole praśasti of 634/635 CE on the Meguti Jain temple. In it he claims fame equal to Kālidāsa's and Bhāravi's.

type:LABEL: person
name: Narasiṃhavarman I (Māmalla)
summary: A Pallava king (630–668 CE), son of Mahendravarman I, after whose title Māmalla Mamallapuram is named. Several of its monolithic monuments and reliefs are attributed to his reign.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṛṣṇa I (Rāṣṭrakūṭa)
summary: A Rāṣṭrakūṭa king (c. 756–773 CE) to whom later copper plates (Vadodara plates of Karkarāja II, c. 812–813; Kadaba grant) attribute the Kailāsa temple at Ellora.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mānadeva
summary: A Licchavi king of Nepal (464–505 CE) whose pillar inscription at Changu Narayan (Saṃvat 386, conventionally 464 CE) is among the oldest dated records of the Kathmandu Valley. He issued coins called mānāṅka.

type:LABEL: person
name: Dyah Lokapāla (Rakai Kayuwangi)
summary: A ruler of the Medang (Mataram) kingdom of Central Java who issued the Śivagṛha inscription of 856 CE immediately after the abdication of Rakai Pikatan (Jatiningrat).

type:LABEL: person
name: Candragupta Maurya
summary: The founder of the Maurya empire (c. 321–297 BCE), at whose court in Pāṭaliputra Megasthenes served as Seleucid ambassador.

type:LABEL: person
name: Megasthenes
summary: A Greek historian and Seleucid ambassador to Candragupta Maurya at Pāṭaliputra (c. 300 BCE; died c. 290 BCE). His lost Indica survives in excerpts by Arrian, Diodorus and Strabo, including the report of the Sourasenoi who honoured 'Herakles'. Strabo already distrusted him.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kālidāsa
summary: The classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist, author of Abhijñānaśākuntalam, Raghuvaṃśa and Meghadūta. His dates are debated and he is often placed in the Gupta period (c. 4th–5th century CE). The Aihole inscription of 634/635 CE, which names him, is the firm terminus ante quem.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhāravi
summary: A Sanskrit poet, author of the Kirātārjunīya, which retells Arjuna's penance and his fight with Śiva disguised as a hunter. The Aihole inscription of 634/635 CE names him beside Kālidāsa, giving a terminus ante quem; he is usually placed in the 6th century CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Alexander Cunningham
summary: A British army engineer and archaeologist (1814–1893), founder and first head of the Archaeological Survey of India (1861). His tour reports recorded, among many sites, Besnagar and the Heliodorus pillar, Udayagiri, Eran, Deogarh and Nachna.

type:LABEL: person
name: John Marshall
summary: A British archaeologist (1876–1958), Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902–1928). He directed the excavations at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa and proposed the 'proto-Śiva' reading of the Paśupati seal (Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, 1931). He also reported the 1909 discovery of the Heliodorus inscriptions.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ernest J. H. Mackay
summary: A British archaeologist (1880–1943) who directed excavations at Mohenjo-daro in 1927–31. In Further Excavations at Mohenjo-daro (1938) he numbered the 'Paśupati' seal 420 and assigned it to his Intermediate I period.

type:LABEL: person
name: Doris Meth Srinivasan
summary: An American art historian of early Indian art whose studies (1975–76; 1979; 1997) criticised the proto-Śiva reading of the Paśupati seal and analysed early Vaiṣṇava (caturvyūha) and multi-headed imagery.

type:LABEL: person
name: B. B. Lal
summary: An Indian archaeologist (1921–2022), Director-General of the ASI (1968–1972). He excavated Hastinapur (1950–52) and Purana Qila, and argued for a link between Painted Grey Ware sites and Mahābhārata places.

type:LABEL: person
name: S. R. Rao
summary: Shikaripura Ranganatha Rao (1922–2013), Indian archaeologist who excavated Lothal and led marine archaeology at Dwarka and Bet Dwarka for the National Institute of Oceanography. He argued that the remains were Kṛṣṇa's Dvārakā (The Lost City of Dvārakā, 1999). His claimed decipherment of the Indus script is not accepted by mainstream scholarship.

type:LABEL: person
name: V. S. Sukthankar
summary: Vishnu Sitaram Sukthankar (1887–1943), Indologist and first general editor of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute's Critical Edition of the Mahābhārata (from 1925 until his death). He also worked on the Besnagar inscriptions; his transliteration is among those adapted for the Heliodorus reading on Wikipedia.

type:LABEL: person
name: D. R. Bhandarkar
summary: Devadatta Ramkrishna Bhandarkar (1875–1950), Indian epigraphist and archaeologist. He excavated at Besnagar (1913–15) and edited the Hāthībāḍā Brāhmī inscription in Epigraphia Indica vol. 22.

type:LABEL: person
name: Georg Bühler
summary: A German Indologist (1837–1898) who, with F. Kielhorn, collected thousands of manuscripts for the Bombay government from 1868, now at BORI, including Rigveda manuscripts. He published the first complete edition of the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription (1883) and, with Bhagvanlal Indraji, early Nepalese inscriptions including the Changu Narayan pillar.

type:LABEL: person
name: Franz Kielhorn
summary: A German Indologist (1840–1908) who collected manuscripts for the Bombay Presidency (1868–1882), now part of BORI's holdings, and published the standard revised edition of the Aihole inscription in Epigraphia Indica vol. VI.

type:LABEL: person
name: J. F. Fleet
summary: John Faithfull Fleet (1847–1917), British epigraphist whose Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum vol. III (1888) remains the standard edition of Gupta-period inscriptions. He correctly read the Bhārata-war date of the Aihole inscription in 1879.

type:LABEL: person
name: Dieter Schlingloff
summary: A German Indologist who studied Sanskrit manuscripts from the Turfan finds. His 1969 article identified the parvan list of the Mahābhārata in the Spitzer manuscript as the oldest extant list.

type:LABEL: person
name: Eli Franco
summary: An Indologist who published the two-volume edition of the Spitzer manuscript (2004) and proposed a palaeographic date of c. 200–230 CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Paul Bernard
summary: A French archaeologist who directed the DAFA excavations at Aï Khanoum after Daniel Schlumberger, until work stopped in 1978. The 1970 hoard with the Agathocles drachms of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva came from his excavations.

type:LABEL: person
name: I. K. Sarma
summary: Inguva Karthikeya Sarma, Indian archaeologist who led the ASI excavations around the Gudimallam liṅga in 1973–74.

type:LABEL: person
name: H. D. Sankalia
summary: Hasmukh Dhirajlal Sankalia (1908–1989), Indian archaeologist of Deccan College. He led the 1963 onshore excavation at Dwarka and, in Ramayana: Myth or Reality? (1973), questioned the historicity and geography of the Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: person
name: J. G. de Casparis
summary: Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis (1916–2002), Dutch epigraphist of Indonesia. He edited the Śivagṛha inscription (Prasasti Indonesia II, 1956) and identified its Śiva temple compound with Prambanan.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Maurya empire
summary: The first empire of most of the Indian subcontinent (c. 322–185 BCE), founded by Candragupta Maurya. Megasthenes was sent to its court at Pāṭaliputra.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Indo-Greek kingdoms
summary: Greek-ruled kingdoms of the north-west of the subcontinent (c. 180 BCE – c. 10 CE), offshoots of Greco-Bactria. Their kings issued bilingual coins, and their envoy Heliodorus set up the Besnagar pillar for Vāsudeva.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Śuṅga dynasty
summary: A north and central Indian dynasty (c. 185–73 BCE) founded by Puṣyamitra after the last Maurya. Some scholars once identified Bhāgabhadra of the Heliodorus pillar with a Śuṅga king; the identification is now doubted.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Sātavāhana dynasty
summary: A Deccan dynasty whose early queen Nāganikā commissioned the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription. Its chronology is debated between a short chronology (from the 1st century BCE) and a long one (from the late 3rd century BCE), ending in the early 3rd century CE.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Northern Satraps of Mathurā
summary: Indo-Scythian (Śaka) satraps who governed Mathurā around the turn of the Common Era, including Rājuvula and his son Śoḍāsa. Dedicatory inscriptions of their time record shrines of Vāsudeva and the Vṛṣṇi heroes.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kuṣāṇa empire
summary: A Central Asian dynasty that ruled Bactria and northern India (c. 1st–3rd century CE). Its coinage carried a mixed pantheon including Oesho, Skanda-Kumāra and the Buddha, and its Mathurā workshops produced early Hindu, Buddhist and Jain images.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Gupta empire
summary: A north Indian empire (c. 320–550 CE) whose kings styled themselves paramabhāgavata. Their period produced the Udayagiri Varāha, Deogarh, Eran and much of the classical iconography of Viṣṇu, Śiva and the Goddess. The Gupta era begins in 319/320 CE.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Aulikara dynasties
summary: Two lines of rulers in western Mālwa with seats at Daśapura (Mandasor), known almost entirely from inscriptions such as Gangdhar (423/424 CE), Mandasor (436/437 CE) and the Sondani pillars of Yaśodharman (6th century).

type:LABEL: polity
name: Hūṇa (Alchon) kingdom
summary: The Alchon Huns, a Central Asian power that under Toramāṇa (c. 493–515) and Mihirakula ruled the Punjab and parts of central India. The Eran boar inscription records a Vaiṣṇava local ruler under Toramāṇa.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Licchavi kingdom of Nepal
summary: The early historic kingdom of the Kathmandu Valley (c. 400–750 CE). Its Sanskrit inscriptions, beginning with Mānadeva's Changu Narayan pillar, record Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva foundations.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kalacuris of Māhiṣmatī (early Kalacuris)
summary: A western Indian dynasty of the 6th century under whose king Kṛṣṇarāja the Elephanta Great Cave is now generally thought to have been completed.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Cālukyas of Bādāmi
summary: A Deccan dynasty (543–753 CE) based at Vātāpi (Bādāmi). Its rulers Kīrtivarman I, Maṅgaleśa and Pulakeśin II patronised the Bādāmi caves (Cave 3 dated 578 CE) and the Aihole praśasti (634/635 CE).

type:LABEL: polity
name: Pallava dynasty
summary: A Tamil–Andhra dynasty (c. 3rd century – 897 CE) based at Kāñcīpuram. The rock-cut monuments and reliefs of Mamallapuram were created under its 7th–8th-century kings.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Rāṣṭrakūṭa dynasty
summary: A Deccan dynasty (c. 753–982 CE) to whose king Kṛṣṇa I the Kailāsa temple at Ellora is attributed by later copper plates.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Medang (Mataram) kingdom, Java
summary: A Javanese kingdom (c. 732–1016 CE) of Central and later East Java, patron of Borobudur and of the Śaiva temple compound of Prambanan, consecrated according to the Śivagṛha inscription of 856 CE.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Cōḻa dynasty
summary: A Tamil dynasty whose imperial line (c. 848–1279 CE, from Vijayālaya) patronised great temples and the bronze-casting tradition that produced the classic Naṭarāja.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Khmer empire
summary: The empire centred on Angkor (802–1431 CE). Pre-Angkorian Cambodian kingdoms, such as the one that produced the Phnom Da sculptures (6th century), preceded it.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Candela dynasty
summary: A central Indian dynasty (c. 831–1315 CE) best known for the temples of Khajuraho.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Eastern Gaṅga dynasty
summary: An Odishan dynasty whose imperial phase (c. 1078–1434 CE, from Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga) built the Jagannātha temple at Puri and the Sun temple at Konark. Earlier Gaṅga rulers of Kaliṅga are known from the 5th–6th century.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Vijayanagara empire
summary: A south Indian empire (1336–1646 CE) with its capital at Hampi.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune
summary: A research institute founded in Pune in 1917. It produced the Critical Edition of the Mahābhārata (1933–1966) and holds the former Government Manuscripts Library of the Bombay Presidency, including the 30 Rigveda manuscripts inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register (2007).

type:LABEL: institution
name: Archaeological Survey of India
summary: India's national archaeological agency, founded in 1861 under Alexander Cunningham. It excavated Mohenjo-daro (before 1947), Hastinapur and Purana Qila, protects monuments such as Udayagiri, Eran, Deogarh and Gudimallam, and runs an underwater archaeology wing.

type:LABEL: institution
name: UNESCO
summary: UNESCO, whose World Heritage Centre maintains the World Heritage List (Mohenjo-daro 1980; Elephanta 1987; Mamallapuram, Ellora, Prambanan and others), whose Living Heritage Entity maintains the Intangible Cultural Heritage lists (Vedic chanting, Rāmlīlā, Kūṭiyāṭṭam, Royal Ballet of Cambodia), and whose Memory of the World Register includes the BORI Rigveda manuscripts (2007).

type:LABEL: institution
name: National Museum, New Delhi
summary: India's national museum. Among its holdings are the 'Paśupati' seal from Mohenjo-daro, allocated to India at Partition, and the main collection of loose sculpture from the Deogarh Daśāvatāra temple.

type:LABEL: institution
name: National Archives, Kathmandu
summary: Nepal's national archive, holding a major collection of early palm-leaf manuscripts, including the Skandapurāṇa manuscript dated 810/811 CE (NAK 2-229). Its holdings were microfilmed by the Nepal-German projects.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Cleveland Museum of Art
summary: An art museum in Cleveland, Ohio, whose Open Access programme releases collection images under CC0. Relevant holdings include the Naṭarāja 1930.331, the gold archer coin of Candragupta II 1977.62 and the Phnom Da Kṛṣṇa Govardhana 1973.106.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam
summary: The national museum of the Netherlands. It displays the Cōḻa Naṭarāja AK-MAK-187 on loan from the Royal Asian Art Society in the Netherlands.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Bharat Kala Bhavan, Banaras Hindu University
summary: The art and archaeology museum of Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi. It holds the Gupta-period Kṛṣṇa Govardhanadhara from Varanasi.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin
summary: The Berlin State Library, which holds most of the Spitzer manuscript (SHT 810) among the Sanskrit manuscripts of the German Turfan expeditions.

type:LABEL: institution
name: British Library
summary: The national library of the United Kingdom, which holds some fragments of the Spitzer manuscript (Or 15005/…).

type:LABEL: institution
name: Government Museum, Mathurā
summary: The archaeological museum of Mathurā, holding the Mora well inscription (GMM Q.1), a Vṛṣṇi-hero torso from Mora and the Vasu doorjamb (GMM 13.367), together with major Kuṣāṇa sculpture.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Government Museum, Udaipur
summary: A state museum in Udaipur, Rajasthan, reported to hold fragments of the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions.

type:LABEL: institution
name: National Museum of Indonesia, Jakarta
summary: Indonesia's national museum, holding the Śivagṛha inscription (D.28).

type:LABEL: institution
name: CSIR-National Institute of Oceanography, Goa
summary: India's national oceanographic institute. Its Marine Archaeology Centre, led first by S. R. Rao, conducted the underwater explorations off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Norton Simon Foundation / Museum, Pasadena
summary: The California collection that bought the Sivapuram Naṭarāja in 1973 and, under a 1976 settlement with the Government of India, held it for ten years before returning it.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Délégation archéologique française en Afghanistan (DAFA)
summary: The French archaeological mission in Afghanistan, which excavated Aï Khanoum (1964–1978) under Daniel Schlumberger and Paul Bernard.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation / Cataloguing Projects
summary: German–Nepalese projects (NGMPP, then NGMCP) that microfilmed and catalogued manuscripts in Nepal, including the 810/811 CE Skandapurāṇa manuscript (microfilm B 11/4).

type:LABEL: institution
name: National Mission for Manuscripts
summary: A Government of India mission (Ministry of Culture) for documenting and conserving manuscripts. It submitted the Rigveda nomination to UNESCO's Memory of the World on behalf of BORI.

type:LABEL: deity
name: The Mothers (Mātṛkās)
summary: A group of goddesses, the 'Mothers', whose shrine is first dated epigraphically in the Gangdhar inscription of 423/424 CE, which calls it a terrifying abode of the divine Mothers. Groups of Mātṛkās (later usually seven, the Saptamātṛkās) are common in Kuṣāṇa and Gupta sculpture.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: text
name: Indica of Megasthenes (fragments)
summary: A lost Greek ethnography of India by Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE). It survives only in excerpts and paraphrases by Diodorus (1st century BCE), Strabo (1st century CE) and Arrian (Indica, 2nd century CE), and is the earliest foreign description of Indian religious life. It includes the report of 'Herakles' honoured by the Sourasenoi.

type:LABEL: inscription
name: Tamil inscriptions of the Rājarājeśvaram, Thanjavur
summary: The long Tamil inscriptions on the walls and base of the Bṛhadīśvara (Rājarājeśvaram) temple, recording Rājarāja I’s and his successors’ gifts, the temple’s endowments, staff and bronzes; edited by E. Hultzsch in South Indian Inscriptions vol. II.

type:LABEL: character
name: Pūtanā
summary: Child-killing female being sent by Kaṃsa to poison the infant Kṛṣṇa with her breast-milk; he sucks out her life. The Harivaṃśa calls her a bird (śakunī) and Kaṃsa's nurse, the Bhāgavata a rākṣasī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tṛṇāvarta
summary: Whirlwind demon sent by Kaṃsa who carries the infant Kṛṣṇa into the sky and is strangled by him; the episode is found in the Bhāgavata, not in the Harivaṃśa or Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aghāsura
summary: Serpent demon, younger brother of Pūtanā and Baka in the Bhāgavata, who swallows the cowherd boys and calves; Kṛṣṇa enters his mouth and kills him by expanding.

type:LABEL: character
name: Dhenuka
summary: Donkey-shaped demon guarding the palm grove (Tālavana), killed by Balarāma, who hurls him into the palm trees.

type:LABEL: character
name: Cāṇūra
summary: Kaṃsa's champion wrestler, killed by Kṛṣṇa in the arena at Mathurā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Muṣṭika
summary: Kaṃsa's wrestler, set against Balarāma and killed by him in the Mathurā arena.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kuvalayāpīḍa
summary: Kaṃsa's war-elephant posted at the gate of the arena to crush Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma; Kṛṣṇa kills it and takes its tusk.

type:LABEL: character
name: Akrūra
summary: Yādava elder, son of Śvaphalka, sent by Kaṃsa to bring Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Mathurā; on the way he sees them, and Viṣṇu/Śeṣa, in the waters of the Yamunā. In the Syamantaka story he keeps the jewel.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kālayavana
summary: 'Black Yavana' king who besieges Mathurā; Kṛṣṇa lures him into the cave of the sleeping Mucukunda, whose glance burns him to ashes.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mucukunda
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Māndhātṛ, who after helping the gods sleeps in a cave with the boon that whoever wakes him will be burnt by his glance; he burns Kālayavana and then praises Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Satrājit
summary: Yādava owner of the Syamantaka jewel (given him by the Sun in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas), father of Satyabhāmā; later killed by Śatadhanvan for the jewel.

type:LABEL: character
name: Prasena
summary: Brother of Satrājit who wears the Syamantaka jewel while hunting and is killed by a lion.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śatadhanvan
summary: Yādava who kills Satrājit to take the Syamantaka jewel, leaves it with Akrūra and is killed by Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Jāmbavatī
summary: Daughter of the bear-king Jāmbavān, given to Kṛṣṇa after their fight over the Syamantaka jewel; mother of Sāmba.

type:LABEL: character
name: Naraka (Narakāsura, Bhauma)
summary: Asura king of Prāgjyotiṣa, son of the Earth (Bhūmi), who carries off Aditi's earrings and thousands of maidens; Kṛṣṇa kills him and frees the women.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bāṇa (Bāṇāsura)
summary: Thousand-armed asura, eldest son of Bali and devotee of Śiva, whose daughter Uṣā loves Aniruddha; in the ensuing war Kṛṣṇa cuts off all but two of his arms and Śiva intercedes for his life.

type:LABEL: character
name: Uṣā (daughter of Bāṇa)
summary: Daughter of the asura Bāṇa who sees Aniruddha in a dream; her friend Citralekhā brings him to her by magic, which leads to the war between Kṛṣṇa and Bāṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aniruddha
summary: Son of Pradyumna and grandson of Kṛṣṇa, carried to Bāṇa's city by Citralekhā to be with Uṣā; in Pāñcarātra theology also the name of the fourth vyūha.

type:LABEL: character
name: Citralekhā
summary: Uṣā's companion, daughter of Bāṇa's minister Kumbhāṇḍa, who paints the portraits by which Uṣā recognises Aniruddha and brings him to her.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sudāmā (Kucela), Kṛṣṇa's brāhmaṇa friend
summary: Poor brāhmaṇa schoolfellow of Kṛṣṇa who brings him a handful of flattened rice and returns home to find himself made rich. The Bhāgavata leaves him unnamed ('a certain brāhmaṇa', 10.80.6); the names Sudāmā/Kucela belong to later tradition.

type:LABEL: character
name: Uddhava
summary: Yādava counsellor and friend of Kṛṣṇa who carries his message to the gopīs and, before the destruction of the Yādavas, receives his final teaching (the Uddhava Gītā, BhP 11).

type:LABEL: character
name: Nalakūbara and Maṇigrīva
summary: Sons of Kubera cursed by Nārada to stand as twin arjuna trees (yamalārjuna) until the child Kṛṣṇa, dragging the mortar to which he is tied, uproots them (Bhāgavata).

type:LABEL: character
name: The gopīs (cowherd women of Vraja)
summary: The cowherd women of Vraja who love Kṛṣṇa; their nocturnal dance with him (the rāsa) and their longing in separation are central to Bhāgavata devotion.

type:LABEL: place
name: Tālavana (the palm grove)
summary: Palm grove near Vṛndāvana guarded by the donkey-demon Dhenuka (narrative place).

type:LABEL: place
name: Prāgjyotiṣa (Naraka's city)
summary: City of the asura Naraka in the epic and Purāṇic stories; identified by tradition and by early medieval inscriptions with Kāmarūpa in Assam.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śoṇitapura (Bāṇa's city)
summary: City of the asura Bāṇa where Aniruddha is held captive; later local tradition identifies it with Tezpur in Assam.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa and Pūtanā
summary: The infant Kṛṣṇa sucks the life out of Pūtanā, who has come to poison him with her breast. The Harivaṃśa makes her a bird and places the episode after the overturning of the cart; the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas tell it first.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The overturning of the cart (Śakaṭa)
summary: The infant Kṛṣṇa, lying under a cart, kicks it over with his foot. In the Harivaṃśa and Viṣṇu Purāṇa it is simply a cart; the Bhāgavata summary lists it with the demons and later tradition names a cart-demon, Śakaṭāsura.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Tṛṇāvarta, the whirlwind demon
summary: Sent by Kaṃsa, the whirlwind demon Tṛṇāvarta carries the infant Kṛṣṇa into the sky; Kṛṣṇa grows heavy, seizes his throat and kills him. A Bhāgavata addition, absent from the Harivaṃśa and Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The butter thief bound to the mortar (Dāmodara) and the twin arjuna trees
summary: Yaśodā ties the mischievous child Kṛṣṇa to a mortar by a rope round his belly (hence Dāmodara, 'rope-belly'); dragging it, he uproots two arjuna trees. The Bhāgavata frames this with his butter-stealing and makes the trees Kubera's cursed sons.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa kills Aghāsura
summary: The serpent-demon Agha opens his mouth like a cave; the cowherd boys and calves walk in, and Kṛṣṇa enters, swells within his throat and kills him, restoring the boys. Bhāgavata only.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Brahmā steals the calves and cowherd boys
summary: To test Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā hides the calves and cowherd boys for a year; Kṛṣṇa becomes all of them, and Brahmā, seeing every one as four-armed Viṣṇu, praises him (BhP 10.14). Bhāgavata only.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Balarāma kills Dhenuka in the palm grove
summary: When the boys want the palm fruit of the Tālavana, the donkey-demon Dhenuka attacks Balarāma, who seizes him by the hind legs and dashes him against the palm trees; his kin are also killed.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa takes the gopīs' garments
summary: Unmarried gopīs keep a month-long vow to Kātyāyanī to win Kṛṣṇa as husband; when they bathe naked in the Yamunā he takes their clothes up a tree and returns them when they come out with joined hands, promising to fulfil their wish. Bhāgavata only.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The rāsa dance (rāsa-līlā)
summary: On autumn nights Kṛṣṇa sports and dances with the cowherd women of Vraja. The Harivaṃśa gives a short erotic description; the Viṣṇu Purāṇa adds his disappearance, the gopīs' search by his footprints and the circular rāsa dance; the Bhāgavata expands it into five chapters (the rāsa-pañcādhyāyī) with the flute, the 'Gopī-gīta' and Kṛṣṇa multiplied between each pair of women.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Akrūra's journey to Vraja and the vision in the Yamunā
summary: Kaṃsa sends Akrūra to fetch Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Mathurā. Akrūra goes rejoicing, takes them amid the gopīs' grief, and while bathing in the Yamunā sees the two of them — and Viṣṇu on Śeṣa — within the water.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kālayavana and Mucukunda
summary: Besieged by Jarāsandha and by the invincible Kālayavana, Kṛṣṇa moves the Yādavas to Dvārakā and lures Kālayavana into a cave where King Mucukunda sleeps; woken by a kick, Mucukunda burns Kālayavana with his glance and recognises Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Syamantaka jewel
summary: A wonder-working jewel passes from Satrājit (or Prasena) to Prasena, who is killed by a lion; the bear-king Jāmbavān kills the lion. Suspected of theft, Kṛṣṇa tracks it to Jāmbavān's cave, fights him, receives the jewel and Jāmbavatī, and returns it; later Śatadhanvan kills Satrājit and the jewel ends with Akrūra.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa kills Naraka (Narakāsura)
summary: Indra complains that Naraka, son of the Earth and lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, has taken Aditi's earrings and thousands of maidens. Kṛṣṇa, riding Garuḍa with Satyabhāmā, kills Muru and Naraka, returns the earrings and marries the freed women.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Kṛṣṇa's killing of Naraka is commemorated on Naraka Caturdaśī / Dīpāvalī
summary: In much of western and southern India the day before (or the first day of) Dīpāvalī is Naraka Caturdaśī, observed as the day Kṛṣṇa (or Satyabhāmā) killed Naraka. The Purāṇic narratives of the slaying do not themselves found the festival; the association is festival tradition with late textual support.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Uṣā, Aniruddha and the war with Bāṇa
summary: Bāṇa's daughter Uṣā dreams of a lover; her friend Citralekhā identifies him as Aniruddha and carries him off from Dvārakā. Bāṇa imprisons him; Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Pradyumna attack Śoṇitapura, defeat Śiva's fever and Śiva himself, and cut off Bāṇa's arms until Śiva intercedes.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kṛṣṇa's poor brāhmaṇa friend (Sudāmā/Kucela) and the flattened rice
summary: A destitute brāhmaṇa, Kṛṣṇa's schoolfellow, visits him in Dvārakā with a handful of flattened rice; Kṛṣṇa eats it with delight and the friend returns to find his hut a palace. Bhāgavata only.

type:LABEL: text
name: Uddhava Gītā (Haṃsa Gītā), Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 11
summary: Kṛṣṇa's last and longest teaching, given to Uddhava before the destruction of the Yādavas (BhP 11.6–29): renunciation, the avadhūta's twenty-four teachers, bhakti-yoga, the guṇas and the Haṃsa teaching.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tārakākṣa
summary: Eldest of the three asura sons of Tāraka who rule the three cities (Tripura); his is the city of gold.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kamalākṣa
summary: Second son of Tāraka, lord of the silver city of Tripura.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Vidyunmālin
summary: Third son of Tāraka, lord of the iron city of Tripura.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Maya (the asura architect)
summary: Asura master-builder and magician who builds the three cities of Tripura (and, in the Mahābhārata, the Pāṇḍavas' assembly hall); the Matsya and Śiva Purāṇas let him survive the burning.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śiva burns the three cities (Tripura)
summary: Three asura brothers obtain three flying cities of gold, silver and iron, built by Maya, that can be destroyed only when they align, by a single arrow. The gods build Śiva a chariot of the cosmos; with Viṣṇu as (part of) the arrow he burns the cities in one shot. Later versions add Viṣṇu's subversion of the asuras' piety and his drinking of their reviving nectar.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhṛṅgin (Bhṛṅgi)
summary: Emaciated, three-legged gaṇa and devotee of Śiva; in the Vāmana and other Purāṇas the asura Andhaka, impaled on Śiva's trident and purified, becomes Bhṛṅgin.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śiva subdues Andhaka
summary: Andhaka, a blind son born to Śiva and Pārvatī (from her sweat when she covers Śiva's eyes, in the Śiva Purāṇa) and adopted by the asura Hiraṇyākṣa, grows into a tyrant who desires Pārvatī. Śiva impales him on his trident; purified, he praises Śiva and becomes a gaṇa (Bhṛṅgin).

type:LABEL: character
name: Jalandhara
summary: Asura born from the ocean (from the fire of Śiva's third eye, in the Śiva Purāṇa) who conquers the gods and covets Pārvatī; Śiva kills him with a discus drawn with his toe in the water.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vṛndā (wife of Jalandhara)
summary: Chaste wife of Jalandhara, daughter of Kālanemi, whose fidelity protects her husband; Viṣṇu deceives her by taking Jalandhara's form, she curses him and enters the fire. Later tradition links her with the tulasī plant.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śiva kills Jalandhara
summary: The ocean-born asura Jalandhara defeats the gods and even Viṣṇu, then demands Pārvatī. While Viṣṇu breaks the chastity of his wife Vṛndā by impersonating Jalandhara, Śiva kills him with the discus Sudarśana, which he draws in the water with his toe; in the Liṅga Purāṇa Viṣṇu later obtains that discus from Śiva by worshipping him with a thousand names.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śaṅkhacūḍa
summary: Dānava son of Dambha, protected by an amulet of Viṣṇu and by his wife Tulasī's chastity; Śiva kills him after Viṣṇu, disguised, obtains the amulet and violates Tulasī's vow.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tulasī (wife of Śaṅkhacūḍa)
summary: Wife of the dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa who, deceived by Viṣṇu in her husband's form, curses him to become a stone (the śālagrāma) and herself becomes the Gaṇḍakī river and the tulasī plant (Śiva Purāṇa).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śaṅkhacūḍa, Tulasī and the origin of the śālagrāma
summary: The dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa, invincible while he wears Viṣṇu's amulet and his wife Tulasī remains chaste, is killed by Śiva after Viṣṇu, disguised, takes the amulet and Tulasī's chastity. Tulasī curses Viṣṇu to become stone; she becomes the Gaṇḍakī river, whose stones are the śālagrāmas.

type:LABEL: character
name: Gajāsura (son of Mahiṣa)
summary: Elephant-asura, son of Mahiṣāsura, whom Śiva kills at Kāśī and whose hide he wears (hence Kṛttivāsas); the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga marks the spot.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śiva kills Gajāsura and wears his hide (Kṛttivāsas)
summary: Śiva kills the elephant-asura Gajāsura, son of Mahiṣa, at Kāśī, wears his hide and establishes the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga there.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kāma (Kāmadeva)
summary: God of desire, armed with a flowered bow and arrows, who is sent by the gods to rouse Śiva's love for Pārvatī and is burnt to ashes by the fire of Śiva's third eye, becoming 'bodiless' (Anaṅga).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Rati
summary: Wife of Kāma, personifying sexual delight, whose lament over his ashes and prayer to Śiva lead to the promise of his restoration.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śiva burns Kāma
summary: Sent by Indra to make the ascetic Śiva fall in love with Pārvatī (so that a son can be born to kill Tāraka), Kāma shoots his flower-arrow; Śiva's third eye blazes and reduces him to ashes. Rati laments; Kāma lives on bodiless (Anaṅga) and is later restored.

type:LABEL: character
name: Himavat (Himavān), king of mountains
summary: The personified Himālaya, king of mountains, husband of Menā and father of Pārvatī (Umā, Haimavatī) in the Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: character
name: Menā (wife of Himavat)
summary: Wife of the mountain-king Himavat and mother of Pārvatī; the Śiva Purāṇa makes her a mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs and dwells on her horror at Śiva's appearance as bridegroom.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Pārvatī's austerities and her marriage to Śiva
summary: After Kāma is burnt, Pārvatī wins Śiva by fierce austerities; Śiva, disguised as a brahmacārin, tests her resolve by reviling himself, then reveals himself. The Seven Sages negotiate with Himavat and the wedding is celebrated in the mountain's palace.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The origin of Ardhanārīśvara (Śiva as half-woman)
summary: Two Purāṇic patterns: Rudra is born from Brahmā's anger with a body half male and half female and is told to divide himself (Viṣṇu, Mārkaṇḍeya, Kūrma); or Śiva appears to Brahmā, who cannot make creation multiply, as the androgynous Ardhanārīśvara and separates the Goddess from his body so that sexual creation can begin (Śiva Purāṇa, Liṅga).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śiva drinks the poison of the churning (Nīlakaṇṭha)
summary: The deadly poison (hālāhala/kālakūṭa) that rises first from the churned ocean threatens the worlds; at the gods' plea Śiva drinks it and holds it in his throat, which turns blue. The episode is absent from the constituted texts of both epic critical editions.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kālī kills Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (Cāmuṇḍā)
summary: Sent by Śumbha to seize the Goddess, the generals Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa provoke her anger; Kālī springs from her brow, devours their army and beheads both, and the Goddess names her Cāmuṇḍā (Devī Māhātmya 7).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The slaying of Raktabīja and the battle of the Mothers
summary: Every drop of the asura Raktabīja's blood produces a new Raktabīja; the Mothers (Mātṛkās) — the śaktis of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Varāha, Narasiṃha and Indra — join the fight, and Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā drinks his blood so that Caṇḍikā can kill him (Devī Māhātmya 8).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Brāhmī (Brahmāṇī)
summary: Brahmā's śakti among the Mothers, riding a haṃsa with rosary and water-pot (Devī Māhātmya 8); one of the Saptamātṛkās of later iconography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Māheśvarī
summary: Śiva's śakti among the Mothers, riding a bull and holding the trident (Devī Māhātmya 8); one of the Saptamātṛkās of later iconography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kaumārī
summary: Skanda's (Kumāra's) śakti among the Mothers, holding the spear and riding a peacock (Devī Māhātmya 8); one of the Saptamātṛkās of later iconography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vaiṣṇavī
summary: Viṣṇu's śakti among the Mothers, on Garuḍa with conch, discus, mace, bow and sword (Devī Māhātmya 8); one of the Saptamātṛkās of later iconography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vārāhī
summary: The śakti of Viṣṇu's boar form among the Mothers, boar-faced (Devī Māhātmya 8); one of the Saptamātṛkās of later iconography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Nārasiṃhī
summary: The śakti of Narasiṃha among the Mothers, in man-lion form (Devī Māhātmya 8); one of the Saptamātṛkās of later iconography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Aindrī (Indrāṇī)
summary: Indra's śakti among the Mothers, thunderbolt in hand, on the elephant (Devī Māhātmya 8); one of the Saptamātṛkās of later iconography.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Śivadūtī
summary: Fierce form of the Goddess in Devī Māhātmya 8 who sends Śiva as her messenger to the asuras and is therefore called Śivadūtī.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Gaṇeśa's birth from Pārvatī and his beheading by Śiva (Śiva Purāṇa)
summary: Wanting a door-keeper loyal only to her, Pārvatī fashions a son from the dirt of her body; he bars Śiva from her bath, defeats Śiva's gaṇas and the gods, and Śiva cuts off his head with his trident. To appease the furious Goddess and her Mothers, the gods fit him with an elephant's head, revive him and make him lord of the gaṇas, to be worshipped first.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śani's glance beheads the infant Gaṇeśa (Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa)
summary: Śani (Saturn), whose glance destroys, reluctantly looks at Pārvatī's newborn son at her insistence; the child's head falls off. Viṣṇu flies on Garuḍa, cuts the head from a sleeping elephant with his discus and joins it to the child.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Pārvatī's elephant-headed child from bath-unguent (Matsya Purāṇa)
summary: Pārvatī shapes a figure with an elephant's head from the unguent rubbed off her body and throws it into the Gaṅgā; it grows huge, the Gaṅgā calls him her son, and the gods worship him as Gāṅgeya, while Brahmā gives him lordship over the Vināyakas.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śiva becomes the elephant-faced obstacle-maker at the gods' request (Liṅga Purāṇa)
summary: Because the asuras prosper through their rites, the gods ask Śiva for a maker of obstacles; Śiva himself takes the form of the elephant-faced Gaṇeśvara, born from Ambikā, and is charged to obstruct the dharma of the daityas and protect the devout.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Gaṇeśa born from Śiva's laughter and cursed with an elephant head (Varāha Purāṇa)
summary: When the gods ask Śiva for a remover of obstacles to the wicked, a radiant youth springs from Śiva's laughter; when Umā gazes at his beauty, the angry Śiva curses him to have an elephant's face and a pot belly — and from Śiva's sweat many elephant-headed Vināyakas arise.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Siddhi (consort of Gaṇeśa)
summary: With Buddhi, one of the two daughters of Prajāpati Viśvarūpa married to Gaṇeśa in the Śiva Purāṇa; personifies accomplishment.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Buddhi (consort of Gaṇeśa)
summary: With Siddhi, Gaṇeśa's wife in the Śiva Purāṇa; personifies intelligence. Their sons are Kṣema and Lābha.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Gaṇeśa and Skanda race around the world
summary: Śiva and Pārvatī promise to marry first whichever son circles the earth first. Skanda sets off; Gaṇeśa bathes, seats his parents, worships and circumambulates them seven times, declaring that this equals circling the earth. He is married to Siddhi and Buddhi; Skanda returns, feels cheated and withdraws to Mount Krauñca.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Gaṇeśa writes down the Mahābhārata at Vyāsa's dictation
summary: In the frame found in many manuscripts and the vulgate (Bombay ed. 1.1.75–79), Brahmā advises Vyāsa to take Gaṇeśa as scribe; Gaṇeśa agrees on condition that the dictation never pauses, and Vyāsa composes knotty verses to gain time. The critical edition excludes the passage from the constituted text.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Gaṇeśa-as-scribe frame is a late interpolation in the Mahābhārata
summary: The story of Gaṇeśa writing the Mahābhārata at Vyāsa's dictation is absent from the constituted text of the Critical Edition and is regarded as a late insertion, though it occurs in a majority of the Ādiparvan manuscripts collated.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Mohinī distributes the nectar
summary: When the asuras seize the nectar produced by the churning, Viṣṇu takes the form of an enchanting woman; the infatuated asuras let her divide it, and she gives it all to the gods. Rāhu, disguised among the gods, is beheaded by the discus.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Śiva and Mohinī
summary: Śiva asks Viṣṇu to show him the enchantress form; seeing Mohinī playing with a ball he loses his composure and pursues her, his seed falling to earth where it becomes gold and silver; Viṣṇu then praises Śiva's mastery of māyā (Bhāgavata).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: How Viṣṇu came to have a horse's head (Hayagrīva)
summary: Versions differ: the Nārāyaṇīya has Viṣṇu assume the horse-headed form to recover the Vedas stolen by Madhu and Kaiṭabha; the Devī Bhāgavata says that a termite, sent by the gods, gnawed the bowstring on which the sleeping Viṣṇu rested his head, the string snapped and beheaded him, and a horse's head was fitted so he could kill the horse-headed demon Hayagrīva.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Anasūyā
summary: Wife of the sage Atri, proverbial for chastity, mother of Dattātreya, Durvāsas and Soma, born of portions of Viṣṇu, Śiva and Brahmā (Bhāgavata).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The birth of Dattātreya, Durvāsas and Soma to Atri and Anasūyā
summary: Atri performs austerities for a son like the Lord of the world; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva appear together and are born as his sons by Anasūyā — Soma from Brahmā's portion, Datta from Viṣṇu's, Durvāsas from Śiva's (Bhāgavata).

type:LABEL: character
name: Kardama
summary: Prajāpati who marries Devahūti, daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu; their son is Kapila (Bhāgavata).

type:LABEL: character
name: Devahūti
summary: Daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of Kardama and mother of Kapila, to whom Kapila teaches devotional Sāṃkhya (Bhāgavata 3.25–33).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kapila teaches his mother Devahūti
summary: Born to Kardama and Devahūti, Kapila — counted an avatāra — teaches his mother a devotional (bhakti-oriented) Sāṃkhya and yoga, and she attains liberation (Bhāgavata 3.24–33).

type:LABEL: character
name: Nābhi
summary: King of Ajanābha/Himavarṣa, grandson of Priyavrata, husband of Merudevī and father of Ṛṣabha in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas (and in Jain tradition, the last kulakara and father of Ṛṣabha).

type:LABEL: character
name: Bharata (son of Ṛṣabha; Jaḍa Bharata)
summary: Eldest son of Ṛṣabha after whom, in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas, Bhāratavarṣa is named; he renounces the throne, is reborn as a deer through attachment to a fawn, and then as the outwardly dull (jaḍa) brāhmaṇa who teaches King Rahūgaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ṛṣabhanātha (first Jain tīrthaṅkara)
summary: In Jain tradition, Ṛṣabha (Ādinātha), the first of the twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras of the present age, son of the kulakara Nābhi and Marudevī, who teaches humanity the arts and renounces kingship.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ṛṣabha's rule and renunciation (Bhāgavata Purāṇa)
summary: Ṛṣabha, son of Nābhi and Merudevī and a descent of Viṣṇu, rules Ajanābha, gives the kingdom to Bharata, and wanders as a naked avadhūta until his body burns in a forest fire; the Bhāgavata adds that a king of Koṅka-Veṅka-Kuṭaka, Arhat, hearing of him, will spread a heterodox path in the Kali age.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bharata reborn as a deer and as Jaḍa Bharata
summary: King Bharata retires to the forest, becomes attached to an orphaned fawn and is reborn a deer; reborn again as a brāhmaṇa he feigns dullness, is pressed into carrying King Rahūgaṇa's palanquin, and teaches the king non-dual knowledge.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vena
summary: Wicked king, son of Aṅga, who forbids sacrifice and is killed by the sages; from his churned body come the Niṣāda and then Pṛthu (Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bhūmi (the Earth, Pṛthivī)
summary: The Earth personified as a goddess, who flees from Pṛthu as a cow and yields her milk when he makes Manu the calf; also the mother of Naraka and, in Vaiṣṇava theology, a consort of Viṣṇu (Bhūdevī).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Pṛthu milks the Earth
summary: Born from the churned arm of the dead king Vena, Pṛthu finds the earth withholding her produce; she flees as a cow, he pursues her with his bow, and she agrees to give milk if a calf is provided. With Svāyambhuva Manu as calf he milks out the crops; other beings milk her with their own calves and vessels. The earth is named Pṛthivī after him.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ajāmila
summary: Fallen brāhmaṇa of Kānyakubja who, dying, calls out to his son named Nārāyaṇa; Viṣṇu's messengers rescue him from Yama's, demonstrating the power of the divine name (Bhāgavata 6.1–2).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ajāmila saved by the name 'Nārāyaṇa'
summary: Ajāmila, a brāhmaṇa who has abandoned his duties for a slave-woman, calls out his youngest son's name 'Nārāyaṇa' at death; Viṣṇu's attendants stop Yama's messengers, arguing that even an inadvertent utterance of the name removes sin. Ajāmila repents and attains Vaikuṇṭha.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambarīṣa (son of Nābhāga)
summary: Ikṣvāku king and devotee of Viṣṇu; when Durvāsas, offended that Ambarīṣa broke his Dvādaśī fast before the sage's return, sends a demon against him, Viṣṇu's discus Sudarśana pursues Durvāsas through the worlds until he begs the king's pardon (Bhāgavata 9.4–5).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ambarīṣa, Durvāsas and the discus
summary: At the end of his Dvādaśī vow King Ambarīṣa sips water before the delayed sage Durvāsas returns; the angry sage creates a fiery being to kill him; Viṣṇu's discus destroys it and chases Durvāsas through the three worlds, until Viṣṇu tells him to seek the forgiveness of his devotee.

type:LABEL: character
name: Jaya and Vijaya (Viṣṇu's door-keepers)
summary: Twin door-keepers of Vaikuṇṭha who bar the child-sages Sanaka and his brothers and are cursed to three demonic births — as Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, and Śiśupāla and Dantavakra — each time slain by Viṣṇu (Bhāgavata).

type:LABEL: character
name: The four Kumāras (Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra)
summary: Mind-born sons of Brahmā who remain eternal children and celibate sages; in the Bhāgavata they curse Jaya and Vijaya and are counted the first descent of Viṣṇu (BhP 1.3.6).

type:LABEL: character
name: Dantavakra
summary: King of Karūṣa, ally of Śiśupāla and enemy of Kṛṣṇa, who kills him; the Bhāgavata makes him and Śiśupāla the third birth of Jaya and Vijaya.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The curse of Jaya and Vijaya
summary: Sanaka and his brothers, appearing as naked boys, are stopped at the gate of Vaikuṇṭha by Jaya and Vijaya; they curse the door-keepers to be born as asuras. Viṣṇu accepts the curse but promises their return: after three births as his enemies, each ended by him, they rejoin him.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Triśaṅku's heaven
summary: King Satyavrata (Triśaṅku), wanting to ascend to heaven in his body, is refused by Vasiṣṭha and cursed into a caṇḍāla by Vasiṣṭha's sons; Viśvāmitra, whose family Triśaṅku had fed in a famine (Harivaṃśa), sends him up by his own power; thrown down by Indra, he is held head-down in a new heaven Viśvāmitra creates.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vasiṣṭha's wish-granting cow (Śabalā / Nandinī)
summary: The wish-fulfilling cow of the sage Vasiṣṭha whose seizure by King Viśvāmitra starts their feud; Vālmīki calls her Śabalā, the Mahābhārata Nandinī (daughter of Surabhi); she produces armies that defeat the king.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Viśvāmitra tries to seize Vasiṣṭha's cow
summary: King Viśvāmitra, hosted by Vasiṣṭha from his wish-granting cow, tries to take her; she produces armies that crush his forces, and Vasiṣṭha's brahmanic power defeats his weapons. Humiliated, Viśvāmitra undertakes austerities to become a brahmarṣi — the origin of a lasting feud.

type:LABEL: narrative
