name: The battle of Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra as two birds (āḍi and baka)
summary: Enraged that Viśvāmitra has ruined Hariścandra and killed his sons, Vasiṣṭha curses him to become a baka (heron); Viśvāmitra curses Vasiṣṭha to become an āḍi bird; their fight shakes the worlds until Brahmā restores and reconciles them (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 9).

type:LABEL: character
name: Śaibyā (wife of Hariścandra)
summary: Queen of Hariścandra, sold into servitude with her son Rohitāśva when the king keeps his word to Viśvāmitra (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Hariścandra's ordeal of truth
summary: To keep a promise to Viśvāmitra, King Hariścandra gives up his kingdom, sells his wife Śaibyā and son Rohitāśva and himself becomes the servant of a caṇḍāla at the cremation ground; when his wife brings their dead son there, the gods (Dharma, Indra) reveal the test and restore them.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Holikā and Prahlāda
summary: In the legend told for Holī, Holikā, sister of Hiraṇyakaśipu and immune to fire, sits in a pyre with the child Prahlāda to burn him; she burns and he survives. The Nārada Purāṇa's festival rubric names Holikā 'a rākṣasī who frightened Prahlāda', burned in the Phālguna full-moon bonfire — or, 'in another opinion', the burning of Kāma.

type:LABEL: place
name: Bhūmaṇḍala (the earth-disc of seven continents)
summary: In Purāṇic cosmography the flat, circular earth: seven ring-shaped continents (dvīpas), each twice the size of the last, separated by seven oceans, with Mount Meru at the centre of Jambudvīpa and the Lokāloka mountain at the rim.

type:LABEL: place
name: Jambudvīpa
summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: the central, innermost continent, named after its giant jambū (rose-apple) tree, with Meru at its centre; Bhāratavarṣa is its southern division.

type:LABEL: place
name: Plakṣadvīpa
summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: the second continent in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata lists, named after its plakṣa (fig) tree; absent from the Matsya list.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śālmalidvīpa
summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: continent named after its śālmali (silk-cotton) tree; third in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata lists, fifth in the Matsya.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kuśadvīpa
summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: continent named after its clump of kuśa grass; fourth in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata lists, third in the Matsya.

type:LABEL: place
name: Krauñcadvīpa
summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: continent named after Mount Krauñca; fifth in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata lists, fourth in the Matsya.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śākadvīpa
summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: continent named after its śāka (teak) tree, whose inhabitants worship Viṣṇu in the form of the Sun (ViP 2.4.70); later tradition derives the Śākadvīpīya (Maga) brāhmaṇa sun-priests from it; second in the Matsya list.

type:LABEL: place
name: Puṣkaradvīpa
summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: the outermost continent, divided by the ring-mountain Mānasottara and named after its great lotus (puṣkara), Brahmā's seat.

type:LABEL: place
name: Gomedakadvīpa
summary: In the Matsya Purāṇa's cosmography, the sixth continent (named after Mount Gomeda), which takes the place of Plakṣadvīpa in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata lists.

type:LABEL: place
name: Lavaṇoda (the Salt Ocean)
summary: One of the seven ring-oceans of Purāṇic cosmography: the salt ocean surrounding Jambudvīpa. The texts differ on which continent it encircles.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ikṣurasoda (the Ocean of Sugarcane Juice)
summary: One of the seven ring-oceans of Purāṇic cosmography: the ocean of sugarcane juice. The texts differ on which continent it encircles.

type:LABEL: place
name: Suroda (the Ocean of Wine)
summary: One of the seven ring-oceans of Purāṇic cosmography: the ocean of surā (wine/liquor). The texts differ on which continent it encircles.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ghṛtoda (the Ocean of Clarified Butter)
summary: One of the seven ring-oceans of Purāṇic cosmography: the ocean of ghee. The texts differ on which continent it encircles.

type:LABEL: place
name: Dadhimaṇḍoda (the Ocean of Curds/Whey)
summary: One of the seven ring-oceans of Purāṇic cosmography: the ocean of curd-water. The texts differ on which continent it encircles.

type:LABEL: place
name: Svādūdaka (the Ocean of Sweet Water)
summary: One of the seven ring-oceans of Purāṇic cosmography: the outermost ocean of fresh water, beyond which lies the golden land and the Lokāloka range. The texts differ on which continent it encircles.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mount Meru (Sumeru)
summary: The golden cosmic mountain at the centre of Jambudvīpa and of the earth-disc, around which the sun and stars revolve; the Viṣṇu Purāṇa gives it a height of 84,000 yojanas above ground and 16,000 below, 32,000 wide at the top and 16,000 at the base, like the pericarp of the earth-lotus.

type:LABEL: place
name: Bhāratavarṣa
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: the southern varṣa of Jambudvīpa, 'north of the ocean and south of the Himālaya, where the descendants of Bharata live' (ViP 2.3.1), the only 'land of action' (karmabhūmi); the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas name it after Bharata son of Ṛṣabha, the Mahābhārata's genealogy after Bharata son of Śakuntalā.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kiṃpuruṣavarṣa
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: the varṣa north of Bhārata, where (in the Bhāgavata) Hanumān worships Rāma.

type:LABEL: place
name: Harivarṣa
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: the third southern varṣa, where (in the Bhāgavata) Prahlāda worships Viṣṇu as Narasiṃha.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ilāvṛtavarṣa
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: the central varṣa around Meru, where (in the Bhāgavata) Śiva is the only male and worships Saṅkarṣaṇa.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ramyakavarṣa
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: a northern varṣa, where (in the Bhāgavata) Manu worships the Fish (Matsya).

type:LABEL: place
name: Hiraṇmayavarṣa
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: a northern varṣa, where (in the Bhāgavata) Aryaman worships the Tortoise (Kūrma).

type:LABEL: place
name: Uttarakuru
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: the northernmost varṣa, a land of long-lived, happy people, where (in the Bhāgavata) the Earth worships the Boar (Varāha).

type:LABEL: place
name: Bhadrāśvavarṣa
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: the varṣa east of Meru, where (in the Bhāgavata) Bhadraśravas worships Viṣṇu as Hayaśīrṣa (Hayagrīva).

type:LABEL: place
name: Ketumālavarṣa
summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: the varṣa west of Meru, where (in the Bhāgavata) Viṣṇu is worshipped in the form of Kāmadeva.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mānasottara (the ring-mountain of Puṣkaradvīpa)
summary: Circular mountain dividing Puṣkaradvīpa into an inner and outer half, over which the sun's chariot runs in the Bhāgavata's astronomy.

type:LABEL: place
name: Lokāloka (the world/no-world mountain)
summary: The ring-mountain at the edge of the earth-disc, beyond the ocean of sweet water and a golden land, dividing the lit world (loka) from the unlit (aloka).

type:LABEL: concept
name: The fourteen worlds (caturdaśa-bhuvana)
summary: The Purāṇic vertical cosmos of seven upper worlds — Bhūr (earth), Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapas and Satya — and seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas), whose names differ between texts.

type:LABEL: place
name: Bhūrloka (the earth)
summary: One of the seven upper worlds of Purāṇic cosmology: the earth, as far as sun and moon illumine it.

type:LABEL: place
name: Bhuvarloka (the atmosphere)
summary: One of the seven upper worlds of Purāṇic cosmology: the region between earth and sun, of the siddhas and munis.

type:LABEL: place
name: Svarloka (Svarga, heaven)
summary: One of the seven upper worlds of Purāṇic cosmology: the heaven of the gods between the sun and the pole star (Dhruva).

type:LABEL: place
name: Maharloka
summary: One of the seven upper worlds of Purāṇic cosmology: the world above the pole star, home of beings who live through a kalpa.

type:LABEL: place
name: Janaloka
summary: One of the seven upper worlds of Purāṇic cosmology: the world above Maharloka, of Brahmā's mind-born sons (Sanandana and others).

type:LABEL: place
name: Tapoloka
summary: One of the seven upper worlds of Purāṇic cosmology: the world of the ascetic Vairājas, four times higher above Janaloka.

type:LABEL: place
name: Satyaloka (Brahmaloka)
summary: One of the seven upper worlds of Purāṇic cosmology: the highest world, Brahmā's, from which there is no rebirth.

type:LABEL: place
name: Atala
summary: One of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas); paradisal subterranean realms of daityas, dānavas and nāgas.

type:LABEL: place
name: Vitala
summary: One of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas); paradisal subterranean realms of daityas, dānavas and nāgas.

type:LABEL: place
name: Nitala
summary: One of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas) (Viṣṇu Purāṇa list only); paradisal subterranean realms of daityas, dānavas and nāgas.

type:LABEL: place
name: Gabhastimat
summary: One of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas) (Viṣṇu Purāṇa list only); paradisal subterranean realms of daityas, dānavas and nāgas.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mahātala
summary: One of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas); paradisal subterranean realms of daityas, dānavas and nāgas.

type:LABEL: place
name: Sutala
summary: One of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas); paradisal subterranean realms of daityas, dānavas and nāgas. In the Bhāgavata, Bali dwells in Sutala after Vāmana's three strides.

type:LABEL: place
name: Talātala
summary: One of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas) (Bhāgavata list only); paradisal subterranean realms of daityas, dānavas and nāgas.

type:LABEL: place
name: Rasātala
summary: One of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas) (Bhāgavata list only); paradisal subterranean realms of daityas, dānavas and nāgas. Often used generically for the underworld, e.g. where Varāha finds the sunken earth.

type:LABEL: place
name: Pātāla (the netherworlds)
summary: The seven subterranean worlds below the earth, 'more delightful than heaven' (Nārada's report, ViP 2.5.5), with Śeṣa beneath them; also the name of the lowest of the seven.

type:LABEL: place
name: Naraka (the hells)
summary: The places of punishment below the netherworlds and above the waters, ruled by Yama, where sinners suffer for set periods before rebirth; the Viṣṇu Purāṇa names some twenty-eight with the sins that lead to each, the Bhāgavata twenty-eight (or twenty-one).

type:LABEL: place
name: Raurava
summary: One of the named hells (narakas): for liars (ViP) / for those who harm living beings, who are attacked by ruru creatures (BhP).

type:LABEL: place
name: Asipatravana (the sword-leaf forest)
summary: One of the named hells (narakas): a forest whose leaves are swords.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kṛmibhojana
summary: One of the named hells (narakas): where the sinner is eaten by worms or must eat them.

type:LABEL: place
name: Vaitaraṇī (the hell-river)
summary: One of the named hells (narakas): a river of filth, blood and pus at the border of Yama's realm.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kumbhīpāka
summary: One of the named hells (narakas): where those who cook living creatures are boiled in oil.

type:LABEL: place
name: Tāmisra
summary: One of the named hells (narakas): the first hell of the Bhāgavata, of darkness, for those who seize another's wealth, wife or children.

type:LABEL: place
name: Andhatāmisra
summary: One of the named hells (narakas): 'blinding darkness', for those who deceive a husband or wife.

type:LABEL: place
name: Vaikuṇṭha (Viṣṇu's world)
summary: The world of Viṣṇu, beyond the cosmos, attained by his devotees; the Bhāgavata describes its gates guarded by Jaya and Vijaya (3.15). In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa 'Vaikuṇṭha' is still chiefly a name of Viṣṇu himself (born of Vikuṇṭhā in the Cākṣuṣa manvantara, 3.1.41).

type:LABEL: place
name: Goloka (Kṛṣṇa's cow-world)
summary: The highest heaven of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā above Vaikuṇṭha in later Kṛṣṇaite Purāṇas (Brahmavaivarta, Nārada), absent from the Bhāgavata.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śvetadvīpa (the White Island)
summary: Island in the north of the Milk Ocean inhabited by white, radiant devotees of Nārāyaṇa, visited by Nārada in the Nārāyaṇīya; the Bhāgavata calls it Viṣṇu's beloved abode beside the Milk Ocean.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: text
name: Kalki Purāṇa
summary: A late Upapurāṇa narrating the future birth of Kalki in the village of Śambhala to Viṣṇuyaśas and Sumati, his education by Paraśurāma, his marriage and his destruction of the Kali age; probably composed in Bengal in the mid-second millennium CE.

type:LABEL: text
name: Saura Purāṇa
summary: A Śaiva Upapurāṇa despite its name ('of the Sun'), spoken by Sūrya; it praises Vārāṇasī and its liṅgas and includes Purūravas and Urvaśī (ch. 31). Hazra dated it between c. 950 and 1050 CE in north-western India.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ekāmra Purāṇa
summary: Odia-region Upapurāṇa (a sthala-purāṇa) glorifying Ekāmra-kṣetra — Bhubaneswar — and its Śiva as Kṛttivāsa (the Liṅgarāja), with the Bindusāgara tank and the surrounding shrines.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kāśīkhaṇḍa (Skanda Purāṇa 4)
summary: The fourth khaṇḍa of the printed Skanda Purāṇa, a hundred-chapter māhātmya of Kāśī (Vārāṇasī) as Śiva's royal city where death brings liberation, cataloguing its liṅgas, tīrthas and guardian deities; it reached its present form around the mid-13th century.

type:LABEL: text
name: Revākhaṇḍa (printed as Skanda Purāṇa 5.3; assigned to the Vāyu Purāṇa)
summary: The 232-chapter Revākhaṇḍa, a māhātmya of the Narmadā (Revā) and its tīrthas from Amarakaṇṭaka and Oṃkāra to the sea, printed since 1910 as Skanda Purāṇa 5.3; its GRETIL editor, J. Neuss, argues from the manuscripts that it originally belonged to the Vāyu Purāṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa (116 chapters)
summary: A shorter, 116-chapter Revākhaṇḍa of the Narmadā that its editor regards as the genuine Skanda Purāṇa Revākhaṇḍa, absent from the printed Skanda Purāṇa; it gives special place to Oṃkāra (e.g. RKS 47, 'oṃkāramahimānuvarṇana').

type:LABEL: claim
name: The 232-chapter Revākhaṇḍa printed as Skanda Purāṇa 5.3 belongs to the Vāyu Purāṇa
summary: According to its GRETIL editor Jürgen Neuss, all available manuscripts assign the long Revākhaṇḍa printed by the Veṅkaṭeśvara Press (1910) as Skanda Purāṇa 5.3 to the Vāyu Purāṇa; a distinct 116-chapter Revākhaṇḍa is the Skanda's own.

type:LABEL: text
name: Veṅkaṭācala Māhātmya (Skanda Purāṇa 2.1)
summary: The first section of the Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa of the printed Skanda Purāṇa, forty chapters glorifying the Veṅkaṭa hill (Tirumala) and its lord Śrīnivāsa/Veṅkaṭeśvara, opening with Nārada's vision of Yajñavarāha on Meru.

type:LABEL: text
name: Puruṣottamakṣetra (Jagannātha) Māhātmya (Skanda Purāṇa 2.2)
summary: Part of the printed Skanda Purāṇa: the second section of the Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa, glorifying Puruṣottama-kṣetra (Puri) and Jagannātha, including the story of King Indradyumna and the wooden image.

type:LABEL: text
name: Badarikāśrama Māhātmya (Skanda Purāṇa 2.3)
summary: Part of the printed Skanda Purāṇa: the third section of the Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa, glorifying Badarī, the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa in the Himālaya.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ayodhyā Māhātmya (Skanda Purāṇa 2.8)
summary: Part of the printed Skanda Purāṇa: the eighth section of the Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa, a guide to the tīrthas of Ayodhyā, critically edited and dated by Hans Bakker.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 103–112 (Prayāga-māhātmya)
summary: Ten chapters of the Matsya Purāṇa in which Mārkaṇḍeya tells Yudhiṣṭhira the glory of Prayāga, the confluence of Gaṅgā and Yamunā: bathing, dying and giving there bring liberation.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gayā Māhātmya (Vāyu Purāṇa 105–112)
summary: Māhātmya of Gayā, the pilgrimage centre for śrāddha offerings to the ancestors: the asura Gaya, on whose body the gods' sacrifice is performed, and Viṣṇu's footprint (Viṣṇupada) that pins him down. Transmitted as the last chapters of the Vāyu Purāṇa; critically edited by Claude Jacques (1962).

type:LABEL: text
name: Saromāhātmya of the Vāmana Purāṇa (Kurukṣetra-māhātmya)
summary: A māhātmya of the lake (saras) and tīrthas of Kurukṣetra, inserted after chapter 23 of the Vāmana Purāṇa in A. S. Gupta's edition: Kuru's ploughing, the Sarasvatī, and Śiva as Sthāṇu at Sthāṇvīśvara (Thanesar).

type:LABEL: character
name: Vikukṣi (Śaśāda)
summary: Eldest son of Ikṣvāku, expelled for eating a hare meant for the śrāddha offering and hence called Śaśāda ('hare-eater'); succeeds his father.

type:LABEL: character
name: Purañjaya (Kakutstha)
summary: Son of Vikukṣi who fights the asuras riding on Indra in the form of a bull, standing on its hump (kakud) — hence Kakutstha, eponym of the Kākutsthas.

type:LABEL: character
name: Anenas (son of Kakutstha)
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Purañjaya Kakutstha.

type:LABEL: character
name: Pṛthu (Ikṣvāku king, son of Anenas)
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Anenas; distinct from Pṛthu Vainya, son of Vena (char:prithu).

type:LABEL: character
name: Viśvagaśva (Viśvagandhi)
summary: Son of Pṛthu in the Ikṣvāku line; the Bhāgavata calls him Viśvagandhi.

type:LABEL: character
name: Cāndra (Candra), Ikṣvāku king
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Viśvagaśva/Viśvagandhi.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yuvanāśva (I), son of Cāndra
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Cāndra and father of Śrāvasta.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śrāvasta
summary: Ikṣvāku king who founded the city of Śrāvastī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bṛhadaśva (Ikṣvāku king)
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Śrāvasta and father of Kuvalayāśva; distinct from the sage Bṛhadaśva who tells Yudhiṣṭhira the Nala story.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kuvalayāśva (Dhundhumāra)
summary: Ikṣvāku king who, empowered by Viṣṇu's energy and with his 21,000 sons, killed the asura Dhundhu for the sage Uttaṅka and was called Dhundhumāra; all but three of his sons perished in Dhundhu's fiery breath.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Dṛḍhāśva
summary: One of the three sons of Kuvalayāśva who survived Dhundhu's fire; continues the line.

type:LABEL: character
name: Haryaśva (I), son of Dṛḍhāśva
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Dṛḍhāśva.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nikumbha (Ikṣvāku king)
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Haryaśva.

type:LABEL: character
name: Saṃhitāśva
summary: Son of Nikumbha in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's list; the Bhāgavata names Bahulāśva in this place.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bahulāśva
summary: Son of Nikumbha in the Bhāgavata's list, where the Viṣṇu Purāṇa has Saṃhitāśva.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛśāśva (Ikṣvāku king)
summary: Ikṣvāku king, father of Prasenajit/Senajit.

type:LABEL: character
name: Prasenajit (Senajit), Ikṣvāku king
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Kṛśāśva and father of Yuvanāśva II; the Bhāgavata calls him Senajit.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yuvanāśva (II), father of Māndhātṛ
summary: Sonless Ikṣvāku king who drinks by mistake the consecrated water meant for his queen and himself bears Māndhātṛ, who is born from his side and fed on Indra's finger.

type:LABEL: character
name: Purukutsa
summary: Son of Māndhātṛ who, taken to the netherworld by the river Narmadā, destroys the Mauneya gandharvas for the nāgas; father of Trasadasyu.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambarīṣa (son of Māndhātṛ)
summary: Son of Māndhātṛ, adopted by his grandfather (BhP); ancestor of the Hārīta brāhmaṇas. Distinct from Ambarīṣa son of Nābhāga (char:ambarisha).

type:LABEL: character
name: Yauvanāśva (son of Ambarīṣa)
summary: Son of Māndhātṛ's son Ambarīṣa and father of Harīta.

type:LABEL: character
name: Harīta (Hārīta), ancestor of the Hārītas
summary: Son of Yauvanāśva from whom the Āṅgirasa Hārītas descend.

type:LABEL: character
name: Trasadasyu (son of Purukutsa, Purāṇic genealogy)
summary: Son of Purukutsa and the Narmadā in the Purāṇic Ikṣvāku list. The Bhāgavata also gives the name Trasaddasyu to Māndhātṛ himself (9.6.33).

type:LABEL: character
name: Anaraṇya
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Trasadasyu, killed by Rāvaṇa on his campaign of conquest (Viṣṇu Purāṇa).

type:LABEL: character
name: Pṛṣadaśva (son of Anaraṇya)
summary: Son of Anaraṇya in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's list; absent from the Bhāgavata's.

type:LABEL: character
name: Haryaśva (II), descendant of Anaraṇya
summary: Ikṣvāku king: son of Pṛṣadaśva in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, son of Anaraṇya in the Bhāgavata.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vasumanas
summary: Son of Haryaśva in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's list; absent from the Bhāgavata's.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tridhanvan
summary: Son of Vasumanas and father of Trayyāruṇa in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's list.

type:LABEL: character
name: Trayyāruṇa
summary: Father of Satyavrata (Triśaṅku) in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's list.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aruṇa (Ikṣvāku king)
summary: Son of Haryaśva in the Bhāgavata's list.

type:LABEL: character
name: Tribandhana
summary: Son of Aruṇa and father of Satyavrata (Triśaṅku) in the Bhāgavata's list, where the Viṣṇu Purāṇa has Tridhanvan → Trayyāruṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Harita (son of Rohita)
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Rohita/Rohitāśva and grandson of Hariścandra.

type:LABEL: character
name: Cañcu
summary: Son of Harita in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa; father of Vijaya and Sudeva.

type:LABEL: character
name: Campa (founder of Campāpurī)
summary: Son of Harita in the Bhāgavata, founder of the city of Campā; father of Sudeva.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sudeva (Ikṣvāku king)
summary: Brother of Vijaya and son of Cañcu (ViP), or son of Campa and father of Vijaya (BhP).

type:LABEL: character
name: Vijaya (Ikṣvāku king)
summary: Son of Cañcu (ViP) or of Sudeva (BhP); father of Ruruka/Bharuka.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ruruka
summary: Son of Vijaya in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa; the Bhāgavata names Bharuka.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bharuka
summary: Son of Vijaya in the Bhāgavata, where the Viṣṇu Purāṇa names Ruruka.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vṛka (Ikṣvāku king)
summary: Father of Bāhu/Bāhuka.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bāhu (Bāhuka), father of Sagara
summary: Ikṣvāku king driven from his kingdom by the Haihayas and Tālajaṅghas, who dies near the hermitage of the sage Aurva while his pregnant queen, poisoned by a co-wife, carries Sagara ('born with poison').

type:LABEL: character
name: Śruta (son of Bhagīratha)
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Bhagīratha (who brought down the Gaṅgā), in both the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata lists.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nābhāga (son of Śruta)
summary: Son of Śruta in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's list; the Bhāgavata names 'another Nābha'.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ambarīṣa (son of Nābhāga son of Śruta)
summary: Ikṣvāku king in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's post-Bhagīratha list; not in the Bhāgavata's. Distinct from the devotee Ambarīṣa (char:ambarisha) and Māndhātṛ's son.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nābha (son of Śruta)
summary: Son of Śruta in the Bhāgavata ('another Nābha'), where the Viṣṇu Purāṇa has Nābhāga → Ambarīṣa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sindhudvīpa
summary: Ikṣvāku king, father of Ayutāyus.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ayutāyus
summary: Ikṣvāku king, father of Ṛtuparṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ṛtuparṇa
summary: Ikṣvāku king, friend of Nala, who knows the 'heart of dice' and exchanges it for Nala's horse-lore.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sarvakāma
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Ṛtuparṇa and father of Sudāsa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sudāsa (Ikṣvāku king, father of Saudāsa)
summary: Son of Sarvakāma and father of Saudāsa Mitrasaha; distinct from the Ṛgvedic Sudās (char:sudas).

type:LABEL: character
name: Saudāsa (Mitrasaha, Kalmāṣapāda)
summary: Ikṣvāku king cursed by Vasiṣṭha to become a man-eating rākṣasa for twelve years after being tricked into serving him human flesh; the curse-water burns his feet spotted (kalmāṣa). His son Aśmaka is begotten by Vasiṣṭha.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aśmaka
summary: Son of Saudāsa's queen (Madayantī) by Vasiṣṭha, born after seven years when she struck the womb with a stone (aśman).

type:LABEL: character
name: Mūlaka (Nārīkavaca)
summary: Son of Aśmaka, hidden among women when the earth was emptied of kṣatriyas (by Paraśurāma), hence 'woman-armoured' (Nārīkavaca).

type:LABEL: character
name: Daśaratha (son of Mūlaka)
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Mūlaka; distinct from Daśaratha father of Rāma (char:dasharatha).

type:LABEL: character
name: Ilivila (Aiḍaviḍi)
summary: Son of Daśaratha son of Mūlaka; the Bhāgavata calls him Aiḍaviḍi.

type:LABEL: character
name: Viśvasaha
summary: Ikṣvāku king, father of Khaṭvāṅga (Dilīpa).

type:LABEL: character
name: Dhundhu
summary: Asura, son of Madhu and Kaiṭabha in the Mahābhārata, who sleeps beneath the sands near the hermitage of Uttaṅka and shakes the earth with his breath; killed by Kuvalayāśva.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kuvalayāśva kills Dhundhu (Dhundhumāra)
summary: At the request of the sage Uttaṅka, King Kuvalayāśva, empowered by Viṣṇu, digs out the asura Dhundhu from the desert sands with his sons and kills him, though the asura's fiery breath consumes all but three of the sons; the king is thereafter called Dhundhumāra.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The birth of Māndhātṛ from his father's body
summary: The sonless King Yuvanāśva, thirsty in the night, drinks the water the sages had consecrated for his queen; he conceives, the child is born from his side, and Indra lets him suck his finger, saying 'He will suck me' (māṃ dhāsyati) — whence the name Māndhātṛ.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Saudāsa becomes the man-eater Kalmāṣapāda
summary: Tricked by a rākṣasa disguised as Vasiṣṭha, King Saudāsa Mitrasaha serves his guru human flesh and is cursed to be a man-eating rākṣasa for twelve years; his curse-water, thrown on his own feet, spots them (Kalmāṣapāda). As a rākṣasa he devours a brāhmaṇa and is cursed by the widow; Vasiṣṭha later begets Aśmaka on his queen.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: collection
name: Mahāpurāṇas
summary: The conventional set of eighteen 'great' Purāṇas. The tradition agrees on the number eighteen but not on the membership: lists such as Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6 and Bhāgavata 12.7 name a Śaiva Purāṇa where the Matsya and Nārada lists name the Vāyu (the Kūrma names both).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Upapurāṇas
summary: 'Secondary' Purāṇas, also conventionally eighteen, whose lists disagree even more than those of the Mahāpurāṇas; several (Viṣṇudharmottara, Kālikā, Narasiṃha, Devī Bhāgavata in some lists) are as old or as influential as Mahāpurāṇas.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Dharmaśāstra
summary: The Sanskrit genre of normative treatises on dharma (Manu, Yājñavalkya, Nārada, Viṣṇu and others), together with their commentaries and digests; included here because Manusmṛti 1 supplies one of the earliest yuga reckonings.

type:LABEL: text
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa of six books (aṃśas), narrated by Parāśara to Maitreya, often taken as the Purāṇa that best preserves the five 'marks' (pañcalakṣaṇa); book 5 is a sustained life of Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa
summary: The most influential Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, in twelve books (skandhas), narrated by Śuka to King Parīkṣit; its tenth book on Kṛṣṇa's life became a foundation of later Kṛṣṇa devotion, and 1.3.28 declares Kṛṣṇa 'Bhagavān himself'.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śiva Purāṇa
subtype: Mahāpurāṇa (contested; some lists give the Vāyu instead)
summary: A large Śaiva compilation organised in saṃhitās (seven in the common Bombay text: Vidyeśvara, Rudra, Śatarudra, Koṭirudra, Umā, Kailāsa, Vāyavīya) that narrates Śiva's manifestations, the Liṅgodbhava and Śaiva ritual.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vāyu Purāṇa
summary: One of the oldest Purāṇas, Śaiva in orientation and closely parallel to the Brahmāṇḍa (the two are thought to derive from one original); the Mahābhārata (CE 3.189.14) already refers to a purāṇa 'proclaimed by Vāyu'.

type:LABEL: text
name: Liṅga Purāṇa
summary: A Śaiva Mahāpurāṇa centred on the liṅga as Śiva's form; it narrates the Liṅgodbhava, in which Brahmā as a swan and Viṣṇu as a boar fail to find the ends of a fiery pillar (1.17), and prescribes how the scene is to be sculpted (1.76.60–61).

type:LABEL: text
name: Skanda Purāṇa
summary: The largest Purāṇa by reputation (81,100 verses per BhP 12.13.7), known in print as a vast compendium of khaṇḍas (Māheśvara, Vaiṣṇava, Brahma, Kāśī, Avantī, Nāgara, Prabhāsa) rich in tīrtha-māhātmyas; scholars distinguish it from the much earlier 'original' Skandapurāṇa preserved in Nepalese manuscripts.

type:LABEL: text
name: Skandapurāṇa (early recension, Nepalese manuscripts)
aliases: Original Skandapurāṇa|Ambikākhaṇḍa (colophon title in some MSS)
summary: The 'original' Skandapurāṇa, a Pāśupata-milieu Śaiva Purāṇa composed probably in the late 6th or early 7th century (perhaps at Vārāṇasī) and transmitted in Nepalese palm-leaf manuscripts, one of which, dated 810 CE, is the oldest dated Purāṇa manuscript known; it is being critically edited by the Groningen–Leiden Skandapurāṇa project.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa
summary: A comparatively non-sectarian and probably early Mahāpurāṇa narrated by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya to the wise birds; it contains the Devī Māhātmya (chapters 81–93 in the common text).

type:LABEL: text
name: Devī Māhātmya
summary: A 13-chapter, c. 700-verse glorification of the Goddess embedded in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in which a supreme Goddess slays Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣāsura and Śumbha–Niśumbha; Coburn calls it the 'crystallization' of the Goddess tradition.

type:LABEL: text
name: Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa
summary: An early Mahāpurāṇa closely parallel to the Vāyu (both probably descend from one source); its extant versions embed later works such as the Lalitopākhyāna and, in some printings, the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Matsya Purāṇa
summary: A Mahāpurāṇa presented as taught by Viṣṇu in fish form to Manu (1.10–2.19); it preserves a detailed list of the eighteen Purāṇas with verse counts and the five marks (53), the doctrine of ten manifestations caused by Bhṛgu's curse (47), and Satī's 108 tīrtha-names (13).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kūrma Purāṇa
summary: A Mahāpurāṇa said to be taught by Viṣṇu as the tortoise; though framed as Vaiṣṇava it is strongly Śaiva in content (including the Īśvara Gītā) and its list of the Purāṇas names both a Śaiva (fourth) and a Vāyavīya (after the Gāruḍa).

type:LABEL: text
name: Vāmana Purāṇa
summary: A Mahāpurāṇa named after the dwarf avatāra that, despite its title, treats Śiva and the Goddess extensively (including a version of Dakṣa's sacrifice and the slaying of Mahiṣa); critically edited by A. S. Gupta (1967).

type:LABEL: text
name: Varāha Purāṇa
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa framed as Varāha's teaching to the Earth whom he has rescued; largely concerned with vows, ritual and tīrthas (notably Mathurā), and generally regarded as relatively late.

type:LABEL: text
name: Garuḍa Purāṇa
summary: An encyclopaedic Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa taught by Viṣṇu to Garuḍa, best known for its section on death and the afterlife (Pretakalpa); its opening avatāra list (1.1.14–33) reproduces Bhāgavata 1.3 almost verbatim, and 1.86.10–11 gives a ten-avatāra list.

type:LABEL: text
name: Padma Purāṇa
summary: A very large Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa (55,000 verses per BhP 12.13.4) extant in divergent Bengal and Devanāgarī recensions arranged in khaṇḍas; widely cited for its classification of the Purāṇas by the three guṇas.

type:LABEL: text
name: Agni Purāṇa
summary: An encyclopaedic Mahāpurāṇa taught by Agni to Vasiṣṭha; it opens with the avatāras of Viṣṇu (chapters 2–16, using the expression daśāvatāra) and gives iconographic rules for the ten (49), alongside chapters on ritual, polity, medicine, poetics and grammar.

type:LABEL: text
name: Brahma Purāṇa
summary: Counted 'first of all Purāṇas' (ViP 3.6.20), the extant Brahma Purāṇa is largely a compilation of tīrtha material for Orissa (Puruṣottama/Puri, Koṇārka) and the Godāvarī, much of it borrowed from other Purāṇas and generally dated late.

type:LABEL: text
name: Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa
summary: A Kṛṣṇa-centred Mahāpurāṇa in four khaṇḍas (Brahma, Prakṛti, Gaṇapati, Kṛṣṇajanma) in which Rādhā is an exalted cosmic consort; its extant form is largely a 15th–16th-century Bengal recasting of an older work.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nārada Purāṇa
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa (also Nāradīya; distinct from the Bṛhannāradīya Upapurāṇa) whose Pūrvabhāga contains a detailed synopsis (anukramaṇī) of all eighteen Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhaviṣya Purāṇa
summary: The 'Purāṇa of the future', a heterogeneous compilation with an early core on vows and Sun worship (shared with the Sāmba Purāṇa) and a Pratisargaparvan that 'prophesies' Mughal and even British-era history — accretions dated to the 18th–19th centuries.

type:LABEL: text
name: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa
summary: A twelve-book Śākta Purāṇa that reworks the Bhāgavata model around the Goddess as supreme reality; Śāktas count it as the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata', while most lists and scholars treat it as an Upapurāṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Manusmṛti
summary: The most influential Dharmaśāstra, a verse treatise presented as Manu's (and Bhṛgu's) teaching; its first chapter gives a cosmogony and a yuga reckoning of 12,000 years for the four ages (1.68–73), the base of the Purāṇic scheme.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kālikā Purāṇa
summary: A Śākta Upapurāṇa from the Kāmarūpa (Assam–north Bengal) region that glorifies the goddess Kāmākhyā, prescribes her worship including animal sacrifice, and tells how parts of Satī's corpse fell to earth, Kāmarūpa receiving her yoni.

type:LABEL: text
name: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa
summary: An encyclopaedic Vaiṣṇava Upapurāṇa, associated with Kashmir, whose third book contains the Citrasūtra, the most detailed early Sanskrit treatise on painting and image-making, with iconographic rules for many deities.

type:LABEL: text
name: Narasiṃha Purāṇa
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Upapurāṇa (already named as an 'upabheda' of 18,000 verses in Matsya 53.60) devoted to Narasiṃha; its Prahlāda narrative occupies chapters 40–44 of the Jena edition.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sāmba Purāṇa
summary: A Saura Upapurāṇa (named among the upabhedas in Matsya 53.62) narrating how Kṛṣṇa's son Sāmba, cured of leprosy by the Sun, installed Sun worship with Maga priests from Śākadvīpa; it shares material with the Bhaviṣya.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gaṇeśa Purāṇa
summary: A Gāṇapatya Upapurāṇa in two parts (Upāsanā- and Krīḍā-khaṇḍa) that presents Gaṇeśa as the supreme deity and includes the Gaṇeśa Gītā; usually dated to the first half of the 2nd millennium.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mudgala Purāṇa
summary: A Gāṇapatya Upapurāṇa organised around eight incarnations of Gaṇeśa (Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadanta, Mahodara, Gajānana, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnarāja, Dhūmravarṇa) who conquer personified vices.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āryabhaṭīya
summary: Āryabhaṭa's astronomical treatise (499 CE), which states that he was 23 years old when 3,600 years of the Kali age had elapsed (3.10) — the basis of the later standard computation of the Kali epoch to 3102 BCE; it divides the mahāyuga into four equal quarters (3.10, cf. 1.5).

type:LABEL: text
name: Amarakośa
summary: Amarasiṃha's Sanskrit thesaurus (c. 5th–7th c. CE), which glosses purāṇa as 'pañcalakṣaṇam' (1.6.5) — an early datable witness to the five-mark definition.

type:LABEL: text
name: Devī Gītā
summary: The 'Song of the Goddess', chapters 7.31–40 of the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa, in which the Goddess teaches Himālaya, modelled on the Bhagavad Gītā.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Viṣṇu
summary: A Vedic god of the three strides who in the epics and Purāṇas becomes, for Vaiṣṇavas, the supreme being who preserves the world and descends in avatāras; the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas are his principal Purāṇic scriptures.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Nārāyaṇa
summary: A cosmic deity whose name is interpreted as 'resting on the waters'; first prominent in late Vedic texts and the Mahābhārata's Nārāyaṇīya, he is identified with Viṣṇu and Vāsudeva and is the sleeping god from whose navel Brahmā is born.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Śiva
summary: The great god of Śaiva traditions, identified, from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad onward, with the Vedic Rudra; in the Purāṇas he is the ascetic and householder of Kailāsa, destroyer of Tripura and of Dakṣa's sacrifice, and, in the Liṅgodbhava, the infinite pillar of fire beyond Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Brahmā
summary: The four-faced creator god of the Purāṇas, born on the lotus from Viṣṇu's navel in Vaiṣṇava accounts; his cult declined, and Purāṇic myths such as the Liṅgodbhava often show him humbled.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Devī (the Goddess)
summary: The Great Goddess (Mahādevī) of Śākta theology, conceived as the supreme power (śakti) of whom all goddesses are forms; the Devī Māhātmya (c. 5th–6th c.) is the first Sanskrit text to present her as supreme.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Durgā
summary: The warrior form of the Goddess, above all as slayer of the buffalo-demon Mahiṣa (Mahiṣāsuramardinī); the Devī Māhātmya describes her formation from the gods' collected radiance and her arming with their weapons.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Pārvatī
summary: Daughter of the mountain Himavat and wife of Śiva, mother of Skanda and Gaṇeśa; Purāṇas present her as the rebirth of Dakṣa's daughter Satī who wins Śiva by asceticism.
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Lakṣmī
summary: Goddess of fortune, prosperity and royal glory (Śrī), consort of Viṣṇu; in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas she rises from the churned Ocean of Milk and chooses Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kālī
summary: The dark, terrifying form of the Goddess who in the Devī Māhātmya springs from Ambikā's brow to slay Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (and is then named Cāmuṇḍā) and drinks the blood of Raktabīja.
earliest_material: 9th–10th c. CE (traditionally c. 864 under Queen Hīrādevī)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Gaṇeśa
summary: Elephant-headed god of beginnings and remover of obstacles, son of Pārvatī (and Śiva); the Purāṇas give competing accounts of his birth and head, and Gāṇapatya Upapurāṇas make him supreme.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Skanda
summary: Warrior son of Śiva (born in the epics and Purāṇas with the help of Agni, Gaṅgā and the Kṛttikās), general of the gods and slayer of the demon Tāraka; the early Skandapurāṇa is named after him.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Gaṅgā
summary: The goddess of the Ganges, brought down from heaven by Bhagīratha's austerities and caught in Śiva's hair; she also appears as mother of Bhīṣma and as one of Skanda's nurses.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Matsya
summary: The fish avatāra of Viṣṇu who saves Manu (and the seeds of creatures, or the Vedas) from the flood; in the earlier Śatapatha and Mahābhārata versions the fish is unnamed or identifies itself as Brahmā.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kūrma
summary: The tortoise avatāra who supports Mount Mandara during the churning of the ocean; in the Mahābhārata critical text the supporting tortoise is the 'king of tortoises' Akūpāra, not Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Varāha
summary: The boar avatāra who dives into the cosmic waters to raise the Earth; the image of the boar-headed god lifting Bhūdevī (e.g. Udayagiri, early 5th c.) is among the earliest monumental avatāra sculptures.
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: deity
name: Narasiṃha
summary: The man-lion avatāra who emerges from a pillar to kill the demon-king Hiraṇyakaśipu at twilight, on the threshold, with his claws, circumventing the demon's boon and protecting his devotee Prahlāda.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vāmana
summary: The dwarf avatāra, born to Aditi, who asks the asura king Bali for three steps of land and, growing into Trivikrama, recovers the three worlds; the myth develops the Ṛgvedic three strides of Viṣṇu.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: deity
name: Mohinī
summary: The enchantress form taken by Viṣṇu to distribute the nectar of immortality to the gods rather than the asuras; in Śaiva and later Purāṇic myth she is also the mother, with Śiva, of Ayyappa/Hariharaputra.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: deity
name: Dhanvantari
summary: The physician of the gods who emerges from the churned ocean carrying the pot of nectar; the Bhāgavata counts him among Viṣṇu's avatāras (12th) and as founder of Āyurveda.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: deity
name: Hayagrīva (Hayaśiras)
summary: The horse-headed form of Viṣṇu who recovers the Vedas; the Nārāyaṇīya names the Haṃsa and Hayaśiras manifestations (MBh CE 12.326.94), and the Bhāgavata lists Hayaśīrṣa among the descents (2.7.11). Distinct from the demon Hayagrīva of BhP 8.24.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: deity
name: Dattātreya
summary: Son of Atri and Anasūyā counted as an avatāra of Viṣṇu (BhP 1.3.11; 2.7.4; HV 31.93) and as a teacher of yoga; later traditions treat him as a joint form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Śeṣa (Ananta)
summary: The cosmic serpent on whom Viṣṇu reclines between creations; in MBh (CE) 1.16.6–7 Ananta uproots Mount Mandara for the churning, and Balarāma is regarded as his incarnation in many texts.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vīrabhadra
summary: The fierce being created by Śiva from a lock of his matted hair to destroy Dakṣa's sacrifice after Satī's death (BhP 4.5.2–3).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Cāmuṇḍā
summary: The name given to Kālī after she brings the heads of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa to the Goddess (DM 7 = MkP 87.26); she is also one of the Seven Mothers (Saptamātṛkā) in DM 8.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kauśikī (Ambikā)
summary: The radiant goddess who issues from the body-sheath (kośa) of Pārvatī in DM 5 (MkP 85.40–44) and confronts Śumbha and Niśumbha; the Harivaṃśa already foretells a Kauśikī, dwelling on the Vindhya, who will slay them.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vindhyavāsinī (Nidrā/Ekānaṃśā)
summary: The goddess Nidrā ('Sleep') whom Viṣṇu sends to be born of Yaśodā as Kṛṣṇa's substitute; the Harivaṃśa foretells that she will have an eternal seat on the Vindhya, love meat-offerings and be worshipped on the ninth lunar day.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Kāmākhyā
summary: The goddess worshipped in the yoni-shaped rock at Nīlācala near Guwahati, glorified in the Kālikā Purāṇa as the place where Satī's yoni fell.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Garuḍa
summary: The king of birds, son of Vinatā and enemy of serpents, who becomes Viṣṇu's mount; the Garuḍa Purāṇa is framed as Viṣṇu's teaching to him, and the Heliodorus pillar (2nd c. BCE) was a garuḍadhvaja for Vāsudeva.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Nandin (Nandī)
summary: Śiva's bull mount and chief attendant (gaṇa), represented as a seated bull facing the liṅga in Śaiva temples; earlier texts also know a theriomorphic bull of Śiva (Vṛṣabhadhvaja).

type:LABEL: character
name: Paraśurāma
summary: Rāma 'with the axe', the Bhārgava son of Jamadagni and Reṇukā who exterminated the kṣatriyas twenty-one times; counted as Viṣṇu's avatāra in the Nārāyaṇīya, Harivaṃśa, Bhāgavata (16th) and in the standard ten (6th).

type:LABEL: character
name: Kalki
summary: The avatāra expected at the end of the Kali age, born to the brahmin Viṣṇuyaśas in the village of Śambhala, who will ride a horse, destroy the wicked and restore the Kṛta age.

type:LABEL: character
name: Prahlāda
summary: Son of the demon-king Hiraṇyakaśipu who, despite persecution, remains devoted to Viṣṇu; his father's death at the hands of Narasiṃha and his teaching make him the model devotee of the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: character
name: Hiraṇyakaśipu
summary: Daitya king, son of Kaśyapa and Diti, who by Brahmā's boon could be killed by neither man nor beast, by day nor night, inside nor outside; Narasiṃha kills him for persecuting his son Prahlāda.

type:LABEL: character
name: Hiraṇyākṣa
summary: Daitya brother of Hiraṇyakaśipu who drags the Earth into the cosmic waters; he is slain by Varāha (BhP 3.17–19; MBh CE 12.326.73).

type:LABEL: character
name: Bali (Mahābali)
summary: Asura king, grandson of Prahlāda and son of Virocana, who conquered the three worlds and gave Vāmana three steps of land; sent to the netherworld Sutala, he is promised Viṣṇu's protection (BhP 8.22.35). In Kerala he is remembered at Onam as Māveli.

type:LABEL: character
name: Dhruva
summary: Prince, son of Uttānapāda and Sunīti, who, slighted by his stepmother Suruci, performed austerities as a child and was granted the immovable station of the Pole Star.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mārkaṇḍeya
summary: Long-lived sage who survives the cosmic dissolution and narrates the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and the Devī Māhātmya; in the Mahābhārata he recounts the flood of Manu and the yugas to Yudhiṣṭhira (MBh CE 3.185–189).
earliest_textual: within the epic’s growth, c. 3rd century BCE – 3rd century CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Nārada
summary: Divine sage and musician who carries news between worlds; the Nārāyaṇīya has him receive the Pāñcarātra revelation at Śvetadvīpa, and the Bhāgavata counts him as Viṣṇu's third descent (BhP 1.3.8).

type:LABEL: character
name: Dakṣa
summary: A Prajāpati, father of many daughters including Satī; his sacrifice, from which he excludes Śiva, is destroyed by Śiva's forces (Vīrabhadra), and he is given a goat's head in several Purāṇic versions.

type:LABEL: character
name: Satī
summary: Daughter of Dakṣa and first wife of Śiva, who gives up her body at her father's sacrifice; Purāṇas treat her as reborn as Pārvatī, and Śākta texts derive the pīṭhas from her.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mahiṣāsura
summary: The buffalo demon who, having conquered the gods and become 'Indra', is slain by the Goddess formed from their combined radiance (DM 2–3 = MkP 82–83).

type:LABEL: character
name: Manu (Vaivasvata)
summary: Son of Vivasvat (the Sun), the Manu of the present (seventh) manvantara and progenitor of humanity, saved from the flood by the fish; the Bhāgavata identifies him with the royal sage Satyavrata, lord of the Draviḍas.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)
earliest_material: regnal year 6 of Rājendra I = c. 1018 CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhagīratha
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Dilīpa, whose austerities brought the Gaṅgā down to earth to purify the ashes of his ancestors, the sons of Sagara; hence her name Bhāgīrathī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Sagara
summary: Ikṣvāku king 'born with poison' whose sixty thousand sons, searching for his sacrificial horse, dug out the ocean (sāgara) and were burned by the sage Kapila; his descendants' quest leads to the descent of the Gaṅgā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Hariścandra
summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Triśaṅku, proverbial for truthfulness; in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa he loses kingdom, wife and son to keep his word to Viśvāmitra. The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa's Hariścandra (Śunaḥśepa story) is an earlier tradition.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yayāti
summary: King of the Lunar line, son of Nahuṣa, husband of Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā; cursed with old age by Śukra (Kāvya), he exchanged it for his son Pūru's youth and divided the earth among his five sons.

type:LABEL: character
name: Gajendra
summary: The lord of elephants on Mount Trikūṭa, seized by a crocodile in a lake, who prays to the supreme being and is freed by Hari arriving on Garuḍa; formerly the Pāṇḍya king Indradyumna (BhP 8.2–4).

type:LABEL: character
name: Madhu
summary: One of the two demons born from Viṣṇu's ear-wax during his cosmic sleep who threaten Brahmā; Viṣṇu slays them after the Goddess (as Yoganidrā) releases him (DM 1).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaiṭabha
summary: Madhu's companion demon in DM 1; with Madhu he is slain by Viṣṇu (hence Viṣṇu's epithet Madhusūdana / Kaiṭabhajit).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Śumbha
summary: Asura king who, with his brother Niśumbha, conquers the gods and seeks the Goddess in marriage; she slays him in DM 10 (MkP 90). The Harivaṃśa already predicts their death at the hands of Vindhyavāsinī (HV CE 47.49).

type:LABEL: character
name: Niśumbha
summary: Younger brother of Śumbha, slain by the Goddess in DM 9 (MkP 89).

type:LABEL: character
name: Caṇḍa
summary: Asura general of Śumbha, beheaded with Muṇḍa by Kālī (DM 7 = MkP 87).

type:LABEL: character
name: Muṇḍa
summary: Asura general paired with Caṇḍa, slain by Kālī; their names yield the epithet Cāmuṇḍā (MkP 87.26).

type:LABEL: character
name: Raktabīja
summary: Asura from each drop of whose blood a new demon arose; Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā drinks his blood so the Goddess can slay him (DM 8 = MkP 88).

type:LABEL: character
name: Tāraka
summary: Asura made invincible except by a son of Śiva; his oppression of the gods motivates Śiva's marriage to Pārvatī and the birth of Skanda, who slays him. The Matsya counts the Tārakāmaya war fifth of twelve deva–asura wars (47.43).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Andhaka
summary: Blind asura, in Śaiva myth Śiva's own son adopted by Hiraṇyākṣa, who desires Pārvatī and is impaled on Śiva's trident, then made a gaṇa; the Matsya counts the Andhaka war eighth (47.44).

type:LABEL: character
name: Hayagrīva (the demon)
summary: Dānava who steals the Vedas from Brahmā's mouths at the end of a kalpa and is slain by Viṣṇu as Matsya (BhP 8.24.8, 8.24.57); distinct from Viṣṇu's horse-headed form.

type:LABEL: character
name: Rāhu
summary: Dānava who drinks the nectar disguised as a god; the Sun and Moon expose him, Viṣṇu severs his head with the discus, and his undying head pursues them, causing eclipses (MBh CE 1.17.4–8).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Virocana
summary: Asura son of Prahlāda and father of Bali (MBh CE 12.326.74).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Śukra (Kāvya, Uśanas)
summary: Bhārgava preceptor of the asuras, father of Devayānī; his curse ages Yayāti (ViP 4.10.5) and he warns Bali against Vāmana.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kapila
summary: Sage, traditional founder of Sāṃkhya, counted the fifth descent in BhP 1.3.10; Sagara's sons, accusing him of stealing their father's horse, are burned by his glance (BhP 9.8.10; ViP 4.4).

type:LABEL: character
name: Jamadagni
summary: Bhārgava sage, father of Paraśurāma, killed by the sons of Kārtavīrya Arjuna.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kārtavīrya Arjuna
summary: Thousand-armed Haihaya king slain by Paraśurāma (HV CE 31.101; BhP 9.15).

type:LABEL: character
name: Suratha
summary: Dispossessed king of the Devī Māhātmya's frame story who, with the merchant Samādhi, learns of the Goddess from the sage Medhas and receives a boon to become the next Manu, Sāvarṇi (DM 1, 13).

type:LABEL: character
name: Medhas
summary: The sage (ṛṣi) who narrates the Devī Māhātmya to Suratha and Samādhi.

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyavrata
summary: Royal sage, lord of the Draviḍas, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, who catches a small fish in the Kṛtamālā river and becomes Vaivasvata Manu 'in this kalpa' (BhP 8.24.10–13, 58); kept as a separate id because only the Bhāgavata makes the identification.

type:LABEL: character
name: Indradyumna (Pāṇḍya king)
summary: Pāṇḍya king, 'best of the Draviḍas', devoted to Viṣṇu, cursed by Agastya to become the elephant Gajendra (BhP 8.4.7–11). Distinct from the Indradyumna of the Puri temple legend.

type:LABEL: character
name: Hūhū
summary: Gandharva cursed by Devala to become the crocodile that seized Gajendra; freed when Hari killed the crocodile (BhP 8.4.3).

type:LABEL: character
name: Viṣṇuyaśas
summary: The brahmin of Śambhala in whose house Kalki is to be born (BhP 12.2.18; HV CE 31.148).

type:LABEL: character
name: Buddha (as avatāra of Viṣṇu)
summary: The Buddha as he appears in Purāṇic avatāra lists — a descent of Viṣṇu 'to delude the enemies of the gods' (BhP 1.3.24), the ninth of the standard ten. This id represents the Purāṇic figure; the historical Buddha and the Buddhist traditions are separate.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ikṣvāku
summary: Eldest son of Vaivasvata Manu and founder of the Solar dynasty at Ayodhyā (ViP 3.1.33; BhP 8.13.2; VR CE 1.69.19).
earliest_material: regnal year 6 of Rājendra I = c. 1018 CE

type:LABEL: character
name: Triśaṅku
summary: Ikṣvāku king, father of Hariścandra (ViP 4.3.17), who sought to ascend bodily to heaven with Viśvāmitra's help.

type:LABEL: character
name: Rohita (Rohitāśva)
summary: Son of Hariścandra (ViP 4.3.17 'rohitāśva').

type:LABEL: character
name: Māndhātṛ
summary: Ikṣvāku universal monarch, son of Yuvanāśva (VR CE 1.69.22); the Matsya counts him the fifth of Viṣṇu's seven human manifestations due to Bhṛgu's curse (47.242).

type:LABEL: character
name: Asamañjas
summary: Son of Sagara and father of Aṃśumat (VR CE 1.69.25; ViP 4.4).

type:LABEL: character
name: Aṃśumat
summary: Grandson of Sagara who found the sacrificial horse near Kapila and was told that his grandson would bring down the Gaṅgā (ViP 4.4.18–24).

type:LABEL: character
name: Dilīpa
summary: Name of more than one Ikṣvāku king: Dilīpa son of Aṃśumat and father of Bhagīratha (ViP 4.4.24–25; VR 1.69.26), and Dilīpa Khaṭvāṅga, ancestor of Raghu in ViP 4.4.47–49. This id is the father of Bhagīratha.
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: character
name: Khaṭvāṅga (Dilīpa)
summary: Ikṣvāku king who, told he had one muhūrta to live, merged himself in Vāsudeva (ViP 4.4.47); father of Dīrghabāhu and ancestor of Raghu (ViP 4.4.49; BhP 9.10.1).

type:LABEL: character
name: Dīrghabāhu
summary: Son of Khaṭvāṅga and father of Raghu in ViP 4.4.49 and BhP 9.10.1.

type:LABEL: character
name: Raghu
summary: Ikṣvāku king after whom the line is called Raghuvaṃśa; grandfather of Rāma via Aja in ViP 4.4.49 and BhP 9.10.1, but placed much earlier, as son of Kakutstha, in VR (CE) 1.69.26.
earliest_textual: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

type:LABEL: character
name: Aja
summary: Father of Daśaratha: son of Raghu in ViP 4.4.49 and BhP 9.10.1, but son of Nābhāga in VR (CE) 1.69.30.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nābhāga (Vālmīki's genealogy)
summary: In VR (CE) 1.69.30 the son of Yayāti and father of Aja; kept distinct from the Nābhāga son of Manu (BhP 8.13.2) because the identity of homonymous kings across lists is not established.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ilā
summary: Child of Manu's sacrifice, alternately female and male (Sudyumna); as Ilā she bears Purūravas to Budha, linking the Solar and Lunar lines (ViP 4.1.10–13).

type:LABEL: character
name: Budha
summary: Son of Soma (the Moon) and Tārā, the planet Mercury; father of Purūravas by Ilā (ViP 4.1.12–13; 4.6).

type:LABEL: character
name: Āyu
summary: Eldest son of Purūravas and Urvaśī (ViP 4.7.1; 4.8.1), father of Nahuṣa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nahuṣa
summary: Lunar king, son of Āyu, who for a time replaced Indra and was cursed to become a serpent; father of Yayāti (ViP 4.8.2; 4.10.1; BhP 9.18.3). The Vālmīki genealogy also has a Nahuṣa among Rāma's ancestors (VR CE 1.69.29).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Devayānī
summary: Daughter of Śukra, wife of Yayāti and mother of Yadu and Turvasu (ViP 4.10.4; BhP 9.18.33).

type:LABEL: character
name: Śarmiṣṭhā
summary: Daughter of the asura king Vṛṣaparvan, wife of Yayāti and mother of Druhyu, Anu and Pūru (ViP 4.10.4; BhP 9.18.33).

type:LABEL: character
name: Yadu
summary: Eldest son of Yayāti and Devayānī, ancestor of the Yādavas (and thus of Kṛṣṇa); denied the succession for refusing his father's old age.

type:LABEL: character
name: Turvasu
summary: Son of Yayāti and Devayānī (ViP 4.10.4).

type:LABEL: character
name: Druhyu
summary: Son of Yayāti and Śarmiṣṭhā (ViP 4.10.4).

type:LABEL: character
name: Anu
summary: Son of Yayāti and Śarmiṣṭhā (ViP 4.10.4).

type:LABEL: character
name: Pūru
summary: Youngest son of Yayāti and Śarmiṣṭhā who accepted his father's old age and inherited the central kingdom; ancestor of the Pauravas, Bharatas and Kurus.

type:LABEL: character
name: Pṛthu
summary: King Pṛthu Vainya, son of Vena, who 'milked' the earth of plants and resources; counted as the ninth descent in BhP 1.3.14.

type:LABEL: character
name: Uttānapāda
summary: Son of Svāyambhuva Manu and father of Dhruva by Sunīti and of Uttama by Suruci (ViP 1.11).

type:LABEL: character
name: Ṛṣabha
summary: Son of Nābhi and Merudevī, an ascetic king counted as the eighth descent in BhP 1.3.13 (and 2.7.10); Jain tradition knows Ṛṣabha as the first Tīrthaṅkara — the relation between the two is a matter of scholarly discussion.

type:LABEL: character
name: Durgā's lion
summary: The lion (siṃha) given to the Goddess by Himavat (DM 2 = MkP 82.29), on which she rides as Siṃhavāhinī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Skanda's peacock
summary: The peacock (mayūra) that serves as Skanda's mount; in the Mahābhārata it is a gift to the young god (recall), and later iconography almost always shows it.

type:LABEL: character
name: Mūṣaka (Gaṇeśa's mouse)
summary: The mouse or rat that serves as Gaṇeśa's mount, sometimes interpreted as a subdued demon (e.g. Gajamukha/Krauñca in later Purāṇic tellings).

type:LABEL: character
name: Brahmā's haṃsa
summary: The swan/goose that is Brahmā's mount; in the Liṅgodbhava Brahmā himself becomes a swan to fly upward (LiP 1.17.38).

type:LABEL: character
name: Makara
summary: The crocodile-like water creature on which Gaṅgā stands in temple-door iconography.

type:LABEL: character
name: Akūpāra (king of tortoises)
summary: The 'king of tortoises' whom gods and asuras ask to bear Mount Mandara during the churning in the Mahābhārata critical text (MBh CE 1.16.10–11); later Purāṇas make the tortoise Viṣṇu himself (Kūrma).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: character
name: Nahuṣa (Vālmīki's Ikṣvāku genealogy)
summary: In VR (CE) 1.69.29 a king of the Ikṣvāku line, son of Ambarīṣa and father of Yayāti; kept distinct from the Lunar Nahuṣa (son of Āyu) because the identity of the homonyms is not stated by the sources.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yayāti (Vālmīki's Ikṣvāku genealogy)
summary: In VR (CE) 1.69.30 a king of the Ikṣvāku line, son of Nahuṣa and father of Nābhāga, grandfather of Aja; kept distinct from the Lunar Yayāti.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vāsuki
summary: King of the serpents who serves as the churning rope round Mount Mandara (MBh CE 1.16.12; ViP 1.9.82; VR CE 1.44.17).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: concept
name: Avatāra
summary: The 'descent' of a deity, above all Viṣṇu, into a bodily form to restore dharma; the theory develops from the Bhagavad Gītā's 'yuge yuge' (4.7–8) and the Nārāyaṇīya's prādurbhāvas into the Purāṇic lists of ten, twenty-two or 'innumerable' avatāras.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Daśāvatāra (the ten avatāras)
summary: The conventional set of ten avatāras of Viṣṇu; the term occurs in the Agni Purāṇa (16.12; 49.1), and the set becomes canonical in medieval art and liturgy (e.g. Jayadeva's Gītagovinda), though the eighth and ninth places vary (Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma; Buddha).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Yuga
summary: One of the four ages — Kṛta (Satya), Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali — of declining dharma that together make a mahāyuga; Manusmṛti 1.68–71 gives 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 years plus dawn and dusk, totalling 12,000 'a yuga of the gods'.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kalpa
summary: A day of Brahmā, a thousand mahāyugas (Manu 1.72; ViP 1.3.15) containing fourteen manvantaras (ViP 1.3.16); the present kalpa is called Vārāha, the first of the second half (parārdha) of Brahmā's life (ViP 1.3.27–28).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Manvantara
summary: The period of a Manu, 'a little over seventy-one' mahāyugas (ViP 1.3.18; BhP 3.11.24; Manu 1.79), each with its own Indra, gods and seven sages; fourteen make a kalpa and the present is the seventh, of Vaivasvata Manu.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Mahāyuga (caturyuga)
summary: The cycle of the four yugas, 12,000 divine years (Manu 1.71; ViP 1.3.11; BhP 3.11.18), computed as 4,320,000 human years where a divine year is taken as 360 human years.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pralaya (dissolution)
summary: The dissolution of the worlds; the Bhāgavata distinguishes four kinds — occasional (naimittika, at the end of a day of Brahmā), elemental (prākṛtika), constant (nitya) and final (ātyantika) (12.7.17) — and Viṣṇu sleeps on the cosmic ocean in the interval.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pañcalakṣaṇa (five marks of a Purāṇa)
summary: The classical definition of a Purāṇa by five topics — sarga (creation), pratisarga (re-creation/dissolution), vaṃśa (genealogy), manvantara (ages of the Manus) and vaṃśānucarita (dynastic history) — stated in the Amarakośa and in several Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Trimūrti
summary: The triad of Brahmā (creation), Viṣṇu (preservation) and Śiva (destruction) as aspects of one reality; affirmed in non-sectarian and Smārta contexts, while sectarian Purāṇas subordinate two to the third.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śakti pīṭha
summary: A seat of the Goddess, especially as derived from the parts of Satī's body; the number (4, 51, 108) and the derivation from a dismembered corpse vary — the Matsya instead has Satī herself name 108 tīrthas where she is to be worshipped (13.26–53).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Tīrtha
summary: A 'crossing-place' — a sacred ford, river-bank or site where pilgrimage and bathing are held to be efficacious; Purāṇic māhātmyas (glorifications) are the principal textual charters of tīrthas.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Jyotirliṅga
summary: The twelve 'liṅgas of light', self-manifest forms of Śiva at named sites (Somanātha, Mallikārjuna, Mahākāla, Kedāra, Viśveśvara and others), listed in the Śiva Purāṇa (Koṭirudra-saṃhitā) and in a widely recited stotra.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vyūha
summary: The four 'emanations' of the Pāñcarātra theology — Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha — set out in the Nārāyaṇīya (MBh CE 12.326.68–69), from Aniruddha of whom Brahmā arises.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The churning of the ocean
summary: Gods and asuras churn the ocean with Mount Mandara and the serpent Vāsuki to obtain amṛta; the versions differ on who supports the mountain, who takes the poison, what emerges and how the nectar is withheld from the asuras.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Varāha raises the Earth
summary: Viṣṇu as a cosmic boar dives into the waters and raises the submerged Earth on his tusk; in the Bhāgavata he also slays Hiraṇyākṣa.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era
earliest_material: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Narasiṃha and Prahlāda
summary: Hiraṇyakaśipu persecutes his devoted son Prahlāda; Viṣṇu bursts from a pillar as the man-lion and kills him at twilight on the threshold with his claws, honouring the letter of Brahmā's boon.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Vāmana and Bali
summary: Viṣṇu, born as the dwarf son of Aditi, asks the asura king Bali for three steps, grows to cosmic size as Trivikrama, recovers the worlds for Indra and sends Bali to the netherworld.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice
summary: Dakṣa excludes Śiva from his sacrifice; Satī gives up her body; Śiva's emanation Vīrabhadra and his hosts destroy the rite and Dakṣa is punished and restored.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The birth of Skanda
summary: Śiva's seed, too potent to bear, passes through Agni and Gaṅgā and is nursed by the six Kṛttikās; the child Skanda is made general of the gods and slays Tāraka. Versions differ on the bearers and the mother's role.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Goddess slays Mahiṣāsura
summary: The gods, defeated by the buffalo-demon, emit their radiance which coalesces into the Goddess; armed with their weapons and riding Himavat's lion she destroys his army and kills him as he emerges from the buffalo (DM 2–3).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The appearance of the fiery liṅga (Liṅgodbhava)
summary: Brahmā and Viṣṇu quarrel over supremacy; an endless pillar of fire appears; Brahmā as a swan flies up and Viṣṇu as a boar digs down, and neither finds its end; Śiva reveals himself within it.
earliest_material: c. 700 CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha, c. 690–728)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The liberation of Gajendra
summary: The king of elephants, seized by a crocodile in a lake on Mount Trikūṭa, prays to the supreme person; Hari comes on Garuḍa, kills the crocodile with his discus and frees him, and both are released from curses.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The story of Dhruva
summary: The child Dhruva, rejected from his father's lap, undertakes fierce austerity and is granted by Viṣṇu the highest immovable station, the Pole Star.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The descent of the Gaṅgā
summary: Sagara's sixty thousand sons, burned by Kapila, can be purified only by the Gaṅgā; after generations Bhagīratha's austerities bring her down, Śiva breaks her fall in his hair, and she flows over the ashes.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Matsya avatāra and the flood
summary: A small fish begs Manu's protection, grows enormous, warns of a deluge and tows his boat, tied to its horn, to safety; in the Purāṇas the fish is Viṣṇu and the story is set at the end of a manvantara or kalpa.
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Satī's body and the origin of the Śakti Pīṭhas
summary: After Satī's death Śiva wanders carrying her corpse; it is divided and its parts fall at places that become seats (pīṭhas) of the Goddess — a late, Śākta development of the Dakṣa story.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha
summary: During Viṣṇu's cosmic sleep two demons born from his ear-wax threaten Brahmā; Brahmā praises the Goddess as Yoganidrā, she releases Viṣṇu, and he slays them (DM 1).
earliest_textual: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha
summary: The asura brothers seek the Goddess in marriage; she destroys their generals Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa and Raktabīja with Kālī and the Mothers, then Niśumbha and Śumbha (DM 5–10).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Sagara's sons and Kapila
summary: Sagara's sixty thousand sons dig through the earth in search of the sacrificial horse, find it near the sage Kapila, accuse him and are burned to ashes; Aṃśumat recovers the horse.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Yayāti and the exchange of old age
summary: Cursed by Śukra with premature old age, Yayāti asks his sons to take it; only Pūru agrees, and he becomes heir to the central realm while the others receive the peripheries.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Ilā/Sudyumna and the birth of Purūravas
summary: From a flawed rite of Manu a daughter Ilā is born, changed into a man (Sudyumna) and back; as Ilā she bears Purūravas to Budha, son of the Moon — the junction of the Solar and Lunar lines.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The advent of Kalki
summary: At the end of the Kali age Kalki is born at Śambhala to Viṣṇuyaśas, rides a swift horse given by the gods, destroys the dasyus posing as kings, and inaugurates a new Kṛta age.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Bhṛgu's curse and Viṣṇu's repeated births
summary: In the Matsya, Viṣṇu kills Bhṛgu's wife during a war of gods and asuras; Bhṛgu curses him to be born repeatedly among humans, which explains seven human manifestations after three divine ones (MatsP 47.235–251).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Goddess formed from the gods' radiance
summary: The radiance (tejas) issuing from the angry Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, Indra and the other gods merges into a single female form whose body parts each derive from one god, and the gods arm her with copies of their weapons (DM 2 = MkP 82.8–31).

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa / Ikṣvāku)
summary: The royal line descended from Vivasvat (the Sun) through Vaivasvata Manu and Ikṣvāku, ruling from Ayodhyā; it includes Māndhātṛ, Hariścandra, Sagara, Bhagīratha, Raghu, Aja, Daśaratha and Rāma. The sequence of kings differs markedly between the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and the Purāṇas.
earliest_material: regnal year 4 of Sundara Cōḻa (c. 961 CE)

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Lunar dynasty (Candravaṃśa / Aila)
summary: The royal line descended from Soma (the Moon) through Budha and Ilā's son Purūravas (hence 'Aila'), then Āyu, Nahuṣa and Yayāti, whose sons Yadu and Pūru found the Yādava and Paurava–Kuru branches.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Pauravas (descendants of Pūru)
summary: The branch of the Lunar line descended from Yayāti's son Pūru, including Bharata, Kuru and the Kurus of the Mahābhārata (ViP 4.19–20; BhP 9.20–22).

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Bhārgavas (descendants of Bhṛgu)
summary: The priestly clan of Bhṛgu, including Śukra (Kāvya), Ṛcīka, Jamadagni and Paraśurāma; Goldman traces their prominence in the Mahābhārata.

type:LABEL: lineage
name: Daityas (sons of Diti)
summary: The asuras descended from Kaśyapa and Diti — Hiraṇyakaśipu, Hiraṇyākṣa, Prahlāda, Virocana, Bali — perennial rivals of the gods (Ādityas, sons of Aditi).

type:LABEL: place
name: Kāśī (Vārāṇasī)
summary: The city on the Gaṅgā held to be Śiva's own (Avimukta, 'never forsaken'), where death brings liberation; glorified in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa and the subject of an early māhātmya in the original Skandapurāṇa.

type:LABEL: place
name: Prayāga
summary: The confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā (with the invisible Sarasvatī) at present Prayagraj, called 'king of tīrthas' in Purāṇic māhātmyas (e.g. Matsya Purāṇa, recall) and site of the Kumbha Melā.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mount Kailāsa
summary: Śiva's mountain abode in Purāṇic cosmography, traditionally identified with Mount Kailash (Gang Rinpoche) in western Tibet, sacred also to Buddhists, Jains and Bon.

type:LABEL: place
name: Gaṅgā river
summary: The Ganges, personified as the goddess Gaṅgā; Purāṇic geography traces her descent from Viṣṇu's foot through the heavens to Śiva's hair and the earth.

type:LABEL: place
name: Sarasvatī river (Vedic)
summary: The river praised in the Ṛgveda and remembered in later texts as disappearing in the desert (at Vinaśana) and flowing invisibly to join the Gaṅgā and Yamunā at Prayāga; its identification with the Ghaggar–Hakra is debated.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ocean of Milk (Kṣīrasāgara)
summary: The cosmic ocean of Purāṇic cosmography that is churned for the amṛta and on which Viṣṇu reclines; Mount Trikūṭa rises from it (BhP 8.2.1).

type:LABEL: place
name: Mount Mandara
summary: The mountain used as the churning-stick in the churning of the ocean; MBh (CE) 1.16.3 makes it 11,000 yojanas high. Tradition identifies a Mandar hill near Bhagalpur, Bihar.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mount Trikūṭa
summary: Three-peaked mountain in the Ocean of Milk, scene of Gajendra's rescue (BhP 8.2.1–2).

type:LABEL: place
name: Naubandhana peak (Himavat)
summary: The Himālayan peak where, in the Mahābhārata, the fish has the sages tie Manu's boat, 'still famous today' as Naubandhana (MBh CE 3.185.44–47); ŚB 1.8.1.6 has the 'northern mountain' (vedic domain).

type:LABEL: place
name: Malaya mountains
summary: The southern (Western Ghats) mountain range where, in the Matsya Purāṇa, King Manu performs austerities before meeting the fish (MatsP 1.12).

type:LABEL: place
name: Kṛtamālā river
summary: River in the Draviḍa country where Satyavrata catches the small fish (BhP 8.24.12); traditionally identified with the Vaigai at Madurai.

type:LABEL: place
name: Vindhya mountains
summary: The central Indian range on which the Harivaṃśa gives the goddess Nidrā/Kauśikī an eternal seat (HV CE 47.48); the shrine of Vindhyavāsinī near Mirzapur continues the tradition.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kāmarūpa
summary: Region of the lower Brahmaputra valley (Assam) glorified in the Kālikā Purāṇa as the most sacred land of the Goddess, where Satī's yoni fell at Nīlācala (Kāmākhyā).

type:LABEL: place
name: Śambhala (village of Kalki)
summary: The village where Kalki is to be born in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas (BhP 12.2.18); local traditions identify it with Sambhal (Uttar Pradesh), and it is distinct from the Buddhist Kālacakra Śambhala.

type:LABEL: place
name: Madhuvana
summary: Forest on the Yamunā near Mathurā where Dhruva performs austerities (BhP 4.8.42).

type:LABEL: place
name: Badarī (Viśālā)
summary: Himālayan hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa; in MBh (CE) 3.185.4 Manu performs austerities at Viśālā Badarī, and Nārada hastens there at the end of the Nārāyaṇīya (12.326.99).

type:LABEL: place
name: Kanakhala
summary: Place near Haridwar on the Gaṅgā identified in tradition and in several Purāṇic tellings (recall) as the site of Dakṣa's sacrifice.

type:LABEL: place
name: Gaṅgāsāgara
summary: The mouth of the Hooghly branch of the Gaṅgā (Sagar Island), where tradition places Kapila's hermitage and the ashes of Sagara's sons.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vaiṣṇava traditions
summary: Traditions that worship Viṣṇu (with Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, Rāma and other forms) as supreme; their Purāṇic canon centres on the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas and the avatāra doctrine.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śaiva traditions
summary: Traditions that worship Śiva as supreme, from the Pāśupatas and the 'Śaiva age' of early medieval India (Sanderson) to Śaiva Siddhānta, Kashmir Śaivism and Vīraśaivism; their Purāṇas include the Liṅga, Śiva, Vāyu, Kūrma and Skanda.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śākta traditions
summary: Traditions that worship the Goddess (Devī, Śakti) as supreme; the Devī Māhātmya (c. 5th–6th c.) is their first great Sanskrit text, followed by the Kālikā and Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇas and Tantric literature.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Smārta tradition
summary: Brahmanical orthopraxy based on the smṛti (Dharmaśāstra, Purāṇa), associated with the worship of five deities (pañcāyatana: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa) and, since the medieval period, with Advaita monasteries.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Early Bhāgavata (Vāsudeva) devotion
summary: The early devotional cult of Vāsudeva (and Saṅkarṣaṇa) whose adherents called themselves bhāgavata; the Heliodorus pillar's donor styles himself 'bhāgavata' (late 2nd c. BCE), and the tradition flows into later Vaiṣṇavism.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Pāśupata Śaivism
summary: The earliest known Śaiva ascetic order, tracing itself to Lakulīśa (c. 2nd c. CE); its milieu shaped the Vāyu, Liṅga, Kūrma and the early Skandapurāṇa.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Saura (Sun) worship
summary: Worship of Sūrya as supreme, prominent in western and northern India between the Gupta and early medieval periods, with Maga priests from 'Śākadvīpa'; textual charters are the Sāmba and parts of the Bhaviṣya and Brahma Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Gāṇapatya
summary: Traditions that worship Gaṇeśa as supreme, crystallised in the Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Upapurāṇas (2nd millennium) and in Maharashtrian centres such as Morgaon and Chinchwad.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Kali age began in 3102 BCE
summary: The traditional Indian astronomical epoch of the Kali-yuga (midnight 17/18 February 3102 BCE, Ujjain, as computed in later siddhāntas), derived backwards from planetary models; Āryabhaṭa's 499 CE statement implies it, and the 634 CE Aihole inscription counts 3,735 years from the Bhārata war.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Devī Bhāgavata is the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata'
summary: The Śākta position that the 'Bhāgavata' of the eighteen-lists is the Devī Bhāgavata, supported by the Matsya's description of the Bhāgavata as beginning with the Gāyatrī and containing the slaying of Vṛtra (MatsP 53.20–21); Vaiṣṇava tradition and most scholars hold it to be the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, with the Devī Bhāgavata an Upapurāṇa.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The term 'mahāpurāṇa' is late
summary: Rocher's observation that the term mahāpurāṇa occurs rarely in Purāṇic literature and is probably late; in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa critical edition the half-verse calling the eighteen 'mahāpurāṇas' is an insertion (3.6.23*8).

type:LABEL: claim
name: Vāsudeva was worshipped by self-styled bhāgavatas by the 2nd century BCE
summary: The scholarly conclusion, from the Heliodorus pillar (Besnagar), the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī and Mora well inscriptions and the coins of Agathocles, that a devotional cult of Vāsudeva (and Saṅkarṣaṇa) existed in the last centuries BCE, long before the Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Śiva was worshipped in iconic and liṅga form by the early centuries CE
summary: The conclusion, from the Gudimallam liṅga and Kuṣāṇa coinage (Wima Kadphises' deity with bull), that Śiva worship in liṅga and anthropomorphic form predates the Śaiva Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Devī Māhātmya was in circulation by 608 CE
summary: A verse of the Devī Māhātmya's eleventh chapter is quoted in a dated inscription of 608 CE, giving a firm terminus ante quem for at least part of the text.

type:LABEL: person
name: Āryabhaṭa
summary: Indian astronomer-mathematician (b. 476 CE) whose Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE) states his age in the Kali era and adopts a mahāyuga of four equal quarters.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.3 (units of time, yugas, kalpa)
summary: Parāśara's account of time: nimeṣa to day, human and divine years (1.3.8–10), the caturyuga of 12,000 divine years (1.3.11–14), 1,000 caturyugas as Brahmā's day with fourteen Manus (1.3.15–16), a manvantara of a little over 71 caturyugas = 852,000 divine or 306,720,000 human years (1.3.18–21), and the present Vārāha kalpa (1.3.27–28).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.4 (Varāha raises the Earth)
summary: The boar form taken at the beginning of the present kalpa to raise the Earth from the waters, with the Earth's hymn.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.9 (Durvāsas' curse and the churning)
summary: Durvāsas' curse deprives Indra of Śrī; on Viṣṇu's advice gods and asuras churn the Ocean of Milk; Viṣṇu as tortoise; the nāgas take the poison; Śrī rises and goes to Hari's chest.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.11–12 (Dhruva)
summary: The story of Dhruva's austerity and his elevation to the pole.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.16–20 (Prahlāda)
summary: Prahlāda's devotion and persecution by Hiraṇyakaśipu; the father's death at Narasiṃha's hands is stated at 1.20.32.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.1 (the manvantaras)
summary: The six past Manus (Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa) and the present seventh, Vaivasvata, with its Indra Purandara, seven sages and Manu's sons (3.1.6–7, 30–34).

type:LABEL: passage
