name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6 (the eighteen Purāṇas and the five marks)
summary: Vyāsa's Purāṇa-saṃhitā given to Romaharṣaṇa; the list of eighteen purāṇas (3.6.20–23) and the five topics treated in all (3.6.24); the term 'mahāpurāṇa' only in insertion 3.6.23*8.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.4 (Sagara to Rāma)
summary: Sagara's sons and Kapila, Aṃśumat, Dilīpa and Bhagīratha (4.4.1–25); Khaṭvāṅga, Dīrghabāhu, Raghu, Aja, Daśaratha and the fourfold birth of Viṣṇu as Rāma and his brothers (4.4.47–49).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.10 (Yayāti)
summary: Nahuṣa's six sons; Yayāti's sons by Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā; Śukra's curse and the exchange of old age.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.24 (dynasties of the Kali age)
summary: The 'future' dynasties (Nandas, Mauryas, Śuṅgas … Guptas) and the onset of Kali when Kṛṣṇa departed; Kali lasts 360,000 human years (4.24.32–33, as the e-text reads).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.38 (after Kṛṣṇa's departure)
summary: Arjuna leads the Yādava women from Dvārakā; on the day Hari left the earth, Kali descended (5.38.8) and the sea flooded Dvārakā.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3 (the twenty-two avatāras)
summary: The cosmic Person as seed of avatāras (1.3.1–5) and the numbered list of twenty-two descents (1.3.6–25), declared innumerable (1.3.26); 1.3.28 distinguishes partial descents from Kṛṣṇa, 'Bhagavān himself'.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.7 (Brahmā's catalogue of līlāvatāras)
summary: Brahmā tells Nārada of Viṣṇu's sportive descents — Varāha, Suyajña, Kapila, Datta, the Kumāras, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Pṛthu, Ṛṣabha, Hayaśīrṣa, Matsya, Kūrma, Nṛsiṃha, Hari (for Gajendra), Vāmana, Haṃsa, Manu, Dhanvantari, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa with Balarāma, Vyāsa, the deluder of the demons and the chastiser of Kali.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11 (time and the yugas)
summary: Maitreya's account of the four yugas as 12,000 divine years (3.11.18–20), Brahmā's day of a thousand caturyugas and fourteen Manus (3.11.22–24).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.2–7 (Dakṣa's sacrifice)
summary: Dakṣa's enmity, Satī's death, Vīrabhadra's destruction of the sacrifice (4.5.2–3) and the restoration.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.8–12 (Dhruva)
summary: Dhruva's austerity at Madhuvana (4.8.42) and ascent to the viṣṇupada (4.12.25).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 7 (Prahlāda and Narasiṃha)
summary: Hiraṇyakaśipu's boon and persecution of Prahlāda; Narasiṃha's emergence from the pillar (7.8.17–19) and Prahlāda's hymn (7.9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.2–4 (Gajendramokṣa)
summary: Mount Trikūṭa (8.2.1), the elephant's prayer (8.3), the rescue and the former births of the elephant (Indradyumna) and the crocodile (Hūhū) (8.4.3–11).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.5–12 (the churning and Mohinī)
summary: The churning with Viṣṇu as tortoise, Śiva drinking the hālāhala (8.7.43), Lakṣmī choosing Mukunda (8.8.24), Mohinī distributing the nectar (8.9) and Śiva's infatuation (8.12).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.13 (the present and future manvantaras)
summary: Vaivasvata (Śrāddhadeva) as the present seventh Manu, his ten sons, gods, Indra Purandara, seven sages, and Vāmana's birth in this period (8.13.1–6).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.15–23 (Bali and Vāmana)
summary: Bali's conquest, Aditi's vow and Vāmana's birth, the gift of three steps (8.19.20), Trivikrama's strides (8.20.34) and Bali's elevation to Sutala (8.22.35).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.24 (Matsya)
summary: The fish avatāra: Hayagrīva steals the Vedas (8.24.8); King Satyavrata of the Draviḍas catches the fish in the Kṛtamālā (8.24.10–13); the deluge, the boat, the teaching; Satyavrata becomes Vaivasvata Manu (8.24.58).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 9 (the royal dynasties)
summary: The Solar line from Manu's sons (Ikṣvāku, Sagara 9.8, Bhagīratha 9.9, Raghu–Aja–Daśaratha 9.10.1, Rāma 9.10–11) and the Lunar line (Purūravas 9.14, Paraśurāma 9.15–16, Yayāti 9.18–19, Pauravas and Yādavas 9.20–24).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 10 (Kṛṣṇa)
summary: The life of Kṛṣṇa from birth at Mathurā and childhood in Vraja to the killing of Kaṃsa and life at Dvārakā; the most influential Purāṇic book in Kṛṣṇa devotion.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.2 (Kali age and Kalki)
summary: The decline of the Kali age and the birth of Kalki in the house of Viṣṇuyaśas at Śambhala (12.2.16–20).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.7 (marks of a Purāṇa; list of eighteen)
summary: Ten characteristics of a Purāṇa, with the remark that some count five (12.7.9–10); the eighteen Purāṇas (12.7.23–24).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.13 (verse counts of the Purāṇas)
summary: Verse counts of the eighteen Purāṇas, totalling 400,000, the Bhāgavata having 18,000 (12.13.4–9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 1 (Madhu and Kaiṭabha) = MkP 81
summary: Frame story of Suratha, Samādhi and Medhas; Brahmā's hymn to Yoganidrā; the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 2–4 (Mahiṣāsura) = MkP 82–84
summary: The gods' radiance becomes the Goddess and is armed (MkP 82.8–31); battle with Mahiṣa's army (82); his death (83); the gods' hymn (84).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 5–10 (Śumbha and Niśumbha) = MkP 85–90
summary: Ambikā/Kauśikī emerges from Pārvatī (85.40–44); Dhūmralocana (86); Kālī and Cāmuṇḍā (87.5, 87.26); Raktabīja (88); Niśumbha (89); Śumbha (90).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 7 (Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa; Kālī) = MkP 87
summary: Kālī springs from the angry Ambikā's brow (87.5), slays Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa and is named Cāmuṇḍā (87.26).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Māhātmya 11 (Nārāyaṇī-stuti) = MkP 91
summary: The gods' hymn to the Goddess as Nārāyaṇī, including the verse 'sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye…' (MkP 91.9) quoted in the 608 CE Dadhimatī-mātā inscription.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Manusmṛti 1.68–73 (lengths of the yugas)
summary: Kṛta 4,000 years with dawn and dusk of 400 each; the other three decreasing by a thousand and a hundred; the 12,000 'yuga of the gods'; a thousand such make Brahmā's day (cf. 1.64–67 time units; 1.79 manvantara of 71 divine yugas).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 1–2 (the fish and Manu)
summary: King Manu's austerity on the Malaya; the growing fish recognised as Keśava/Janārdana; the flood at the end of the Cākṣuṣa manvantara; the boat tied to the horn with a serpent rope.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 13 (Satī and the 108 tīrthas)
summary: At Dakṣa's sacrifice Satī announces she will abandon the body born of him, names 108 tīrthas with her names there (13.26–53) and burns herself; she is reborn as Pārvatī (13.59).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 47 (Bhṛgu's curse and Viṣṇu's manifestations)
summary: Twelve deva–asura wars (47.41–45); Bhṛgu's curse; three divine and seven human manifestations of Viṣṇu (47.235–251): Dattātreya, Māndhātṛ, Jāmadagnya, Rāma, Vedavyāsa, Buddha, Kalki.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Matsya Purāṇa 53 (the Purāṇas, their extent and marks)
summary: Descriptions, verse counts and gifts for the eighteen (53.12–58), the upabhedas (53.60–63), the five marks (53.65) and the guṇa correlation (53.68–69).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.1 (avatāra list)
summary: A list of twenty-two avatāras nearly verbatim with BhP 1.3.6–25 (1.1.14–33), Buddha called 'jinasuta' (1.1.32).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Garuḍa Purāṇa 1.86 (ten manifestations)
summary: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛhari, Vāmana, Rāma (Bhārgava), Rāma Dāśarathi, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha and Kalki (1.86.10–11).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 2–16 (the avatāras narrated)
summary: Matsya (2), Kūrma (3), Varāha to Paraśurāma (4), Rāma (5–11), Harivaṃśa (12), Mahābhārata (13–15), Buddha and Kalki (16), closing with 'viṣṇor daśāvatārākhyān' (16.12).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Agni Purāṇa 49 (iconography of the ten avatāras)
summary: Prescriptions for images of Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Balarāma (plough and pestle), Buddha and Kalki (49.1–9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Liṅga Purāṇa 1.17 (Liṅgodbhava)
summary: Brahmā's account of the quarrel with Viṣṇu, the fiery liṅga, his swan form and Viṣṇu's boar form (1.17.31–45).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Liṅga Purāṇa 1.76 (image of the Liṅgodbhava)
summary: Prescription for an image with Candraśekhara within the flaming liṅga, Brahmā as swan above and Viṣṇu as boar below (1.76.60–61).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Śiva Purāṇa, Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā 5–9 (Liṅgodbhava and the ketakī)
summary: The pillar of fire between Brahmā and Viṣṇu; Brahmā's false witness, the ketakī flower (1.7.19–27).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1 (five marks and list of eighteen)
summary: The pañcalakṣaṇa (1.1.12) and a list of the Purāṇas that keeps Śaiva fourth and ends with the Vāyavīya and 'the eighteenth, called Brahmāṇḍa' (1.1.13–15).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.31–40 (Devī Gītā)
summary: The Goddess's teaching to Himālaya, transmitted separately as the Devī Gītā.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Caṅkam (Sangam) literature
summary: The earliest corpus of Tamil poetry — the Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai) and Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu) — together with the grammar Tolkāppiyam, composed roughly between the turn of the era and the 5th–6th century CE, with later layers such as the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Tirumurai
summary: The twelve-book canon of Tamil Śaiva devotional literature: Tēvāram (1–7), Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (8), Tiruvicaippā and Tiruppallāṇṭu (9), Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram (10), a miscellany including the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai (11) and Cēkkiḻār’s Periya Purāṇam (12).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās
summary: The scriptures of the Pāñcarātra tradition — traditionally 108, with over 200 known titles — including the Sāttvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya (“three gems”), the Ahirbudhnya, Pārameśvara, Īśvara and Lakṣmī Tantra.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śaiva Āgamas (Siddhānta tantras)
summary: The Sanskrit scriptures of the Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally twenty-eight Āgamas with subsidiary Upāgamas, beginning with the Kāmika; the earliest surviving tantra of the wider Mantramārga is the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śākta Tantras
summary: Tantras centred on the Goddess and her retinue (yoginīs, Kālī, Tripurasundarī, Kubjikā), including the Brahmayāmala (Picumata) of the early Vidyāpīṭha, the Kaula texts and later Śrīvidyā literature.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Maṅgalkāvya
summary: Bengali narrative poems (c. 13th–18th c.) celebrating the power of local or Purāṇic deities — Manasā, Caṇḍī, Dharma Ṭhākur, Annadā — and the establishment of their worship among reluctant devotees.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Sthala-purāṇas (temple and place legends)
summary: Texts recounting the sacred history of a particular shrine or town — its deity’s manifestation, divine marriages, miracles and royal patrons — in Sanskrit (often as māhātmyas within Purāṇas) and in Tamil and other languages.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tolkāppiyam
summary: The oldest extant Tamil grammar and poetics, in three books (phonology, morphology, “subject-matter” — poruḷ). Its Akattiṇaiyiyal assigns presiding deities to the landscapes: Māyōṉ to the forest-pasture (mullai), Cēyōṉ to the hills (kuṟiñci), Vēntaṉ to farmland (marutam) and Varuṇaṉ to the shore (neytal).

type:LABEL: text
name: Paripāṭal
summary: A late Caṅkam anthology (fifth of the Eight Anthologies) of musical poems: of the 24 that survive complete, 7 are addressed to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa), 8 to Murukaṉ (Cevvēḷ) and 9 to the river Vaikai at Madurai.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai
summary: Nakkīrar’s poem “guiding [the devotee] to Murukaṉ,” the first of the Ten Idylls and also included in Tirumurai 11. It describes six places where Murukaṉ is present and blends Tamil and northern (Skanda) imagery.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruppāvai
summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s thirty Tamil verses in the voice of cowherd girls who rise before dawn in the month of Mārkaḻi to wake one another and Kṛṣṇa for a vow (nōṉpu). It is part of the Divya Prabandham and recited daily in Śrīvaiṣṇava worship.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nācciyār Tirumoḻi
summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s 143 Tamil verses of longing for union with Viṣṇu–Kṛṣṇa, including the celebrated dream of her wedding to him (vāraṇam āyiram), part of the Divya Prabandham.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruvāymoḻi
summary: Nammāḻvār’s 1,102-verse Tamil poem to Viṣṇu, in a hundred decads; Śrīvaiṣṇavas call it the Tamil (Drāviḍa) Veda and it was the subject of the first Śrīvaiṣṇava commentary, Piḷḷāṉ’s Āṟāyirappaṭi.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruvācakam
summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s Tamil hymns to Śiva, forming (with his Tirukkōvaiyār) Tirumurai book 8; intensely personal poems of grace, longing and Śiva as dancer at Tillai (Chidambaram).

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruvempāvai
summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s twenty-verse pāvai poem within the Tiruvācakam, in which young women wake each other at dawn in Mārkaḻi to bathe and praise Śiva — a Śaiva counterpart of Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tirumantiram
summary: Tirumūlar’s Tamil verse treatise on Śaiva doctrine, yoga and tantra (c. 3,000 verses), Tirumurai book 10, regarded as the earliest Tamil statement of Śaiva Siddhānta ideas; its date is much disputed.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam
summary: The Tamil sthala-purāṇa of Madurai narrating the sixty-four “sacred sports” (tiruviḷaiyāṭal) of Śiva as Cuntarēcuvarar, including his marriage to the warrior-princess Taṭātakai (Mīnākṣī). The best-known version is by Parañcōti Muṉivar.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kanta Purāṇam
summary: Kacciyappa Civācāriyar’s Tamil Skanda Purāṇa, recounting Murukaṉ’s birth and his war against the asura Cūrapatmaṉ (Śūrapadma), traditionally first recited at the Kumarakōṭṭam shrine in Kanchipuram.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āndhra Mahābhāratamu
summary: The Telugu Mahābhārata of the “poet trinity” (kavitrayam): Nannaya began it under the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra (11th c.), Tikkana wrote fifteen books from the Virāṭa onward (13th c.), and Errana completed the Araṇya book (14th c.).

type:LABEL: text
name: Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu
summary: Telugu Rāmāyaṇa in dvipada couplets by Gona Budda Reddy (pen-name Raṅganātha), 13th–14th c. Its singable metre suited folk and puppet performance; it contains popular episodes absent from Vālmīki, such as the squirrel who helps build the bridge and Lakṣmaṇa drawing a protective line.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu (Pōtana)
summary: Bammera Pōtana’s 15th-century Telugu rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, dedicated not to a king but to Rāma; much loved for its Gajendra-mokṣa and Kṛṣṇa narratives.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vikramārjuna Vijaya (Pampa Bhārata)
summary: The Kannada Mahābhārata in campū form by the Jain poet Pampa, completed c. 941 CE at the court of the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya Arikēsari II; Pampa equates his patron with the hero Arjuna.

type:LABEL: text
name: Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī (Gadugina Bhārata)
summary: Kumāravyāsa’s Kannada Mahābhārata (first ten books) in bhāminī ṣaṭpadi six-line stanzas, completed c. 1430 under the Vijayanagara king Dēvarāya II; it remains a living recitation text (gamaka) in Karnataka.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vacanas of Basavaṇṇa
summary: The free-verse Kannada sayings (vacana) attributed to Basava, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, criticising temple ritual and caste and exalting the devotee’s body as Śiva’s temple.

type:LABEL: text
name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu
summary: Eḻuttacchaṉ’s 16th-century Malayalam rendering of the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa in the “parrot-song” form, in which a parrot recites the story; it is read aloud in Kerala households during the month of Karkkaṭakam.

type:LABEL: text
name: Saptakāṇḍa Rāmāyaṇa (Assamese)
summary: Mādhava Kandali’s 14th-century Assamese rendering of Vālmīki, made for the Barāhī (Kachari) king Mahāmāṇikya — among the earliest renderings of a Sanskrit epic into a modern Indo-Aryan language. Its first and last books were lost and replaced in the 16th century by Mādhavadeva (Ādi) and Śaṅkaradeva (Uttara).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kīrtana Ghoṣā
summary: Śaṅkaradeva’s Assamese collection of devotional narrative songs, largely drawn from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the core scripture recited in the nāmghars and sattras of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śāraḷā Mahābhārata
summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s 15th-century Odia Mahābhārata, begun under the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva (r. 1435–1467). It follows the Bhārata outline but adds many episodes and Odia local colour, written in colloquial, unsanskritised Odia.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa
summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia narrative of a war against a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa of the land of Vilaṅkā, after the defeat of the ten-headed one — a theme shared with the Sanskrit Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa’s Sahasra-Rāvaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Odia Bhāgabata
summary: Jagannātha Dāsa’s Odia rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (late 15th – early 16th c.), in a simple nine-syllable metre; it became the most widely read devotional book of Odisha and the basis of village Bhāgabata-ghara reading houses.

type:LABEL: text
name: Manasāmaṅgal
summary: Bengali Maṅgalkāvya narratives of the snake goddess Manasā, centred on the merchant Cā̃d Sadāgar’s refusal to worship her and the devotion of his daughter-in-law Behulā, who wins back her dead husband Lakhindar.

type:LABEL: text
name: Caitanya Caritāmṛta
summary: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Bengali–Sanskrit biography and theology of Caitanya (early 17th c.), which the Gauḍīya tradition treats as definitive; it presents Caitanya as Kṛṣṇa who took on the emotion and complexion of Rādhā.

type:LABEL: text
name: Eknāthī Bhāgavata
summary: Eknāth’s Marathi ovī commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (the Uddhava-gītā), 16th c.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tukārām Gāthā
summary: The collection of Marathi abhaṅgas attributed to Tukārām (traditionally c. 4,500), sung by Vārkarī pilgrims on the road to Pandharpur.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sūrsāgar
summary: The “Ocean of Sūr”: the corpus of Braj Bhāṣā songs attributed to Sūrdās, chiefly on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood and the love of Rādhā and the gopīs, arranged in later recensions in twelve books after the Bhāgavata. Most of the received corpus is later than Sūr; Hawley and Bryant reconstruct an early core from manuscripts.

type:LABEL: text
name: Hanumān Cālīsā
summary: Forty-verse Awadhi hymn to Hanumān, traditionally attributed to Tulsīdās and now the most widely recited Hindu devotional hymn in North India.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vākhs of Lal Ded
summary: Kashmiri four-line mystical sayings (vākh) attributed to the 14th-century yoginī Lal Ded (Lallā), venerated by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa; they survived orally and were first written down systematically in the 20th century.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gāhā Sattasaī
summary: An anthology of 700 Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit love verses attributed to the Sātavāhana king Hāla; dated between the 1st and 7th centuries (before Bāṇa, 7th c.). One verse mentions Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, the earliest known literary mention of her.

type:LABEL: text
name: Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa
summary: A Sanskrit Śākta-inflected Rāma narrative in 27 sargas framed as a secret telling by Vālmīki to Bharadvāja. Sītā is born to Mandodarī, and in the climax she takes the form of Mahākālī and destroys the thousand-headed Sahasra-Rāvaṇa after Rāma falls unconscious.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhaṭṭikāvya (Rāvaṇavadha)
summary: Bhaṭṭi’s 6th–7th-century Sanskrit mahākāvya telling the Rāma story while illustrating the rules of Pāṇini’s grammar; it was the model for the first half of the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Uttarapurāṇa of Guṇabhadra
summary: The 9th-century Digambara Jain Sanskrit universal history completing Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa; its Rāma section follows a different Jain line from Vimalasūri, making Sītā the daughter of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, abandoned at birth because of a prophecy.

type:LABEL: text
name: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
summary: A Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra (c. 4th–5th c.) whose frame story has the Buddha visiting Laṅkā at the invitation of its king Rāvaṇa, who questions him on the dharma.

type:LABEL: text
name: Hikayat Seri Rama (Malay)
summary: The Malay prose Rāma narrative, put into its present form between the 13th and 17th centuries, with Islamic framing in some versions (Dasaratha as a descendant of the prophet Adam). Its oldest manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, was acquired by Archbishop Laud by 1633.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yama Zatdaw (Burmese)
summary: The Burmese Rāma tradition (Yamayana), known in Bagan-period terracottas as the Dasaratha Jātaka and in literature from a 1527 pyo poem; it was reshaped in the Konbaung period by Thai court drama brought back after the conquest of Ayutthaya.

type:LABEL: text
name: Phra Lak Phra Lam (Lao)
summary: The Lao Rāma epic, framed as a jātaka: Phra Lam is a previous birth of the Buddha, and Rāvaṇa (Hapmanasouane) is his cousin, compared with Devadatta or Māra. Versions were recorded on palm leaf from the 15th to the early 19th century.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jayākhya Saṃhitā
summary: One of the “three gems” of the Pāñcarātra canon, a ritual and theological saṃhitā edited in 1931; its date is disputed, from an early proposal of c. 5th c. to later scholarship placing it around the 8th–9th c.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sāttvata Saṃhitā
summary: Among the oldest and most authoritative Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (one of the “three gems”), with a commentary by Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa; date disputed.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā
summary: Pāñcarātra saṃhitā known for its doctrine of the Sudarśana (Viṣṇu’s discus) and its cosmology; the subject of Schrader’s pioneering 1916 study, which placed it early, a dating later scholars question.

type:LABEL: text
name: Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā
summary: The earliest surviving tantra of the Śaiva Mantramārga, in five books; its editors date the oldest layer (Mūlasūtra) to c. 450–550 CE. It preserves an early stage of Śaiva Siddhānta ritual and the transition from the Atimārga.

type:LABEL: text
name: Brahmayāmala (Picumata)
summary: An early Vidyāpīṭha tantra of the Bhairava stream, centred on Kapālīśabhairava and the goddess Caṇḍā Kāpālinī with their yoginīs; studied by Hatley as a key source for early Śākta-Śaiva yoginī cults.

type:LABEL: text
name: Civañāṉapōtam (Śivajñānabodham)
summary: Meykaṇṭār’s 13th-century twelve-sūtra Tamil treatise that founded the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta school; tradition calls it a rendering of twelve Sanskrit verses from the Raurava Āgama, a claim scholars treat cautiously.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tantrāloka
summary: Abhinavagupta’s encyclopaedic Sanskrit exposition of Trika Śaiva ritual and doctrine (c. 1000 CE), in thirty-seven chapters, based above all on the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nāthamuni
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (9th–10th c.) of Vīranārāyaṇapuram (Kāṭṭumaṉṉārkōyil), credited with collecting and arranging the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham and setting it to music; grandfather of Yāmuna.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-compiler of Tirunāraiyūr (10th–11th c.) who arranged the Tēvāram and other hymns into the first eleven books of the Tirumurai; tradition links his work to Rājarāja I.

type:LABEL: person
name: Māṇikkavācakar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint, author of the Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (Tirumurai 8); hagiography makes him a minister of a Pāṇḍya king who renounced office after meeting Śiva at Tirupperuntuṟai. Most scholars place him in the 9th century, though earlier dates are proposed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Cēkkiḻār
summary: Tamil poet and minister at the court of the Cōḻa king Kulōttuṅka II (12th c.), author of the Periya Purāṇam.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nakkīrar
summary: Tamil poet to whom the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai is attributed; tradition (including the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam) makes him the president of the Madurai academy (caṅkam) who dared to challenge Śiva’s poem.

type:LABEL: person
name: Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ
summary: The “venerable prince-ascetic,” brother of the Cēra king Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ according to the prologue of the Cilappatikāram, to whom the epic is attributed; the attribution rests on a later prologue and is doubted.

type:LABEL: person
name: Periyāḻvār
summary: Āḻvār of Śrīvilliputtūr (8th–9th c.), author of the Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi with its celebrated poems of Kṛṣṇa’s infancy and of the Tiruppallāṇṭu; foster-father of Āṇṭāḷ.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nannaya
summary: Telugu poet (11th c.), “first poet” (ādikavi) of Telugu, who began the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu at the request of the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tikkana
summary: Telugu poet and minister (13th c.) who rendered fifteen books (Virāṭa to Svargārohaṇa) of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Errana
summary: Telugu poet (14th c.) at the court of Prolaya Vēma Reḍḍi who completed the Araṇya book of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Gona Budda Reddy (Raṅganātha)
summary: Telugu poet (13th–14th c.), author under the pen-name Raṅganātha of the dvipada Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bammera Pōtana
summary: Telugu poet (15th c.) of Bammera near Warangal, author of the Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu, who according to tradition refused to dedicate his work to the king of Rācakoṇḍa and offered it to Rāma.

type:LABEL: person
name: Pampa (Ādikavi Pampa)
summary: Jain Kannada poet (902–c. 955) at the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya court of Arikēsari II, author of the Ādipurāṇa (941) and the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kumāravyāsa
summary: Kannada poet (Nāraṇappa, early 15th c.) of Gadag, author of the Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī, active under Dēvarāya II of Vijayanagara.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tuñcattu Rāmānujaṉ Eḻuttacchaṉ
summary: Malayalam poet (16th c.), called the father of modern Malayalam literature, author of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu and a Mahābhāratam Kiḷippāṭṭu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mādhava Kandali
summary: Assamese poet (14th c.) who rendered Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa into Assamese for the Barāhī king Mahāmāṇikya.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śrīmanta Śaṅkaradeva
summary: Assamese saint, poet, dramatist and founder of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism (traditionally 1449–1568, after the hagiographies), author of the Kīrtana Ghoṣā, the Aṅkīyā Nāṭ one-act plays and the Bargīt songs, and of the Uttara kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mādhavadeva
summary: Assamese poet and chief disciple of Śaṅkaradeva (16th c.), author of the Nām Ghoṣā and of the Ādi kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śāraḷā Dāsa
summary: Odia poet (15th c.) of the reign of the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva, author of the Odia Mahābhārata, the Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa and the Caṇḍī Purāṇa; his name, “by the grace of Sāraḷā,” refers to his goddess.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jagannātha Dāsa
summary: Odia poet (late 15th – 16th c.) of Puri, one of the Pañcasakhā, author of the Odia Bhāgabata and founder of the Atibaḍī tradition.

type:LABEL: person
name: Eknāth
summary: Marathi poet-saint of Paiṭhaṇ (c. 1533–1599), author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata and the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa, who produced a corrected text of the Jñāneśvarī in 1584.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tukārām
summary: Marathi poet-saint of Dehū (1608 or 1598 – 1649/1650), a grocer by caste whose abhaṅgas to Viṭṭhala are central to the Vārkarī pilgrimage.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nāmdev
summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1270–1350), a tailor of Pandharpur, devotee of Viṭṭhala and contemporary of Jñāneśvar; songs attributed to him are also in the Sikh Ādi Granth.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sūrdās
summary: Braj Bhāṣā poet-singer of the 16th century to whom the Sūrsāgar is attributed; hagiography makes him blind and a disciple of Vallabha, claims modern scholarship treats as later constructions.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lal Ded (Lalleśvarī)
summary: Kashmiri yoginī-poet of the 14th century, revered by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa, to whom the vākhs are attributed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Narsinh Mehtā
summary: Gujarati poet-saint of Junagadh (c. 1414 – 1480s), honoured as the Ādi Kavi of Gujarati, devotee of Kṛṣṇa and author of the bhajan “Vaiṣṇava jana to.”

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja
summary: Gauḍīya poet-theologian of Vṛndāvana (16th–17th c.), author of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

type:LABEL: person
name: Meykaṇṭār
summary: Tamil Śaiva theologian (13th c.) of Tiruveṇṇainallūr, author of the Civañāṉapōtam and founder of the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta lineage.

type:LABEL: person
name: Abhinavagupta
summary: Kashmirian Śaiva philosopher and aesthetician (fl. c. 975–1025), author of the Tantrāloka, of commentaries on Utpaladeva’s Pratyabhijñā and of the Abhinavabhāratī on the Nāṭyaśāstra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok)
summary: First king of the Chakri dynasty of Siam (r. 1782–1809), founder of Bangkok, under whom the canonical Ramakien was compiled (1797–1807), partly by the king himself.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kulōttuṅka Cōḻa II
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 1133–1150) at whose court Cēkkiḻār composed the Periya Purāṇam; Śaiva tradition associates him with the expansion of the Chidambaram temple.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lakṣmaṇasena
summary: King of the Sena dynasty of Bengal (r. c. 1178–1206), at whose court tradition places Jayadeva together with the poets Umāpatidhara, Śaraṇa, Govardhana and Dhoyī.

type:LABEL: person
name: Arikēsari II
summary: Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya ruler (10th c.), a feudatory of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Kṛṣṇa III, patron of Pampa, who equated him with Arjuna in the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā) of Pandharpur
summary: The deity of Pandharpur in Maharashtra, standing with hands on hips upon a brick, worshipped by Vārkarīs as a form of Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu; scholars debate his origins (pastoral hero-stone, Jain, Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava elements).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Māyōṉ (Tamil)
summary: The “dark one,” presiding deity of the mullai (forest-pasture) landscape in the Tolkāppiyam, and in Caṅkam poetry a dark cowherd god (also called Māl, Tirumāl) later identified with Viṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa. Kept distinct from deity:vishnu and joined by IDENTIFIED_WITH.

type:LABEL: character
name: Nappiṉṉai (Piññai)
summary: The Tamil cowherd girl beloved of Kṛṣṇa (Māyavaṉ) in the Cilappatikāram’s round-dance of the cowherdesses and in the Āḻvārs’ hymns, where she is his consort; some scholars see her as a southern parallel or precursor of Rādhā, others identify her with Nīḷā Devī.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vaḷḷi
summary: Murukaṉ’s Tamil consort, a hunter (kuṟava) girl of the hills whom the god woos in disguise; she stands beside Teyvāṉai (Devasenā), daughter of Indra, in Tamil tradition.

type:LABEL: character
name: Suvannamaccha
summary: Mermaid princess, daughter of Thotsakan (Rāvaṇa), in Thai and other Southeast Asian Rāma tellings; sent to sabotage the causeway to Laṅkā, she falls in love with Hanumān and bears him a son, Macchanu.

type:LABEL: character
name: Macchanu
summary: Son of Hanumān and the mermaid Suvannamaccha in the Ramakien, half monkey and half fish, who later meets and fights his father before they recognise each other.

type:LABEL: character
name: Thotsakan
summary: The ten-faced king of Laṅkā in the Thai Ramakien — the counterpart of Rāvaṇa (the name renders Daśakaṇṭha) — who in this telling is the father of Sida, keeps his heart outside his body, and dies when Hanumān crushes it.

type:LABEL: character
name: Māyā-Sītā (the illusory Sītā)
summary: The illusory double or reflection of Sītā who, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, is the one Rāvaṇa abducts while the real Sītā is kept safe in Agni.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhāmaṇḍala
summary: In Jain Rāma tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya and successors), Sītā’s twin brother, carried off at birth and raised as a vidyādhara prince, who falls in love with Sītā from her portrait and seeks her hand before learning that she is his twin sister.
earliest_textual: c. 1st–5th c. CE (not later than the 3rd c. in the commonest view)

type:LABEL: character
name: Sahasra-Rāvaṇa (the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa)
summary: A thousand-headed elder brother or double of Rāvaṇa who, in the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa, is destroyed by Sītā in the form of Mahākālī after Rāma is struck down; a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa is also fought in Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Kaṇṇaki
summary: Heroine of the Cilappatikāram, who proves her executed husband Kōvalaṉ innocent before the Pāṇḍya king, burns Madurai with her curse and is deified as the chaste goddess Pattiṉi, worshipped in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Sri Lanka.
earliest_material: modern buildings (date not given in the reference)

type:LABEL: place
name: Pandharpur
summary: Town on the Bhīmā (Candrabhāgā) river in Maharashtra, seat of the Viṭṭhala temple and goal of the Vārkarī pilgrimages (vārī) of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śrīvilliputtūr
summary: Temple town in Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, home of Periyāḻvār and Āṇṭāḷ according to tradition, with twin shrines of Āṇṭāḷ and Vaṭapatrasāyī (Raṅganātha).

type:LABEL: place
name: Nevāsā
summary: Town on the Pravarā near its confluence with the Godāvarī (Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra), identified by tradition as the place where the Jñāneśvarī was composed, home of the Mohinīrāja (Mahālayā) temple named in the colophon.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vārkarī
summary: The Marathi devotional tradition of Viṭṭhala of Pandharpur, carried by pilgrims (vārkarī) who walk to Pandharpur twice a year singing the abhaṅgas of Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev, Eknāth, Tukārām and other saints.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Ekaśaraṇa Dharma
summary: The Assamese Vaiṣṇava movement founded by Śaṅkaradeva (15th–16th c.): exclusive refuge in Kṛṣṇa through congregational singing and hearing of his name and deeds, organised in sattras and village nāmghars; Rādhā is not worshipped alongside Kṛṣṇa.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Puṣṭimārga
summary: The Kṛṣṇa tradition founded by Vallabha (16th c.), centred on Śrīnāthjī and the “eight seals” (aṣṭachāp) of poets, among whom it counts Sūrdās.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Rāmānandī
summary: The North Indian Vaiṣṇava ascetic order tracing itself to Rāmānanda, centred on Rāma and Sītā; it claims Tulsīdās and is traditionally associated with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Rāmlīlā
summary: North Indian staged performance of the Rāma story based on Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, held around Dussehra over ten to twelve days or (at Ramnagar, Varanasi) a month; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2005).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kūṭiyāṭṭam
summary: Sanskrit theatre of Kerala performed by Cākyār and Nampyār families in temple theatres (kūttampalam), with long elaborations of single acts of Sanskrit plays (including Rāma plays); inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2001).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Yakṣagāna
summary: Dance-drama of coastal Karnataka, led by a singer-narrator (bhāgavata), performing episodes (prasaṅga) from the Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata; an inscription of 1556 at Kurugodu records land given to performers.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kathakaḷi
summary: Kerala dance-drama that crystallised in the 16th–17th centuries from Rāmanāṭṭam (attributed to the Kottarakkara Tampurāṉ) and Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam (of the Zamorin Mānavēdaṉ), performing Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata stories.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Wayang
summary: Indonesian puppet and shadow theatre (wayang kulit and related forms) led by a dalang with gamelan, performing stories from the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa among others; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Khon
summary: Thai masked dance-drama performing episodes of the Ramakien, historically a court art; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2018 as “Khon, masked dance drama in Thailand.”

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Royal Ballet of Cambodia
aliases: Khmer classical dance|Robam Preah Reach Trop
summary: Khmer classical court dance, whose repertoire includes Reamker episodes; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Triyampawai–Trippawai ceremony
summary: Thai royal Brahman new-year ceremony (December–January) whose name comes from two Tamil devotional poems — Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai and Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai — and during which hymns from these collections are chanted; it was historically linked to the Giant Swing in Bangkok.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Cāḷukyas of Vēmulavāḍa
summary: A 9th–10th-century dynasty in northern Telangana, feudatories of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, patrons of the Kannada poet Pampa under Arikēsari II.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Rattanakosin Kingdom (Chakri dynasty)
summary: The Siamese kingdom ruled from Bangkok by the Chakri dynasty from 1782, under whose first kings the Ramakien was compiled and the Wat Phra Kaew murals painted.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Sena dynasty of Bengal
summary: Dynasty ruling Bengal in the 11th–13th centuries, whose king Lakṣmaṇasena is traditionally Jayadeva’s patron.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Prambanan Rāmāyaṇa reliefs illustrate the Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa
summary: The claim that the 9th-century Rāmāyaṇa reliefs on the Śiva and Brahmā temples at Prambanan follow the Old Javanese Kakawin. Since Stutterheim (1925) scholars have noted episodes that diverge from the Kakawin and suggest another, possibly oral, telling.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Sūrdās was a disciple of Vallabha
summary: The Puṣṭimārga hagiographic claim (Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā) that Sūrdās was initiated by Vallabha and became one of the aṣṭachāp poets; Hawley argues the connection is a later sectarian construction.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Basava founded the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition
summary: The traditional claim that Basava founded the Liṅgāyata community; modern scholars using Kalacuri-period inscriptions and the vacana corpus often see him as a reformer and organiser of an existing Śaiva milieu.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Dasaratha Jātaka preserves an older form of the Rāma story than Vālmīki
summary: Argued in the 19th century (notably by Albrecht Weber) because of the jātaka’s simpler plot and sibling-marriage motif; most later scholars regard it as a Buddhist reworking of a story already known in Rāmāyaṇa form, though its verses may be old.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Dīpāvalī (Diwali)
summary: The autumn festival of lamps, spread over about five days around the new moon of Āśvina/Kārttika and observed across India and the diaspora. Different regions and communities give it different reasons — Kṛṣṇa’s killing of Narakāsura, Lakṣmī’s worship, Bali’s yearly reign, Rāma’s return to Ayodhyā, Kālī’s worship in Bengal, and Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa for Jains — which are recorded here as separate, unharmonised associations. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2025.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Naraka Caturdaśī
summary: The 14th of the dark half of Āśvina (Kārttika in the pūrṇimānta reckoning), the day before the Dīpāvalī new moon: a dawn oil-bath, a lamp lit for Naraka, and, in the south and west, the celebration of Kṛṣṇa’s killing of Narakāsura. Kane argues that the day was originally named for propitiating Yama against hell (naraka), and that the Narakāsura legend was attached later.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Lakṣmī Pūjā of Dīpāvalī
summary: The worship of Lakṣmī (with Kubera in some digests) on the new-moon night of Āśvina/Kārttika, the central night of Dīpāvalī in much of north and west India; merchants close their old account books and open new ones. The Bhaviṣyottara (ch. 140) and the Nīlamata Purāṇa (Sukhasuptikā) describe the night with lamps everywhere and the driving out of Alakṣmī (ill luck) at midnight.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kālī Pūjā (Bengal)
summary: The worship of Kālī on the new-moon night of Kārttika in Bengal, Assam and Odisha — the same night on which much of India worships Lakṣmī for Dīpāvalī. Kane notes that in Bengal Kālī is worshipped on this day; McDermott traces its spread as a large public festival in Bengal from the eighteenth century.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Balipratipadā
summary: The first day of the bright half of Kārttika, the day after the Dīpāvalī new moon, on which Bali, the asura king sent to the netherworld by Vāmana, is worshipped and said to reign for a day; it is also the day of dice-play (dyūta-pratipad) and, in the north, of Govardhana Pūjā. The Bhaviṣyottara (140.47–73) prescribes drawing Bali with his queen Vindhyāvalī and worshipping him with the mantra “salutation to you, O king Bali, son of Virocana … the future Indra”.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Govardhana Pūjā and Annakūṭa
summary: Worship of Mount Govardhana and the offering of a “mountain of food” (annakūṭa) to Kṛṣṇa on Kārttika śukla 1, the day after the Dīpāvalī new moon, recalling Kṛṣṇa’s turning the cowherds from Indra’s worship to the hill and lifting it against Indra’s storm. Central in Braj and in the Puṣṭimārga temples.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Bhrātṛdvitīyā (Bhai Dūj / Yamadvitīyā)
summary: The second day of the bright half of Kārttika, closing Dīpāvalī, on which sisters feed and bless their brothers; the Bhaviṣya tells that Yamunā fed her brother Yama on this day, hence the name Yamadvitīyā.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Holī
summary: The spring festival of the Phālguna full moon: a bonfire (Holikā-dahana) on the full-moon night, followed by the throwing of coloured water and powder. Kane traces the name to Holākā, a usage known to Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsā sūtras (as explained by Śabara) and the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya, and regards it in origin as a spring festival; popular legend explains the bonfire by the burning of Holikā, who tried to kill Prahlāda, while Braj celebrates Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa’s play with colours.

type:LABEL: character
name: Holikā (sister of Hiraṇyakaśipu)
summary: In the legend most widely told for Holī, the sister of the asura king Hiraṇyakaśipu, immune to fire, who sat in a pyre with the child Prahlāda to burn him; she was consumed and Prahlāda survived. The bonfire on the eve of Holī is called Holikā-dahana after her.

type:LABEL: character
name: Ḍhauṇḍhā (Dhondhā), the ogress of the Bhaviṣyottara
summary: An ogress, daughter of Mālin, who in the Bhaviṣyottara’s account of Holī troubled children in king Raghu’s realm; protected by Śiva’s boon from gods, men, weapons and weather, she could be overcome only by boisterous boys, and died when they lit a bonfire with rakṣoghna mantras on the Phālguna full moon.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Dolayātrā (Dol Pūrṇimā)
summary: The swing festival of Kṛṣṇa on the Phālguna full moon in Bengal and Odisha, Bengal’s form of Holī: an image of Govinda is installed on a swing in a sixteen-pillared pavilion, bathed and swung, with coloured powder (abir). Śūlapāṇi wrote a Dolayātrāviveka on it, recording the tradition that king Indradyumna began the swing festival in Vṛndāvana. Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas keep the day as Caitanya’s birthday (Gaura Pūrṇimā).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Navarātri
summary: The nine nights of the Goddess from the first to the ninth of the bright half of Āśvina (with a spring Navarātri in Caitra), observed across India in regional forms — Durgā Pūjā in Bengal, Garbā and Dāṇḍiyā in Gujarat, Golu doll displays in Tamil Nadu, Dasarā in Mysore — and closing with Vijayadaśamī. The Devī Māhātmya is recited during the nine days.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Durgā Pūjā (Bengal)
summary: Bengal’s great autumn festival of the Goddess, worshipped with her children (Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya) in clay images made from Gaṅgā clay, from Mahālayā through the 6th–9th days to immersion on Vijayadaśamī; in Kolkata it has become a city-wide public art festival of community pavilions (pandals). “Durga Puja in Kolkata” was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2021.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vijayadaśamī (Dasarā / Dussehra)
summary: The tenth of the bright half of Āśvina, the day after Navarātri, one of the three most auspicious days of the year: worship of the goddess Aparājitā and of the śamī tree, crossing the village boundary (sīmollaṅghana), worship of weapons and tools, and — in north India — the burning of Rāvaṇa’s effigy at the end of the Rāmlīlā. In Bengal it is the day of Durgā’s immersion (Bijayā).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Mysore Dasarā
summary: The ten-day royal Dasarā of Mysore (Karnataka), centred on the goddess Cāmuṇḍeśvarī of Chamundi Hill, who in local tradition killed Mahiṣāsura there; the Wodeyar kings held a durbar and the procession of the goddess on an elephant (Jambū Savārī) closes the festival on Vijayadaśamī. It continues the royal Mahānavamī of the Vijayanagara court.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Mahāśivarātri
summary: The “great night of Śiva”, the 14th of the dark half of Māgha (Phālguna by the pūrṇimānta reckoning), kept with fasting, worship of the liṅga with bilva leaves and an all-night vigil (jāgaraṇa). The Garuḍa, Skanda, Padma and Agni Purāṇas contain its māhātmya, illustrated by the story of a hunter who, keeping awake in a bilva tree, unknowingly worshipped a liṅga below and won liberation.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī
summary: The celebration of Kṛṣṇa’s birth on the 8th of the dark half of Bhādrapada (Śrāvaṇa in the pūrṇimānta reckoning), with a fast and a vigil until midnight, the hour at which the Bhāgavata says Kṛṣṇa appeared to Devakī. In Maharashtra the next day’s Gopāḷkālā includes the breaking of pots of curd (Dahi Handi).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Rāma Navamī
summary: The celebration of Rāma’s birth on the 9th of the bright half of Caitra, with a fast and midday worship. The Rāmcaritmānas dates the birth to “the holy navamī tithi of the month of Madhu (Caitra), bright fortnight, at abhijit (midday)”, and dates its own beginning to a Rāma Navamī; the constituted text of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Critical Edition narrates the birth without naming a month or tithi.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Gaṇeśa Caturthī
summary: The festival of Gaṇeśa on the 4th of the bright half of Bhādrapada, when a clay image is installed, worshipped for one to ten days and immersed in water. Kane treats the domestic vrata in ch. VIII of his History; in Maharashtra Bal Gangadhar Tilak promoted a public (sārvajanik) form from 1893, which became a mass civic festival.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Sārvajanik Gaṇeśotsav (public Gaṇeśa festival)
summary: The public, neighbourhood-organised form of Gaṇeśa Caturthī with large images in street pavilions and processions to immersion, promoted by Bal Gangadhar Tilak in Pune from 1893 as a vehicle of Hindu mobilisation and nationalist politics; it spread through Maharashtra and to Mumbai, Hyderabad and the diaspora.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
summary: Marathi nationalist leader, journalist and scholar (1856–1920), editor of Kesari, who from 1893 promoted public Gaṇeśa festivals and from 1895 the Śivājī festival in Maharashtra; also author of The Orion (1893) and The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903) on Vedic chronology.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Makara Saṅkrānti
summary: The day the sun is reckoned to enter Capricorn (Makara), about 14 January in traditional almanacs, kept with bathing, gifts of sesame and sugarcane and, in Gujarat, kite-flying (Uttarāyaṇ); it corresponds to Pongal in Tamil Nadu and Māgh Bihu in Assam. Kane notes that the traditional date lags the true winter solstice (21 December) by about twenty-three days because of the precession of the equinoxes.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Gaṅgāsāgar Melā
summary: The pilgrimage and bathing fair at the mouth of the Hooghly on Sagar Island (West Bengal) at Makara Saṅkrānti, where tradition places the hermitage of Kapila and the descent of the Gaṅgā that freed the ashes of Sagara’s sons.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Pongal (Tai Pongal)
summary: The Tamil harvest festival at the beginning of the month of Tai (mid-January), named after the dish of new rice boiled over in milk and offered to the Sun; it runs over three or four days — Bhōgi, Pongal, Māṭṭu Pongal (for cattle) and Kāṇum Pongal. Kane notes that it corresponds to the Makara Saṅkrānti of northern and western India and lasts three days.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Onam
summary: The harvest festival of Kerala in the month of Ciṅṅam (August–September), culminating on Tiruvōṇam with floral carpets (pūkkaḷam), the feast (sadya), boat races and the Pulikaḷi; Malayali tradition holds that it welcomes the annual return of the just asura king Mahābali, sent to the netherworld by Vāmana. The earliest Tamil reference, in the Caṅkam poem Maduraikkāñci, instead calls Ōṇam the day of Māyōṉ (Viṣṇu) who overcame the asuras.

type:LABEL: text
name: Maduraikkāñci
summary: A Caṅkam poem of 782 lines by Māṅkuṭi Marutaṉār, one of the Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu), addressed to the Pāṇḍya king Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ and describing a day and night in Madurai; it contains the earliest known mention of the Ōṇam festival (lines 590–591).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Chhaṭh Pūjā
summary: A festival of the Sun (Sūrya) and of the goddess Chhaṭhī Maiyā kept chiefly in Bihar, Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh and the Nepal Tarai on the 6th of the bright half of Kārttika, six days after Dīpāvalī: after days of fasting, worshippers stand in rivers and ponds to offer arghya to the setting and then the rising sun. It has travelled with Bhojpuri- and Maithili-speaking migrants to Indian cities and the diaspora.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Chhaṭhī Maiyā
summary: The mother goddess worshipped with the Sun at Chhaṭh in Bihar and neighbouring regions, regarded as a protector of children; often identified in modern accounts with Ṣaṣṭhī, the goddess of the sixth day after birth, and sometimes called the Sun’s sister or consort.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Ratha Yātrā of Puri
summary: The chariot festival of Jagannātha at Puri on the second day of the bright half of Āṣāḍha: Jagannātha, Balabhadra and Subhadrā are drawn on three newly built wooden chariots along the Bada Danda to the Guṇḍicā temple and back after nine days. The Gajapati king sweeps the chariots (chera pahanra). Caitanya’s ecstatic dancing before the chariots is a central scene of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Thaipusam
summary: The Tamil festival of Murukaṉ on the Pūcam asterism of the month of Tai (January–February), when devotees carry kāvaṭi burdens, milk pots and lances piercing the body in fulfilment of vows; tradition says it commemorates Pārvatī’s gift of the vēl (lance) to Murukaṉ for his war against the asura Cūrapatmaṉ. It is kept at Paḻaṉi and other Murukaṉ shrines and, on the largest scale, in Malaysia (Batu Caves, since the 1890s), Singapore and Mauritius.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kumbh Melā
summary: The “festival of the sacred pitcher”, a mass bathing pilgrimage held in rotation at Prayāga (Allahabad/Prayagraj), Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik, each roughly every twelve years by an astronomical reckoning, so that one of the four falls about every three years; UNESCO calls it “the largest peaceful congregation of pilgrims on earth”. Its primary bearers are the ascetic akhāṛās and āśramas. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2017.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Kumbh Melā is an ancient institution with a continuous history at its four sites
summary: The popular and official view presents the Kumbh Melā as of great antiquity, sometimes citing Xuanzang’s seventh-century account of a great gathering at Prayāga; Maclean argues from colonial and pilgrim-priest records that the Allahabad Kumbh in its present form and name is a nineteenth-century development of the annual Māgh Melā.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Pandharpur Vārī (Āṣāḍhī pilgrimage)
summary: The annual foot-pilgrimage of the Vārkarīs to Viṭṭhala at Pandharpur for Āṣāḍhī Ekādaśī (June–July): hundreds of thousands walk for about three weeks in organised groups (diṇḍīs) singing abhaṅgas, escorting palanquins (pālkhīs) bearing the sandals (pādukās) of the saints — chiefly Jñāneśvar’s from Āḷandī and Tukārām’s from Dehū. A second, smaller vārī falls on Kārttikī Ekādaśī.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Ayyappa (Ayyappan, Śāstā)
summary: The celibate forest god of Śabarimala in Kerala, worshipped as Dharmaśāstā and as Hariharaputra, the son born of Śiva and Viṣṇu in his female form Mohinī; local tradition also tells of the foundling prince Maṇikaṇṭhan of Pandalam who killed the buffalo-demoness Mahiṣī. His cult draws millions of male pilgrims each season.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śabarimala pilgrimage
summary: The season-long pilgrimage (mid-November to January) to the hill shrine of Ayyappa at Śabarimala in the Western Ghats of Kerala. Pilgrims keep a 41-day vow (vratam) of celibacy, vegetarian diet and black or blue dress, address one another as “Ayyappa”, and climb carrying the irumuḍi bundle of offerings; the season culminates at Makaravilakku (Makara Saṅkrānti). Many visit the shrine of Vāvar, a Muslim companion of Ayyappa, at Erumeli on the way.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kāṁvaṛ (Kāvaḍ) Yātrā
summary: The pilgrimage of the month of Śrāvaṇa in which devotees of Śiva (kāṁvaṛiyās), dressed in saffron, carry Gaṅgā water in pots slung from a shoulder pole (kāṁvaṛ) — from Haridwar, Gaumukh or Sultanganj — on foot to pour over the liṅgas of their home temples or of Baidyanāth at Deoghar. It has grown since the 1980s into one of the largest annual pilgrimages in north India.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Garbā of Gujarat
summary: The ritual and devotional circle dance of Gujarat performed during Navarātri around a perforated earthenware pot lit with an oil lamp (garbo) or an image of the mother goddess Ambā, moving counter-clockwise while singing and clapping, slow at first and building to whirling. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2023.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Yoga (UNESCO living-heritage element)
summary: The practice of yoga as a living tradition — postures, meditation, controlled breathing and chanting aimed at self-realisation and liberation — inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2016 on India’s nomination. UNESCO describes it as traditionally transmitted from guru to disciple and now also through āśramas, schools and media worldwide.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Muṭiyēṯṯu
summary: A ritual dance-drama of central Kerala enacting the battle between the goddess Kāḷī (Bhadrakāḷī) and the demon Dārika, performed by the whole village after the summer harvest in the goddess temples (Bhagavati kāvus) along the Chalakudy, Periyar and Moovattupuzha rivers; a great image of Kāḷī (kaḷam) is first drawn on the temple floor in coloured powders. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2010.

type:LABEL: character
name: Dārika
summary: An asura of Kerala tradition who, by a boon that no mortal could kill him, oppressed the worlds until Bhadrakāḷī, born from Śiva’s third eye, slew him; the story is enacted in Muṭiyēṯṯu and other Bhagavati rituals of Kerala.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Kāḷī slays Dārika
summary: The Kerala myth of the goddess Bhadrakāḷī’s war against the asura Dārika, whom no mortal could kill; Nārada informs Śiva, who decrees that Dārika shall die by the Goddess. It is the plot of Muṭiyēṯṯu and of songs and rites in the Bhagavati temples of central Kerala.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Rammāṇ
summary: A religious festival and masked ritual theatre held each year in late April in the twin villages of Saloor-Dungra (Chamoli, Uttarakhand) in honour of the village tutelary god Bhūmiyāl Devtā, combining recitation of a version of the Rāma story and other legends with songs and masked dances; only the Bhaṇḍārīs may wear the most sacred mask, that of Narasiṃha. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2009.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Bhūmiyāl Devtā (Saloor-Dungra)
summary: The tutelary village god of Saloor-Dungra in the Garhwal Himalaya, in whose honour and temple the Rammāṇ festival is held; the family that hosts the god during the year keeps a strict daily routine.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Chhau
summary: A masked and martial dance tradition of eastern India in three styles — Seraikella (Jharkhand), Purulia (West Bengal) and Mayurbhanj (Odisha), the first two masked — enacting episodes from the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa, local folklore and abstract themes, closely tied to the spring festival Caitra Parva. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2010.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Saṅkīrtana of Manipur
summary: The ritual singing, drumming and dancing of the Vaiṣṇavas of the Manipur plains, performed at temples, festivals and life-cycle rites: two drummers and about ten singer-dancers narrate the life and deeds of Kṛṣṇa in a hall or courtyard ringed by seated devotees, and the performance is regarded as a visible manifestation of God. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2013.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Tradition of Vedic chanting (UNESCO element)
summary: The oral transmission of the four Vedas by memorised recitation with exact accentuation and the mnemonic recitation patterns (pāṭhas), proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003 and inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Sbek Thom (Khmer shadow theatre)
summary: Cambodian shadow theatre with two-metre-high, non-articulated puppets cut from a single hide, held up before a fire-lit screen by dancers while two narrators and an orchestra perform scenes of the Reamker, the Khmer Rāmāyaṇa, over several nights with up to 160 puppets. Proclaimed a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed in 2008.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Lkhon Khol Wat Svay Andet
summary: Khmer masked dance-drama performed by men in the community around the Buddhist monastery of Wat Svay Andet on the Mekong east of Phnom Penh, to propitiate the Neak Ta guardian spirits for the community and its harvest; spirit mediums attend the performance. Inscribed in 2018 on UNESCO’s List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Three genres of traditional dance in Bali
summary: Balinese dance in its three genres — sacred (wali), semi-sacred (bebali) and for public enjoyment (balih-balihan) — performed to gamelan by male and female dancers in gold-painted costumes, and transmitted informally to children from an early age. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2015.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Geet-Gawai (Bhojpuri folk songs in Mauritius)
summary: A pre-wedding ceremony of Bhojpuri-speaking Mauritians of Indian descent, held at the bride’s or groom’s home, combining rituals, prayers, songs honouring Hindu gods and goddesses, the drum (dholak) and dance; it begins with five married women sorting turmeric, rice, grass and money in a cloth. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2016.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Sant tradition (nirguṇa bhakti)
summary: The loose lineage of north and west Indian poet-saints — Nāmdev, Kabīr, Raidās, Dādū and others — who addressed a formless (nirguṇa) Lord, usually named Rām or Hari, through the divine Name and the true guru, and criticised caste, image-worship and ritual. Scholars treat “sant” as a family resemblance rather than an organised sect; Kabīr Panth, Dādū Panth and the Sikh Gurus draw on it.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rāmānanda
summary: North Indian Vaiṣṇava teacher (14th–15th c.), traditionally of Vārāṇasī, revered as founder of the Rāmānandī order; hagiography from the Bhaktamāl onward makes Kabīr, Raidās and others his disciples, which historians treat as a later construction of lineage.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kabīr
summary: Weaver-poet of Vārāṇasī (15th c.), raised in a Muslim julāhā family, the most quoted of the north Indian Sants: his sākhīs, padas and ramainīs address a formless Rām, mock both brāhmaṇ and mullā, and insist on the Name and the true guru. Verses in his name are preserved in three main collections — the eastern Bījak, the Rajasthani (Dādūpanthī) Kabīr Granthāvalī and the Sikh Ādi Granth.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kabīr Panth
summary: The religious community of Kabīr’s followers, organised in monastic and householder branches (notably the Kabīr Chaurā at Vārāṇasī and the Dharamdāsī branch of central India), which treats Kabīr as the true guru and the Bījak (or the Kabīr Sāgar) as scripture.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bījak
summary: The “Seed” or “Account”: the collection of Kabīr’s ramainīs, śabdas and sākhīs canonical in the Kabīr Panth, representing the eastern (Bhojpuri-coloured) transmission of his poetry.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kabīr Granthāvalī (Rajasthani recension)
summary: The western collection of Kabīr’s verses transmitted in Dādūpanthī manuscripts of Rajasthan and edited in the twentieth century; with the Bījak and the Sikh Ādi Granth one of the three main recensions of Kabīr.

type:LABEL: person
name: Raidās (Ravidās)
summary: Leatherworker (camār) poet-saint of Vārāṇasī (15th–16th c.) whose songs to a formless Lord reject caste hierarchy; preserved in the Sikh Ādi Granth and the Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī, he is revered as guru by the Ravidassia community and, in Rajasthani legend, as Mīrābāī’s guru.

type:LABEL: text
name: Padas of Raidās
summary: The songs attributed to Raidās, transmitted in the Sikh Ādi Granth (about forty śabads), in the Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī of Rajasthan and in later collections; edited and translated by Callewaert and Friedlander (1992).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Ravidassia (Ravidās Panth)
summary: The community of followers of Guru Ravidās, largely of Dalit (camār) background in Punjab and its diaspora; historically close to Sikh practice, its leading centre, Dera Sachkhand Ballan, proclaimed it a distinct religion in 2010 with the Amritbāṇī of Ravidās as scripture.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mīrābāī
summary: Rajput princess-poet of Merta and Mewar (16th c.), devotee of Kṛṣṇa as Giridhar Gopāl, whose legend of defiance of her in-laws and of caste and gender norms is told across north India; the earliest datable reference to her is a stanza in Nābhādās’s Bhaktamāl (c. 1600). Hundreds of songs bear her name, nearly all of uncertain authorship.

type:LABEL: text
name: Padāvalī of Mīrābāī
summary: The large and open corpus of songs (padas) in Rajasthani, Braj and Gujarati attributed to Mīrābāī, addressed to Kṛṣṇa as lover and husband; very few are found in early dated manuscripts.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nābhādās
summary: Rāmānandī poet of Galtā near Jaipur (late 16th–early 17th c.), author of the Bhaktamāl, the “Garland of Devotees”, the first comprehensive hagiographical anthology of north Indian bhakti.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhaktamāl
summary: Nābhādās’s Braj Bhāṣā “Garland of Devotees” (c. 1600), some two hundred short chappay stanzas on devotees from the mythic past to his contemporaries — Kabīr, Raidās, Mīrā, Sūrdās, Tulsīdās and many others — and the earliest datable reference for several of them. Priyādās’s commentary (1712) expanded it into narrative hagiography.

type:LABEL: person
name: Priyādās
summary: Gauḍīya-influenced poet of Vṛndāvan who completed in 1712 the Bhaktirasabodhinī, a verse commentary on the Bhaktamāl that turned its terse stanzas into the miracle-rich stories of the saints known today.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhaktirasabodhinī
summary: Priyādās’s Braj commentary (1712) on Nābhādās’s Bhaktamāl, the main source of the popular stories of Kabīr, Mīrā, Tulsīdās and others.

type:LABEL: person
name: Dādū Dayāl
summary: Sant poet of Rajasthan (1544–1603), a cotton-carder by tradition, whose followers founded the Dādū Panth; the Dādūpanthīs compiled the Pañcvāṇī anthologies preserving the songs of Kabīr, Nāmdev, Raidās and Hardās with Dādū’s own.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vinaya Patrikā
summary: Tulsīdās’s “Petition of Humility”, 279 Braj Bhāṣā hymns framed as a petition to Rāma’s court, addressed first to Gaṇeśa, Śiva, Hanumān and other deities and then to Rāma; valued for its personal devotion and its theology of the Name.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kavitāvalī
summary: Tulsīdās’s Braj collection of kavitt, savaiyā and other stanzas retelling the Rāma story in seven kāṇḍas, with a long Uttarakāṇḍa of personal and social verses on Kali-age Banaras and the power of Rāma’s name.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gītāvalī
summary: Tulsīdās’s Braj Rāmāyaṇa in songs: 328 padas in seven kāṇḍas set to rāgas, elaborating some episodes and abridging others.

type:LABEL: text
name: Hanumān Bāhuk
summary: A Braj prayer of 44 stanzas to Hanumān, traditionally composed by Tulsīdās in old age when he suffered acute pain in his arm (c. 1607).

type:LABEL: person
name: Viṭṭhalnāth (Gusāiṃjī)
summary: Younger son and successor of Vallabha (1515–1586) who organised the Puṣṭimārga’s temple liturgy of eight daily darśans and, by tradition in 1565, named eight poets — the Aṣṭachāp — whose songs were to be sung in it.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Aṣṭachāp (the “eight seals”)
summary: The eight poet-singers recognised by Viṭṭhalnāth as the authorised singers of the Puṣṭimārga liturgy at the Śrīnāthjī temple on Govardhana: Sūrdās, Kumbhandās, Paramānanddās and Kṛṣṇadās (counted as Vallabha’s disciples) and Nanddās, Chītasvāmī, Govindasvāmī and Caturbhujdās (Viṭṭhalnāth’s). Their padas form the core of havelī saṅgīt.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kumbhandās
summary: Farmer-poet of Jamunavato near Govardhana, the earliest of Vallabha’s disciples among the Aṣṭachāp; Puṣṭimārga hagiography tells that he refused the emperor’s summons to Fatehpur Sikri.

type:LABEL: person
name: Paramānanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet from Kannauj, a disciple of Vallabha, whose Braj padas on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood are collected as the Paramānandsāgar.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṛṣṇadās (Aṣṭachāp)
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet of Gujarati origin and long-time manager (adhikārī) of the Śrīnāthjī temple under Vallabha and Viṭṭhalnāth.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth, celebrated for the refined Braj of his Rāspañcādhyāyī and Bhramargīt, which recast Bhāgavata episodes.

type:LABEL: person
name: Chītasvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a Mathurā Caube priest who became Viṭṭhalnāth’s disciple.

type:LABEL: person
name: Govindasvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet and musician, a disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth, who lived near Govardhana.

type:LABEL: person
name: Caturbhujdās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, son of Kumbhandās and a disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth.

type:LABEL: text
name: Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā
summary: The Braj prose “Accounts of Eighty-four Vaiṣṇavas”, Puṣṭimārga hagiographies of Vallabha’s disciples (including Sūrdās and the other early Aṣṭachāp poets), attributed to Gokulnāth and transmitted with Harirāy’s commentary (17th c.).

type:LABEL: person
name: Rūpa Gosvāmī
summary: Senior of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvan (1489–1564), a former minister of the Bengal sultanate who met Caitanya at Prayāga; in the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi he recast Sanskrit aesthetic theory (rasa) as a theology of devotion, and wrote the Kṛṣṇa dramas Vidagdhamādhava and Lalitamādhava.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sanātana Gosvāmī
summary: Elder brother of Rūpa and one of the Six Gosvāmīs (1488–1558), instructed by Caitanya at Vārāṇasī according to the Caitanya Caritāmṛta; author of the Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta and a commentary on the Bhāgavata’s tenth book, and traditionally of the ritual code Haribhaktivilāsa.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jīva Gosvāmī
summary: Nephew of Rūpa and Sanātana and the systematic theologian of the Gauḍīya school (c. 1513–c. 1598), author of the six Sandarbhas, which ground Caitanya’s teaching in the Bhāgavata, and founder of the Rādhā-Dāmodara temple in Vṛndāvan.

type:LABEL: person
name: Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs (1503–1578), from a Śrīvaiṣṇava family of Śrīraṅgam, traditionally co-author of the Haribhaktivilāsa and founder of the Rādhāramaṇa temple in Vṛndāvan.

type:LABEL: person
name: Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs (1505–1579), remembered as a reciter of the Bhāgavata in Vṛndāvan.

type:LABEL: person
name: Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī
summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs, a renunciant son of a wealthy Bengali family who lived for years at Rādhākuṇḍa; his memories of Caitanya’s last years at Puri are a main source for Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Works of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvan
summary: The Sanskrit theological, ritual, aesthetic and dramatic works of Rūpa, Sanātana, Jīva and their colleagues (16th c.) that define Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava doctrine and practice.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu
summary: Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Sanskrit “Ocean of the Nectar of Devotional Rasa”, which classifies devotion (bhakti) and its emotions with the categories of Sanskrit poetics, making bhakti itself the supreme rasa. Its closing verse says it was completed while the author dwelt in Gokula, in a Śaka year given by a word-numeral.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ujjvalanīlamaṇi
summary: Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Sanskrit treatise on the erotic mode of devotion (madhura-rasa), a sequel to the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, which classifies Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds and makes Rādhā, with Candrāvalī, the chief of his eternal beloveds in Vraja.

type:LABEL: text
name: Haribhaktivilāsa
summary: The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava ritual digest (16th c.) on initiation, daily worship, festivals and conduct, attributed to Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī with a commentary ascribed to Sanātana.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ṣaṭ Sandarbha
summary: Jīva Gosvāmī’s six “Treatises” (Tattva-, Bhagavat-, Paramātma-, Kṛṣṇa-, Bhakti- and Prīti-sandarbha), a systematic theology of the Gauḍīya school built on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vṛndāvana Dāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Bengali poet (1507–1589), disciple of Nityānanda, whose Caitanya Bhāgavata is the first full-length Bengali biography of Caitanya.

type:LABEL: text
name: Caitanya Bhāgavata
summary: Vṛndāvana Dāsa’s Bengali verse biography of Caitanya (16th c.), the earliest full-length life in Bengali, concentrating on his youth in Navadvīpa and his early ministry; it presents him as Kṛṣṇa (and Rādhā) descended.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śikṣāṣṭaka
summary: Eight Sanskrit verses of instruction on the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names, humility and longing, attributed to Caitanya and quoted in the last chapter of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta; the only verses Gauḍīyas ascribe to him directly.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śākta Padāvalī (Bengali songs to the Goddess)
summary: The Bengali song literature to Kālī and Umā from the eighteenth century onward — Śyāmā-saṅgīt to Kālī and the Āgamanī–Bijayā songs of Umā’s homecoming at Durgā Pūjā — initiated by Rāmprasād Sen and Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rāmprasād Sen
summary: Bengali Śākta poet of Halisahar (c. 1718/1723–c. 1775) whose intimate, often reproachful songs to Kālī as mother (Rāmprasādī) created the genre of Śyāmā-saṅgīt; patronised by Rājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia, who gave him the title Kavirañjana.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: Bengali Śākta poet and tantric practitioner (1769–1821), court poet of the Mahārājā of Burdwan, who after Rāmprasād shaped the Śākta padāvalī, including the Āgamanī songs of Umā’s homecoming.

type:LABEL: person
name: Baḍu Caṇḍīdās
summary: Bengali poet to whom the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan is ascribed (late 14th–15th c.?). Songs signed “Caṇḍīdās” — with the epithets Baḍu, Dvija and Dīna — appear to belong to more than one poet, a puzzle known as the Caṇḍīdās problem.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan
summary: A Bengali dramatic song-cycle of the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa ascribed to Baḍu Caṇḍīdās, known from a single incomplete manuscript found in the early twentieth century in a cowshed in Bankura district and published by the Bangiya Sahitya Parishad; among the earliest monuments of Middle Bengali.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vidyāpati
summary: Maithili and Sanskrit poet, scholar and courtier of the Oinwāra kings of Mithilā (c. 1352–1448), whose Maithili songs of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa were taken up by Bengali Vaiṣṇavas (and imitated in Brajabuli), while his songs to Śiva (nacārī) and his Sanskrit works on Durgā worship show a Smārta devotion to several deities.

type:LABEL: text
name: Padāvalī of Vidyāpati
summary: The Maithili love-songs (padas) of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and songs to Śiva and the Goddess attributed to Vidyāpati, transmitted in Mithilā, Nepal and Bengal; Caitanya is said to have delighted in them.

type:LABEL: text
name: Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī
summary: Vidyāpati’s Sanskrit manual of the autumn worship of Durgā, cited by Kane among the special treatises on the Durgotsava/Navarātra.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nām Ghoṣā
summary: Mādhavadeva’s Assamese “Proclamation of the Name”, about a thousand verses in praise of the Name of Kṛṣṇa (Rāma/Hari), with Śaṅkaradeva’s Kīrtana Ghoṣā a principal scripture of the Ekaśaraṇa sattras and nāmghars.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Bargīt
summary: The “great songs” of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva (15th–16th c.) in Brajāvalī, set to rāgas but not necessarily to tāla, sung to open services in the sattras and nāmghars of the Ekaśaraṇa Dharma.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Aṅkīyā Nāṭ and Bhāonā
summary: The one-act devotional plays in Brajāvalī created by Śaṅkaradeva in the early sixteenth century, mostly on Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, and their performance (bhāonā) in the nāmghars and sattras of Assam, directed and narrated by a sūtradhāra.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Sattriya
summary: The dance tradition of the Ekaśaraṇa sattras, created within the bhāonā performances of Śaṅkaradeva’s plays and maintained by celibate monks; recognised among India’s classical dances by the Sangeet Natak Akademi in 2000.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Sattra (Vaiṣṇava monasteries of Assam)
summary: The monastic and congregational institutions of the Ekaśaraṇa Dharma — chiefly on Majuli and in upper Assam — that preserve its scriptures, Bargīt, plays and dance under a sattrādhikār.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Pañcasakhā (the “five friends” of Odia literature)
summary: The five sixteenth-century Odia poet-saints — Balarāma Dāsa, Jagannātha Dāsa, Acyutānanda Dāsa, Yaśovanta Dāsa and Ananta Dāsa — who rendered Sanskrit scriptures into Odia and joined Jagannātha devotion with a meditative, nirguṇa-leaning Vaiṣṇavism, sometimes called Utkalīya Vaiṣṇavism.

type:LABEL: person
name: Balarāma Dāsa
summary: Eldest of the Odia Pañcasakhā, author of the Jagamohana (Dāṇḍi) Rāmāyaṇa, the Lakṣmī Purāṇa and the Bhakti-tattva of the “Bata Abakasha”; tradition calls him Krupāsiddha.

type:LABEL: person
name: Acyutānanda Dāsa
summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet and saint, prolific author of Mālikās (prophetic verses), genealogical and devotional works, and a figure of popular prophecy in Odisha.

type:LABEL: person
name: Yaśovanta Dāsa
summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet, remembered for devotional and yogic songs (the Prema Bhakti Brahma Gītā and Mālikās are attributed to him).

type:LABEL: person
name: Ananta Dāsa
summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet, author by tradition of the Hetu-udaya Bhāgavata and devotional songs.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jagamohana Rāmāyaṇa (Dāṇḍi Rāmāyaṇa)
summary: Balarāma Dāsa’s Odia Rāmāyaṇa (early 16th c.), in the popular dāṇḍi metre, a free retelling rather than a translation of Vālmīki, long recited in Odisha’s village prayer-houses.

type:LABEL: person
name: Janābāī
summary: Marathi Vārkarī poet-saint (d. 1350 by tradition), a low-caste orphan who served as a maid in Nāmdev’s household at Pandharpur; her abhaṅgas address Viṭṭhal with startling intimacy as mother, friend and helper in her chores.

type:LABEL: person
name: Muktābāī
summary: Younger sister of Jñāneśvar (13th c.) and Vārkarī poet of about forty abhaṅgas, remembered in tradition as the teacher of the yogī Cāṅgdev.

type:LABEL: person
name: Cokhāmeḷā
summary: Vārkarī poet-saint of the Mahār (untouchable) caste (13th–14th c.), of Mangalvedhe, a companion of Nāmdev; barred from the Viṭṭhal temple, he sang of the god outside it, and his samādhi lies at the foot of the temple steps in Pandharpur. He is a key figure for modern Dalit memory.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bahiṇābāī
summary: Marathi Vārkarī poet-saint (1628–1700), a brāhmaṇ woman who took Tukārām as her guru in a vision and whose autobiography in abhaṅgas (Ātmanivedana) records the conflict of devotion with her married life.

type:LABEL: person
name: Samarth Rāmdās
summary: Marathi saint (c. 1608–1682), devotee of Rāma and Hanumān, founder of the Rāmdāsī order and of Hanumān shrines across Maharashtra, author of the Dāsbodh and the Manāce Ślok; later tradition makes him guru to the Maratha king Śivājī.

type:LABEL: text
name: Dāsbodh
summary: Rāmdās’s Marathi “Advice to the Servant” (1654), 7,751 ovīs in twenty chapters of ten sub-chapters each, a dialogue of guru and disciple on devotion, knowledge and worldly conduct, dictated to his disciple Kalyāṇ Svāmī.

type:LABEL: text
name: Manāce Ślok
summary: Rāmdās’s 205 Marathi verses “to the mind”, a widely memorised didactic poem urging the mind toward Rāma.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vaiṣṇava jana to
summary: Narsinh Mehtā’s Gujarati pad defining the true devotee of Viṣṇu by ethical conduct — feeling others’ pain, humility, freedom from greed — rather than caste or ritual; it was sung daily in Gandhi’s āśrams.

type:LABEL: person
name: Premānand Bhaṭṭ
summary: Gujarati poet and professional storyteller (māṇbhaṭ, 1636–1714) of Vadodara, master of the ākhyāna — sung narratives of Purāṇic and bhakti stories such as Okhāharaṇ, Nalākhyān and Sudāmā-caritra, and of Narsinh Mehtā’s life.

type:LABEL: person
name: Swaminarayan (Sahajānand Svāmī)
summary: Ascetic and religious founder (1781–1830), born Ghanaśyām Pāṇḍe near Ayodhyā, who after years of wandering was initiated by Rāmānand Svāmī in Gujarat in 1800 and succeeded him in 1802; his followers worship him as the supreme manifestation of God (Puruṣottama), and the Swaminarayan Sampradāya grew from his reforms.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Swaminarayan Sampradāya
summary: A Vaiṣṇava tradition founded in Gujarat in the early nineteenth century around Sahajānand Svāmī (Swaminarayan), rooted in Rāmānuja’s Viśiṣṭādvaita, organised around the dioceses of Ahmedabad and Vadtal and temples built in his lifetime, and spread by Gujarati migrants to East Africa, Britain and North America.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vacanāmṛt
summary: The 273 Gujarati discourses of Swaminarayan delivered between 1819 and 1829, compiled by five senior disciples and approved by him; the principal theological scripture of the Swaminarayan Sampradāya.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śikṣāpatrī
summary: Swaminarayan’s code of conduct in 212 Sanskrit verses (1826) for his followers; on 26 February 1830 at Rajkot he presented a copy to Sir John Malcolm, Governor of Bombay, which is now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: BAPS (Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha)
summary: A Swaminarayan denomination formed in 1905 by Shastri Yagnapurushdas (Shastriji Maharaj), teaching that Swaminarayan (Puruṣottama) remains present through a succession of gurus who embody Akṣara, beginning with Guṇātītānand Svāmī; known worldwide for its large stone mandirs, including Neasden (London) and Robbinsville (New Jersey).

type:LABEL: person
name: Shastriji Maharaj (Shastri Yagnapurushdas)
