summary: Swaminarayan monk and scholar (1865–1951) who in 1905 left the Vadtal diocese to found BAPS around the Akṣara–Puruṣottama doctrine.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Haridāsa (Dāsa Kūṭa)
summary: The movement of Kannada devotional singers — “servants of Hari” — within the Mādhva (Dvaita) tradition, from Śrīpādarāja and Vyāsatīrtha to Purandaradāsa and Kanakadāsa and later Vijayadāsa, whose simple Kannada songs (kīrtanas, ugābhogas, suḷādis) carried Dvaita devotion to the people and shaped Carnatic music.

type:LABEL: person
name: Purandaradāsa
summary: Kannada Haridāsa poet-composer (c. 1484–1564), a wealthy merchant who became a disciple of Vyāsatīrtha; his songs signed “Purandara Viṭhala” and his graded exercises made him the “grandfather” (pitāmaha) of Carnatic music.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kanakadāsa
summary: Kannada Haridāsa poet (1509–1609 or 1606), of the Kuruba (shepherd) community, disciple of Vyāsatīrtha; Udupi tradition says Kṛṣṇa turned to face him through a window in the temple wall (Kanakana kiṇḍi) when he was barred from entering. Author of the Mohanataraṅgiṇi and the allegory Rāmadhānya Caritre.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mohanataraṅgiṇi
summary: Kanakadāsa’s Kannada narrative poem (in sāṅgatya metre) on Kṛṣṇa’s life at Dvārakā, including the love of Uṣā and Aniruddha.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rāmadhānya Caritre
summary: Kanakadāsa’s Kannada allegory in which ragi (finger millet), the grain of the poor, wins a debate with rice before Rāma and earns the name rāmadhānya — read as a protest against caste privilege.

type:LABEL: person
name: Annamācārya (Annamayya)
summary: Telugu composer of Tāḷḷapāka (1408–1503) who sang to Veṅkaṭeśvara of Tirumala; family tradition credits him with some 32,000 saṅkīrtanas, of which about 14,900 survive engraved on copper plates kept at Tirumala, the earliest large body of songs in the kīrtana form.

type:LABEL: text
name: Saṅkīrtanas of Annamācārya
summary: The Telugu (and some Sanskrit) songs of Annamācārya on Veṅkaṭeśvara, in devotional (adhyātma) and erotic (śṛṅgāra) modes, preserved on the Tāḷḷapāka copper plates at Tirumala; translated in part by Narayana Rao and Shulman (2005).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Carnatic music
summary: The classical music tradition of south India, built on rāga and tāla and on a repertoire of devotional song (kṛti, kīrtana, padam, varṇam) — from the Haridāsas and Annamācārya to the eighteenth–nineteenth-century “Trinity” of Tyāgarāja, Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tyāgarāja
summary: Telugu composer of Tiruvaiyaru in the Thanjavur country (1767–1847), the most celebrated of the Carnatic “Trinity”, whose hundreds of kṛtis — among them the five Pañcaratna kṛtis — are songs of devotion to Rāma; he is said to have refused royal patronage.

type:LABEL: person
name: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar
summary: Sanskrit-language composer of the Carnatic “Trinity” (1775/76–1835), signing as “Guruguha”; his some 500 kṛtis describe the deities, temples and tantric worship of dozens of shrines, including the Kamalāmbā Navāvaraṇa kṛtis of Tiruvārūr.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śyāma Śāstri
summary: Eldest of the Carnatic “Trinity” (1762–1827), a priest of the goddess Kāmākṣī (Bangāru Kāmākṣī) at Thanjavur, whose compositions are almost all addressed to the Goddess.

type:LABEL: text
name: Pañcaratna kṛtis
summary: Five Telugu kṛtis of Tyāgarāja in the rāgas Nāṭa, Gauḷa, Ārabhi, Varāḷi and Śrī, sung together by assembled musicians at his annual ārādhanā at Tiruvaiyaru.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Tyāgarāja Ārādhanā
summary: The annual music festival at Tyāgarāja’s samādhi on the Kāvēri at Tiruvaiyaru on the anniversary of his death (Puṣya bahuḷa pañcamī), culminating in the collective singing of the Pañcaratna kṛtis.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu (Kañcarla Gopanna)
summary: Telugu devotee-composer (c. 1620–1688), revenue official under the Qutb Shāhī sultans of Golconda, who by tradition spent government money rebuilding the Rāma temple at Bhadrācalam, was imprisoned for twelve years and released when Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa repaid the sum; author of kīrtanas and the Dāśarathi Śatakam.

type:LABEL: text
name: Dāśarathi Śatakam
summary: A Telugu śatakam of about a hundred verses addressed to Rāma, son of Daśaratha, attributed to Kañcarla Gopanna (Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu).

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṣetrayya
summary: Telugu composer of padams (c. 1600–1680) from Muvva in the Krishna delta, whose love songs to Muvva Gopāla (Kṛṣṇa), voiced mostly by courtesans and women, became central to the repertoire of dance (devadāsī and later Bharatanāṭyam).

type:LABEL: text
name: Padams of Kṣetrayya
summary: Several hundred surviving Telugu padams (of thousands attributed) signed with the mudrā “Muvva Gopāla”, translated in part in When God Is a Customer (1994).

type:LABEL: person
name: Akka Mahādēvi
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet-saint of the twelfth century from Uḍutaḍi, who renounced marriage (and, in legend, clothing) for her divine husband Śiva as Cennamallikārjuna, “the lord white as jasmine”, and joined the gathering of Basava and Allama at Kalyāṇa before ending her life on Śrīśaila; some 430 vacanas are attributed to her.

type:LABEL: person
name: Allama Prabhu
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva mystic poet of the twelfth century, presiding figure of the Anubhava Maṇṭapa of Kalyāṇa in tradition, whose enigmatic vacanas to Guhēśvara (“lord of the caves”) criticise ritual and teach the unity of self and Śiva.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vacanas of Akka Mahādēvi
summary: The Kannada free-verse sayings (vacanas) signed “Cennamallikārjuna”, about 430 attributed to Akka Mahādēvi.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vacanas of Allama Prabhu
summary: The Kannada vacanas signed “Guhēśvara” attributed to Allama Prabhu, admired for paradox and riddling imagery.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śūnya Sampādane
summary: A fifteenth-century Kannada anthology that arranges the vacanas of Allama, Basava, Akka Mahādēvi and others as dialogues in the Anubhava Maṇṭapa around Allama, the “attainment of the void”; compiled in several redactions in the Vijayanagara period.

type:LABEL: person
name: Aruṇakirinātar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet of Tiruvaṇṇāmalai (c. 1370–1450 on Zvelebil’s dating), author of the Tiruppukaḻ, rhythmically intricate songs to Murukaṉ at his shrines, and of the Kantar Anupūti and Kantar Alaṅkāram.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruppukaḻ
summary: Aruṇakirinātar’s “Holy Praise”, some 1,300 surviving Tamil songs to Murukaṉ in elaborate rhythmic patterns (cantam), arranged by the shrines they praise; the Project Madurai edition numbers the songs 1–1326.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mēlputtūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri
summary: Kerala Sanskrit poet and grammarian (1560–1646/1666), author of the Prakriyāsarvasva on Pāṇinian grammar and of the Nārāyaṇīyam, a condensation of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa in a thousand verses addressed to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nārāyaṇīyam
summary: A Sanskrit devotional poem of 100 cantos (daśakas), 1,034 verses, condensing the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and addressed throughout to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr (“pavanapurapate”). Its last verse ends with the phrase “āyurārogyasaukhyam”, which as a kali-day chronogram gives a date in 1586 CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Pūntānam Nampūtiri
summary: Malayalam devotional poet (1547–1640) of Keezhattoor, devotee of Guruvāyūrappan, author of the Jñānappāna; Guruvāyūr legend contrasts his simple bhakti, which the god preferred, with Bhaṭṭatiri’s learned Sanskrit.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jñānappāna
summary: Pūntānam’s Malayalam “Song of Divine Wisdom” (16th c.), a meditation in simple verse on the transience of life and devotion to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ (Vaḷḷalār)
summary: Tamil saint and poet (1823–1874) of Marutūr near Chidambaram, who preached compassion to all living beings (jīvakāruṇyam), founded the Samaraca Cutta Caṉmārka Caṅkam (1865), a free kitchen at Vadalur (1867) and the Sathya Gnana Sabai (1872) to a formless “Arutperuñjōti” (Grace-Light); his collected hymns, the Tiruvaruṭpā, provoked the “Aruṭpā–Maruṭpā” controversy with Śaiva Siddhāntins.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Samaraca Cutta Caṉmārkam (Vaḷḷalār’s path)
aliases: Samarasa Suddha Sanmarga Sathya Sangam|Vallalar movement
summary: The universalist movement founded by Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ in 1865, centred on the worship of God as light and on feeding the hungry, with its Sathya Gnana Sabai at Vadalur (1872).

type:LABEL: text
name: Tiruvaruṭpā
summary: The collected Tamil hymns of Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ, arranged in six tirumuṟais, the first parts published in his lifetime (1867); their claim to scriptural status was attacked by Āṟumuka Nāvalar in the “Aruṭpā–Maruṭpā” dispute.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhānubhakta Ācārya
summary: Nepali poet (1814–1868) honoured as Ādikavi, the first poet of Nepali, for his Nepali Rāmāyaṇa; also known for verse letters and satire written while imprisoned. His birthday (Bhānu Jayantī) is a cultural holiday in Nepal and among Nepali speakers in India.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhānubhakta Rāmāyaṇa
summary: Bhānubhakta’s Nepali Rāmāyaṇa in seven kāṇḍas, circulated orally and in manuscript and published complete in 1887 by Motirām Bhaṭṭa; regarded as the first Nepali epic and a foundation of the literary language. Hutt treats it as based on the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śivastotrāvalī
summary: Utpaladeva’s “Garland of Hymns to Śiva”, twenty Sanskrit stotras of personal devotion grounded in Pratyabhijñā non-dualism, collected after him with a commentary by Kṣemarāja; still recited by Kashmiri Paṇḍits.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rūpa Bhavānī
summary: Kashmiri Paṇḍit woman mystic and poet (c. 1621–1721), whose Kashmiri vākhs in the line of Lal Ded express Śaiva yogic experience; she is commemorated by Kashmiri Paṇḍits on her birth anniversary (Sahib Saptami).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Old Javanese kakawin and parwa literature
summary: The court literature of Java and Bali in Old Javanese: prose renderings of Mahābhārata books (parwa, from the late 10th c.) and long poems in Sanskrit metres (kakawin) retelling epic and Purāṇic stories — Rāmāyaṇa, Arjunawiwāha, Kṛṣṇāyana, Bhāratayuddha, Hariwangsa and others — preserved mainly in Balinese palm-leaf manuscripts.

type:LABEL: person
name: Airlangga
summary: King in East Java (r. 1019–1042), of Balinese birth, who restored the kingdom after the fall of Dharmawangsa Teguh’s court (c. 1016) and is named in the Arjunawiwāha as the poet Mpu Kanwa’s king; his Pucangan inscription of 1041 recounts his career.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mpu Kanwa
summary: Old Javanese poet of King Airlangga’s court (early 11th c.), known only from his Arjunawiwāha, in whose last stanza (36.2) he names himself, the work and the king.

type:LABEL: text
name: Arjunawiwāha (Kakawin)
summary: Mpu Kanwa’s Old Javanese kakawin “Arjuna’s Wedding” (11th c.), the oldest dated kakawin after the Rāmāyaṇa: Arjuna’s ascetic penance, his resistance to the nymphs sent to test him, the fight with Śiva as a hunter over the boar Muka, and his victory for Indra over the demon Niwātakawaca, rewarded with marriage to the nymphs. It retells the Mahābhārata’s Āraṇyakaparvan episodes and remained a favourite of Javanese and Balinese wayang.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jayabhaya (king of Kaḍiri)
summary: King of Kaḍiri (Daha) in East Java (r. c. 1130/1135–1157), known from inscriptions of 1135, 1136 and 1144 under the consecration name Śrī Warmeśwara, patron of the Bhāratayuddha; later Javanese tradition made him a prophet-king (the Jangka Jayabaya prophecies).

type:LABEL: person
name: Mpu Sedah
summary: Old Javanese court poet of King Jayabhaya of Kaḍiri, who began the Bhāratayuddha in 1157; Javanese legend that he was put to death for modelling Śalya’s queen on the king’s consort is dismissed by Zoetmulder as having no basis in the text.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mpu Panuluh
summary: Old Javanese court poet who completed the Bhāratayuddha begun by Mpu Sedah and wrote the kakawins Hariwangsa and Ghaṭotkacāśraya (12th c.).

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhāratayuddha (Kakawin)
summary: The Old Javanese kakawin of the Mahābhārata war, begun by Mpu Sedah and completed by Mpu Panuluh for King Jayabhaya of Kaḍiri; a chronogram in its prologue (“sang akuda suddha candrama”) gives Śaka 1079, 1157 CE — the paraphrase even yields the day, 6 September 1157. It became the basis of the Javanese and Balinese tradition of the great war.

type:LABEL: text
name: Hariwangsa (Kakawin)
summary: Mpu Panuluh’s Old Javanese kakawin (12th c.) on Kṛṣṇa’s abduction of Rukmiṇī and the war with Jarāsandha, drawing on the Harivaṃśa tradition; edited by A. Teeuw (1950).

type:LABEL: text
name: Ghaṭotkacāśraya (Kakawin)
summary: Mpu Panuluh’s Old Javanese kakawin (12th c.) on Ghaṭotkaca’s help to Abhimanyu in winning his bride — an episode not found in the Sanskrit Mahābhārata.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kṛṣṇāyana (Kakawin)
summary: Mpu Triguṇa’s Old Javanese kakawin on Kṛṣṇa’s abduction of Rukmiṇī, written at the court of King Warsajaya (early 12th c.).

type:LABEL: person
name: Mpu Triguṇa
summary: Old Javanese poet of King Warsajaya’s court (early 12th c.), author of the Kṛṣṇāyana kakawin.

type:LABEL: text
name: Wirāṭaparwa (Old Javanese prose)
summary: The Old Javanese prose rendering of the Mahābhārata’s Virāṭaparvan, made at the court of King Dharmawangsa Teguh; its epilogue records that it was recited before the king over a month, which Zoetmulder computes as 14 October–12 November 996 CE — one of the earliest dated works of Old Javanese literature.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Agama Hindu Dharma (Balinese Hinduism)
summary: The Hindu religion of Bali (and of Hindu communities elsewhere in Indonesia), joining temple-centred Śaiva and Buddhist priestly ritual inherited from Java with local ancestor and village temple cults. Under Indonesia’s state requirement of monotheism, Balinese reformers recast it around Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa as one supreme God and secured its recognition by the Ministry of Religion around 1958–59; the Parisada Hindu Dharma was founded as its council in 1959, and “Agama Hindu Bali” became the national “Agama Hindu” in the 1960s.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Parisada Hindu Dharma Indonesia
summary: The council of Indonesian Hindus, founded in Bali in 1959 as Parisada Dharma Hindu Bali and later renamed for the whole country, which standardises doctrine and represents Hinduism to the state.

type:LABEL: text
name: Maharadia Lawana (Maranao)
summary: A Maranao epic song from the Lake Lanao region of Mindanao (Philippines) whose hero is Maharadia Lawana — Rāvaṇa — to whom the gods grant immortality; a local, Islamised telling of the Rāma story. Juan R. Francisco heard it sung by Maranao bards in 1968 and published an English rendering with the Maranao scholar Nagasura Madale (1969), arguing that the story reached the Philippines between the 17th and 19th centuries through Javanese and Malay contacts.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Hinduism in Mauritius
summary: The Hindu traditions of Mauritius, brought by indentured labourers from Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Andhra and Maharashtra from the 1830s; Hindus are the largest religious group (about 48% in the 2022 census), the only Hindu plurality in Africa. Its signature observances are the Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage to Ganga Talao (Grand Bassin), Thaipusam and Tamil kāvaṭi, and the Bhojpuri Geet-Gawai.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Grand Bassin (Ganga Talao) pilgrimage
summary: The Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage of Mauritian Hindus, many walking from across the island carrying decorated kāṁvaṛ, to the crater lake Grand Bassin, renamed Ganga Talao and ritually linked with the Gaṅgā; the island’s largest Hindu festival and, for Eisenlohr, a “cultural touchstone” of Indo-Mauritian identity.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Indo-Caribbean Hinduism
summary: The Hinduism of the descendants of Indian indentured labourers in Trinidad and Tobago (from 1845), British Guiana/Guyana (from 1838) and Suriname (from 1873), largely of Bhojpuri-speaking north Indian origin: Sanātanī temple and pandit organisations, Rāmāyaṇ (Mānas) recitation and Rāmlīlā, Phagwah (Holī) and Divālī as public festivals. Guyana has the highest proportion of Hindus in the Western Hemisphere.

type:LABEL: institution
name: Sanatan Dharma Maha Sabha (Trinidad and Tobago)
summary: The largest Hindu organisation of Trinidad and Tobago, formed in 1952 when Bhadase Sagan Maraj merged two Sanātanī bodies; it runs some 150 mandirs, over fifty schools and broadcast media.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Rāmlīlā of Trinidad
summary: Open-air village performances of the Rāma story in Trinidad, based on Tulsīdās’s Mānas and staged by Indo-Trinidadian communities from the late nineteenth century, culminating in the burning of Rāvaṇa’s effigy around Dussehra.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Phagwah (Caribbean Holī)
summary: The Caribbean form of Holī among Indo-Guyanese, Indo-Trinidadians and Indo-Surinamese, named from the Bhojpuri month Phāgun, with chowtal singing and the throwing of coloured water (abeer); a public holiday in Guyana and Suriname.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Hinduism in Fiji
summary: The Hinduism of Indo-Fijians, descendants of indentured labourers brought to the sugar plantations between 1879 and 1916; about a quarter of Fiji’s population (24% in 2017). Rāmāyaṇ maṇḍalīs reciting the Mānas, Sanātanī and Ārya Samāj organisations and south Indian fire-walking are among its institutions; Kelly (1991) studies its colonial-era politics of virtue.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Hinduism in Malaysia
summary: The Hinduism of Malaysia’s Indian (mostly Tamil) community, about 6% of the population (2020), formed largely by nineteenth- and early twentieth-century labour migration to the plantations; its great public festival is Thaipusam at Batu Caves near Kuala Lumpur, with its 43-metre Murukaṉ statue.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Hinduism in South Africa
summary: The Hinduism of Indian South Africans, mainly in KwaZulu-Natal, descended chiefly from indentured labourers brought to Natal from 1860 to 1911 and from later “passenger” migrants; Tamil, Telugu, Hindi- and Gujarati-speaking traditions coexist, with fire-walking festivals for Draupadī and Kāvaṭi for Murukaṉ.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Hindu temple-building in Britain
summary: The growth of British Hindu congregations from converted houses and halls in the 1960s–70s, after migration from India and East Africa, to purpose-built temples such as the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir at Neasden (1995) and many regional and sectarian mandirs; the temples belong to the temple records, this record to the community movement.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Hindu temple-building in the United States
summary: The establishment of temples by Indian professionals who arrived after the 1965 Immigration Act — among the first the Ganesha temple of the Hindu Temple Society of North America in Flushing, New York, and the Sri Venkateswara temple at Penn Hills, Pittsburgh (both consecrated 1977) — often built by south Indian craftsmen on Āgamic plans and serving pan-Hindu congregations.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: ISKCON (International Society for Krishna Consciousness)
summary: A Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava movement founded in New York on 13 July 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda, which spread the chanting of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra, Caitanya’s theology and his own translations of the Gītā and Bhāgavata among Western converts and later the Indian diaspora; its headquarters are at Māyāpur, West Bengal. It holds Ratha Yātrās in cities worldwide.

type:LABEL: person
name: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
summary: Bengali Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava teacher (1896–1977), initiated in the Gauḍīya Maṭh line of Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī, who sailed to New York in 1965 aged 69 and founded ISKCON in 1966; his English translations and commentaries on the Bhagavad Gītā, Bhāgavata Purāṇa and Caitanya Caritāmṛta became the movement’s scriptures.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Āgamas and Tantras
summary: The large body of post-Vedic scriptures (Āgama, Tantra, Saṃhitā) of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra and Śākta traditions, which regulate initiation, mantra, temple building, image worship, festivals and yoga.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Devotional (bhakti) literature
summary: Devotional poetry, song and hagiography addressed to Śiva, Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa/Rāma, the Goddess and other deities in Tamil, Kannada, Telugu, Marathi, Hindi dialects, Bengali, Assamese, Odia, Gujarati, Kashmiri and other languages, from the Tamil saints of c. 6th–9th c. onward.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Regional and vernacular retellings
summary: Tellings of the Rāma and Bhārata narratives (and of Purāṇic material) in Indian languages, in later Sanskrit, and in Jain and Buddhist traditions. Each telling is recorded as a work with its own date, author and theology, not as a deviation from an original.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Southeast Asian adaptations
summary: Rāma and other Indic narratives as written, carved, recited and performed in Java, Bali, Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Myanmar and the Malay world, from the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (late 9th–early 10th c.) to the Thai Ramakien of Rama I (1797–1807).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kamba Rāmāyaṇam (Irāmāvatāram)
summary: The Tamil Rāma epic of the poet Kampaṉ, in six kāṇṭams of viruttam verse (c. 10,500 stanzas in the standard edition), dated variously between the 9th and 12th centuries. It is the most celebrated Tamil telling and is shaped by Tamil poetics and Śrīvaiṣṇava devotion.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rāmcaritmānas
summary: Tulsīdās’s Awadhi Rāma epic in seven kāṇḍs of caupāī–dohā verse, begun at Ayodhyā in Saṃvat 1631 (1574 CE) according to the poem itself. It is the dominant Rāma text of North India and the basis of the Rāmlīlā.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa
summary: The Bengali Rāma narrative (Śrīrām Pā̃cālī) attributed to Kṛttibās Ojhā, composed probably in the 15th century in the pā̃cālī form for recitation and singing, and the most widely read Rāmāyaṇa in Bengal.

type:LABEL: text
name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa
summary: A Sanskrit Rāma narrative in seven kāṇḍas presented as a Śiva–Pārvatī dialogue within the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, re-reading the story through Advaita Vedānta: Rāma is the supreme Brahman and events are his līlā. Dated to roughly the 13th–15th c.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tēvāram
summary: The Tamil Śaiva hymns (patikams) of Campantar, Appar and Cuntarar (7th–8th c.), forming the first seven books of the Tirumurai; about 796 hymns survive. The hymns praise Śiva at named temples, which tradition counts as the 275 Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talams.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nālāyira Divya Prabandham
summary: The “Four Thousand Sacred Compositions”: Tamil hymns of the twelve Āḻvārs (c. 6th–9th c.) praising Viṣṇu at named shrines, compiled by Nāthamuni in the 9th–10th century. Śrīvaiṣṇavas regard it as a Tamil Veda and recite it in temple worship.

type:LABEL: text
name: Periya Purāṇam
summary: Cēkkiḻār’s 12th-century Tamil hagiography of the sixty-three Śaiva saints (Nāyaṉmār), composed at the Cōḻa court of Kulōttuṅka II and placed as the twelfth and last book of the Tirumurai.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gītagovinda
summary: Jayadeva’s 12th-century Sanskrit lyrical poem in twelve cantos (24 songs, aṣṭapadī) on the love, separation and reunion of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. It is the first major Sanskrit work centred on Rādhā and is sung nightly in the Jagannātha temple, Puri.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jñāneśvarī
summary: Jñānadeva’s Marathi ovī commentary (Bhāvārthadīpikā) on the Bhagavad Gītā in eighteen chapters, completed in Śaka 1212 (1290 CE) according to its colophon. It is the foundational scripture of the Vārkarī tradition and among the earliest major works of Marathi literature.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (Old Javanese)
summary: The Old Javanese Rāmāyaṇa in kakawin (Indic-metre court poetry), the longest kakawin of the Hindu-Buddhist period, composed in Central Java c. 856–930 CE. Its first half closely follows the Sanskrit Bhaṭṭikāvya rather than Vālmīki.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ramakien (Thai)
summary: The Thai national Rāma epic. Earlier Ayutthaya-period versions were largely lost in 1767; the canonical recension was compiled under King Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok) in 1797–1807, partly written by the king, and a shorter version for dance-drama was made under Rama II.

type:LABEL: text
name: Reamker (Khmer)
summary: The Khmer Rāma epic (Rāmakerti, “Glory of Rāma”), whose surviving text dates from the 16th–17th c. (first part) and later centuries. It recasts the story in Theravāda Buddhist terms and is a mainstay of Cambodian court dance and Lkhon Khol masked theatre.

type:LABEL: text
name: Paumacariya of Vimalasūri (Jain)
summary: The earliest Jain telling of the Rāma story, in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit, by Vimalasūri. Its own colophon dates it 530 (variant 520) years after Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa; scholars disagree on how to convert this and many place the work between the 1st and 5th centuries CE.

type:LABEL: text
name: Dasaratha Jātaka (Buddhist)
summary: Jātaka no. 461 of the Pali canon’s Jātaka collection: a birth-story in which Rāma-paṇḍita, the Bodhisatta, his brother Lakkhaṇa and their sister Sītā, children of King Dasaratha of Bārāṇasī, live twelve years in the Himalaya. There is no abduction and no Rāvaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Cilappatikāram
summary: The Tamil epic of Kaṇṇaki and Kōvalaṉ attributed to Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ, in three books set in the Cōḻa, Pāṇḍya and Cēra capitals, probably composed around the 5th–6th century. It contains early Tamil depictions of Kṛṣṇa, Murukaṉ and Koṟṟavai worship.

type:LABEL: character
name: Rādhā
summary: The cowherd beloved of Kṛṣṇa. She is not named in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; the earliest datable literary mentions are scattered Prakrit and Sanskrit verses (Gāhā Sattasaī, 9th-c. poetics), she becomes the heroine of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (12th c.), and the supreme goddess of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Gauḍīya theology.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Murukaṉ (Tamil)
summary: The Tamil god of the hills, Cēyōṉ (“the red one”) of the Tolkāppiyam, praised in the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai. From the late Caṅkam period he converges with the northern Skanda-Kārttikeya; the two are kept as separate ids here, joined by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Pāñcarātra
summary: The Vaiṣṇava ritual and theological tradition of the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās, centred on Vāsudeva-Nārāyaṇa and the doctrine of four emanations (vyūha: Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha). It governs worship in many South Indian Vaiṣṇava temples, including Srirangam.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śaiva Siddhānta
summary: The dualist, Veda-congruent school of the Śaiva Mantramārga, based on the Siddhānta Āgamas (traditionally 28), systematised by Kashmirian exegetes (Sadyojyoti, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha) and later by Aghoraśiva at Chidambaram. In Tamil it fused with the Tirumurai hymns through Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (13th c.).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śrīvaiṣṇava
summary: The South Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition that joins the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs (as a “Tamil Veda”) with Sanskrit Vedānta (Viśiṣṭādvaita) and Pāñcarātra temple ritual, centred on Viṣṇu with Śrī (Lakṣmī). Its ācāryas include Nāthamuni, Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and Vedānta Deśika.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava
summary: The Bengal Vaiṣṇava tradition stemming from Caitanya (1486–1534), centred on the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, with a theology elaborated by the Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana and a hagiographic canon including Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata
summary: The Kannada-speaking Śaiva tradition associated with Basava (12th c.) and the vacana poets (Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahādēvi and others), marked by wearing the personal iṣṭaliṅga, devotion to Śiva alone, and — in the vacanas — criticism of caste, temple ritual and Brahmanical sacrifice.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Kashmir Śaivism (Trika)
summary: The non-dualist Śaiva traditions of Kashmir — Trika, Krama, Spanda and the Pratyabhijñā philosophy of Somānanda and Utpaladeva — culminating in Abhinavagupta (c. 975–1025) and Kṣemarāja.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Jain tradition
summary: The Jain religion, here recorded chiefly as the source of its own Rāma and Kṛṣṇa tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya, Raviṣeṇa’s Padmapurāṇa, Svayambhū’s Paumacariu, Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa, Hemacandra) and of Jain poets in Kannada and Tamil such as Pampa.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Buddhist tradition
summary: The Buddhist religion, here recorded as the source of the Dasaratha Jātaka, of the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra’s frame story with Rāvaṇa, and of the Theravāda-framed Rāma tellings of mainland Southeast Asia (Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam as a jātaka; Khmer Reamker; Thai Ramakien).

type:LABEL: person
name: Kampaṉ (Kambar)
summary: Tamil poet, author of the Irāmāvatāram (Kamba Rāmāyaṇam), patronised by Caṭaiyappa Vaḷḷal of Tiruveṇṇainallūr. His date is disputed between the 9th and the 12th century, with most modern scholars favouring the 12th.

type:LABEL: person
name: Tulsīdās
summary: Awadhi and Braj poet (d. 1623), author of the Rāmcaritmānas (begun 1574), the Vinaya Patrikā, Kavitāvalī and other Rāma-devotional works; he lived in Ayodhyā and above all in Kāśī (Vārāṇasī).

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṛttibās Ojhā
summary: Bengali poet to whom the Śrīrām Pā̃cālī (Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa) is attributed; tradition places him at Phuliyā on the Bhāgīrathī and in the 15th century, though the identification of the king he mentions is disputed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jayadeva
summary: Sanskrit poet of the late 12th century, author of the Gītagovinda; tradition makes him a poet at the court of Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal, and both Bengal and Odisha claim his birthplace “Kindubilva.” Two hymns attributed to him are in the Sikh Ādi Granth.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jñāneśvar
summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1275–1296), disciple of his elder brother Nivṛttinātha, author of the Jñāneśvarī (1290) and the Amṛtānubhava, and revered as a founder of the Vārkarī tradition of Viṭṭhala devotion.

type:LABEL: person
name: Āṇṭāḷ
summary: The only woman among the twelve Āḻvārs, foster-daughter of Periyāḻvār at Śrīvilliputtūr, author of the Tiruppāvai (30 verses) and Nācciyār Tirumoḻi (143 verses in the standard count); she is usually dated to the 8th–9th century.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nammāḻvār
summary: The foremost Āḻvār (Caṭakōpaṉ, Māṟaṉ) of Kurukūr (Āḻvārtirunagari) in the far south of Tamil Nadu, author of the Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses) and three shorter works; scholars date him to the 8th–9th century.

type:LABEL: person
name: Appar (Tirunāvukkaracar)
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint of the 7th century, author of Tirumurai books 4–6. The Periya Purāṇam tells that he was first a Jain monk named Dharmasena, returned to Śaivism, and brought the Pallava king Mahendravarman I back to Śiva.

type:LABEL: person
name: Campantar (Tiruñāṉacampantar)
summary: Tamil Śaiva child-poet of Cīrkāḻi (7th c.), author of Tirumurai books 1–3 — the largest share of the Tēvāram. The Periya Purāṇam narrates his contest with Jain monks at Madurai and the return of the Pāṇḍya king to Śaivism.

type:LABEL: person
name: Cuntarar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint of the 8th century (Cuntaramūrtti), author of Tirumurai book 7; his Tiruttoṇṭattokai lists the devotees whom the Periya Purāṇam later expanded into the sixty-three Nāyaṉmār. Tradition calls him the “friend of Śiva” and links him to Tiruvārūr.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rāmānuja
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya and Vedāntin of Śrīperumbudūr, chief exponent of Viśiṣṭādvaita and author of the Śrībhāṣya; he reorganised worship at Srirangam and, during a sojourn in the Hoysala country, at Melkote. Traditional dates are 1017–1137; many scholars prefer 1077–1157.

type:LABEL: person
name: Caitanya
summary: Bengali Vaiṣṇava saint (1486–1534), born at Navadvīpa, who spent his last two decades at Puri; the Gauḍīya tradition regards him as Kṛṣṇa, and as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body. The eight-verse Śikṣāṣṭaka is the only work accepted as his.

type:LABEL: person
name: Basava
summary: Kannada Śaiva poet and minister at the Kalacuri court of Bijjala II at Kalyāṇa (12th c.), whose vacanas, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, are central to the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vimalasūri
summary: Jain (Śvetāmbara) monk-poet, author of the Prakrit Paumacariya, the earliest surviving Jain Rāma narrative. His date depends on the disputed reading of his colophon (530 years after Mahāvīra) and is placed by scholars anywhere from the 1st to the 5th century CE.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Sapta Purī (the seven liberating cities)
summary: The seven cities — Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā (Haridvāra), Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā (Ujjayinī) and Dvārakā — named in a widely recited Sanskrit verse as the places that grant liberation (mokṣa); a pan-Indian pilgrimage set rather than a single route.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pañca Kedāra (five Kedāras of Garhwal)
summary: Five Śiva shrines in the Garhwal Himalaya — Kedārnāth, Tuṅgnāth, Rudranāth, Madhyamaheśvar and Kalpeśvar — joined by a legend in which Śiva, fleeing the Pāṇḍavas in the form of a bull, reappears in five parts at the five sites.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Aṣṭavināyaka (eight Gaṇeśa shrines of Maharashtra)
summary: A pilgrimage circuit of eight Gaṇeśa temples around Pune in Maharashtra — Morgaon, Siddhatek, Pali, Mahad, Theur, Lenyadri, Ozar and Ranjangaon — each holding a self-manifest (svayambhū) image with its own legend.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Navagraha temples of the Kaveri delta
summary: A set of nine temples near Kumbakonam and Mayiladuthurai in Tamil Nadu, each associated in tradition with one of the nine planetary deities (navagraha); eight are Śiva temples with a graha shrine, and only Sūryanār Kōvil is dedicated to the graha (Sūrya) as principal deity.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Ahom kingdom
summary: Kingdom of the Brahmaputra valley (Assam) founded by Tai-speaking Ahoms in the 13th century; its later kings, notably Gadādhar Siṃha and Śiva Siṃha, patronised Śaiva and Śākta temples around Guwahati.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Māṇikya dynasty of Tripura
summary: Ruling house of the kingdom of Tripura (Twipra) from the 15th century until 1949; Dhanya Māṇikya is credited with founding the Tripura Sundarī temple at Udaipur.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kingdom of Manipur
summary: Meitei kingdom of the Manipur valley; from the 18th century its rulers adopted Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism and built the royal Govindajī temple at Imphal.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Utpala dynasty of Kashmir
summary: Kashmiri dynasty founded by Avantivarman (r. c. 855–883), builder of the Avantisvāmin and Avantīśvara temples at Avantipura; its history is told in Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Gurjara-Pratīhāra dynasty
summary: North Indian imperial dynasty (c. 8th–11th c.) based at Kanauj, under whose rule many of the early Māru-Gurjara and central Indian Nāgara temples (Osian, Bateshwar) were built.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kacchapaghāta dynasty
summary: Dynasty of the Gwalior region (c. 10th–12th c.); a later inscription at Mitaoli associates the circular Causaṭh Yoginī temple with the Kacchapaghāta king Devapāla.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kalacuris of Tripurī
summary: Dynasty of the upper Narmadā valley (Ḍāhala), with its capital at Tripurī near Jabalpur, c. 7th–13th c.; the Bhedaghat Causaṭh Yoginī temple and the early temples at Amarkantak are attributed to their period.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Bundelā kingdom of Orchha
summary: Rajput state of Bundelkhand founded in 1531 with its capital at Orchha; its rulers built the Rām Rājā and Caturbhuj temples.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Marāṭhā state (Chhatrapatis and Peśvās)
summary: The Marāṭhā state founded by Śivājī (crowned 1674), later directed by the Peśvās from Pune until 1818; Marāṭhā rulers, ministers and generals rebuilt or endowed many temples across western and northern India.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kingdom of Mysore (Woḍeyar dynasty)
summary: South Indian kingdom ruled by the Woḍeyars (with the interregnum of Haidar ʿAlī and Ṭīpū Sulṭān), patrons of the Cāmuṇḍeśvarī temple on Chamundi Hill.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Cāḷukyas of Kalyāṇī (Western Cāḷukyas)
summary: Deccan dynasty (973–1189) whose ornate temples at Lakkundi, Itagi and elsewhere define the “Kalyāṇī Cāḷukya” or later Cāḷukya style.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Cāḷukyas of Veṅgī (Eastern Cāḷukyas)
summary: Dynasty of coastal Andhra (c. 624–1070) to whom the Bhīmeśvara temple at Draksharama is attributed.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Malla kings of Mallabhūm (Bishnupur)
summary: Bengal dynasty of Mallabhūm whose 17th-century Vaiṣṇava rulers, converts under Śrīnivāsa Ācārya’s influence, built the brick and laterite temples of Bishnupur.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Mughal empire
summary: Empire of the Timurid Mughals (1526–1857); under Akbar Hindu nobles such as Mān Siṃh of Amber built major temples (Govindadeva at Vrindavan, 1590), while some later rulers ordered temples demolished.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kachvāhā kingdom of Amber (Jaipur)
summary: Rajput kingdom of Amber, later Jaipur; its rulers served the Mughals and patronised Kṛṣṇa temples in Braj and, from 1714–35, rehoused the Govindadeva image at Jaipur.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Shah dynasty of Nepal
summary: The Gorkha (Shah) dynasty that unified Nepal from 1768 until the abolition of the monarchy in 2008; patrons of Kathmandu valley shrines such as Manakāmanā and Dakṣiṇkālī.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Jaffna kingdom (Āryacakravarti dynasty)
summary: Tamil kingdom of northern Sri Lanka (c. 13th c.–1619) under the Āryacakravartis; tradition and the Yālppāṇa Vaipava Mālai credit it with the first Nallur Kandaswamy temple.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Chenla
summary: Khmer polity (6th–8th c.) known from Chinese sources and Sanskrit and Khmer inscriptions; Īśānavarman I’s capital Īśānapura is identified with Sambor Prei Kuk.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Pagan kingdom
summary: Burmese kingdom centred on Bagan (c. 849–1297); among its thousands of Buddhist monuments the Nathlaung Kyaung is the one surviving Vaiṣṇava temple.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Majapahit
summary: East Javanese kingdom (1293–c. 1527) whose state temple Penataran carries Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇāyana reliefs.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Irukkuvēḷ chiefs of Kodumbalur
summary: Tamil chiefly family of Kodumbalur, allies and feudatories of the early Cōḻas, to whom the Mūvarkōvil temples are attributed by inscription.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Śailodbhava dynasty
summary: Dynasty of Koṅgoda in coastal Odisha (c. 6th–8th c.) under whom the earliest surviving Bhubaneswar temples, including Paraśurāmeśvara, were built.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Bhauma-Kara dynasty
summary: Dynasty of Odisha (c. 8th–10th c.) with Śākta and Buddhist patronage; the Vaitāl Deul at Bhubaneswar is generally placed in their period.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Guhilas of Mewar
summary: Rajput dynasty of Mewar (Guhilas, later Sisodiyās), whose rulers style themselves the dīvān (regent) of Ekaliṅgajī, the tutelary Śiva of the Eklingji temple.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Umānanda temple, Guwahati
summary: Śiva temple on Umananda (Peacock) Island in the Brahmaputra at Guwahati, first built in 1694 on the orders of the Ahom king Gadādhar Siṃha; badly damaged in the 1897 Assam earthquake and later rebuilt.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hayagrīva Mādhava temple, Hajo
summary: Viṣṇu temple on Maṇikūṭa hill at Hajo near Guwahati whose present stone building is attributed to the Koch ruler Raghudeva Nārāyaṇa (late 16th c.); it is also revered by some Buddhists as the place of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ugratārā temple, Guwahati
summary: Śākta temple of the goddess Ugratārā at Latasil/Uzan Bazaar in Guwahati, built by the Ahom king Śiva Siṃha in 1725; local tradition links it to the navel of Satī.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Madan Kāmdev temple ruins
summary: Ruined complex of stone temples at Baihata Chariali near Guwahati, dated on stylistic grounds to about the 10th–12th centuries, with erotic and divine sculpture associated in local tradition with Kāmadeva.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tripura Sundarī temple, Udaipur (Tripura)
summary: Śākta temple on a tortoise-backed hillock at Udaipur, Tripura, founded according to tradition by Mahārāja Dhanya Māṇikya around 1501; counted among the 51 Śakti pīṭhas as the place where Satī’s right foot fell.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Unakoti rock reliefs
summary: Śaiva rock-cut reliefs and loose images on a forested hill near Kailashahar, Tripura, ascribed on stylistic grounds to the 7th–9th centuries; the central Unakotīśvara Kāla Bhairava head is about 9 m high.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śrī Govindajī temple, Imphal
summary: Royal Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava temple of Rādhā-Govinda beside the old palace of the Manipur kings at Imphal; first built in 1846, rebuilt after an 1868 earthquake and reconsecrated in 1876, with the images reinstalled in the present temple in 1908.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tuṅgnāth temple
summary: The highest of the Pañca Kedāra shrines (c. 3,680 m) below Chandrashila peak in Rudraprayag district, Uttarakhand, where the arms of the bull-form Śiva are worshipped; its priests are local Brahmins of Makkumath.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rudranāth temple
summary: Natural-rock Śiva shrine at about 2,290 m in the Garhwal Himalaya, the fourth Pañca Kedāra, where Śiva’s face (mukha) is worshipped.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Madhyamaheśvar temple
summary: Śiva temple at Gaundar in Rudraprayag district, the Pañca Kedāra shrine where the navel or middle (madhya) of the bull-form Śiva is worshipped.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kalpeśvar temple
summary: Small rock shrine in the Urgam valley of Chamoli district, the fifth Pañca Kedāra and the only one accessible all year, where Śiva’s matted hair (jaṭā) is worshipped.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vaidyanātha temple, Baijnath (Kangra)
summary: Nāgara Śiva temple at Baijnath in the Kangra valley, built in 1204 CE by two merchants, Ahuka and Manyuka, according to its own inscriptions; Śiva is worshipped as Vaidyanātha, “lord of physicians”.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hiḍimbā Devī temple, Manali
summary: Wooden pagoda-roofed temple at Manali built in 1553 over a rock worshipped as the goddess Hiḍimbā, whom local tradition identifies with the rākṣasī wife of Bhīma in the Mahābhārata.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bhīmakālī temple, Sarahan
summary: Tower-like wooden-and-stone temple of the goddess Bhīmakālī at Sarahan, the tutelary goddess of the former Bushahr rulers, built in the Himalayan kāṭh-kuṇi technique; it is regarded locally as being as holy as the Śakti pīṭhas.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa temple group, Chamba
summary: Group of stone śikhara temples with wooden canopies in Chamba town, Himachal Pradesh, whose main Viṣṇu temple is attributed to Rājā Sāhila Varman, the 10th-century founder of Chamba; a gilded finial was added in 1678.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Masrur rock-cut temples
summary: Monolithic complex of Nāgara temples carved from a sandstone ridge in the Kangra valley in the early 8th century, dedicated chiefly to Śiva with Viṣṇu, Devī and Sūrya imagery; unfinished and earthquake-damaged.

type:LABEL: place
name: Amarnāth cave
summary: Glacial cave at about 3,888 m in the Lidder–Sind watershed of Kashmir where an ice stalagmite is worshipped as a self-formed liṅga of Śiva (Amareśvara); the summer yātrā is one of the largest Himalayan pilgrimages.

type:LABEL: place
name: Vaiṣṇo Devī cave shrine
aliases: Vaishno Devi Temple|Mata Vaishno Devi|Trikuta Devi
summary: Cave shrine on Trikūṭa mountain above Katra in Jammu, where the goddess Vaiṣṇo Devī is worshipped in three natural rock forms (piṇḍīs) identified with Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī; one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in India.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kṣīra Bhavānī temple, Tulmul
summary: Spring shrine of the goddess Rājñā (Kṣīra Bhavānī) at Tulmul near Srinagar, whose present marble temple in the spring-fed pool was built under Mahārāja Pratāp Siṃh in the 1910s; its annual Jyeṣṭha aṣṭamī fair is the main festival of Kashmiri Paṇḍits.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Avantisvāmin temple, Avantipura
summary: Ruined Viṣṇu temple at Avantipura on the Jhelum, built by King Avantivarman (r. c. 855–883) of the Utpala dynasty, as recorded by Kalhaṇa; with the nearby Avantīśvara Śiva temple it is a key example of Kashmiri stone architecture.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pandrethan Śiva temple, Srinagar
summary: Small, well-preserved Kashmiri stone temple of the 8th–9th century standing in a spring-fed tank at Pandrethan, the site of the ancient capital (Purāṇādhiṣṭhāna) east of Srinagar.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śaṅkarācārya (Jyeṣṭheśvara) temple, Srinagar
summary: Stone Śiva temple on the hill above Srinagar known to Kalhaṇa as Gopādri; its date is disputed between an early medieval core and a later superstructure, and its modern name links it to Ādi Śaṅkara.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jvālāmukhī temple
summary: Śākta temple at Jawalamukhi in the Kangra valley where natural gas flames issuing from the rock are worshipped as the goddess Jvālā; counted among the Śakti pīṭhas (the tongue of Satī in common lists).

type:LABEL: place
name: Haridvāra (Haridwar)
summary: City where the Gaṅgā leaves the Śivālik hills for the plains, one of the Sapta Purī (as Māyā) and one of the four Kumbha Melā sites; its main bathing ghāṭ is Har kī Pauṛī.

type:LABEL: place
name: Har kī Pauṛī, Haridwar
summary: The principal bathing ghāṭ of Haridwar, held to bear the footprint of Viṣṇu (Hari) at the Brahmakuṇḍ, focus of the evening Gaṅgā āratī and the Kumbha Melā baths.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ṛṣikeśa (Rishikesh)
summary: Pilgrimage town on the Gaṅgā above Haridwar, traditionally where Viṣṇu appeared as Hṛṣīkeśa to the sage Raibhya; a centre of ascetic āśramas and, since the 20th century, of international yoga.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rani ki Vav (Queen’s Stepwell), Patan
summary: Monumental seven-storey stepwell at Patan, Gujarat, built for the Caulukya queen Udayamatī in the 11th century and conceived as an inverted temple; its walls carry hundreds of sculptures, overwhelmingly Vaiṣṇava, including the avatāras of Viṣṇu. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2014).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ambājī temple, Arasur
summary: Śākta temple of Ambā at Ambaji in the Arāvallī hills of north Gujarat, where there is no image: a sacred yantra in a niche is dressed to show the goddess; worship here is attested by at least the 14th century and the site is counted as the heart pīṭha of Satī in common lists.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kālikā Mātā temple, Pavagadh
summary: Goddess temple on the summit of Pavagadh hill inside the Champaner-Pavagadh World Heritage property, with a core of the 10th–11th centuries and images of Mahākālī flanked by Kālī and Bahucarā Mātā; its spire was rebuilt and a flag raised in 2022.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śāmaḷājī temple
summary: Viṣṇu temple at Shamlaji in north Gujarat whose present building dates from the 15th–16th centuries on an earlier (perhaps 11th-century) foundation; the site was a major 6th-century sculpture centre, and the sanctum image of Viṣṇu as Gadādhara is probably of the 7th–8th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ekaliṅgajī temple, Kailashpuri
summary: Śiva temple complex near Udaipur housing the tutelary deity of the rulers of Mewar, who govern as his dīvān; tradition credits Bappā Rāwal (8th c.), but the present main temple results from 15th-century rebuildings culminating under Rāṇā Rāimal (r. 1473–1509).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śrīnāthjī temple, Nathdwara
summary: Principal temple of the Puṣṭimārga, built at Nathdwara in Mewar in 1672 to house the image of Śrīnāthjī (Kṛṣṇa raising Govardhana) brought from Braj to protect it from Mughal iconoclasm; the temple is laid out as a residence (havelī) rather than a temple.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Osian temple group (Harihara temples)
summary: Cluster of 8th–12th-century Hindu and Jain temples at the desert oasis of Osian near Jodhpur, among the earliest Māru-Gurjara monuments; it includes three Harihara temples, a Sūrya temple, the Sacciyā Mātā temple and the Mahāvīra temple of 783.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Baroli temples
summary: Walled group of eight 10th-century Śiva and other temples at Baroli near Rawatbhata, Rajasthan, in the Pratīhāra-period Nāgara style; the best preserved, the Ghaṭeśvara Mahādeva, enshrines a liṅga with five faces.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kiradu temples
summary: Ruined group of at least five temples near Barmer in the Thar desert, of which the Someśvara Śiva temple is the best preserved; inscriptions of 1153–1178 link them to vassals of the Caulukyas, while art historians date the Someśvara anywhere from c. 1020 to the 12th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Galtājī, Jaipur
summary: Temple and spring-tank complex in a ravine of the hills east of Jaipur, a seat (gaddī) of the Rāmānandī order since the early 15th century, when Payohārī Kṛṣṇadās displaced the yogīs who lived there.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śrī Maṅgeśa temple, Priol (Goa)
summary: Śiva temple of the Gauḍa Sārasvata Brahmins at Mangueshi in Ponda, Goa, re-founded here in 1560 when the deity was carried out of Portuguese-ruled territory; the present building is of the later 18th–19th century, with a third building phase in 1890.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Viṭṭhala-Rukmiṇī temple, Pandharpur
summary: Main temple of Viṭhobā (Viṭṭhala) and Rakhumāī at Pandharpur on the Bhīmā, goal of the Vārkarī pilgrimages; inscriptions show a small shrine set up in 1189, a gateway in 1237 and a temple built in 1273–77, though the standing structure is mainly of the 17th century or later.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Khaṇḍobā temple, Jejuri
summary: Hill temple of Khaṇḍobā (Mallāri Mārtaṇḍa), the warrior and pastoral god of the Deccan worshipped by farmers, Dhangar herders and Brahmins alike; worship is attested from the 12th–13th century and the present complex was built and enlarged under Marāṭhā and Holkar patronage.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mahālakṣmī (Ambābāī) temple, Kolhapur
summary: Goddess temple in Kolhapur, counted among the Śakti pīṭhas and one of the “three and a half” pīṭhas of Maharashtra; a reference work claims construction in 634 CE, but its Hemāḍpantī fabric is generally of the 11th–13th centuries.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tuḷajā Bhavānī temple, Tuljapur
summary: Twelfth-century temple of the goddess Bhavānī at Tuljapur, built according to the reference by the Kadamba feudatory Māradadeva; family deity of the Bhosale house of Śivājī and of many Marathi castes, and one of Maharashtra’s Śakti pīṭhas.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Dhūmar Leṇā (Ellora Cave 29)
summary: One of the earliest and largest Hindu excavations at Ellora, a Śaiva cave-temple beside the Elaganga waterfall with a free-standing liṅga shrine and large reliefs of Śiva’s myths; probably 6th century and possibly Kalacuri.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rāmeśvara cave (Ellora Cave 21)
summary: Early Śaiva cave-temple at Ellora, credited to the Kalacuris of Māhiṣmatī before the Rāṣṭrakūṭa expansion, whose entrance is flanked by large figures of the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rāvaṇ kī Khāī (Ellora Cave 14)
summary: Hindu cave-temple at Ellora of the 7th–8th century, excavated before the neighbouring Daśāvatāra cave (Cave 15), with reliefs of Durgā, Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu and Śiva; its popular name refers to a relief of Rāvaṇa lifting Kailāsa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mayūreśvara temple, Morgaon
summary: Fortified Gaṇeśa temple at Morgaon near Baramati, the first and last shrine of the Aṣṭavināyaka circuit and the foremost centre of the Gāṇapatya tradition, where Gaṇeśa is held to have slain the demon Sindhu riding a peacock.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Siddhivināyaka temple, Siddhatek
summary: Gaṇeśa temple on the Bhīmā at Siddhatek, the only Aṣṭavināyaka shrine in Ahmednagar district; the present temple was built in the late 18th century by Ahilyābāī Holkar.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ballāḷeśvara temple, Pali
summary: Gaṇeśa temple at Pali in Raigad district, the only Aṣṭavināyaka named after a devotee (the boy Ballāḷa); built in 1640 by Moreśvar Viṭṭhal Sindkar and rebuilt in stone in 1760 by Nānā Phaḍṇavīs.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Varadavināyaka temple, Mahad
summary: Gaṇeśa temple at Mahad near Khopoli in Raigad district, built or restored in 1725 by the Peśvā general Rāmjī Mahādev Bivalkar to house an image reportedly found in the adjoining tank in 1690.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Cintāmaṇi temple, Theur
summary: One of the larger Aṣṭavināyaka temples, at Theur near Pune, where Gaṇeśa recovered the wish-granting jewel for the sage Kapila; a favoured shrine of the Peśvā Mādhavrāv I, who died there in 1772.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Girijātmaja (Lenyadri cave 7)
summary: Aṣṭavināyaka shrine in cave 7 of the Lenyadri group near Junnar — a Buddhist vihāra of the 1st–3rd century CE later adapted to the worship of Gaṇeśa as Girijātmaja, “son of Pārvatī”.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vighneśvara temple, Ozar
summary: Aṣṭavināyaka temple at Ozar on the Kukaḍī river near Junnar, where Gaṇeśa defeated the obstacle-demon Vighnāsura; renovated in 1967.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mahāgaṇapati temple, Ranjangaon
summary: Aṣṭavināyaka temple at Ranjangaon near Pune, where Gaṇeśa is held to have been worshipped by Śiva before the destruction of Tripura; the reference consulted dates the temple to the 9th–10th century, a claim not supported there by evidence.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rām Rājā temple, Orchha
summary: Palace-temple at Orchha where Rāma is worshipped as a reigning king (rājā), with a daily armed guard of honour; tradition holds that Queen Gaṇeś Kuṃvarī brought the image from Ayodhyā in 1574–75 and that it refused to move from her palace into the Caturbhuj temple built for it.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kāla Bhairava temple, Ujjain
summary: Temple of Kāla Bhairava, guardian deity of Ujjain, on the Kṣiprā, where liquor is offered to the god; the present building shows Marāṭhā-period work over an older temple, and Paramāra-period images (9th–13th c.) have been found on the site.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bateshwar temple group (Morena)
summary: Ravine site of nearly 200 small sandstone Śiva, Viṣṇu and Śakti temples north of Gwalior, built from about 750–800 to the 11th century in the early Pratīhāra Nāgara style; mostly collapsed, many were reassembled by the ASI from 2005.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Causaṭh Yoginī temple, Mitaoli
summary: Circular hypaethral temple on a hill at Mitaoli near Morena with 64 (65) cells around a central Śiva shrine; an inscription of 1323 credits it to the Kacchapaghāta king Devapāla, though the building is usually placed in the 11th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Causaṭh Yoginī temple, Bhedaghat
summary: Large circular yoginī temple (Golakī Maṭha) on a hill above the Narmadā at Bhedaghat near Jabalpur, built in the early 11th century under the Kalacuri king Yuvarāja II, with 81 rather than 64 yoginī shrines; a Gaurī-Śaṅkara shrine was added in its court in 1155.

type:LABEL: place
name: Amarakaṇṭaka (Amarkantak)
summary: Plateau tīrtha in the Maikal hills where the Narmadā (and the Son) rise, with a group of Kalacuri-period stone temples beside the Narmadā source tank; a place of pilgrimage and of the Narmadā parikramā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kṛṣṇa Janmasthān temple complex, Mathurā
summary: Temple complex in Mathurā built from 1953 (completed 1982) on the site revered as Kṛṣṇa’s birthplace, beside the Shahi Idgah mosque raised after Aurangzeb ordered the great Keśavadeva temple destroyed in 1670; the site has a long history of temple building and destruction and is the subject of ongoing litigation.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Govindadeva temple, Vrindavan
aliases: Govind Dev Temple|Govind Dev ji Mandir, Vrindavan
summary: Monumental red-sandstone temple at Vrindavan built for the Gauḍīya image of Govindadeva by Rājā Mān Siṃh of Amber, dated by inscription to 1590; its upper storeys were lost after the image was taken away for safety in 1670, and the image now resides at Jaipur.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Govind Dev Jī temple, Jaipur
summary: Temple in the City Palace complex of Jaipur that has housed the Govindadeva image of Vrindavan since the early 18th century; regular worship was established in 1719 and the deity was housed in its present building by Savāī Jai Siṃh II, founder of Jaipur.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bāṅke Bihārī temple, Vrindavan
summary: Popular Vrindavan temple, built around 1862–64, housing the image of Bāṅke Bihārī — Kṛṣṇa in the three-bend pose, understood as the united form of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa — said to have been revealed to Svāmī Haridās at Nidhivan.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hanumān Gaṛhī, Ayodhyā
summary: Fortress-like hill temple of Hanumān in Ayodhyā, held by the Nirvāṇī akhāṛā of Rāmānandī bairāgīs; the present temple grew under Awadh nawabi land grants in the 18th–19th centuries, and an 1855 dispute over it was a major Hindu–Muslim conflict in Ayodhyā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vindhyavāsinī temple, Vindhyachal
summary: Temple of the goddess Vindhyavāsinī on the Gaṅgā at Vindhyachal near Mirzapur, centre of a triangular pilgrimage with the Kālī Khoh and Aṣṭabhujā shrines; the goddess is the one promised an eternal seat on the Vindhya in the Harivaṃśa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Saṅkaṭ Mocan Hanumān temple, Varanasi
summary: Hanumān temple by the Assī river in Varanasi, held to have been founded by Tulsīdās where he had a vision of Hanumān; most of the present complex dates from the mid-20th century. The temple’s mahants founded the Sankat Mochan Foundation (1982) for cleaning the Gaṅgā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Paraśurāmeśvara temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: The best-preserved early temple of Bhubaneswar, a small sandstone rekhā deuḷa of about the mid-7th century (Śailodbhava period) dedicated to Śiva, with a hall carrying reliefs and a lintel of eight (not nine) planetary deities.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vaitāl Deuḷ, Bhubaneswar
summary: Eighth-century Bhubaneswar temple of the Tantric goddess Cāmuṇḍā (Kapālinī) with an unusual oblong khākharā roof crowned by three finials, resembling a South Indian gopura; its interior holds a fierce eight-armed Cāmuṇḍā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Brahmeśvara temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: Pañcāyatana Śiva temple in Bhubaneswar securely dated by a (now lost) inscription to the 18th regnal year of the Somavaṃśī king Udyotakeśarī, c. 1058, when his mother Kolāvatī Devī built it.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rājarāṇī temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: Mid-11th-century Bhubaneswar temple, probably originally the Indreśvara, named after the yellow-red sandstone called rājarāṇī; it has no image in worship, and its richly carved deuḷa with clustered miniature spires and dikpāla figures is a model of mature Kaliṅga design.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ananta Vāsudeva temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: Thirteenth-century Vaiṣṇava temple in Bhubaneswar, a Śaiva city, built in the time of the Eastern Gaṅga king Bhānudeva by Candrikā Devī, daughter of Anaṅgabhīma III; Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Subhadrā are worshipped here, and its kitchen supplies a large daily offering.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sākṣīgopāla (Satyabādī Gopīnātha) temple
summary: Kṛṣṇa temple at Sakhigopal on the Bhubaneswar–Puri road whose image, in the well-known legend, walked behind a young Brahmin to bear witness (sākṣī) to a promise of marriage; pilgrims to Puri traditionally visit it.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Virajā (Birajā) temple, Jajpur
summary: Goddess temple at Jajpur whose present building is of the 11th century (later renovated), housing a two-armed Durgā spearing Mahiṣa; Jajpur is called Virajā-kṣetra and the shrine is counted among the Śakti pīṭhas (the navel of Satī in common lists).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Temples of Bishnupur
summary: Group of brick and laterite temples built by the Malla kings of Bishnupur between about 1600 and 1800, the finest ensemble of Bengal’s curved-roof (cālā) and ratna temples with terracotta panels of the Kṛṣṇa līlā and the epics; on India’s UNESCO Tentative List since 1997–98.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rāsmañca, Bishnupur
summary: Pyramidal brick-and-laterite pavilion at Bishnupur commissioned around 1600 by the Malla king Bīr Hāmbīr, where the images of the town’s temples were brought for public display during the Rāsa festival (until 1932).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Keṣṭa Rāy (Joṛ Bāṅglā) temple, Bishnupur
summary: Twin-hut (joṛ-bāṅglā) brick temple of Kṛṣṇa at Bishnupur founded in 1655 by the Malla king Raghunāth Siṃha according to its plaque, the largest surviving joṛ-bāṅglā and famed for its terracotta panels.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śyām Rāy (Pañcaratna) temple, Bishnupur
summary: Five-pinnacled (pañcaratna) brick temple of Kṛṣṇa as Śyām and Rādhā at Bishnupur, founded in 1643 by Raghunāth Siṃha according to its plaque, with dense terracotta panels.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tārāpīṭh temple
summary: Tantric temple of the goddess Tārā beside a cremation ground at Tarapith in Birbhum, West Bengal, famous for the 19th-century saint Bāmākhepā; regarded by devotees as a Śakti pīṭha (where Satī’s eye fell, in local tradition).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nava Kailāśa (108 Śiva temples), Kalna
summary: Two concentric rings of 74 and 34 small cālā-roofed Śiva temples at Kalna, built in 1809 under the Mahārājās of Bardhaman; Kalna also has the 25-pinnacled Lālajī (1739) and the Pratāpeśvara (1849) temples.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ḍhākeśvarī National Temple, Dhaka
summary: State-owned “National Temple” of Bangladesh in Old Dhaka, dedicated to Ḍhākeśvarī (“Goddess of Dhaka”), traditionally founded by the Sena king Ballāla Sena in the 12th century; the original image was taken to Kolkata in 1947–50, and the temple became Bangladesh’s principal Hindu shrine after the destruction of the Ramna Kālī temple in 1971.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kāntajī (Kantanagar) temple, Dinajpur
summary: Nine-spired (navaratna) brick temple of Kṛṣṇa (Kānta) and Rukmiṇī at Kantanagar, Dinajpur, begun in 1704 by Mahārājā Prāṇnāth and completed in 1752 by his son Rāmnāth; its walls are covered with terracotta panels of the Kṛṣṇa-līlā, the epics and contemporary life.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Candranāth temple, Sitakunda
summary: Hilltop Śiva shrine on Chandranath hill above Sitakunda near Chittagong, counted among the Śakti pīṭhas as the place where Satī’s right arm fell; the Rājmālā chronicle credits its founding to a 12th-century ruler, Biśvambhar Śūr.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Puthia temple complex
aliases: Puthia Temple Complex|Bhubaneshwar Shiva Temple, Puthia
summary: Cluster of 19th-century temples of the Puthia zamindar family in Rajshahi, Bangladesh — the largest group of historic temples in the country — including the Śiva temple of 1823 built by Rānī Bhuvanmayī Devī and the pañcaratna Govinda temple.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kṛṣṇa temple and maṭha, Udupi
aliases: Udupi Sri Krishna Matha|Udupi Krishna Temple
summary: Kṛṣṇa temple at Udupi founded according to Dvaita tradition by Madhvācārya in the 13th century, administered in two-year turns (paryāya) by the eight Udupi maṭhas; devotees view the image through a latticed window associated with the poet-saint Kanakadāsa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vidyāśaṅkara temple, Śṛṅgeri
summary: Stone temple at Śṛṅgeri on the Tuṅgā built as a memorial to the pontiff Vidyāśaṅkara and usually dated to 1338, in the founding years of Vijayanagara; its twelve hall pillars carry the zodiac signs, arranged so that the sun’s rays fall on the sign of the month.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śāradāmbā temple and Śṛṅgeri maṭha
summary: Seat of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya Śāradā Pīṭha at Śṛṅgeri, one of the four cardinal Advaita monasteries traditionally founded by Ādi Śaṅkara, with its temple of the goddess Śāradā; the institution’s documented history begins in the 14th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mahābaleśvara temple, Gokarna
summary: Seaside Śiva temple at Gokarna on the Karnataka coast enshrining the ātmaliṅga that, in the legend, Rāvaṇa was tricked into setting down here; a Tēvāram shrine praised by the Nāyaṉmār, though the present complex is largely of the Vijayanagara period.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mūkāmbikā temple, Kollur
summary: Goddess temple at Kollur at the foot of Kodachadri in coastal Karnataka, where Mūkāmbikā is worshipped in a self-formed liṅga with a golden line dividing Śiva and Śakti; an important pilgrimage for devotees from Kerala and Karnataka, associated in tradition with Ādi Śaṅkara.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Cāmuṇḍeśvarī temple, Chamundi Hill
summary: Goddess temple on Chamundi Hill above Mysuru, tutelary deity of the Woḍeyar kings and “state goddess” (nāḍa devī) of Karnataka; the reference dates the original shrine to the 12th century, its stair of 1,000 steps to 1659 and the installation of the image to 1664.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kāśīviśveśvara temple, Lakkundi
summary: Eleventh-century double temple at Lakkundi (Gadag district), with facing sanctums for Śiva and Sūrya sharing one hall, regarded as one of the finest examples of the fully developed Kalyāṇī Cāḷukya style.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mahādeva temple, Itagi
summary: Śiva temple at Itagi (Koppal district) built c. 1112 by Mahādeva, a commander of the Kalyāṇī Cāḷukya king Vikramāditya VI; its inscription calls it the “emperor among temples” (devālaya-cakravarti).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Lakṣmī Devī temple, Doddagaddavalli
summary: Four-shrined temple of Mahālakṣmī at Doddagaddavalli near Hassan, built c. 1113 by the merchant Kullahaṇa Rāhuta and his wife Sahaja Devī; the earliest of the Hoysaḷa-period temples, with shrines also for Kālī, Viṣṇu and a Śiva liṅga.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vīrabhadra temple, Lepakshi
summary: Vijayanagara temple of Vīrabhadra at Lepakshi built c. 1530–40 by the brothers Virūpaṇṇa and Vīraṇṇa, governors at Penukonda under Acyutadevarāya; famous for its painted ceilings — among the largest surviving Vijayanagara murals — its hanging pillar and a giant monolithic Nandī.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Varāha-Lakṣmī-Narasiṃha temple, Simhachalam
summary: Hill temple near Visakhapatnam whose image, a fused Varāha and Narasiṃha, is kept covered in sandal paste except on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā; its present stone temple was built in 1268 under the Eastern Gaṅga king Narasiṃhadeva I, and the complex holds some 500 inscriptions.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ahobilam Narasiṃha shrines
summary: Group of nine Narasiṃha shrines in the Nallamala hills of Andhra Pradesh, at Lower and Upper Ahobilam, held to mark where Narasiṃha killed Hiraṇyakaśipu; the shrines received heavy Vijayanagara patronage from the Sāḷuvas (15th c.) and Tuḷuvas (16th c.) and include a Divya Deśam.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Thousand Pillar (Rudreśvara) temple, Hanamkonda
summary: Star-shaped triple-shrined (trikūṭa) temple of Śiva, Viṣṇu and Sūrya at Hanamkonda built by the Kākatīya king Rudradeva and dated by his inscription to 1163; on India’s UNESCO Tentative List with Warangal fort.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bhīmeśvara temple, Draksharama
summary: Large Śiva temple at Draksharama in the Godāvarī delta, one of the five Pañcārāma shrines and attributed to the Eastern Cāḷukya king Bhīma I (c. 892–922); the goddess Māṇikyāmbā here is counted among the eighteen Śakti pīṭhas.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sītā-Rāmacandrasvāmī temple, Bhadrachalam
summary: Rāma temple on the Godāvarī at Bhadrachalam built in the second half of the 17th century by Kañcarla Gopanna (Bhakta Rāmadāsu), a revenue official of the last Qutb Shāhī sultan, with diverted state revenue; the annual Śrī Rāma Navamī wedding festival draws vast crowds.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mahānandīśvara temple, Mahanandi
summary: Śiva temple below the Nallamala hills, one of the nine Nandi shrines (Nava Nandulu), with spring-fed tanks of clear water; the reference states the original structure was built by the Bādāmi Cāḷukyas in the 7th century, with additions in the 10th and 15th centuries.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kanaka Durgā temple, Vijayawada
aliases: Sri Durga Malleswara Swamy Varla Devasthanam|Indrakeeladri
summary: Hill temple of Kanaka Durgā with Mallēśvara on Indrakīlādri above the Kṛṣṇā at Vijayawada, where Arjuna is said to have performed the penance that won Śiva’s weapon; a Kākatīya-era inscription of 1229 records a gift to Mallēśvara here.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jogulāmbā temple, Alampur
summary: Goddess temple in the Navabrahma temple complex at Alampur near the Tuṅgabhadrā–Kṛṣṇā confluence, counted fifth of the eighteen Mahā Śakti pīṭhas; the old shrine was destroyed in 1390 and the present temple was rebuilt in 2005.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śārṅgapāṇi temple, Kumbakonam
summary: Large Viṣṇu temple at Kumbakonam (Tirukkuṭantai), a Divya Deśam praised by seven Āḻvārs, with a sanctum built as a chariot drawn by horses and elephants; the site was a Vaiṣṇava centre by the 7th–8th century and the present complex is largely Cōḻa to Nāyaka.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ādi Kumbheśvara temple, Kumbakonam
summary: Principal Śiva temple of Kumbakonam, where Śiva is worshipped as the liṅga formed from the pot (kumbha) of nectar carried by the deluge; a Tēvāram shrine whose masonry dates from the 9th-century Cōḻas with Vijayanagara and Nāyaka expansion.

type:LABEL: place
name: Mahāmaham tank, Kumbakonam
summary: Large temple tank in Kumbakonam where, once every twelve years (when Jupiter enters Leo in the month of Māsi), the Mahāmaham festival is held; tradition holds that the sacred rivers of India bathe here then, and the 1992 festival drew about a million pilgrims.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tyāgarāja temple, Tiruvarur
summary: Vast Śiva temple of Tiruvārūr, seat of Tyāgarāja (Somāskanda) and of the goddess Kamalāmbikā, praised in the Tēvāram; Cōḻa masonry from the 9th century, with a long inscription of Rājendra I listing gold and copper gifts, and the largest temple chariot in Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kāmākṣī temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Principal goddess temple of Kāñcī, where Kāmākṣī is worshipped seated in yogic posture with the Śrīcakra before her; founded according to the reference in the Pallava period, it was rebuilt in the 14th and 17th centuries and its present image was reinstalled in 1783 after a long exile.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Āṇṭāḷ and Vaṭapatraśāyī temples, Srivilliputhur
summary: Twin temple complex at Srivilliputhur — the Viṣṇu temple of Vaṭapatraśāyī (inscriptions from the 10th century) and the shrine of the poet-saint Āṇṭāḷ, revered as a form of the goddess — with a towering gopura that is the emblem of the Tamil Nadu government.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kaḷḷaḻakar temple, Alagar Koyil
summary: Viṣṇu temple of Kaḷḷaḻakar (Tirumāliruñcōlai) in the hills north of Madurai, praised in the Cilappatikāram and by the Āḻvārs; its deity’s yearly journey to Madurai for Mīnākṣī’s wedding, reorganised by Tirumalai Nāyaka, joins the city’s Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava festivals.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nellaiyappar–Kāntimatī temple, Tirunelveli
summary: Twin Śiva and goddess temple of Tirunelveli on the Tāmraparṇī, a Tēvāram shrine attributed to the 7th-century Pāṇḍya Neṭumāṟaṉ (Kūṉ Pāṇḍiyaṉ), with musical pillars and a chain-hall (1647) linking the two temples.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sthāṇumālaya temple, Suchindram
summary: Temple at Suchindram near Kanyakumari whose single liṅga is worshipped as the Trimūrti — Sthāṇu (Śiva), Māl (Viṣṇu) and Ayaṉ (Brahmā); with Cōḻa inscriptions of Parāntaka I (10th c.), its present form is largely 17th-century Nāyaka, with Travancore additions.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Koraṅganātha temple, Srinivasanallur
summary: Small, exquisitely carved early Cōḻa Viṣṇu temple at Srinivasanallur on the Kāvērī, dated on style to the early 10th century (c. 920s, Parāntaka I); its inscriptions do not record its foundation.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vijayālaya Cōḻīśvaram, Narttamalai
summary: Rock-sited stone Śiva temple at Narttamalai with a circular sanctum inside a square vimāna, among the earliest Cōḻa-region structural temples; its inscription credits it to the Muttaraiyar chief Sāttaṉ Paḻiyili in the 7th year of the Pallava Nṛpatuṅga (c. 862), not to Vijayālaya Cōḻa whose name it bears.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mūvarkōvil, Kodumbalur
summary: Group of originally three west-facing Śiva shrines at Kodumbalur, two surviving, built by the Irukkuvēḷ chief Būti Vikramakesarī according to his inscription; refined late 9th–10th-century early Cōḻa-style vimānas.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sūryanār Kōvil
summary: Temple of the Sun near Aduthurai, built under Kulottuṅga I (r. c. 1070–1120) as the Kulottuṅgacōḻa-Mārttāṇḍālaya according to its inscription; the only Navagraha temple whose principal deity is the graha himself, with Uṣā and Pratyuṣā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kailāsanātha temple, Tiṅkaḷūr
summary: Śiva temple at Tiṅkaḷūr between Thanjavur and Kumbakonam, the Navagraha shrine of Candra (the Moon); a Cōḻa foundation whose present masonry is Nāyaka (16th c.), mentioned in passing in the Tēvāram (vaippu-talam).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vaidyanātha temple, Vaitheeswaran Koil
summary: Śiva temple of Vaidyanātha, “the divine physician”, near Mayiladuthurai, a Tēvāram shrine and the Navagraha seat of Aṅgāraka (Mars); its five inscriptions are mainly of Kulottuṅga I, and a court and steps were added in 1689.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śvetāraṇyeśvara temple, Tiruveṇkāṭu
summary: Tēvāram Śiva temple at Tiruveṇkāṭu near Poompuhar, the Navagraha seat of Budha; about a hundred inscriptions record gifts from Rājarāja I onward, and an 11th-century bronze Ardhanārīśvara was found in the village.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Āpatsahāyeśvara temple, Āluṅkuṭi
summary: Tēvāram Śiva temple at Alangudi (Tiruvarur district), the Navagraha seat of Guru, worshipped here in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti; Campantar sang ten verses on it, and the present masonry is Nāyaka.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Agnīśvara temple, Kañcaṉūr
summary: Śiva temple at Kanjanur north-east of Kumbakonam, the Navagraha seat of Śukra (Venus), who is held to reside within Śiva here.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Darbhāraṇyeśvara temple, Tirunaḷḷāṟu
summary: Tēvāram Śiva temple at Tirunaḷḷāṟu in Karaikal (Puducherry), the most visited Navagraha shrine because of its Śani (Saturn) shrine, and one of the seven Saptaviṭaṅka sites of the Tyāgarāja cult.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nāganātha temple, Tirunāgeśvaram
summary: Tēvāram Śiva temple of Nāganātha at Tirunāgeśvaram east of Kumbakonam, the Navagraha seat of Rāhu, whose image is bathed with milk that is said to turn blue; the Vaiṣṇava Oppiliyappaṉ Divya Deśam is in the same town.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nāganātha temple, Kīḻapperumpaḷḷam
summary: Śiva temple at Keelaperumpallam near Poompuhar, the Navagraha seat of Ketu; a Cōḻa foundation with present masonry of the Nāyaka period, mentioned in passing in the Tēvāram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kapālīśvara temple, Mylapore
summary: Śiva temple of Mylapore, Chennai, praised in Campantar’s Tēvāram; the present temple was built in the 17th century after the earlier seashore temple (Pallava, 7th c. by tradition) was lost, and its 37 m gopura dates from 1906.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pārthasārathi temple, Triplicane
summary: Viṣṇu temple at Triplicane (Tiruvallikkēṇi), Chennai, a Divya Deśam praised by three Āḻvārs, where Kṛṣṇa is worshipped as Arjuna’s charioteer; Tamil inscriptions from the 8th century (Pallava Dantivarman) and Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār attribute it to a Pallava king.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śabarimala Dharmaśāstā (Ayyappan) temple
aliases: Sabarimala Temple|Sabarimala Sree Dharma Sastha Temple|Sannidhanam
summary: Hill shrine of Ayyappan (Dharmaśāstā) in the Periyar forests of Kerala, reached by pilgrims after a 41-day vow and the climb of the eighteen sacred steps; restored after a fire in 1902 and rebuilt after an arson attack in 1950, it receives millions of pilgrims in the Maṇḍala–Makaravilakku season.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vaṭakkunnātha temple, Thrissur
summary: Walled Śiva temple at the centre of Thrissur, a classic Kerala temple with four gopuras, a kūttambalam theatre and murals of Mahābhārata scenes; tradition attributes it to Paraśurāma, and the Thrissur Pūram festival is held on its grounds.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ettumanoor Mahādeva temple
summary: Major Śiva temple at Ettumanoor near Kottayam whose present building, gopura and walls were reconstructed in 1542 (Kollam era 717); its murals, including a large Naṭarāja, are among the finest in Kerala.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pārthasārathi temple, Aranmula
summary: Kerala-style Kṛṣṇa temple on the Pamba at Aranmula, a Divya Deśam praised by Nammāḻvār, where Kṛṣṇa is worshipped as Arjuna’s charioteer; it is the focus of the Aranmula snake-boat (vaḷḷam kaḷi) regatta and has early-18th-century murals.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Āṭṭukāl Bhagavatī temple, Thiruvananthapuram
summary: Goddess temple in Thiruvananthapuram whose deity, a Bhadrakālī on a vetāla, is identified with Kaṇṇaki, heroine of the Cilappatikāram; its annual Poṅkāla, when women cook offerings in the streets, has been counted among the largest gatherings of women in the world.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Cōṟṟāṉikkara Bhagavatī temple
summary: Goddess temple near Kochi where Rājarājeśvarī is worshipped as Sarasvatī in the morning, Lakṣmī at noon and Durgā in the evening, with Nārāyaṇa; its lower (kīḻkkāvu) shrine of Bhadrakālī is visited for relief from mental illness and spirit possession.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tirunelli Mahāviṣṇu temple
summary: Viṣṇu temple on the side of Brahmagiri hill in Wayanad, called “Sahyamalaka-kṣetra” in Purāṇic māhātmyas and believed to have been founded by Brahmā; the Pāpanāśinī stream nearby is a major place for ancestral rites.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Budhānīlakaṇṭha, Kathmandu valley
summary: Open-air shrine at the foot of Shivapuri hill north of Kathmandu where a colossal stone Viṣṇu lies on the coils of Śeṣa in a tank; the image is generally assigned to the Licchavi period (7th c.), and by tradition Nepal’s kings did not look upon it.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Guhyeśvarī temple, Kathmandu
summary: Tantric goddess temple on the Bāgmatī about 1 km east of Paśupatinātha, revered as a Śakti pīṭha (the place of Satī’s secret parts or knees in different lists); renovated by Pratāp Malla in the 17th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Dakṣiṇkālī temple
summary: Open-air Kālī shrine in a ravine south of Kathmandu at Pharping, famous for animal sacrifices (especially at Dasaĩ); the goddess is shown with her right foot on Śiva’s chest.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Manakāmanā temple, Gorkha
summary: Two-tiered pagoda temple of the wish-granting goddess Manakāmanā (a form of Bhagavatī) on a ridge above the Trishuli–Marsyangdi confluence in Gorkha district, founded by tradition in 1678 by the priest Arman Rayamajhi; a cable car has served it since 1998 (recall).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nyātāpola temple, Bhaktapur
summary: Five-tiered pagoda of the goddess Siddhilakṣmī in Taumadhi square, Bhaktapur — the tallest temple in Nepal (c. 30 m) — built in six months in 1702 for King Bhūpatīndra Malla; it survived the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kṛṣṇa Mandir, Patan
summary: Stone śikhara temple of Kṛṣṇa in Patan Durbar Square built in the 17th century (1637) by King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla, whose upper-storey friezes illustrate the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa with Newari captions; damaged in 2015 and restored by 2018.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Taleju temple, Kathmandu
