summary: Three-roofed temple of Taleju Bhavānī, tutelary goddess of the Malla kings, built in 1564 by Mahendra Malla in Hanumān Ḍhokā (Kathmandu Durbar Square); it is opened to the public only once a year, at Dasaĩ.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nallūr Kantacuvāmi temple, Jaffna
summary: Murukaṉ temple at Nallur, Jaffna, where the god is worshipped as the spear (vēl); the Yālppāṇa Vaipava Mālai records earlier temples of the Jaffna kings, the third destroyed by the Portuguese in 1624, and the present temple was built in 1734 under Dutch rule by Ragunātha Māppāṇa Mudaliyār.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kataragama devālaya complex
summary: Shrine complex in the jungle of southern Sri Lanka of the god Kataragama — a Buddhist guardian deity and, for Hindus, Murukaṉ (Skanda) — venerated by Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Vedda; its annual Esala festival and fire-walking are major pilgrimages.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tirukkētīsvaram temple, Mannar
summary: Śiva temple near the ancient port of Māntai (Mannar), one of the five ancient īśvarams of Sri Lanka and a Tēvāram shrine sung by Campantar and Cuntarar; long ruined after the Portuguese period, it was rebuilt from 1903 by the Nāṭṭukkōṭṭai Nakarattār of Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sītā Amman temple, Sita Eliya
summary: Small temple at Sita Eliya near Nuwara Eliya, Sri Lanka, identified by local tradition with the Aśoka grove where Rāvaṇa held Sītā captive; established in the late 20th century and completed in the early 21st, after old images were found by the stream about a century ago.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śāradā Pīṭha (ruins), Neelum valley
summary: Ruined Kashmiri stone temple of the goddess Śāradā at Sharda in the Neelum valley (Pakistan-administered Kashmir), from the 6th to 12th centuries one of the most famous temple-centres of learning in South Asia; described by Al-Bīrūnī and Kalhaṇa, and a pilgrimage site for Kashmiri Paṇḍits until 1947.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pañcamukhī Hanumān temple, Karachi
summary: Hanumān temple in Karachi, Pakistan, declared protected heritage under the Sindh Cultural Heritage (Preservation) Act 1994; tradition says Rāma visited the site in exile and that the five-faced image of Hanumān was found in the ground here, and the temple is popularly claimed to be about 1,500 years old.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Phnom Bakheng, Angkor
summary: Five-tiered temple-mountain of Śiva on a natural hill at Angkor, the state temple of Yaśovarman I (r. 889–c. 910) at the centre of his new capital Yaśodharapura; later converted to Buddhist use.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Baphuon, Angkor Thom
summary: Three-tiered sandstone temple-mountain of Śiva of the mid-11th century in Angkor Thom, long credited to Udayādityavarman II (recent research argues for Sūryavarman I); a reclining Buddha was built onto its western face c. 1430–40, and the EFEO completed its anastylosis in 2011.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Prasat Thom, Koh Ker
summary: Seven-tiered pyramid and temple complex at Koh Ker (ancient Liṅgapura / Chok Gargyar), capital of the Khmer king Jayavarman IV (r. 928–941) and his son Harṣavarman II until 944; the Koh Ker site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sambor Prei Kuk (Īśānapura)
summary: Pre-Angkorian temple city in Kampong Thom province, identified with Īśānapura, capital of the Chenla king Īśānavarman I (r. c. 616–637); its brick sanctuaries, including octagonal towers with “flying palace” reliefs, are among the earliest Khmer temples. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2017).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Prasat Kravan, Angkor
summary: Five brick towers on a common terrace south of Srah Srang at Angkor, dedicated to Viṣṇu in 921 according to a doorjamb inscription; the interior brick reliefs show Viṣṇu striding (Trivikrama), on Garuḍa, eight-armed, and Lakṣmī.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bakong, Roluos
summary: Earliest sandstone temple-mountain of the Khmer empire, the state temple of Indravarman I at Hariharālaya (Roluos), dedicated to Śiva in 881; its central tower was rebuilt in the 12th century in the Angkor Wat style.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kbal Spean (river of a thousand liṅgas)
aliases: Kbal Spean|Valley of a Thousand Lingas
summary: Stretch of the Stung Kbal Spean stream on the Kulen hills north-east of Angkor whose sandstone bed and banks are carved with rows of liṅgas and reliefs of Viṣṇu Anantaśāyin, Śiva and Umā, and Brahmā; carved in the 11th–12th centuries, so that the water flowing to Angkor was sanctified.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Prasat Phanom Rung
aliases: Prasat Hin Phanom Rung|Phanom Rung Historical Park
summary: Khmer sanctuary of Śiva on the rim of an extinct volcano in Buriram province, Thailand, built between the 10th and 13th centuries; its Nārāyaṇa lintel (Viṣṇu Anantaśāyin), stolen in the 1960s and held by the Art Institute of Chicago from 1967, was returned in 1988 after a public campaign.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Prasat Phimai
summary: Largest Khmer sanctuary in Thailand, at Phimai (ancient Vimāyapura) in Nakhon Ratchasima, built in the late 11th–12th centuries as a Mahāyāna Buddhist temple but carrying Hindu narrative lintels, including Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa scenes.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Devasathan (Royal Brahmin office), Bangkok
summary: Hindu shrine complex near Wat Suthat in Bangkok, founded in 1784 by King Rama I as the seat of the court Brahmins (phram), who trace their lineage to Rameswaram and perform royal ceremonies such as the Triyampawai–Trippawai swing festival.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nathlaung Kyaung, Bagan
summary: Brick Viṣṇu temple inside the old city walls of Bagan, the only surviving Hindu temple among Bagan’s thousands of Buddhist monuments, built in the 10th or 11th century (under Anawrahta or earlier), probably for Indian merchants and artisans.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Po Nagar, Nha Trang
aliases: Ponagar|Tháp Bà Po Nagar|Thiên Y Thánh Mẫu
summary: Cham temple complex on a hill at Nha Trang dedicated to Yan Po Nagar, goddess of the land, identified with Bhagavatī and Mahiṣāsuramardinī; founded before 781, with inscriptions recording royal gifts from 781 to 1143 and standing brick towers mainly of the 11th–13th centuries.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Penataran temple complex, Blitar
summary: Largest Hindu temple complex in East Java, begun in 1197 in the Kediri period and enlarged under Majapahit (dated temple 1369); its main terrace carries Rāmāyaṇa reliefs and its second terrace the Kṛṣṇāyana, in the flat wayang-like East Javanese style.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Gedong Songo temples
summary: Group of small 8th–9th-century Śaiva candi set in five clusters on the slopes of Mount Ungaran in Central Java, among the earliest Hindu temples of Java; an inscription of 1382 shows they were still active in the Majapahit period.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Candi Sukuh
summary: Fifteenth-century terraced pyramid temple on the slope of Mount Lawu in Central Java, consecrated c. 1437 by a chronogram at its gate, with distinctive reliefs on birth, fertility and the Garuḍeya story — among the last Hindu temples built in Java before Islamisation.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pura Tanah Lot, Bali
summary: Balinese sea temple on an offshore rock at Beraban, Tabanan, reachable on foot at low tide, attributed by tradition to the 16th-century priest Dang Hyang Nirārtha; one of the chain of sea temples guarding Bali’s coast.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pura Ulun Danu Bratan, Bali
summary: Water temple on Lake Bratan in the Bali highlands, built in 1633 according to the reference, for the lake goddess Dewi Danu; the lake feeds the irrigation societies (subak) downstream, whose smaller water temples depend on it.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pura Tirta Empul, Tampaksiring
summary: Balinese water temple founded around a holy spring in 962 CE in the Warmadewa period, whose bathing pools (petirtaan) are used for ritual purification (melukat); a source of the Pakerisan river.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bujang Valley candi (Kedah)
aliases: Candi Bukit Batu Pahat|Lembah Bujang candi
summary: Remains of brick and laterite Hindu and Buddhist shrines (candi) in the Bujang Valley of Kedah, Malaysia, part of a trading complex of the 5th–14th centuries; the reconstructed Candi Bukit Batu Pahat is the best-known Śaiva shrine.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sri Mahamariamman temple, Kuala Lumpur
summary: Oldest Hindu temple in Kuala Lumpur, founded in 1873 by K. Thamboosamy Pillai as a family shrine, moved in 1885 to its Jalan Bandar site and rebuilt in brick in 1887; the present temple was completed in 1968 with a five-tiered gopura (1972) and consecrated in 1973.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sri Mariamman temple, Singapore
summary: Singapore’s oldest Hindu temple, on South Bridge Road in Chinatown, founded by Naraina Pillai, who built a simple wood-and-attap shrine there by 1827 after receiving the site in 1823; a gazetted National Monument and the setting of the annual fire-walking (Thimithi) festival.

type:LABEL: temple
name: BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Neasden
aliases: Neasden Temple|BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir London
summary: Carved-stone temple of the BAPS Svāminārāyaṇa organisation in Neasden, London — the first traditional Hindu stone temple in Europe — built from November 1992 and opened in August 1995 under Pramukh Swami Maharaj, using Bulgarian limestone and Indian and Italian marble carved in India and assembled without structural steel.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Swaminarayan Akshardham, Delhi
summary: Large BAPS temple-and-exhibition campus on the Yamuna floodplain in Delhi, created under Pramukh Swami Maharaj and consecrated on 6 November 2005; its carved sandstone and marble central monument houses an image of Svāminārāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: BAPS Swaminarayan Akshardham, Robbinsville
summary: BAPS temple in Robbinsville, New Jersey, built between 2015 and 2023 and dedicated in October 2023, the largest Hindu temple in the Western Hemisphere; its construction involved a 2021 lawsuit over the labour conditions of artisans brought from India.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sri Venkateswara Temple, Penn Hills (Pittsburgh)
summary: Temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara in Penn Hills near Pittsburgh, modelled on Tirumala and consecrated on 8 June 1977 with help from the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams and the Andhra Pradesh endowments department — the first Hindu temple in the United States built by Indian immigrants.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sri Maha Vallabha Ganapati Devasthanam, Flushing
aliases: Ganesh Temple, Flushing|Hindu Temple Society of North America
summary: Gaṇeśa temple in Flushing, Queens, New York, managed by the Hindu Temple Society of North America (founded 1970) and consecrated on 4 July 1977 — among the first Hindu temples built by Indian immigrants in the United States.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ganga Talao (Grand Bassin), Mauritius
summary: Crater lake in southern Mauritius made a Hindu tīrtha after a priest of Triolet, Jhummun Giri, dreamed in 1887 (or the 1890s) that its waters flowed from the Gaṅgā; Gaṅgā water was poured into it in 1972, it was declared a sacred lake in 1998, and the Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage draws hundreds of thousands.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Temple in the Sea (Sewdass Sadhu Shiv Mandir), Trinidad
summary: Small Śiva temple on a causeway in the Gulf of Paria at Waterloo, Trinidad, built single-handedly from 1947 to 1952 by Sewdass Sadhu, an indentured labourer from India, after he was refused land; rebuilt and reopened in 1995 for the 150th anniversary of Indian indentured arrival.

type:LABEL: temple
name: BAPS Hindu Mandir, Abu Dhabi
summary: First traditional carved-stone Hindu temple in Abu Dhabi, on land granted by the UAE government in 2015, consecrated by Mahant Swami Maharaj on 14 February 2024; the largest Hindu temple in West Asia, with over two million visitors in its first year.

type:LABEL: place
name: Yamunā river
summary: Sacred river of northern India rising at Yamunotri and joining the Gaṅgā at Prayāga; personified as the goddess Yamunā, sister of Yama, it is the river of Kṛṣṇa’s Braj (Mathurā and Vṛndāvana) and is named in the Ṛgveda’s river hymn.

type:LABEL: place
name: Sarayū river (Ghaghara at Ayodhyā)
summary: The river on which Ayodhyā stands in the Rāmāyaṇa, identified with the lower Ghaghara (Karnali), locally called Saryu or Sarayū at Ayodhyā; Rāma enters its waters at the end of the Uttarakāṇḍa.

type:LABEL: place
name: Narmadā river
summary: West-flowing river of central India rising at Amarkantak and reaching the Gulf of Khambhat, regarded as among the holiest rivers (some say its sight purifies as bathing in the Gaṅgā does); pilgrims perform a months-long circumambulation (parikramā) of its whole length.

type:LABEL: place
name: Godāvarī river
summary: Longest river of peninsular India, rising at Brahmagiri near Trimbak (Tryambakeśvara) and flowing east to the Bay of Bengal; called “Dakṣiṇa Gaṅgā”, its banks at Nashik (Pañcavaṭī) are a Kumbha Melā site and the setting of Rāma’s forest exile.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kāverī river
summary: Sacred river of the far south, rising at Talakaveri in Kodagu and reaching the sea at Poompuhar; its delta holds many of the great Cōḻa and Tēvāram temples, and the island-temple cities of Srirangapatna and Srirangam.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kṛṣṇā river
summary: River of the Deccan rising at Mahabaleshwar and flowing east to the Bay of Bengal; Śrīśailam stands above its gorge and Vijayawada’s Kanaka Durgā on its bank, and twelve-yearly Puṣkaram festivals are held on it.

type:LABEL: place
name: Sindhu (Indus) river
summary: The Indus, the great river of the Ṛgveda (where “sindhu” also means river in general), rising near Mount Kailāsa and flowing through Ladakh and Pakistan to the Arabian Sea; the name gave rise to “Hindu” and “India” through Persian and Greek.

type:LABEL: place
name: Brahmaputra river
summary: Great river of Tibet, Assam and Bangladesh — one of the few Indian rivers personified as male (“son of Brahmā”) — whose valley holds Kāmākhyā, Umānanda and the Hajo shrines; bathing at Parashuram Kund on its upper course is a major pilgrimage.

type:LABEL: place
name: Tuṅgabhadrā river
summary: River of Karnataka formed by the Tuṅgā (on which Śṛṅgeri stands) and the Bhadrā, flowing past Hampi, where tradition places Rāma’s Kiṣkindhā and the Pampā lake, to join the Kṛṣṇā near Alampur.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kṣiprā (Shipra) river
summary: River of the Malwa plateau on whose east bank Ujjain stands; the twelve-yearly Siṃhastha Kumbha Melā is held on its ghāṭs, and it is revered as a river goddess.

type:LABEL: place
name: Aruṇācala hill
summary: Hill of about 814 m at Tiruvannamalai held to be Śiva himself as a column of fire (the fire-liṅga of the Pañca Bhūta set), circumambulated by pilgrims (giri-pradakṣiṇa) and lit by the great Kārttikai Dīpam beacon each year; also linked with the 20th-century sage Ramaṇa Maharṣi.

type:LABEL: place
name: Govardhana hill
summary: Low sandstone ridge about 8 km long west of Mathurā in Braj, identified with the mountain Kṛṣṇa lifted to shelter the cowherds from Indra’s rain; worshipped as a natural form of Kṛṣṇa (Giriraj) and circumambulated by pilgrims on a 21 km path.

type:LABEL: place
name: Śrīparvata (Śrīśailam hills)
summary: Forested Nallamala hills above the Kṛṣṇā gorge in Andhra Pradesh, the “Śrīparvata” of Sanskrit literature, sacred to Śiva as Mallikārjuna and to the goddess Bhramarāmbā; in early medieval sources a famous centre of Tantric ascetics.

type:LABEL: place
name: Kāñcī (Kanchipuram)
summary: Ancient city in Tamil Nadu, capital of the Pallavas, one of the Sapta Purī and a city of both Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava temples (Śiva Kāñcī and Viṣṇu Kāñcī), with the Kāmākṣī temple and the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi maṭha.

type:LABEL: place
name: Ujjayinī (Ujjain)
summary: Ancient city on the Kṣiprā in Malwa — Avantikā of the Sapta Purī — seat of the Mahākāla jyotirliṅga, the prime meridian of classical Indian astronomy, and site of the twelve-yearly Siṃhastha Kumbha Melā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Thanjavur
summary: Granite Śiva temple built by the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I at his capital Thanjavur and consecrated in 1010 CE; its c. 60 m vimāna was the tallest of its age and the walls carry a large corpus of Rājarāja’s own Tamil inscriptions.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Gangaikondacholapuram
summary: Śiva temple at the new capital founded by Rājendra I after his northern campaign to the Gaṅgā (c. 1025); its vimāna has a gently concave profile, unlike Thanjavur’s straight-sided pyramid. Part of the Great Living Chola Temples World Heritage property.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Airāvateśvara temple, Darasuram
summary: Twelfth-century Śiva temple near Kumbakonam built under the Cōḻa king Rājarāja II; its maṇḍapa is designed as a stone chariot and its reliefs include narrative friezes of the 63 Nāyaṉmār saints.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Naṭarāja temple, Chidambaram
summary: Temple of Śiva as Naṭarāja, the cosmic dancer, worshipped in the gold-roofed Kaṉakasabhā; it is the “ether” (ākāśa) shrine among the five element liṅgas and one of the most celebrated temples sung in the Tēvāram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śrī Raṅganāthasvāmī temple, Srirangam
summary: Island temple of Viṣṇu as Raṅganātha reclining on the serpent, set within seven concentric enclosures on an island of the Kāvēri; first among the 108 Divya Deśams of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mīnākṣī–Sundareśvara temple, Madurai
summary: Twin-shrine temple of the goddess Mīnākṣī and her consort Sundareśvara (Śiva) at the heart of Madurai; its fourteen painted gopuras, the tallest c. 52 m, largely date from Nāyaka rebuilding in the 16th–17th centuries.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rāmanāthasvāmī temple, Rameswaram
summary: Śiva temple on Pamban (Rameswaram) island where, according to tradition, Rāma worshipped a liṅga; it is counted among the twelve jyotirliṅgas and as the southern dhāma of the Char Dham, and is known for its very long pillared corridors.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Aruṇācaleśvara temple, Tiruvannamalai
summary: Large temple at the foot of Aruṇācala hill, worshipped as the fire (agni) liṅga among the five element shrines; the hill itself is identified in tradition with the column of fire of the Liṅgodbhava story.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jambukeśvara temple, Thiruvanaikaval
summary: Śiva temple on Srirangam island worshipped as the water (jala) liṅga among the five element shrines; a spring keeps the sanctum floor moist.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ekāmbareśvara temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Major Śiva temple of Kanchipuram worshipped as the earth (pṛthvī) liṅga among the five element shrines, centred on a sacred mango tree; its southern gopura is among the tallest in South India.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kailāsanātha temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Sandstone Śiva temple built by the Pallava king Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha around 700 CE, with additions by his son Mahendravarman III; one of the earliest large structural temples of Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Eighth-century Pallava Viṣṇu temple built by Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, with three superimposed sanctums and a cloister of relief panels that narrate Pallava dynastic history; a Divya Deśam sung by Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Varadarāja Perumāḷ temple, Kanchipuram
summary: Large Viṣṇu temple of Kanchipuram on the Hastigiri mound, a Divya Deśam closely associated with Rāmānuja; renovated under the Cōḻas from 1053 and expanded by later dynasties.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Group of Monuments at Mamallapuram
summary: Seventh- and eighth-century Pallava port with rock-cut cave temples (maṇḍapas), monolithic rathas, open-air reliefs and the structural Shore Temple; a World Heritage property since 1984.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Shore Temple, Mamallapuram
summary: Granite structural temple on the shore at Mamallapuram, built under Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha around 700–728 CE, combining two Śiva shrines with a shrine of the reclining Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pañca Rathas, Mamallapuram
summary: Five monolithic shrines carved from a single granite outcrop in the 7th century, popularly named after the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī; they model the main types of early Drāviḍa shrine and were never consecrated.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Subrahmaṇya temple, Tirupparankundram
summary: Rock-cut and structural temple of Murukaṉ on a hill outside Madurai, counted first of the six abodes; tradition places Murukaṉ’s marriage to Deivayāṉai (Devasenā) here.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Subrahmaṇya temple, Tiruchendur
summary: Seashore temple of Murukaṉ on the Gulf of Mannar, counted second of the six abodes; tradition places here Murukaṉ’s victory over the demon Śūrapadma, re-enacted in the Skanda Ṣaṣṭhī festival.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi temple, Palani
summary: Hilltop temple of Murukaṉ as the renunciant Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi, counted third of the six abodes and one of the most visited temples in Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Svāminātha temple, Swamimalai
summary: Temple of Murukaṉ as Svāminātha near Kumbakonam, counted fourth of the six abodes; tradition says the child Murukaṉ taught Śiva the meaning of Om here.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Subrahmaṇya temple, Tiruttani
summary: Hill temple of Murukaṉ in northern Tamil Nadu, traditionally counted fifth of the six abodes, where Murukaṉ married the hunter-maiden Vaḷḷi in local tradition.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Murukaṉ temple, Pazhamudircholai
summary: Forest-hill shrine of Murukaṉ above the Aḻakar Kōvil near Madurai, counted sixth of the six abodes.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Guruvāyūr temple
summary: Kerala temple of Kṛṣṇa as Guruvāyūrappaṉ (a four-armed Viṣṇu image worshipped as the child Kṛṣṇa), one of the most visited temples of South India.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Padmanābhasvāmī temple, Thiruvananthapuram
summary: Temple of Viṣṇu reclining on Ananta at the heart of Thiruvananthapuram, a Divya Deśam and the tutelary shrine of the Travancore royal house; the opening of its vaults in 2011 revealed a very large treasure.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Veṅkaṭeśvara temple, Tirumala
summary: Hill temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara on the Tirumala range above Tirupati, among the most visited and richest religious institutions in the world; a Divya Deśam sung by the Āḻvārs.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mallikārjuna temple, Srisailam
summary: Fortified hilltop temple above the Krishna gorge that is counted both as a jyotirliṅga (Mallikārjuna) and as a Śakti Pīṭha (Bhramarāmbā); it is also sung in the Tēvāram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śrīkāḷahastīśvara temple, Srikalahasti
summary: Śiva temple on the Svarṇamukhī river worshipped as the air (vāyu) liṅga among the five element shrines and associated with the hunter-saint Kaṇṇappa; it is sung in the Tēvāram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Paraśurāmeśvara temple, Gudimallam
summary: Village temple near Renigunta whose apsidal sanctum enshrines the Gudimallam liṅga, a realistic liṅga carved with a standing two-armed figure that is among the earliest surviving images connected with Śiva; the liṅga is dated by most scholars between the 2nd/1st c. BCE and the early centuries CE.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Navabrahma temples, Alampur
summary: Group of nine Śiva temples of the Bādāmi Cālukya period (7th–8th c.) near the confluence of the Tuṅgabhadrā and Kṛṣṇā, unusual in the south for their Nāgara (curvilinear) towers; the nearby Jogulāmbā shrine is counted among the eighteen Mahāśakti Pīṭhas.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rāmappa (Rudreśvara) temple, Palampet
summary: Kākatīya Śiva temple at Palampet commissioned in 1213 by the general Recherla Rudra under king Gaṇapati; inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2021 and popularly named after its sculptor.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bādāmi cave temples
summary: Four rock-cut cave temples (three Hindu, one Jain) in the sandstone cliff of Vātāpi, capital of the early Cālukyas; Cave 3, dedicated to Viṣṇu, carries an inscription of Śaka 500 (578 CE), making it one of the earliest precisely dated Brahmanical cave temples.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Meguti Jain temple, Aihole
summary: Jain temple on a hill at Aihole whose east wall bears the Aihole praśasti of Pulakeśin II composed by Ravikīrti and dated Śaka 556 (634/635 CE); it is one of the earliest securely dated structural temples in the Deccan.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Durgā temple, Aihole
summary: Apsidal-ended early Cālukya temple at Aihole (late 7th–early 8th c.) surrounded by a colonnaded ambulatory; its name derives from a later fort (durga) built on it, not from the goddess.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Lāḍ Khān temple, Aihole
summary: Flat-roofed early Cālukya Śiva temple at Aihole, named after a later occupant; its date is a classic problem of Indian architectural history, with proposals ranging from the 5th to the early 8th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Virūpākṣa temple, Pattadakal
summary: The largest temple at Pattadakal, built c. 740–745 CE by Queen Lokamahādevī to commemorate her husband Vikramāditya II’s victory over the Pallavas; its Drāviḍa design closely follows the Kailāsanātha temple of Kanchipuram.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pāpanātha temple, Pattadakal
summary: Mid-8th-century Cālukya Śiva temple at Pattadakal that fuses Nāgara and Drāviḍa elements and is known for its narrative panels from the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kirātārjunīya.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kailāsa temple (Ellora Cave 16)
summary: A complete Drāviḍa temple carved downward and inward from the basalt hillside at Ellora in the 8th century, generally attributed to the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Kṛṣṇa I (r. c. 756–773); its form evokes Mount Kailāsa, Śiva’s abode.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Daśāvatāra cave (Ellora Cave 15)
summary: Two-storeyed rock-cut temple at Ellora whose plan follows the Buddhist vihāras nearby but whose sculpture is Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava; an inscription of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa founder Dantidurga on the back wall of the front maṇḍapa is key to its date.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Elephanta Caves (Cave 1)
summary: Great Śiva cave on Elephanta island in Mumbai harbour, completed in the mid-6th century, whose colossal three-headed Sadāśiva (Maheśamūrti) is among the masterpieces of Indian sculpture.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Virūpākṣa temple, Hampi
summary: Living Śiva temple of Virūpākṣa–Pampāpati on the Tuṅgabhadrā at Hampi, whose small early shrine was enlarged into a vast complex under the Vijayanagara kings; it predates and outlived the imperial city.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hazāra Rāma temple, Hampi
summary: Royal chapel of the Vijayanagara palace zone dedicated to Rāma, whose outer and inner walls are covered with friezes of the Rāmāyaṇa and of royal processions; it is attributed to Devarāya I in the early 15th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vijaya Viṭṭhala temple, Hampi
summary: Vijayanagara temple of Viṭṭhala (a form of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa worshipped at Pandharpur) at Hampi, famous for its “musical” pillars and the stone chariot that serves as Garuḍa’s shrine; mostly built in the 15th–16th centuries, with major additions under Kṛṣṇadevarāya.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Cennakeśava temple, Belur
summary: Hoysaḷa temple of Viṣṇu as Cennakeśava commissioned by King Viṣṇuvardhana in 1117 CE at his early capital Belur; its bracket figures and lathe-turned pillars are hallmarks of the Hoysaḷa style.
earliest_material: first quarter of the 12th century CE

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hoysaḷeśvara temple, Halebidu
summary: Twin-shrined Śiva temple at the Hoysaḷa capital Dvārasamudra (Halebidu), begun c. 1121 under Viṣṇuvardhana by his officer Ketamalla; its friezes carry thousands of sculptures including Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata scenes.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Keśava temple, Somanathapura
summary: Triple-shrined (trikūṭa) Hoysaḷa Viṣṇu temple on a star-shaped plan, consecrated by Somanātha Daṇḍanāyaka, a general of Narasiṃha III; Wikipedia gives 1258 CE while many guides give 1268.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Śiva temple, Ambarnath
summary: Bhūmija-style Śiva temple near Mumbai bearing an inscription of 1060 CE from the Śilāhāra period, one of the best-preserved 11th-century temples of the northern Konkan.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bhīmaśaṅkara temple
summary: Śiva temple in the Sahyādri forest at the source of the Bhīmā river, claimed as the Bhīmaśaṅkara jyotirliṅga (a claim also made for sites in Assam and elsewhere).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Tryambakeśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple near the source of the Godāvarī in the Brahmagiri hills, whose liṅga is a hollow with three small lingas (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva); the present temple was built by the Peshwa Bāḷājī Bājīrāv in the mid-18th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Ghṛṣṇeśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple near Ellora, restored by Mālojī Bhosale in the 16th century and rebuilt in its present red-stone form in the 18th century under Holkar patronage.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vaijanātha temple, Parli
summary: Śiva temple at Parli in Marathwada, one of the candidates for the Vaidyanātha jyotirliṅga (the other main claimant being Deoghar in Jharkhand).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nāganātha temple, Aundha
summary: Hemāḍpanthī-style Śiva temple in Marathwada claimed as the Nāgeśvara jyotirliṅga, one of three competing claimants (with Dwarka and Jageshwar).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Udayagiri caves (Vidiśā)
summary: Group of about twenty rock-cut shrines near Vidiśā excavated under the Gupta king Candragupta II, the only cave site securely tied to a Gupta monarch by inscriptions; Cave 5 holds the monumental relief of Varāha raising the Earth.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
summary: Late Gupta stone temple of Viṣṇu (c. 500–550 CE) on the Betwā, one of the earliest surviving North Indian temples with a tower; its wall panels show Viṣṇu reclining on Śeṣa, Gajendra-mokṣa and Nara-Nārāyaṇa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pārvatī temple, Nachna
summary: Early stone temple at Nachna with a sanctum surrounded by a covered ambulatory and an upper chamber, carved with rock-like rustication; dated by style to the 5th or 6th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bhitargaon brick temple
summary: Late 5th-century Gupta-period brick temple near Kanpur, the oldest surviving roofed brick/terracotta Hindu shrine with a high śikhara; its terracotta panels include Viṣṇu and other Purāṇic subjects.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kaṅkālī Devī temple, Tigawa
summary: Small flat-roofed Gupta-period temple (c. 400–425 CE) with a pillared porch, one of the earliest structural Hindu temples to survive; the doorway shows the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Muṇḍeśvarī temple
summary: Octagonal stone temple on a hill in Kaimur district, Bihar, worshipped for Muṇḍeśvarī and a four-faced liṅga; it is often promoted as the oldest functioning Hindu temple (108 CE), a date most historians of architecture reject.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Sirpur
summary: Brick temple at Sirpur (Śrīpura) in Chhattisgarh with a well-preserved śikhara and stone doorframe, the earliest dated monument of the Sirpur group (c. 595–605 CE per Wikipedia; other accounts c. 650).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kandarīya Mahādeva temple, Khajuraho
summary: The largest and most elaborate of the Khajuraho temples, a Śiva temple of c. 1025–1050 CE built under the Candela king Vidyādhara, whose clustered śikhara rises like a mountain range.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Khajuraho
summary: Candela temple of Vaikuṇṭha Viṣṇu completed by Yaśovarman (Lakṣavarman) and dated by an inscription of Vikrama 1011 (953/954 CE), the earliest securely dated of the great Khajuraho temples.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sun Temple, Konark
summary: Colossal 13th-century temple of Sūrya conceived as the Sun god’s chariot with 24 carved wheels and seven horses, built c. 1250 under the Eastern Gaṅga king Narasiṃhadeva I; the tower collapsed, and the surviving jagamohana is the largest standing part.
earliest_textual: not before the 10th c.; Orissa chapters probably after the 13th c.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jagannātha temple, Puri
summary: Temple of Jagannātha with Balabhadra and Subhadrā, worshipped in wooden images periodically renewed (Navakalevara), at Puri; the present temple was begun by the Eastern Gaṅga king Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga in the 12th century, and Puri is the eastern dhāma of the Char Dham.
earliest_textual: not before the 10th c.; Orissa chapters probably after the 13th c.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Liṅgarāja temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: The largest temple of Bhubaneswar (Ekāmra Kṣetra), an 11th-century Kaliṅga-style Śiva temple whose deity is worshipped as Harihara (Śiva–Viṣṇu); it is attributed to Somavaṃśī kings with later Gaṅga additions.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mukteśvara temple, Bhubaneswar
summary: Small 10th-century Kaliṅga-style Śiva temple in Bhubaneswar (c. 950–975 CE), celebrated for its arched gateway (toraṇa) and refined carving, marking the transition to the mature Odishan style.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Causaṭh Yoginī temple, Hirapur
summary: Small circular, roofless (hypaethral) sandstone shrine near Bhubaneswar housing images of sixty-four yoginīs around a central Kālī/Mahāmāyā, dated to the 9th century and associated with the Bhauma-Kara queen Hīrādevī.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kāmākhyā temple, Guwahati
summary: Principal temple of the goddess Kāmākhyā on Nīlācala hill, Guwahati, where an aniconic yoni-shaped stone in a cave is worshipped; one of the oldest centres of tantric Śākta practice and a Śakti Pīṭha in all major lists. The present temple was rebuilt in 1565 under the Koch king Naranārāyaṇa by his brother Chilarai.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kālīghāṭ temple, Kolkata
summary: Temple of Kālī on the old course of the Hooghly (Ādi Gaṅgā) in Kolkata, counted as a Śakti Pīṭha where the toes of Satī’s right foot fell; the present building was completed in 1809 under the Sābarṇa Rāy Caudhurī family.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Dakṣiṇeśvar Kālī temple
summary: Navaratna-style temple of Kālī as Bhavatāriṇī on the Hooghly north of Kolkata, founded by Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi and consecrated on 31 May 1855; Rāmakṛṣṇa served as its priest.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Viṣṇupada temple, Gaya
summary: Temple at Gaya enshrining a footprint of Viṣṇu in basalt, central to the śrāddha rites for ancestors performed at Gaya; the present temple was rebuilt in 1787 by Ahilyābāī Holkar.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Baidyanātha temple, Deoghar
summary: Complex of 22 temples at Deoghar in Jharkhand, the most widely accepted claimant to the Vaidyanātha jyotirliṅga and also claimed as a Śakti Pīṭha; the month of Śrāvaṇa brings very large kāṃvaṛ pilgrimages carrying Gaṅgā water.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kāśī Viśvanātha temple, Varanasi
summary: Temple of Śiva as Viśvanātha (Viśveśvara), “Lord of the Universe”, at Varanasi, one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas; the present temple was built in 1780 by Ahilyābāī Holkar on a site adjacent to the earlier temple.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Somanātha temple, Prabhas Patan
summary: Seashore Śiva temple at Prabhāsa Pāṭan, first of the twelve jyotirliṅgas in the Śiva Purāṇa list; repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt, the present temple in Māru-Gurjara (Cālukya) style was completed in 1951.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Dvārakādhīśa temple, Dwarka
summary: Temple of Kṛṣṇa as “King of Dvārakā” at Dwarka on the Gujarat coast, the western dhāma of the Char Dham and a Divya Deśam; the present five-storeyed structure dates from the 15th–16th centuries.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Nāgeśvara temple, Dwarka
summary: Śiva temple between Dwarka and Bet Dwarka promoted as the Nāgeśvara jyotirliṅga, one of three competing claimants (with Aundha in Maharashtra and Jageshwar in Uttarakhand).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Sun temple, Modhera
summary: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) temple of Sūrya at Modhera with a stepped tank (Sūrya Kuṇḍa) and a detached dance hall; its shrine was built in the reign of Bhīma I, shortly after 1026–27 CE.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mahākāleśvara temple, Ujjain
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple of Śiva as Mahākāla in Ujjain, whose south-facing (dakṣiṇāmūrti) liṅga is worshipped with the dawn bhasma-ārati; the present temple is an 18th-century Marāṭhā-period reconstruction.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Oṃkāreśvara temple
summary: Jyotirliṅga temple on the island of Māndhātā in the Narmadā, whose island is said to resemble the syllable Om; the jyotirliṅga is shared in tradition with the Amaleśvara (Mamaleśvara) temple on the south bank.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Bhojeśvara temple, Bhojpur
summary: Unfinished 11th-century Śiva temple at Bhojpur near Bhopal attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja, housing one of the largest liṅgas in India; construction drawings engraved on the surrounding rock show how the temple was to be completed.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Brahmā temple, Pushkar
summary: Temple of Brahmā beside the sacred lake of Puṣkara in Rajasthan, among the very few temples in India dedicated to Brahmā; the present structure dates from the 14th century with later rebuilding.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Rām Mandir, Ayodhya
aliases: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Mandir|Ram Janmabhoomi temple
summary: Temple of Rāma in Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, built in the Nāgara (Māru-Gurjara) style after the Supreme Court of India’s judgment of 9 November 2019 and consecrated (prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā) on 22 January 2024; many Hindus regard the site as Rāma’s birthplace (Rāma Janmabhūmi).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kedāranātha temple
summary: High-altitude stone temple of Śiva at about 3,580 m in the Garhwal Himalaya, a jyotirliṅga, one of the Chota Char Dham and the chief of the Pañca Kedāra; it survived the 2013 flash flood that devastated the town.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Badrīnātha temple
summary: Temple of Viṣṇu as Badrīnārāyaṇa at about 3,100 m on the Alaknandā, the northern dhāma of the Char Dham, one of the Chota Char Dham and a Divya Deśam; it was largely rebuilt after the 1803 Garhwal earthquake.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Gaṅgotrī temple
summary: Temple of the goddess Gaṅgā at about 3,100 m on the Bhāgīrathī, one of the Chota Char Dham; the original temple was built in the early 19th century by the Gorkha general Amar Singh Thapa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Yamunotrī temple
summary: Temple of the river goddess Yamunā near the source of the Yamunā in the Garhwal Himalaya, the westernmost of the Chota Char Dham; built in the 19th century by a ruler of Tehri Garhwal and rebuilt after destruction by snow and floods.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jageśvara temple group
summary: Group of more than 100 stone temples (7th–14th c.) in a deodar valley near Almora, claimed locally as the Nāgeśa jyotirliṅga “in the Dāruka forest”; ASI-protected.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mārtaṇḍa Sun temple, Kashmir
summary: Ruined 8th-century temple of Sūrya (Mārtaṇḍa) on a plateau near Anantnag, built by the Kārkoṭa king Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa according to Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī and destroyed in the early 15th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Paśupatinātha temple, Kathmandu
summary: Pagoda-roofed temple of Śiva as Paśupati (“Lord of creatures”) on the Bāgmatī at Deopatan, Kathmandu, Nepal’s principal Hindu shrine; worship here is attested from the Licchavi period, and the present building dates from a renovation of 1692.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Changu Narayan temple
summary: Hilltop Viṣṇu temple east of Kathmandu that preserves the pillar inscription of the Licchavi king Mānadeva (Saṃvat 386, 464 CE), the earliest dated inscription of Nepal; the two-tiered pagoda itself is a later rebuilding, heavily damaged in 2015 and restored.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Jānakī Mandir, Janakpur
summary: White marble-and-stone temple of Sītā (Jānakī) at Janakpur, Nepal, built in 1910 by Queen Vṛṣabhānu of Tikamgarh (Orchha) in a Hindu–Rajput (Mughal-influenced) style; Janakpur is identified by tradition with Mithilā, Sītā’s city.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Muktinātha temple
summary: High-altitude pagoda shrine (c. 3,700 m) in Mustang, Nepal, sacred to Hindus as Viṣṇu Muktinārāyaṇa — a Divya Deśam (Sāḷagrāmam) — and to Tibetan Buddhists as Chumig Gyatsa, an abode of Avalokiteśvara.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Kōṇēsvaram temple, Trincomalee
aliases: Thirukonamalai Konesar|Temple of a Thousand Pillars
summary: Śiva temple on Swami Rock above Trincomalee bay, Sri Lanka, praised in the Tēvāram hymns of Campantar and Cuntarar; the medieval complex was destroyed by the Portuguese in 1622–1624 and a fort built from its stones, and the temple was rebuilt in 1952.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Muṉṉēsvaram temple, Chilaw
summary: Śiva temple near Chilaw on Sri Lanka’s west coast, in existence since at least c. 1000 CE; tradition holds that Rāma worshipped Śiva here after the war with Rāvaṇa. It was destroyed twice by the Portuguese and rebuilt in 1753.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Katās Rāj temples
summary: Group of Hindu temples (6th century onward) around a sacred pond in the Salt Range of Punjab, Pakistan; tradition holds that the pond formed from Śiva’s tears after Satī’s death and that the Pāṇḍavas met the Yakṣa here.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Hiṅglāj Mātā cave shrine
summary: Natural cave shrine of the goddess Hiṅgulā in the Hingol valley of Balochistan, Pakistan, counted as a Śakti Pīṭha where part of Satī’s head fell; the spring Hinglaj Yātrā draws very large numbers of pilgrims and is also revered by local Muslims as “Nani”.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Prambanan (Candi Rara Jonggrang)
summary: Ninth-century Hindu temple compound in Central Java with towering shrines to Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu; it is identified with the Śiva temple whose inauguration on 12 November 856 is recorded in the Śivagṛha inscription, and its balustrade reliefs tell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kṛṣṇa story.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Arjuna temple group, Dieng Plateau
summary: Small Śaiva stone temples on the volcanic Dieng Plateau of Central Java (mid-7th to late 8th c.), among the oldest standing stone structures in Java; their Mahābhārata names (Arjuna, Semar, Srikandi, Puntadewa) were given much later by local people.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Angkor Wat
summary: State temple of the Khmer king Sūryavarman II (r. 1113–c. 1150), built as a temple-mountain to Viṣṇu at Yaśodharapura (Angkor); its galleries carry vast bas-reliefs of the churning of the ocean, the Kurukṣetra battle and the war in Laṅkā. From the late 13th century it became a Theravāda Buddhist monastery.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Banteay Srei
summary: Small, exquisitely carved red-sandstone Śiva temple near Angkor consecrated on 22 April 967 CE, unusual in having been built not by a king but by the court official Yajñavarāha; its pediments include Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Preah Vihear temple
summary: Khmer Śiva temple stretched along a north–south axis on a cliff of the Dângrêk escarpment, built mainly in the 11th–12th centuries under Sūryavarman I and Sūryavarman II; the International Court of Justice ruled in 1962 that it lies in Cambodia, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 2008.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Vat Phou
summary: Khmer-period Śiva sanctuary at the foot of Mount Phou Kao (Liṅgaparvata, named for its liṅga-shaped summit) in southern Laos, with structures from the 5th to the 13th century; now a Theravāda Buddhist site and a World Heritage property (2001).

type:LABEL: temple
name: Mỹ Sơn sanctuary
summary: Valley of Cham brick temple-towers in central Vietnam, the principal religious centre of the kings of Champa from the 4th to the 13th century, dedicated chiefly to Śiva as Bhadreśvara; inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1999.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Pura Besakih
summary: The “mother temple” of Balinese Hinduism, a complex of more than twenty temples terraced on the slopes of Mount Agung; in use as a Hindu sanctuary at least since the 14th century.

type:LABEL: temple
name: Batu Caves temple
summary: Murukaṉ shrine in limestone caves north of Kuala Lumpur, completed in 1891 and the focus since 1892 of one of the largest Thaipūsam festivals outside India; a very tall gilded statue of Murukaṉ was unveiled beside the steps in January 2006.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Naṭarāja (Śiva as lord of dance)
summary: Śiva as the king of dancers, above all in the South Indian ānanda-tāṇḍava form standardised in Cōḻa bronzes: four-armed, dancing within a ring of flames on the dwarf Apasmāra, worshipped above all at Chidambaram.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Jagannātha
summary: “Lord of the world”, the deity of Puri worshipped in a stylised wooden image with large round eyes and stump arms, together with Balabhadra and Subhadrā; Vaiṣṇavas regard him as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, while scholars debate the cult’s tribal, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain antecedents.
earliest_material: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

type:LABEL: claim
name: The tribal (Śabara) origin hypothesis for Jagannātha
summary: The scholarly hypothesis that Jagannātha began as a wooden deity of tribal (Śabara) communities of Odisha and was progressively integrated into Brahmanical Vaiṣṇavism and royal cult, culminating under the Eastern Gaṅgas.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The claim that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple dates to 108 CE
summary: The claim, displayed by the ASI and the Bihar State Religious Trust Board, that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple was built in 108 CE and is the oldest functioning Hindu temple in the world.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Veṅkaṭeśvara
summary: Viṣṇu as Lord of the Vēṅkaṭa hill, worshipped at Tirumala in a standing four-armed image; one of the most widely worshipped forms of Viṣṇu in South India and the diaspora.
earliest_material: 966 CE gift of a silver image by the Pallava queen Sāmavai (earliest dated gift commonly cited)

type:LABEL: deity
name: Mīnākṣī
summary: The “fish-eyed” goddess of Madurai, who in the temple’s myth is born as a three-breasted Pāṇḍya princess, conquers the world and marries Śiva as Sundareśvara; she is identified with Pārvatī.
earliest_material: 14th c. CE restoration after Sultanate-period destruction

type:LABEL: deity
name: Raṅganātha
summary: Viṣṇu reclining on the serpent Ādiśeṣa, “lord of the stage (raṅga)”, worshipped above all at Srirangam on the Kāvēri.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Yamunā
summary: The river Yamunā personified as a goddess, daughter of Sūrya and sister of Yama, worshipped at her Himalayan source at Yamunotri and along the river, notably at Mathurā and Vṛndāvana.

type:LABEL: place
name: Hampi
summary: Ruined capital of the Vijayanagara empire on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka, a pilgrimage centre of Virūpākṣa–Pampā and, in local tradition, the Kiṣkindhā of the Rāmāyaṇa; the Group of Monuments at Hampi was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1986.

type:LABEL: place
name: Adam’s Bridge (Rāma Setu)
summary: Chain of limestone shoals and sandbanks, about 48 km long, between Pamban (Rameswaram) Island in India and Mannar Island in Sri Lanka; Hindu tradition identifies it with the causeway built by Rāma’s army to reach Laṅkā.

type:LABEL: place
name: Rameswaram (Pamban island)
summary: Island in the Gulf of Mannar off Tamil Nadu, linked to the mainland by the Pamban bridges, home of the Rāmanāthasvāmī temple and of Dhanushkodi at its south-eastern tip, where pilgrimage tradition places the start of Rāma’s bridge.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rājarāja I
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 985–1014) whose conquests made the Cōḻas the leading power of South India; builder of the Bṛhadīśvara temple at Thanjavur.
earliest_material: early 11th century CE (reigns of Rājarāja I and Rājendra I)

type:LABEL: person
name: Rājendra I
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 1014–1044), son of Rājarāja I, whose northern expedition reached the Gaṅgā and whose navy raided Śrīvijaya; founder of Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rājarāja II
summary: Later Cōḻa king (r. c. 1146–1173) under whom the Airāvateśvara temple at Darasuram was built.

type:LABEL: person
name: Parāntaka I
summary: Early Cōḻa king (r. c. 907–955) credited in copper-plate inscriptions with covering the roof of Naṭarāja’s hall at Chidambaram with gold.
earliest_material: regnal years 12 and 14 of Parāntaka I (c. 919 and 921 CE)

type:LABEL: person
name: Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha
summary: Pallava king (r. c. 690–728) who built the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailāsanātha temple at Kanchipuram, the first large structural temples of Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nandivarman II Pallavamalla
summary: Pallava king (r. c. 731–796) who built the Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple at Kanchipuram; a contemporary of Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vikramāditya II
summary: Cālukya king of Bādāmi (r. c. 733–746) who captured Kanchipuram from the Pallavas; his queens commissioned temples at Pattadakal to commemorate the victory.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lokamahādevī
summary: Queen of the Cālukya king Vikramāditya II who commissioned the Virūpākṣa (Lokeśvara) temple at Pattadakal c. 740–745.

type:LABEL: person
name: Dantidurga
summary: Founder of Rāṣṭrakūṭa imperial power (r. c. 735–756), who overthrew the Cālukyas of Bādāmi; his inscription is carved in Ellora Cave 15.

type:LABEL: person
name: Yaśovarman (Candela)
summary: Candela king (r. c. 925–950) who built the Lakṣmaṇa temple at Khajuraho for an image of Vaikuṇṭha Viṣṇu, as recorded in the inscription of 953/954 CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vidyādhara (Candela)
summary: Candela king (r. c. 1003–1035) in whose reign the Kandarīya Mahādeva temple at Khajuraho was begun; he resisted Mahmud of Ghazni.

type:LABEL: person
name: Narasiṃhadeva I
summary: Eastern Gaṅga king of Odisha (r. 1238–1264) who built the Sun temple at Konark and campaigned against the Bengal sultanate.

type:LABEL: person
name: Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga
summary: Eastern Gaṅga king (r. c. 1078–1147/50) who united Kaliṅga and Utkala and began the present Jagannātha temple at Puri.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ahilyābāī Holkar
summary: Marāṭhā queen and ruler of Indore (r. 1767–1795) who rebuilt or endowed temples, ghāṭs and rest houses across India, including the present Kāśī Viśvanātha temple (1780) and the Viṣṇupada temple at Gaya (1787).

type:LABEL: person
name: Naranārāyaṇa
summary: King of the Koch kingdom (r. 1540–1587) in whose reign the Kāmākhyā temple was rebuilt in 1565.

type:LABEL: person
name: Chilarai
summary: Koch general and brother of King Naranārāyaṇa who, according to an inscription in the temple, rebuilt the Kāmākhyā temple in 1565.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa
summary: Kārkoṭa king of Kashmir (r. c. 724–760) whom Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī credits with the Mārtaṇḍa Sun temple and far-reaching conquests.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhīma I (Caulukya)
summary: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) king of Gujarat (r. c. 1022–1064) during whose reign Mahmud of Ghazni raided Somanātha (1026) and the Modhera Sun temple was built.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhoja (Paramāra)
summary: Paramāra king of Mālava (r. c. 1010–1055), patron and author of works on poetics and architecture, to whom the unfinished Bhojeśvara temple is attributed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sūryavarman II
summary: Khmer king (r. 1113–c. 1150) who built Angkor Wat as his Vaiṣṇava state temple.

type:LABEL: person
name: Yajñavarāha
summary: Brahmin counsellor at the Khmer court (10th c.), tutor of Jayavarman V, credited with founding Banteay Srei (consecrated 967).

type:LABEL: person
name: Rakai Pikatan
summary: Ruler of the Medang (Mataram) kingdom in Central Java in the mid-9th century, whose name painted on a finial of the Śiva temple suggests he began Prambanan.

type:LABEL: person
name: Viṣṇuvardhana (Hoysaḷa)
summary: Hoysaḷa king (r. c. 1108–1152) who commissioned the Cennakeśava temple at Belur in 1117 and under whom the Hoysaḷeśvara temple at Halebidu was begun.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ketamalla
summary: Officer of the Hoysaḷa king Viṣṇuvardhana credited by an inscription with building the Hoysaḷeśvara temple at Halebidu.

type:LABEL: person
name: Somanātha Daṇḍanāyaka
summary: Hoysaḷa general of Narasiṃha III who founded Somanathapura and its Keśava temple in the mid-13th century.

type:LABEL: person
name: Recherla Rudra
summary: Kākatīya general who in 1213 commissioned the Rudreśvara (Rāmappa) temple at Palampet during the reign of Gaṇapati.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kṛṣṇadevarāya
summary: Tuḷuva emperor of Vijayanagara (r. 1509–1529), a major patron of temples including Tirumala, Hampi’s Virūpākṣa and Viṭṭhala temples and Srikalahasti.

type:LABEL: person
name: Devarāya I
summary: Saṅgama king of Vijayanagara (r. c. 1406–1422) to whom the Rāmacandra (Hazāra Rāma) temple in the royal centre is attributed.

type:LABEL: person
name: Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi
summary: Kolkata zamindar and philanthropist (1793–1861) who founded the Dakṣiṇeśvar Kālī temple, consecrated in 1855.

type:LABEL: person
name: Mārtāṇḍa Varma
summary: King of Travancore (r. 1729–1758) who rebuilt the Padmanābhasvāmī temple and in 1750 dedicated his kingdom to Padmanābha.

type:LABEL: person
name: Queen Vṛṣabhānu of Tikamgarh
summary: Queen of the Bundela state of Orchha (Tikamgarh) who built the Jānakī Mandir at Janakpur, completed in 1910.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bāḷājī Bājīrāv (Nānāsāheb Peshwa)
summary: Peshwa of the Marāṭhā state (r. 1740–1761) who built the present Tryambakeśvara temple.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Pāṇḍya dynasty
summary: Tamil dynasty centred on Madurai, attested from the early historic period and powerful again in the 7th–10th and 13th centuries; patrons of rock-cut and structural temples in southern Tamil Nadu.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Nāyakas of Madurai
summary: Telugu-speaking governors of Vijayanagara who became independent rulers of Madurai (c. 1529–1736) and rebuilt the Mīnākṣī temple on a monumental scale.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Hoysaḷa dynasty
summary: Karnataka dynasty (c. 10th–14th c.) whose capitals Belur and Dvārasamudra (Halebidu) gave their name to the ornate Hoysaḷa temple style.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kākatīya dynasty
summary: Telugu dynasty ruling from Warangal (c. 1163–1323), patrons of the Rāmappa and Thousand Pillar temples.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) dynasty of Gujarat
summary: Dynasty ruling Gujarat from Aṇahilapāṭaka (c. 940–1244), patrons of the Māru-Gurjara temple style including Modhera and the medieval Somanātha.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Paramāra dynasty
summary: Dynasty of Mālava (c. 9th–14th c.) ruling from Dhārā, best known for King Bhoja.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kārkoṭa dynasty
summary: Dynasty of Kashmir (c. 625–855) whose greatest king, Lalitāditya, is credited with the Mārtaṇḍa temple.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Koch kingdom
summary: Kingdom in western Assam and northern Bengal founded by Viśva Siṃha in the early 16th century; it rebuilt the Kāmākhyā temple in 1565.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Somavaṃśī dynasty of Odisha
summary: Dynasty of Dakṣiṇa Kosala and Odisha (c. 9th–12th c.) credited with early Bhubaneswar temples including the Mukteśvara and Liṅgarāja.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Holkar state of Indore
summary: Marāṭhā ruling house of Indore (18th c. – 1948), best known for Ahilyābāī Holkar’s temple patronage.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Malla dynasty of Nepal
summary: Rulers of the Kathmandu Valley (c. 1200–1769) under whom much of the valley’s surviving temple architecture was built or rebuilt.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Champa
summary: Cham kingdoms of central and southern Vietnam (c. 2nd–17th c.) whose royal sanctuary at Mỹ Sơn was dedicated to Śiva Bhadreśvara.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Kingdom of Travancore
summary: Kerala kingdom (1729–1949) whose rulers styled themselves servants of Padmanābha (Padmanābhadāsa).

type:LABEL: polity
name: Śilāhāra dynasty (northern Konkan)
summary: Dynasty of the northern Konkan (c. 800–1265) during whose rule the Ambarnath Śiva temple was built.

type:LABEL: polity
name: Pāṇḍuvaṃśīs of Dakṣiṇa Kosala
summary: Dynasty ruling from Śrīpura (Sirpur) in Chhattisgarh in the 6th–7th centuries, patrons of the brick Lakṣmaṇa temple.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Divya Deśams (the 108)
summary: The 108 abodes of Viṣṇu sung by the twelve Āḻvār poet-saints in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham; 105 are in India, one in Nepal (Muktinath/Sāḷagrāmam), and two (Tiruppāṟkaṭal, the milk ocean, and Paramapadam) are beyond the earth.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talaṅkaḷ (the 276 Tēvāram shrines)
summary: The Śiva temples (275 or 276, depending on the list) praised in the Tēvāram hymns of the three Nāyaṉmār Appar, Campantar (Sambandar) and Cuntarar (Sundarar), 7th–9th c.; most are in the Kāvēri delta, with a few in Sri Lanka, northern India and the Himalaya.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Char Dham (the four dhāmas)
summary: Four pilgrimage “abodes” at the corners of India — Badrinath (north), Dwarka (west), Puri (east) and Rameswaram (south) — associated in tradition with Ādi Śaṅkara.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Chota Char Dham (Uttarakhand)
summary: Circuit of four Himalayan shrines in Garhwal — Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath — that became a mass pilgrimage after road access in the second half of the 20th century.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pañca Bhūta Sthalas (five element liṅgas)
summary: Five South Indian Śiva temples each identified with one of the five elements: earth (Kanchipuram Ekāmbareśvara), water (Tiruvanaikaval Jambukeśvara), fire (Tiruvannamalai Aruṇācaleśvara), air (Srikalahasti) and space/ether (Chidambaram).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Āṟupaṭai Vīṭu (six abodes of Murukaṉ)
summary: Six Tamil Nadu shrines of Murukaṉ — Tirupparankundram, Tiruchendur, Palani, Swamimalai, Tiruttani and Pazhamudircholai — traditionally identified with the places named in Nakkīrar’s Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, a guide-poem of the Pattuppāṭṭu.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Rival identifications of jyotirliṅga sites
summary: The question of which modern temple corresponds to several of the twelve jyotirliṅgas named in the Śiva Purāṇa list, where the text gives only a region or an ambiguous name: Vaidyanātha, Nāgeśa, Bhīmaśaṅkara and Oṃkāra/Amaleśvara.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Sāṅkhya
subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
summary: The dualist school that analyses reality into conscious, plural selves (puruṣa) and one unconscious, productive nature (prakṛti) made of three guṇas, which unfolds into twenty-three further principles (tattvas); liberation (kaivalya) comes from discriminating knowledge of the two.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Yoga (Pātañjala darśana)
subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
summary: The darśana founded on Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra, which shares Sāṅkhya’s metaphysics of puruṣa and prakṛti but adds a special self called Īśvara and teaches the stilling of mental fluctuations through the eightfold discipline, culminating in samādhi and kaivalya.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Nyāya
subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
summary: The school of logic and epistemology based on the Nyāya Sūtra of Gautama (Akṣapāda), which recognises four means of valid knowledge (perception, inference, comparison and testimony), develops a theory of debate and of the five-membered inference, and holds that knowledge of the sixteen topics leads to liberation (apavarga).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Navya-Nyāya
summary: The “new” Nyāya inaugurated by Gaṅgeśa’s Tattvacintāmaṇi (14th c.), organised around the four means of knowledge and developing a precise technical language of relations, limitors (avacchedaka) and absences, later centred at Mithilā and Navadvīpa (Raghunātha Śiromaṇi).

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vaiśeṣika
subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
summary: The realist school of natural philosophy based on Kaṇāda’s Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, which classifies everything that exists into categories (padārthas) — substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity and inherence — and holds that eternal atoms combine to form the material world.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Pūrva Mīmāṃsā
subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
summary: The school of Vedic exegesis founded on Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, which defines dharma as what is known through Vedic injunction (codanā), treats the Veda as authorless and intrinsically valid, and develops rules for interpreting ritual texts that shaped Indian law and hermeneutics.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā
summary: The line of Mīmāṃsā following Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (7th c.), which accepts six means of knowledge (adding postulation and non-apprehension) and teaches the intrinsic validity of cognition; continued by Maṇḍana Miśra, Pārthasārathi Miśra and Khaṇḍadeva.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā
summary: The line of Mīmāṃsā following Prabhākara (6th–7th c.), called the “teacher’s view” (gurumata), which accepts five means of knowledge (rejecting non-apprehension as separate) and explains error as non-apprehension (akhyāti); its main later author is Śālikanātha Miśra.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vedānta
subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
summary: The family of schools that interpret the Upaniṣads (the “end of the Veda”), the Brahma Sūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā — the prasthānatrayī — to explain brahman, the self and liberation; its sub-schools (Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Bhedābheda, Dvaitādvaita, Śuddhādvaita, Acintya-bhedābheda) disagree chiefly on how brahman, selves and the world are related.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Bhedābheda Vedānta
summary: The Vedānta view that the self and the world are both different and not different from brahman, held before and after Śaṅkara by Bhartṛprapañca, Bhāskara (8th–9th c.) and Yādavaprakāśa; Nimbārka’s Dvaitādvaita and Caitanya’s Acintya-bhedābheda are later forms.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Viśiṣṭādvaita
summary: The Vedānta of Rāmānuja and the Śrīvaiṣṇava ācāryas, for which brahman is the personal Viṣṇu–Nārāyaṇa possessed of infinite auspicious qualities, and conscious selves and matter are real, eternally distinct modes that form his “body” (śarīra), inseparable from him as qualities from a substance.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Dvaita Vedānta
summary: The realist Vedānta of Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), called Tattvavāda by its followers, which teaches that Viṣṇu alone is independent (svatantra) and that five differences — God/self, God/matter, self/self, self/matter, matter/matter — are real and eternal; liberation is by Viṣṇu’s grace and selves retain graded differences even in release.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Dvaitādvaita (Nimbārka sampradāya)
summary: The Vedānta of Nimbārka and his commentator Śrīnivāsa, a form of bhedābheda in which selves and world are naturally (svābhāvika) both different from and identical with brahman, worshipped as Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Śuddhādvaita
summary: The Vedānta of Vallabha (1479–1531), the doctrinal basis of the Puṣṭimārga: brahman, identified with Kṛṣṇa, becomes the world without undergoing change (avikṛta-pariṇāma), so the world is real and “pure” of māyā; grace (puṣṭi) and devotion are the means.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Acintya-bhedābheda
summary: The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava Vedānta systematised by Jīva Gosvāmī, holding that Kṛṣṇa’s energies (śakti) — internal, external and marginal (the selves) — are simultaneously one with and different from him in a way that is “inconceivable”, i.e. beyond ordinary reasoning yet established by scripture.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Lokāyata (Cārvāka)
summary: The materialist school, known chiefly through its opponents, that accepts perception as the only reliable means of knowledge, denies a self surviving the body, rebirth and the authority of the Veda; its own Bṛhaspati-sūtra survives only in fragments.

type:LABEL: person
name: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the classical summary of Sāṅkhya in about seventy āryā verses; he names himself in SK 71 as receiving the doctrine through a succession of pupils from Kapila, Āsuri and Pañcaśikha.

type:LABEL: person
name: Āsuri
summary: The pupil to whom “the sage” (identified by commentators with Kapila) first taught Sāṅkhya, and who passed it to Pañcaśikha, according to Sāṃkhyakārikā 70 and a quotation in the Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 1.25).

type:LABEL: person
name: Pañcaśikha
summary: An early Sāṅkhya teacher, pupil of Āsuri in the lineage given by Sāṃkhyakārikā 70, said there to have expanded the doctrine; later tradition ascribes to him quotations found in the Yoga Bhāṣya, and he appears as a teacher in the Mahābhārata’s Mokṣadharma.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vijñānabhikṣu
summary: Sixteenth-century scholar who commented on the Sāṃkhyasūtra (Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya), the Yoga Bhāṣya (Yogavārttika) and the Brahma Sūtra (Vijñānāmṛtabhāṣya), arguing that Sāṅkhya, Yoga and a bhedābheda Vedānta agree and that Kapila admitted God.

type:LABEL: person
name: Patañjali (author of the Yoga Sūtra)
summary: The author named in the colophons of the Pātañjalayogaśāstra; tradition often identifies him with the grammarian Patañjali, but most scholars keep the two apart. Maas argues he composed both sūtras and Bhāṣya c. 325–425 CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vyāsa (author of the Yoga Bhāṣya)
aliases: Bhāṣyakāra of the Yoga Sūtra|Vedavyāsa (in tradition)
summary: The name under which tradition transmits the oldest commentary on the Yoga Sūtra (“vyāsabhāṣya” in the colophons); later authors identify him with the epic Vyāsa, while Maas argues the Bhāṣya is Patañjali’s own.

type:LABEL: person
name: Svātmārāma
summary: Compiler of the Haṭhayogapradīpikā (c. 15th c.), the best-known manual of haṭhayoga, which presents haṭha practices as a ladder to rājayoga.

type:LABEL: person
name: Akṣapāda Gautama
summary: The figure to whom the Nyāya Sūtra is ascribed; nothing is known of his life, and the text he is credited with is composite, reaching its final form around the early centuries CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vātsyāyana Pakṣilasvāmin
summary: Author of the Nyāyabhāṣya, the earliest surviving commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra; distinct from Vātsyāyana Mallanāga of the Kāmasūtra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Uddyotakara
summary: Author of the Nyāyavārttika, a sub-commentary defending Vātsyāyana’s Nyāya against the Buddhist logician Dignāga.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vācaspati Miśra
summary: Scholar of Mithilā who wrote standard commentaries on almost every school: the Bhāmatī on Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra commentary, the Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, the Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī, the Tattvavaiśāradī on the Yoga Bhāṣya and works on Mīmāṃsā.

type:LABEL: person
name: Udayana
summary: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosopher of Mithilā, author of the Nyāyakusumāñjali (the classic Nyāya proof of Īśvara), the Ātmatattvaviveka against Buddhism, and the Kiraṇāvalī on Praśastapāda; Gaṅgeśa calls him simply “the Teacher”.

type:LABEL: person
name: Gaṅgeśa
summary: Logician of Mithilā whose Tattvacintāmaṇi, arranged under the four means of knowledge, founded Navya-Nyāya.

type:LABEL: person
name: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi
summary: Navadvīpa logician whose Dīdhiti on the Tattvacintāmaṇi and Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa (revising the Vaiśeṣika categories) made Bengal the centre of Navya-Nyāya.

type:LABEL: person
name: Annaṃbhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tarkasaṃgraha with his own Dīpikā, the standard primer of the combined Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, which opens by listing seven categories including absence.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kaṇāda
summary: The sage to whom the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra is ascribed; Praśastapāda praises “the sage Kaṇāda” in his opening verse. His dates are unknown.
earliest_textual: c. second half of the 6th c. CE

type:LABEL: person
name: Praśastapāda
summary: Author of the Padārthadharmasaṃgraha, the systematic restatement of Vaiśeṣika that fixed its six categories and twenty-four qualities and opened with homage to Īśvara as cause.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jaimini
summary: The teacher to whom the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra is ascribed; the Brahma Sūtra cites “Jaimini” for views on ritual and on the gods (e.g. BS 1.2.28, 1.3.31, 3.4.2), while the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra cites Bādarāyaṇa (MS 1.1.5).

type:LABEL: person
name: Śabarasvāmin
summary: Author of the Śābarabhāṣya, the oldest surviving commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, which embeds an older commentator’s (the Vṛttikāra’s) views and became the base for Kumārila and Prabhākara.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa
summary: Mīmāṃsā philosopher whose Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika and Ṭupṭīkā on Śabara founded the Bhāṭṭa school; he defended the authorless Veda and the intrinsic validity of cognition against Buddhist and other critics.

type:LABEL: person
name: Prabhākara
summary: Mīmāṃsā commentator, author of the Bṛhatī and Laghvī on Śabara, founder of the Prābhākara (“Guru”) school; tradition makes him Kumārila’s pupil, which modern scholars doubt.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śālikanātha Miśra
summary: The principal later Prābhākara author, whose Prakaraṇapañcikā sets out the school’s doctrines and whose Ṛjuvimalā comments on Prabhākara’s Bṛhatī.

type:LABEL: person
name: Pārthasārathi Miśra
summary: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsaka, author of the Śāstradīpikā on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra and the Nyāyaratnākara on Kumārila’s Ślokavārttika.

type:LABEL: person
name: Maṇḍana Miśra
summary: Mīmāṃsā and Advaita author of the Vidhiviveka, Bhāvanāviveka, Vibhramaviveka and the Brahmasiddhi; until the 10th c. his Brahmasiddhi was the most authoritative Advaita treatise besides Śaṅkara’s works, and Vācaspati’s Bhāmatī follows him.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bādarāyaṇa
summary: The teacher to whom the Brahma Sūtra is ascribed; the Sūtra names him in the third person (e.g. BS 1.3.26; 3.4.1; 4.4.7) and the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra cites him (MS 1.1.5). Later tradition identifies him with Vyāsa.

type:LABEL: person
name: Gauḍapāda
summary: Author of the Āgamaśāstra (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā), the earliest surviving systematic Advaita work, which teaches non-origination (ajātivāda) — “no self is born” — and calls duality mere māyā; tradition makes him the teacher of Śaṅkara’s teacher Govinda.

type:LABEL: person
name: Govinda Bhagavatpāda
summary: The teacher of Śaṅkara according to Advaita tradition and the colophons of Śaṅkara’s works (“pupil of the revered Govinda”), himself a pupil of Gauḍapāda; no works of his survive.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sureśvara
summary: Direct pupil of Śaṅkara, author of the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi and of vast verse sub-commentaries (vārttikas) on Śaṅkara’s Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Taittirīya commentaries; hagiography identifies him with Maṇḍana Miśra.

type:LABEL: person
name: Padmapāda
summary: Direct pupil of Śaṅkara whose Pañcapādikā (on the opening of Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra commentary) became, through Prakāśātman’s Vivaraṇa, the basis of the Vivaraṇa school of Advaita.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vidyāraṇya
summary: Advaita author of the Pañcadaśī and Jīvanmuktiviveka, head of the Śṛṅgeri maṭha in the later 14th c. and associated with the founding of Vijayanagara; his identity with Mādhava, brother of Sāyaṇa and author of the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, is traditional and debated.

type:LABEL: person
name: Sadānanda Yogīndra
summary: Author of the Vedāntasāra, a short manual of Advaita (late 15th c.) that became the standard introduction, teaching superimposition (adhyāropa) and its retraction (apavāda) and the fourfold qualification of the student.

type:LABEL: person
name: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī
summary: Bengali Advaitin of Vārāṇasī, author of the Advaitasiddhi (a reply to Vyāsatīrtha’s Nyāyāmṛta), the Siddhāntabindu, the Gūḍhārthadīpikā on the Gītā and the Bhaktirasāyana, which combines Advaita with Kṛṣṇa devotion.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhāskara (Vedāntin)
summary: Bhedābheda Vedāntin whose Brahma Sūtra commentary criticises Śaṅkara and argues that brahman really transforms into the world; distinct from the astronomers Bhāskara I and II.

type:LABEL: person
name: Yāmuna
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher at Srirangam, grandson of Nāthamuni, whose Siddhitraya, Āgamaprāmāṇya and Gītārthasaṃgraha prepared Rāmānuja’s Viśiṣṭādvaita; Rāmānuja salutes him at the opening of the Vedārthasaṃgraha and the Gītābhāṣya.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vedānta Deśika
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava polymath of Kāñcī (1268–1369) who systematised Viśiṣṭādvaita (Tattvamuktākalāpa, Nyāyapariśuddhi, Śatadūṣaṇī, Rahasyatrayasāra) and is revered as the founding authority of the Vaṭakalai branch.

type:LABEL: person
name: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha)
summary: Founder of Dvaita (Tattvavāda) Vedānta, from the Tuḷu country near Udupi, who commented on the Brahma Sūtra (Bhāṣya and Anuvyākhyāna), the Upaniṣads and the Gītā and wrote the Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya, teaching the reality of five differences and Viṣṇu’s supremacy.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jayatīrtha
summary: The “commentator” (ṭīkācārya) of Dvaita, whose Nyāyasudhā on Madhva’s Anuvyākhyāna and Pramāṇapaddhati gave the school its dialectical foundations.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vyāsatīrtha
summary: Dvaita dialectician and rājaguru at the Vijayanagara court under Kṛṣṇadevarāya, author of the Nyāyāmṛta (against Advaita), Tarkatāṇḍava (against Nyāya) and Tātparyacandrikā; patron and teacher of the Haridāsa poets Purandaradāsa and Kanakadāsa.

type:LABEL: person
name: Nimbārka
summary: Founder of Dvaitādvaita Vedānta, author of the Vedāntapārijātasaurabha (a brief Brahma Sūtra commentary) and the Daśaślokī; his date is among the most disputed in Vedānta, from the 7th to the 13th c. CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Śrīnivāsa (Nimbārka school)
summary: Pupil of Nimbārka according to the sampradāya, author of the Vedāntakaustubha, the fuller commentary on the Brahma Sūtra that expounds Nimbārka’s Vedāntapārijātasaurabha.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vallabha (Vallabhācārya)
summary: Telugu brahmin teacher who founded the Puṣṭimārga (“path of grace”) devoted to the child Kṛṣṇa as Śrīnāthjī of Govardhana and its Śuddhādvaita Vedānta; author of the Aṇubhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra, the Subodhinī on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and the Ṣoḍaśagrantha.

type:LABEL: person
name: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
summary: Eighteenth-century Gauḍīya scholar at Jaipur who wrote the Govinda-bhāṣya, the school’s Brahma Sūtra commentary, and commentaries on Jīva’s Sandarbhas, and presented the Gauḍīyas as heirs of Madhva’s lineage.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bhartṛhari
summary: Grammarian-philosopher (5th c.) whose Vākyapadīya teaches that the meaning-bearing word (sphoṭa) is an indivisible whole and that brahman is of the nature of the Word (śabdabrahman).

type:LABEL: person
name: Kauṭilya
summary: The author named in the Arthaśāstra; tradition identifies him with Cāṇakya, minister of Candragupta Maurya (4th c. BCE), while Olivelle and McClish date the surviving text to the 1st–3rd c. CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Vijñāneśvara
summary: Jurist at the court of the Cālukya king Vikramāditya VI of Kalyāṇi, author of the Mitākṣarā on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti, whose doctrine of ownership by birth governed Hindu inheritance in most of India under colonial courts.

type:LABEL: person
name: Jīmūtavāhana
summary: Bengali jurist, author of the Dāyabhāga (part of his Dharmaratna), whose rule that heirs acquire ownership only on the death of the owner governed inheritance in Bengal.

type:LABEL: person
name: Medhātithi
summary: The oldest surviving commentator on the Manusmṛti (Manubhāṣya), probably Kashmirian, cited as an authority by the Mitākṣarā.

type:LABEL: person
name: Piṅgala
summary: Author of the Chandaḥśāstra (Chandaḥsūtra), the Vedāṅga text on metre, whose procedures for enumerating metres (prastāra) use a binary representation of light and heavy syllables.

type:LABEL: person
name: Lagadha
summary: The authority whose “knowledge of time” the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa says it sets out (verse 2: kālajñānaṃ pravakṣyāmi lagadhasya mahātmanaḥ).

type:LABEL: person
name: Āpastamba
summary: Eponymous teacher of a Taittirīya (Black Yajurveda) school whose complete Kalpa Sūtra survives — Śrauta, Gṛhya, Dharma and Śulba Sūtras; Olivelle notes the works may have been composed within the school rather than by one person.

type:LABEL: person
name: Baudhāyana
summary: Eponymous teacher of the oldest Taittirīya ritual school, to whom Śrauta, Gṛhya, Dharma and Śulba Sūtras are ascribed; the Baudhāyana Śulba Sūtra states the relation of the sides and diagonal of a rectangle.

type:LABEL: person
name: Āśvalāyana
summary: Ṛgvedic ritual authority to whom the Āśvalāyana Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras are ascribed; the Kaivalya Upaniṣad opens with an Āśvalāyana asking Brahmā for the highest knowledge.

type:LABEL: person
name: Kātyāyana
summary: Name of the author of the Vārttikas on Pāṇini (3rd c. BCE) and of the Śukla Yajurveda’s Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra and Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhya; whether these are one person is uncertain.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sāṃkhyakārikā
summary: Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s summary of Sāṅkhya in about seventy āryā verses — the oldest surviving systematic Sāṅkhya text — covering suffering and its removal, the three means of knowledge, the twenty-five principles, the guṇas, the plurality of selves and liberation by discrimination.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yuktidīpikā
summary: An anonymous, detailed commentary on the Sāṃkhyakārikā, rediscovered in the 20th c., that preserves otherwise lost views of early Sāṅkhya teachers.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī
summary: Vācaspati Miśra’s concise commentary on the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the most widely studied Sāṅkhya commentary in traditional teaching.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sāṃkhyasūtra
summary: A collection of Sāṅkhya aphorisms ascribed by tradition to Kapila but generally dated to the late medieval period (c. 14th–15th c.), known chiefly through Vijñānabhikṣu’s Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tattvasamāsa
summary: A very short list of Sāṅkhya topics (“eight prakṛtis, sixteen modifications, the puruṣa, the three guṇas …”) ascribed to Kapila, of uncertain but probably late date.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya
summary: Vijñānabhikṣu’s commentary on the Sāṃkhyasūtra (16th c.), which reads Sāṅkhya as compatible with theism and with Vedānta.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
summary: The root text of the Yoga darśana: 195 aphorisms in four chapters (samādhi, sādhana, vibhūti, kaivalya) defining yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind (YS 1.2), teaching the eight limbs (2.29) and ending with kaivalya, the isolation of pure consciousness (4.34).

type:LABEL: text
name: Yoga Bhāṣya (Vyāsabhāṣya)
summary: The oldest commentary on the Yoga Sūtra, transmitted under the name of Vyāsa; it glosses YS 1.1 by stating that “yoga is samādhi” and supplies much of classical Yoga’s doctrine.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tattvavaiśāradī
summary: Vācaspati Miśra’s sub-commentary on the Yoga Bhāṣya, printed with it in Āgāśe’s edition and translated by Woods (1914).

type:LABEL: text
name: Rājamārtaṇḍa
summary: King Bhoja of Dhārā’s brief commentary on the Yoga Sūtra (11th c.), also included in Āgāśe’s 1904 edition.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yogavārttika
summary: Vijñānabhikṣu’s sub-commentary on the Yoga Bhāṣya (16th c.).

type:LABEL: text
name: Haṭhayogapradīpikā
summary: Svātmārāma’s 15th-century compilation of haṭhayoga teachings — postures, breath control, seals (mudrā) and inner sound — which presents haṭha as a means to rājayoga.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nyāya Sūtra
summary: The root text of Nyāya, in five books, which opens by promising liberation from knowledge of sixteen topics — means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, doubt, debate and its faults — and defines the four means of knowledge (NS 1.1.3).

type:LABEL: text
name: Nyāyabhāṣya
summary: Vātsyāyana’s commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra (c. 5th c.), the earliest surviving and the base of all later Nyāya exegesis.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nyāyavārttika
