summary: Uddyotakara’s sub-commentary on the Nyāyabhāṣya (6th–7th c.), written to defend Nyāya against Dignāga’s Buddhist logic.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā
summary: Vācaspati Miśra’s commentary on Uddyotakara’s Nyāyavārttika.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nyāyakusumāñjali
summary: Udayana’s “handful of flowers of reasoning”, the classical Nyāya argument for the existence of Īśvara as creator and author of the Veda, against Mīmāṃsā, Buddhist and Cārvāka objections.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tattvacintāmaṇi
summary: Gaṅgeśa’s “Jewel of Reflection on Reality” (14th c.), in four books on perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony, the founding text of Navya-Nyāya and the object of a vast commentarial literature.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tarkasaṃgraha
summary: Annaṃbhaṭṭa’s primer of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika (17th c.), written “for the easy understanding of beginners”, which lists seven categories including absence (abhāva).

type:LABEL: text
name: Vaiśeṣika Sūtra
summary: The root text of Vaiśeṣika, ascribed to Kaṇāda, which opens “Now we shall explain dharma”, defines dharma as that from which prosperity and the highest good arise, and enumerates nine substances, seventeen qualities and five kinds of motion.

type:LABEL: text
name: Padārthadharmasaṃgraha
summary: Praśastapāda’s systematic exposition of Vaiśeṣika (6th c.), which opens by saluting Īśvara the cause and the sage Kaṇāda, lists six categories (substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence) and counts twenty-four qualities.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mīmāṃsā Sūtra
summary: Jaimini’s sūtras in twelve books, the longest of the darśana root texts, which open “Now, therefore, the inquiry into dharma” and define dharma as a purpose known by Vedic injunction (MS 1.1.2); the bulk sets out rules for interpreting and applying ritual texts.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śābarabhāṣya
summary: Śabarasvāmin’s commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, the oldest surviving and the common base of the Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara schools; it argues that dharma, lying in the future, cannot be known by perception or inference but only through the Veda.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ślokavārttika
summary: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa’s verse exposition of Śabara’s commentary on MS 1.1, a major work of Indian epistemology covering perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation, absence, the self and the authorless Veda, with refutations of Buddhist idealism.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tantravārttika
summary: Kumārila’s prose sub-commentary on Śabara for MS 1.2–3.8, important for its treatment of the authority of smṛti and custom.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bṛhatī
summary: Prabhākara’s large commentary on the Śābarabhāṣya, the root text of the Prābhākara school.

type:LABEL: text
name: Prakaraṇapañcikā
summary: Śālikanātha Miśra’s independent exposition of Prābhākara doctrine in topical chapters (prakaraṇas).

type:LABEL: text
name: Śāstradīpikā
summary: Pārthasārathi Miśra’s Bhāṭṭa commentary on the whole Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, a standard reference for the school.

type:LABEL: text
name: Brahmasiddhi
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra’s Advaita treatise in four chapters (brahman, reasoning, injunction, success), which locates ignorance in individual selves and admits a role for meditation and action; edited by Kuppuswami Sastri in 1937.

type:LABEL: text
name: Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Āgamaśāstra)
summary: Gauḍapāda’s verses in four chapters (āgama, vaitathya, advaita, alātaśānti) on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, the earliest surviving Advaita treatise, teaching that duality is mere māyā (1.17) and that “no self is ever born” (3.48).

type:LABEL: text
name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra
summary: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the foundational work of Advaita Vedānta, which reads the sūtras as teaching one brahman known only from the Upaniṣads and treats the world of plurality as the product of ignorance (avidyā).

type:LABEL: text
name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā
summary: The oldest surviving commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, generally accepted as Śaṅkara’s, which reads the Gītā as teaching liberation by knowledge, with action as preparatory purification.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad
summary: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentary the most securely authentic of his Upaniṣad commentaries; Sureśvara wrote a verse vārttika on it.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad
summary: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, accepted as authentic by Hacker and Mayeda; it reads “tat tvam asi” (CU 6.8.7) as identity of self and brahman.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad
summary: Commentary on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad ascribed to Śaṅkara and accepted as authentic by Hacker and Mayeda.

type:LABEL: text
name: Commentary on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and Kārikā ascribed to Śaṅkara
summary: The commentary on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad together with Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā transmitted under Śaṅkara’s name; its authenticity is questioned more than that of his other Upaniṣad commentaries.

type:LABEL: text
name: Upadeśasāhasrī
summary: The only independent (non-commentarial) work almost universally accepted as Śaṅkara’s, in a prose part on how to teach and a verse part of nineteen chapters; critically edited and translated by Sengaku Mayeda.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vivekacūḍāmaṇi
summary: A popular Advaita verse manual on discrimination (viveka) and liberation, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara; most scholars regard it as a later work (see `claim:vivekachudamani-authorship`).

type:LABEL: text
name: Naiṣkarmyasiddhi
summary: Sureśvara’s treatise arguing that liberation is attained by knowledge alone, not by action combined with knowledge.

type:LABEL: text
name: Pañcapādikā
summary: Padmapāda’s sub-commentary on the opening of Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra commentary (the superimposition preamble and the first four sūtras), the root of the Vivaraṇa school.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhāmatī
summary: Vācaspati Miśra’s sub-commentary on Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra commentary, which follows Maṇḍana Miśra and gave its name to the Bhāmatī school of Advaita (ignorance located in individual selves).

type:LABEL: text
name: Pañcadaśī
summary: A popular Advaita manual in fifteen chapters on discrimination, illumination and bliss, ascribed to Vidyāraṇya (14th c.), with some chapters attributed by tradition to Bhāratītīrtha.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jīvanmuktiviveka
summary: Vidyāraṇya’s treatise on liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which joins Advaita with yogic practice and renunciation; studied by Andrew Fort.

type:LABEL: text
name: Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha
summary: A 14th-century survey of sixteen systems, from Cārvāka through Buddhism, Jainism, the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva schools, grammar and the darśanas, ascribed to Mādhava of Vijayanagara and ordered to lead toward Advaita (which it does not itself expound).

type:LABEL: text
name: Vedāntasāra
summary: Sadānanda’s short manual of Advaita (c. late 15th c.), long the usual introduction to the system, covering the qualified student, superimposition and its retraction, and the mahāvākyas.

type:LABEL: text
name: Siddhāntabindu
summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī’s commentary on the Daśaślokī ascribed to Śaṅkara, edited by P. C. Divanji (1933).

type:LABEL: text
name: Advaitasiddhi
summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī’s point-by-point defence of Advaita against Vyāsatīrtha’s Nyāyāmṛta, which provoked further Mādhva replies (Taraṅgiṇī) and Advaita counter-replies.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aṣṭāvakra Gītā
summary: An anonymous Advaita dialogue between the sage Aṣṭāvakra and king Janaka on the self as pure witness; its date is unknown and probably late (scholarly guesses run from the 8th to the 14th c.).

type:LABEL: text
name: Bhāskara’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra
summary: Bhāskara’s bhedābheda commentary on the Brahma Sūtra (8th–9th c.), which attacks Śaṅkara’s doctrine of illusion and holds brahman’s transformation into the world to be real.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śrībhāṣya
summary: Rāmānuja’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the authoritative statement of Viśiṣṭādvaita, whose long treatment of BS 1.1.1 (the mahāsiddhānta) refutes Advaita’s doctrines of attributeless brahman and of ignorance in seven “untenabilities”.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vedārthasaṃgraha
summary: Rāmānuja’s “Summary of the meaning of the Veda”, an independent treatise that states Viśiṣṭādvaita against Advaita and Bhedābheda, opening with a salute to Yāmuna and teaching that brahman has the whole conscious and unconscious world as its body.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rāmānuja’s commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā
summary: Rāmānuja’s Gītā commentary, which opens with homage to Yāmuna and a long description of Viṣṇu as “husband of Śrī”, and reads the Gītā as teaching devotion (bhakti) as the means to the Lord.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gītārthasaṃgraha
summary: Yāmuna’s summary of the Bhagavad Gītā in 32 verses, which Rāmānuja follows in his Gītā commentary.

type:LABEL: text
name: Siddhitraya
summary: Yāmuna’s three “proofs” — Ātmasiddhi, Īśvarasiddhi and Saṃvitsiddhi — on the self, God and consciousness, foundational for Viśiṣṭādvaita.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tattvamuktākalāpa
summary: Vedānta Deśika’s verse treatise on Viśiṣṭādvaita ontology (substance, non-substance) with his own commentary Sarvārthasiddhi.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nyāyapariśuddhi
summary: Vedānta Deśika’s treatise on epistemology and logic from the Viśiṣṭādvaita standpoint, recasting Nyāya for Śrīvaiṣṇava use.

type:LABEL: text
name: Madhva’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra
summary: Madhva’s short commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, which reads brahman as Viṣṇu, the independent reality, and the sūtras as establishing real difference between God, selves and matter.

type:LABEL: text
name: Anuvyākhyāna
summary: Madhva’s verse commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, supplementing his Bhāṣya; it opens by saluting Nārāyaṇa “whose sole body is the fullness of all qualities” and lists the five differences.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya
summary: Madhva’s verse work “Determining the purport of the Mahābhārata”, which retells the epic and the Rāmāyaṇa as teaching Viṣṇu’s supremacy and states the five real differences in its first chapter.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nyāyasudhā
summary: Jayatīrtha’s massive commentary on Madhva’s Anuvyākhyāna, the dialectical centre of Dvaita scholarship.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nyāyāmṛta
summary: Vyāsatīrtha’s systematic refutation of Advaita (early 16th c.), answered by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī’s Advaitasiddhi.

type:LABEL: text
name: Tarkatāṇḍava
summary: Vyāsatīrtha’s “Dance of Logic”, a critique of Nyāya and Navya-Nyāya positions from the Dvaita standpoint.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vedāntapārijātasaurabha
summary: Nimbārka’s brief commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the root text of Dvaitādvaita; Ramnarace notes that its style resembles pre-Śaṅkara commentaries.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vedāntakaustubha
summary: Śrīnivāsa’s fuller Brahma Sūtra commentary expounding Nimbārka’s Vedāntapārijātasaurabha; translated with it by Roma Bose.

type:LABEL: text
name: Daśaślokī (Nimbārka)
summary: Nimbārka’s ten verses summarising Dvaitādvaita doctrine; not to be confused with the Daśaślokī ascribed to Śaṅkara.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aṇubhāṣya
summary: Vallabha’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the root text of Śuddhādvaita, completed by his son Viṭṭhalanātha.

type:LABEL: text
name: Subodhinī
summary: Vallabha’s commentary on parts of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, central to Puṣṭimārga theology.

type:LABEL: text
name: Govinda-bhāṣya
summary: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa’s Brahma Sūtra commentary (18th c.), written at Jaipur to give the Gauḍīyas a commentary on the third foundation text of Vedānta.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vākyapadīya
summary: Bhartṛhari’s treatise in three books on sentence and word, which opens by identifying brahman with the Word (śabdatattva) and teaches the indivisible sphoṭa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Arthaśāstra
summary: The treatise on government ascribed to Kauṭilya; its account of the sciences (1.2.10) is the earliest dated list naming sāṃkhya, yoga and lokāyata as forms of ānvīkṣikī, “the lamp of all sciences”.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya
summary: The Jain author Haribhadra’s “Compendium of the six views” (8th c.), one of the earliest doxographies; its six are the Buddhist, Naiyāyika, Sāṅkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika and Jaiminīya (Mīmāṃsā) systems — not the later “six orthodox schools”.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śikṣā and Prātiśākhyas
summary: The phonetic limb of the Veda: the Prātiśākhyas, each tied to the text of one Vedic school, which describe sounds, accents and the sandhi rules that convert the word-by-word recitation (padapāṭha) into the continuous text, and later manuals titled Śikṣā (e.g. the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Vyākaraṇa (grammar)
summary: The grammatical limb of the Veda, whose central tradition is the Pāṇinian: Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, Kātyāyana’s Vārttikas and Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya (the “three sages”), continued by Bhartṛhari’s philosophy of language.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Chandas (metrics)
summary: The metrical limb of the Veda, represented by Piṅgala’s Chandaḥśāstra, which covers Vedic and classical metres and devises combinatorial procedures for listing them.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Jyotiṣa (calendar and astronomy)
summary: The limb of the Veda that fixes the times of sacrifice, represented in its Vedāṅga form by the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa (Ṛk and Yajus recensions); later Jyotiḥśāstra grew into mathematical astronomy and astrology.

type:LABEL: text
name: Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya
summary: The phonetic manual of the Śākala school of the Ṛgveda, ascribed to Śaunaka, which describes how Śākalya’s word-by-word text (padapāṭha) is turned into the continuous recited text.

type:LABEL: text
name: Taittirīya Prātiśākhya
summary: The phonetic manual of the Taittirīya school (Black Yajurveda), notable for its detailed articulatory phonetics.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhya
summary: The phonetic manual of the Vājasaneyi (White Yajurveda) school, ascribed to Kātyāyana.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śaunakīyā Caturādhyāyikā (Atharvaveda Prātiśākhya)
summary: The Prātiśākhya of the Śaunakīya Atharvaveda in four chapters, edited and translated by Madhav Deshpande (HOS 52, 1997).

type:LABEL: text
name: Pāṇinīya Śikṣā
summary: A short verse manual of phonetics ascribed by tradition to Pāṇini but later than him, describing places and manners of articulation.

type:LABEL: text
name: Chandaḥśāstra of Piṅgala
summary: Piṅgala’s sūtras on metre, the Vedāṅga text on chandas, whose procedures for enumerating metres of light and heavy syllables (prastāra and related operations) have been analysed as a binary system; Halāyudha’s 10th-c. commentary develops them further.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa
summary: The Vedāṅga text on time-reckoning, in Ṛk (35 numbered verses in the GRETIL e-text) and longer Yajus recensions, presenting the “knowledge of time of the great-souled Lagadha”: a five-year yuga of lunar and solar months with the winter solstice at the beginning of the asterism Śraviṣṭhā.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śrauta Sūtras
summary: Manuals of the solemn (śrauta) sacrifices performed with the three fires — new- and full-moon offerings, agnihotra, soma sacrifices, the agnicayana — each belonging to a Vedic school.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Gṛhya Sūtras
summary: Manuals of the domestic rites performed in the household fire, including the life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) from conception to marriage and death.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Dharma Sūtras
summary: Prose manuals of dharma attached to Vedic schools; four survive — Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana and Vasiṣṭha — which Olivelle dates from about the 3rd c. BCE to around the turn of the era, Āpastamba being the oldest.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śulba Sūtras
summary: Manuals for constructing fire altars with the cord (śulba), the earliest Indian geometry, including constructions of squares and rectangles and the relation of a rectangle’s sides to its diagonal; those of Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Mānava and Kātyāyana survive.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra
summary: The śrauta manual of the Āpastamba school of the Taittirīya (Black Yajurveda), part of the only Kalpa Sūtra that survives complete in all four divisions.

type:LABEL: text
name: Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra
summary: The oldest śrauta manual of the Taittirīya tradition, in a discursive, Brāhmaṇa-like prose.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra
summary: The śrauta manual of the White Yajurveda (Vājasaneyin) school, following the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra
summary: The śrauta manual for the Ṛgvedic hotṛ priest of the Āśvalāyana school, in twelve books.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra
summary: The śrauta manual of the Śāṅkhāyana (Kauṣītaki) school of the Ṛgveda, edited by Hillebrandt.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra
summary: The domestic-ritual manual of the Āśvalāyana school of the Ṛgveda, in four books, covering marriage, the rites of childhood, Vedic study and funerals.

type:LABEL: text
name: Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra
summary: The domestic-ritual manual of the White Yajurveda school, widely followed in north India for life-cycle rites.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra
summary: The domestic-ritual manual of the Āpastamba school (Taittirīya), used with its own mantra collection (Mantrapāṭha).

type:LABEL: text
name: Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra
summary: The dharma manual of the Āpastamba school, in two praśnas; it names the agreement of those who know dharma and the Vedas as authorities (1.1.1.2–3) and lists four āśramas — householder, studentship at the teacher’s house, silence (the wandering ascetic) and forest life — as equally valid paths (2.9.21.1).

type:LABEL: text
name: Gautama Dharma Sūtra
summary: An independent Dharma Sūtra associated with the Sāmaveda, which opens “The Veda is the root of dharma” (1.1) and reports that some allow a choice among āśramas while the teachers recognise only the householder’s (3.1, 3.36).

type:LABEL: text
name: Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra
summary: The dharma manual of the Baudhāyana school (Taittirīya), in four praśnas of which Olivelle takes book 1 and most of book 2 as the older core; like Gautama it reports the teachers’ view that there is only one āśrama (2.6.11.27).

type:LABEL: text
name: Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra
summary: The latest of the four surviving Dharma Sūtras, named after the Ṛgvedic sage Vasiṣṭha but composed by unknown authors; it opens with the inquiry into dharma “for the sake of the highest good of man” (1.1).

type:LABEL: text
name: Baudhāyana Śulba Sūtra
summary: The oldest surviving Śulba Sūtra, with constructions for altar bricks and the statement that the diagonal of a rectangle produces both areas produced separately by its two sides.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra
summary: The altar-geometry manual of the Āpastamba school.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yājñavalkya Smṛti
summary: A concise verse Dharmaśāstra in three books — conduct (ācāra), legal procedure (vyavahāra) and expiation (prāyaścitta) — presented as the teaching of Yājñavalkya to sages; later than Manu and more systematic, it became through the Mitākṣarā the basis of Hindu law in most of India.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mitākṣarā
summary: Vijñāneśvara’s commentary on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti (late 11th – early 12th c.), best known for holding that sons acquire ownership of ancestral property by birth; colonial courts applied it as the law of inheritance outside Bengal.

type:LABEL: text
name: Dāyabhāga
summary: Jīmūtavāhana’s treatise on inheritance (12th c.), part of his Dharmaratna, which holds that heirs acquire ownership only when the owner dies (or renounces), so a father may dispose of ancestral property; it governed Hindu inheritance in Bengal.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nārada Smṛti
summary: The only Dharmaśāstra devoted wholly to law and legal procedure (vyavahāra); it opens by explaining that litigation arose when people ceased to be wholly devoted to dharma, and organises law under eighteen titles (mātṛkā 1.19).

type:LABEL: text
name: Parāśara Smṛti
summary: A Dharmaśāstra on conduct and expiation that presents itself as the law for the Kali age: “in the Kṛta age the dharmas of Manu, in the Tretā those of Gautama, in the Dvāpara those of Śaṅkha and Likhita, in the Kali those of Parāśara” (1.24); Mādhava (14th c.) wrote a major commentary on it.

type:LABEL: text
name: Viṣṇu Smṛti
summary: A Dharmaśāstra framed as Viṣṇu’s teaching to the Earth, incorporating an older Dharma Sūtra of the Kaṭha school and reworked with Vaiṣṇava material; Olivelle dates the redaction to about the 7th c. CE.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kātyāyana Smṛti
summary: A lost legal smṛti on procedure and evidence, reconstructed from quotations in later digests (Kane’s reconstruction is the basis of the GRETIL e-text).

type:LABEL: text
name: Manubhāṣya of Medhātithi
summary: Medhātithi’s commentary on the Manusmṛti, the oldest surviving, frequently cited by later jurists; translated by Ganganatha Jha.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Muktikā canon of 108 Upaniṣads
summary: The list of 108 Upaniṣads given in the Muktikā Upaniṣad, where Rāma teaches Hanumān, grouped by Veda and, in modern presentations, into ten principal (mukhya), Sāmānya-Vedānta, Yoga, Saṃnyāsa, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva and Śākta Upaniṣads; it became the standard canon in South India and in modern printed collections.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Yoga Upaniṣads
summary: The twenty Upaniṣads of the Muktikā list that teach yoga — breath, sound (nāda), the syllable Om, postures and, in many, kuṇḍalinī; dates are widely disputed, from Flood’s 100 BCE–300 CE for some to Bouy’s argument that the collection as transmitted in the South was redacted in the 18th c. under the influence of Nātha haṭhayoga.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads
summary: About twenty Upaniṣads on renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the life of the wandering ascetic; Sprockhoff dates a core group (Āruṇi, Kuṇḍikā, Kaṭhaśruti, Paramahaṃsa, Jābāla, Brahma) before the 3rd c. CE, while others are medieval; nearly all have an Advaita orientation, which Olivelle links to Advaita monastic control of their transmission.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣads
summary: Minor Upaniṣads of the Muktikā list that identify brahman with Viṣṇu or his forms — Narasiṃha, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa (Gopāla), Nārāyaṇa — among them the Tāpanīya Upaniṣads; most are medieval.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Śaiva Upaniṣads
summary: Minor Upaniṣads of the Muktikā list that identify brahman with Śiva–Rudra, such as the Atharvaśiras and Kaivalya; most are of the first or early second millennium CE.

type:LABEL: text
name: Muktikā Upaniṣad
summary: A dialogue in which Rāma teaches Hanumān the kinds of liberation and lists 108 Upaniṣads, the basis of the Muktikā canon; its date is late and uncertain.

type:LABEL: text
name: Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad
summary: A late prose Upaniṣad of the Maitrāyaṇī school (Black Yajurveda) in which king Bṛhadratha is taught by Śākāyanya; it presupposes Sāṅkhya and Yoga ideas (guṇas, a sixfold yoga) and is a key witness for their early history.

type:LABEL: text
name: Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad
summary: The tenth book of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, a collection of mantras and prayers (including Nārāyaṇa and Rudra material) used in later worship; edited and translated by Jean Varenne. Its date is uncertain, usually placed after the early prose Upaniṣads.

type:LABEL: text
name: Jābāla Upaniṣad
summary: One of the oldest Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads, attached to the White Yajurveda, which allows renunciation directly from studentship, householdership or forest life and describes the paramahaṃsa ascetic.

type:LABEL: text
name: Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad
summary: A short Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad describing the highest class of renouncer, the paramahaṃsa; Sprockhoff places it in the last centuries BCE or early CE.

type:LABEL: text
name: Āruṇeya (Āruṇi) Upaniṣad
summary: A Sāmavedic Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad in which Prajāpati teaches Āruṇi the renouncer’s life; part of Sprockhoff’s early group.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kaivalya Upaniṣad
summary: An Atharvan Upaniṣad in which Āśvalāyana asks Brahmā (Parameṣṭhin) for the highest knowledge and is taught faith, devotion and meditation on the self identified with Śiva; Deussen praised its description of the realised person.

type:LABEL: text
name: Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad
summary: A Śaiva Upaniṣad in which Rudra declares to the gods “I alone was first, I am and shall be”, and which identifies Rudra with all gods and beings; its “vow of the head” is associated with Pāśupata practice.

type:LABEL: text
name: Garbha Upaniṣad
summary: A short Upaniṣad describing the body as made of five elements and the development of the embryo, closer to a medical text than to speculative Upaniṣads.

type:LABEL: text
name: Brahmabindu Upaniṣad
summary: A short verse Upaniṣad which teaches that “mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings” (verse 2).

type:LABEL: text
name: Nādabindu Upaniṣad
summary: A Yoga Upaniṣad describing the syllable Om as a bird whose wings, tail and head are its parts, and meditation on inner sound (nāda).

type:LABEL: text
name: Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad
summary: A Yoga Upaniṣad that teaches a six-limbed yoga, placing concentration (dhāraṇā) after meditation (dhyāna) as the Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad does; Deussen thought it older than the Yoga Sūtra.

type:LABEL: text
name: Haṃsa Upaniṣad
summary: A Yoga Upaniṣad on meditation on the self as the “swan” (haṃsa) and on inner sounds; a late text, known before the 17th c. since Dārā Shikoh included it.

type:LABEL: text
name: Paiṅgala Upaniṣad
summary: A Sāmānya Upaniṣad in which Yājñavalkya teaches Paiṅgala the Sāṅkhya-coloured stages of creation and the Advaita doctrine of liberation.

type:LABEL: text
name: Subāla Upaniṣad
summary: A Sāmānya Upaniṣad attached to the White Yajurveda that interprets the Puruṣasūkta and identifies Nārāyaṇa as the supreme being.

type:LABEL: text
name: Vajrasūcī Upaniṣad
summary: A short Upaniṣad that asks who is truly a brahmin and answers that it is not birth, body or learning but realisation of the self; a Buddhist work of the same name is ascribed to Aśvaghoṣa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nṛsiṃha-tāpanīya Upaniṣad
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad in two parts (pūrva and uttara) centred on the Narasiṃha mantra; Farquhar dated it before the 7th c. on the grounds that Gauḍapāda knew it, a dating others find early.

type:LABEL: text
name: Rāma-tāpanīya Upaniṣad
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad in two parts identifying Rāma with brahman and expounding the Rāma mantra; a late text important for Rāma-devotional (Rāmānandī) theology.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gopāla-tāpanī Upaniṣad
summary: A Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad identifying Kṛṣṇa as cowherd (Gopāla) with brahman, valued by the Gauḍīya tradition (Jīva Gosvāmī commented on it); placed after the Nṛsiṃha-tāpanīya and before the 16th c.

type:LABEL: text
name: Gaṇapati Atharvaśīrṣa
summary: A short Upaniṣad identifying Gaṇeśa with brahman, ātman and Om, widely recited in Maharashtra; Courtright and others date it to the 16th–17th c.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śivasaṃkalpa Upaniṣad
summary: A set of verses with the refrain “may my mind be of auspicious resolve” (tan me manaḥ śivasaṃkalpam astu), drawn from the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (VS 34.1–6) and circulated as an Upaniṣad.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Ṣaḍdarśana (the six orthodox darśanas)
aliases: six schools of Hindu philosophy|āstika darśanas
summary: The modern standard grouping of six Veda-accepting (āstika) schools in three pairs — Sāṅkhya–Yoga, Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā–Vedānta. The grouping is late: Haribhadra’s 8th-c. “six views” include Buddhists and Jains, and Nicholson traces the āstika six-fold scheme to doxographers of the 15th–16th c. such as Vijñānabhikṣu and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Āstika and nāstika
summary: The traditional division of views into those that accept (āstika) and reject (nāstika) the authority of the Veda — or, in older usage (e.g. Pāṇini 4.4.60), those who affirm or deny the other world; Buddhists, Jains and Cārvākas are the nāstikas of later doxography.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pramāṇa
summary: A means of valid knowledge. The schools disagree on their number: Cārvāka one (perception), Vaiśeṣika two, Sāṅkhya and Yoga three (SK 4; YS 1.7), Nyāya four (NS 1.1.3), Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā five, Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā and Advaita six (adding postulation and non-apprehension).
earliest_textual: c. 2nd c. BCE – 3rd c. CE (final redaction in the early centuries CE)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Prakṛti
summary: In Sāṅkhya, the single, unconscious, uncreated source of everything except consciousness — the “root nature” (mūlaprakṛti) composed of the three guṇas, which evolves into intellect, ego, mind, senses, subtle and gross elements (SK 3; 22).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Puruṣa (Sāṅkhya)
summary: In Sāṅkhya and Yoga, pure consciousness, the witnessing, inactive self — neither produced nor productive (SK 3) — of which there are many (SK 18); distinct from the cosmic Puruṣa of RV 10.90.
earliest_textual: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Guṇa
summary: The three constituents of prakṛti in Sāṅkhya — sattva (light, illuminating), rajas (active, stimulating) and tamas (heavy, obstructing) — which interact like the parts of a lamp (SK 12–13); in Vaiśeṣika “guṇa” means quality, a different category.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Twenty-five tattvas (Sāṅkhya)
summary: Sāṅkhya’s inventory of reality: puruṣa; prakṛti; and its twenty-three products — intellect (buddhi/mahat), ego (ahaṃkāra), mind, five sense and five action capacities, five subtle and five gross elements (SK 3; 22–25).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Satkāryavāda
summary: The doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its material cause, argued in SK 9 and shared in different forms by Yoga and Vedānta; opposed by Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika’s asatkāryavāda (the effect is a new beginning, ārambha).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kaivalya
summary: The Sāṅkhya–Yoga name for liberation: the isolation of pure consciousness from prakṛti once the guṇas have fulfilled their purpose and resolved back into their source (YS 4.34; SK 68).
earliest_textual: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Samādhi
summary: Meditative absorption, the eighth limb of yoga in which the object alone shines forth “as if empty of its own form” (YS 3.3); the Yoga Bhāṣya glosses yoga itself as samādhi.
earliest_textual: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Aṣṭāṅga yoga (eight limbs)
summary: The eight limbs of Patañjali’s yoga (YS 2.29): restraints (yama), observances (niyama), posture, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation and absorption; the restraints begin with non-violence (2.30).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Kleśa
summary: The five afflictions of Yoga — ignorance, I-am-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life (YS 2.3) — of which ignorance is the field of the others (2.4).
earliest_textual: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Īśvara
summary: The Lord. The darśanas disagree sharply: Yoga defines Īśvara as a special self untouched by affliction and karma (YS 1.24); classical Sāṅkhya and Mīmāṃsā have no creator; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika from Praśastapāda and Udayana argue for God as cause; for Advaita, Īśvara is brahman as associated with māyā; for the theistic Vedāntas, Viṣṇu or Kṛṣṇa is the supreme reality.
earliest_textual: c. 2nd c. BCE – 3rd c. CE (final redaction in the early centuries CE)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Padārtha (Vaiśeṣika categories)
summary: The Vaiśeṣika categories of what exists and can be named: six in Praśastapāda — substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence — and seven, adding absence, in later Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika (Tarkasaṃgraha).
earliest_textual: c. second half of the 6th c. CE

type:LABEL: concept
name: Paramāṇu (atomism)
summary: The Vaiśeṣika doctrine that earth, water, fire and air consist of eternal, partless atoms that combine (as dyads and triads) into perceptible things; criticised by the Brahma Sūtra (2.2.11–17) and by Śaṅkara.
earliest_textual: c. 2nd c. BCE – turn of the era (final form)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Apūrva
summary: In Mīmāṃsā, the “unprecedented” potency produced by a sacrificial act that links it to a result (such as heaven) arriving later; developed by Śabara and Kumārila to explain how a completed act bears fruit.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Apauruṣeyatva
summary: The Mīmāṃsā doctrine that the Veda has no author, human or divine, and is therefore free of the faults that make testimony unreliable; it rests on the claim that the word–meaning relation is original (MS 1.1.5) and that Vedic names refer to expounders, not composers (MS 1.1.30).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Māyā
summary: Power of appearance or illusion. In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (4.10) māyā is prakṛti and the great Lord its wielder (māyin); for Gauḍapāda duality is “mere māyā” (GK 1.17); in Advaita it is the inexplicable power by which brahman appears as the world; Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita reject an illusory world and read māyā as the Lord’s wondrous power.
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Avidyā
summary: Ignorance. For Yoga it is the first affliction, mistaking the impermanent, impure, painful and not-self for their opposites (YS 2.5); for Advaita it is the beginningless ignorance (identified by Śaṅkara with superimposition) through which the one brahman appears as many; Rāmānuja’s critique of its “seven untenabilities” is central to Viśiṣṭādvaita.
earliest_textual: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Adhyāsa
summary: Superimposition: the appearance of one thing in another, as silver in mother-of-pearl; Śaṅkara’s preamble to his Brahma Sūtra commentary treats the mutual superimposition of self and not-self as the root of worldly experience and calls it avidyā.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vivarta
summary: The Advaita account of the world as an apparent, not real, transformation of brahman (like the snake seen in a rope), contrasted with pariṇāma, real transformation, as held by Sāṅkhya and the bhedābheda Vedāntins; the term is systematised by post-Śaṅkara Advaitins.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Līlā
summary: Play: the Brahma Sūtra (2.1.33) answers the objection that a self-sufficient brahman could have no motive to create by saying creation is “mere sport, as in the world” (lokavat tu līlākaivalyam); Gauḍapāda (GK 1.9) mentions and rejects the view that creation is for sport, while the devotional Vedāntas make līlā central.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Jīva
summary: The individual living self. For Advaita the jīva is brahman as limited by ignorance; for Viśiṣṭādvaita it is an eternal, atomic mode of brahman’s body; for Dvaita it is eternally distinct from God and from other jīvas (MBTN 1.69–70); for Acintya-bhedābheda it belongs to the Lord’s marginal (taṭasthā) energy.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Saccidānanda
summary: The characterisation of brahman as being (sat), consciousness (cit) and bliss (ānanda), drawing on Upaniṣadic phrases such as “brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite” (TU 2.1) and “consciousness, bliss is brahman” (BU 3.9.28); the compound itself is post-Upaniṣadic and common in later Vedānta.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Mahāvākyas (the great sayings)
summary: Four Upaniṣadic sentences taken by Advaita as directly teaching the identity of self and brahman — prajñānaṃ brahma (Aitareya 3.3), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (BU 1.4.10), tat tvam asi (CU 6.8.7) and ayam ātmā brahma (Māṇḍūkya 2), one from each Veda; the fourfold scheme is later than Śaṅkara, and Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita read the same sentences differently.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Jīvanmukti
summary: Liberation while still embodied. Sāṅkhya compares the liberated person who lives on to a potter’s wheel still turning from past impetus (SK 67); Advaita accepts it (Vidyāraṇya’s Jīvanmuktiviveka); Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita generally hold that full liberation comes only after death.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Viveka
summary: Discrimination: in Yoga, unwavering discriminating insight (vivekakhyāti) between puruṣa and prakṛti is the means of release (YS 2.26); in Advaita, discrimination of the eternal from the non-eternal is the first of the four qualifications for inquiry into brahman.
earliest_textual: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Sādhana-catuṣṭaya (fourfold qualification)
summary: The four prerequisites Śaṅkara names on BS 1.1.1 for inquiry into brahman: discrimination of eternal and non-eternal, detachment from enjoyment here and hereafter, the six virtues beginning with calm and self-control, and the desire for liberation.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Śarīra–śarīrin relation
summary: Rāmānuja’s model of the God–world relation: conscious selves and matter are the “body” of brahman, inseparable from and wholly dependent on him as a body on its soul, so that brahman “has everything as its body” (Vedārthasaṃgraha 65).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Pañcabheda (five differences)
summary: The five real and eternal differences of Madhva’s Dvaita — between God and selves, God and matter, self and self, self and matter, and matter and matter — stated in the Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya (1.69–70) and the Anuvyākhyāna.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Sphoṭa
summary: The indivisible meaning-bearing unit of language, manifested by sequential sounds, central to Bhartṛhari’s Vākyapadīya and rejected by Mīmāṃsā (Kumārila) and Nyāya.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Bhakti
summary: Devotion or loving participation directed to a deity or teacher; Pāṇini (4.3.95–98) already forms names for devotees of Vāsudeva and Arjuna, the Śvetāśvatara (6.23) speaks of highest bhakti to god and teacher, and the Gītā, the Bhāgavata and the theistic Vedāntas make it the chief means to the Lord.
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Turīya
summary: The “fourth” state beyond waking, dream and deep sleep, identified with the self in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (7) and elaborated by Gauḍapāda.
earliest_textual: around the beginning of the common era

type:LABEL: concept
name: Ahiṃsā
summary: Non-injury, listed in Chāndogya 3.17.4 among the gifts of the inner sacrifice and as the first restraint (yama) of yoga (YS 2.30); Mīmāṃsā debated whether Vedic animal sacrifice violates it.
earliest_textual: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Āśrama (orders of life)
summary: The orders of life — student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer. Olivelle shows that in the oldest Dharma Sūtras they were alternative lifelong choices (ĀpDh 2.9.21.1; GDh 3.1) and that some teachers recognised only the householder (GDh 3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27); the sequential “four stages” is a later classical scheme.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Saṃskāra (life-cycle rites)
summary: The rites of passage prescribed in the Gṛhya Sūtras and Dharmaśāstra — from conception and birth through initiation (upanayana) and marriage to death — whose number varies by text.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Vyavahāra (legal procedure)
summary: Litigation and legal procedure, the subject of the second book of the Yājñavalkya Smṛti and the whole of the Nārada Smṛti, which classifies disputes under eighteen titles (Nārada mātṛkā 1.19).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Dāya (inheritance)
summary: Inheritance and partition of property, on which the two classical schools of Hindu law divide: the Mitākṣarā (ownership by birth) and the Dāyabhāga (ownership on the owner’s death).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Brahma Sūtra 1.1.1–4 (catuḥsūtrī)
summary: The four opening sūtras of the Brahma Sūtra — “Then, therefore, the desire to know brahman”; “from which the origin etc. of this”; “because scripture is its source”; “but that, because of harmony” — on whose reading the Vedānta schools define themselves.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Brahma Sūtra 2.2 (refutation of other systems)
summary: The second pāda of book 2, which rejects in turn Sāṅkhya (2.2.1–10), Vaiśeṣika atomism (2.2.11–17), Buddhist schools (2.2.18–32), the Jains (2.2.33–36), the Pāśupatas (2.2.37–41) and — on Śaṅkara’s reading — the Pāñcarātra doctrine of the origin of the soul (2.2.42–45).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Yoga Sūtra 1.2 (definition of yoga)
summary: “Yoga is the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind” (yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ); with 1.3, when it is achieved the seer abides in its own nature.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Yoga Sūtra 2.29–3.3 (the eight limbs)
summary: The list and definitions of the eight limbs of yoga, from the restraints (2.30) to absorption (3.3).

type:LABEL: passage
name: Sāṃkhyakārikā 69–72 (lineage and Ṣaṣṭitantra)
summary: The closing verses: the doctrine was taught by the supreme sage, given to Āsuri, by Āsuri to Pañcaśikha, and reached Īśvarakṛṣṇa through a succession of pupils; the seventy verses summarise the Ṣaṣṭitantra without its stories and polemics.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.1–3
summary: The sixteen topics whose true knowledge leads to the highest good, the causal chain from false knowledge to suffering whose removal is release, and the four means of knowledge.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.1–5
summary: The opening of Mīmāṃsā: the inquiry into dharma; dharma as a purpose known by injunction; perception cannot know it; the word–meaning relation is original, so the Veda is an independent authority “according to Bādarāyaṇa”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.1–6
summary: The opening of Vaiśeṣika: the explanation of dharma, its definition by prosperity and the highest good, the Veda’s authority as “his” word, and the lists of nine substances, seventeen qualities and five motions.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Gauḍapāda Kārikā 2.32 (the highest truth)
summary: “There is no dissolution, no origination, no one bound, no seeker, no one desirous of liberation and no one liberated — this is the highest truth.”

type:LABEL: passage
name: Arthaśāstra 1.2.10 (ānvīkṣikī)
summary: “Sāṅkhya, Yoga and Lokāyata — this is ānvīkṣikī”: the earliest dated grouping of philosophical traditions under investigative reasoning, which the Arthaśāstra calls “the lamp of all sciences”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya 1.68–70 (the five differences)
summary: Madhva’s statement that Viṣṇu’s qualities, the difference of selves and God, of selves from each other and the world are all real, that the world-stream “endowed with five differences” is real, and that “these five differences are eternal”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.121 (equal ownership of father and son)
summary: “In land acquired by the grandfather, in a corporate holding or in movables, the ownership of father and son is equal” — the verse at the centre of the Mitākṣarā–Dāyabhāga divide.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The author of the Yoga Sūtra is the grammarian Patañjali
summary: A traditional identification, stated in a verse ascribed to Bhoja and in later hagiography, of the Yoga Sūtra’s author with Patañjali the author of the Mahābhāṣya (2nd c. BCE); most modern scholars treat them as different persons on grounds of date and doctrine.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Yoga Sūtra and its Bhāṣya were composed together as one work
summary: Philipp Maas’s thesis that the sūtras and the commentary ascribed to Vyāsa form a single composition, the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, by one author (Patañjali) c. 325–425 CE, rather than a root text with a later commentary.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Maṇḍana Miśra became Śaṅkara’s pupil Sureśvara
summary: The hagiographic tradition (the Śaṅkaradigvijaya literature) holds that the Mīmāṃsaka Maṇḍana Miśra, defeated in debate by Śaṅkara, became his disciple under the monastic name Sureśvara; modern scholars generally regard the two as different authors with different doctrines.

type:LABEL: claim
name: The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi is a work of Śaṅkara
summary: The popular attribution of the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi to Ādi Śaṅkara; most scholars of Śaṅkara (Hacker, Mayeda) regard it as a later Advaita work, because its terminology and its stress on yoga and samādhi differ from the commentaries securely by Śaṅkara.

type:LABEL: claim
name: Nimbārka lived before Śaṅkara (7th c. CE)
summary: A contested dating of Nimbārka: the Nimbārka sampradāya places him in remote antiquity; Roma Bose and others put him in the 12th–13th c., partly on the assumption that he wrote the anti-Mādhva Madhvamukhamardana; Vijay Ramnarace (2014) rejects that attribution and argues for the 7th c. CE.

type:LABEL: person
name: Utpaladeva
summary: Kashmirian Śaiva philosopher and poet, pupil of Somānanda and teacher of Lakṣmaṇagupta (Abhinavagupta’s teacher), who founded the Pratyabhijñā (“Recognition”) philosophy in the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with his own Vṛtti and Vivṛti, and wrote the devotional Śivastotrāvalī.

type:LABEL: text
name: Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā
summary: Utpaladeva’s verses on the “recognition of the Lord”, with his own brief Vṛtti, in four sections (knowledge, action, scripture, summary): the root text of the Pratyabhijñā philosophy of Kashmir Śaivism, critically studied and translated by Raffaele Torella.

type:LABEL: text
name: Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī
summary: Abhinavagupta’s commentary on Utpaladeva’s Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, completed 1014/15 CE according to its colophon as reported by Sanderson; with the longer Vivṛtivimarśinī it is the main exposition of Pratyabhijñā.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nāṭyaśāstra
aliases: Natyashastra|Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra|Nāṭyaveda (as the text calls its subject)
summary: The treatise on drama, dance and music ascribed to the sage Bharata, which presents theatre as a “fifth Veda” created by Brahmā for all social classes from elements of the four Vedas, and which first formulates the theory of rasa and the 108 karaṇas of dance later carved on South Indian temples.

type:LABEL: person
name: Bharata (author of the Nāṭyaśāstra)
summary: The sage to whom the Nāṭyaśāstra is ascribed and who, in its frame story, receives the nāṭyaveda from Brahmā and stages the first performance with his hundred sons; whether one historical author lies behind the name is unknown.

type:LABEL: text
name: Abhinavabhāratī
summary: Abhinavagupta’s commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra (c. 1000 CE), the only surviving early commentary, whose reading of the rasa-sūtra — rasa as a universalised tasting of emotion by the sensitive spectator — became the classical theory of Indian aesthetics.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Nāṭyaśāstra 1.11–18 (the fifth Veda)
summary: The origin story of drama: the gods ask Brahmā for a pastime to be seen and heard and open to all classes; he composes the nāṭyaveda, “a fifth Veda with the itihāsa”, from recitation, song, acting and rasa taken from the four Vedas.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Rasa (aesthetic relish)
summary: The “taste” or relish of an emotion evoked in a cultivated spectator. The Nāṭyaśāstra lists eight rasas — erotic, comic, compassionate, furious, heroic, fearful, odious and marvellous (6.15) — and states that rasa arises from the conjunction of determinants, consequents and transitory states; later theory added a ninth, the tranquil (śānta), and Gauḍīya theology made devotion (bhakti) itself a rasa.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Vedic Saṃhitās
summary: The four mantra collections — Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda (Śukla and Kṛṣṇa) and Atharvaveda — that form the base of the Vedic canon and were transmitted orally by recitation schools (śākhās).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Brāhmaṇas
summary: Prose texts attached to each Vedic school that explain the meaning, origin and correct performance of the śrauta rites, often through myths (ākhyāna) and identifications (bandhu).

type:LABEL: collection
name: Āraṇyakas
summary: Late Vedic texts, studied apart from the village, that treat esoteric or dangerous rites (e.g. the Pravargya) and contain or shade into the oldest Upaniṣads.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Upaniṣads
summary: Texts at the end of the Vedic corpus (hence “Vedānta”) that discuss the self (ātman), brahman, death and rebirth, and liberation; the principal (“early”) Upaniṣads number about thirteen.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Vedāṅgas
summary: The six “limbs of the Veda” — phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), metre (chandas) and astronomy/calendar (jyotiṣa) — developed to preserve, understand and apply the Vedic texts.

type:LABEL: collection
name: Kalpa Sūtras
aliases: Śrauta, Gṛhya and Dharma Sūtras|Śrauta Sūtras|Gṛhya Sūtras|Dharma Sūtras|Śulba Sūtras
summary: Aphoristic manuals of each Vedic school that codify the solemn (śrauta) rites, domestic (gṛhya) rites, rules of conduct (dharma) and altar geometry (śulba).

type:LABEL: text
name: Rigveda
summary: The oldest Vedic collection: 1,028 hymns in ten books (maṇḍalas) addressed chiefly to Indra, Agni and Soma, composed by hereditary poet families and transmitted orally with exceptional fidelity.

type:LABEL: text
name: Samaveda
summary: The Veda of chants (sāman): verses, almost all drawn from the Ṛgveda, arranged for singing by the udgātṛ priests in the soma rites, with separate song-books (gāna) recording the melodies.

type:LABEL: text
name: Yajurveda
summary: The Veda of sacrificial formulas (yajus) recited by the adhvaryu priest who performs the manual acts of the rite; it exists in a “Black” (Kṛṣṇa) branch mixing mantra and explanatory prose and a “White” (Śukla) branch with mantras alone.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā)
summary: The “White” Yajurveda, the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā in forty chapters (Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions), whose mantras are separated from the explanatory prose collected in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.

type:LABEL: text
name: Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda)
summary: The principal Saṃhitā of the Black Yajurveda, in seven books (kāṇḍas) mixing ritual formulas with Brāhmaṇa-style prose explanation; it contains the Śatarudrīya litany to Rudra (TS 4.5).

type:LABEL: text
name: Atharvaveda
summary: The fourth Veda, a collection of hymns and spells for healing, protection, prosperity, love, kingship and domestic life, alongside speculative cosmological hymns; preserved in the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions.

type:LABEL: text
name: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda, the largest and most systematic Brāhmaṇa (“of a hundred paths”), and a source of many narratives later retold in the epics and Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Ṛgvedic Brāhmaṇa for the hotṛ priest in forty adhyāyas (eight pañcikās), best known for the royal consecration (rājasūya) material and the story of Śunaḥśepa (AB 7.13–18).

type:LABEL: text
name: Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Taittirīya school in ten prapāṭhakas; books 7–9 are the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and book 10 the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad.

type:LABEL: text
name: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
summary: The largest and, with the Chāndogya, the oldest Upaniṣad, forming the end of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; it presents Yājñavalkya’s teachings at Janaka’s court, his dialogues with Maitreyī and Gārgī, and the earliest explicit doctrine of karma and rebirth.

type:LABEL: text
name: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
summary: An early prose Upaniṣad of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda school, in eight prapāṭhakas, containing Uddālaka Āruṇi’s instruction of Śvetaketu (“tat tvam asi”), the “five fires” doctrine of rebirth, and the only Vedic mention of a Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī (3.17.6).

type:LABEL: text
name: Taittirīya Upaniṣad
summary: Books 7–9 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, in three vallīs (Śikṣā, Brahmānanda, Bhṛgu), known for the five sheaths of the self and Varuṇa’s instruction of his son Bhṛgu on brahman.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aitareya Upaniṣad
summary: A short Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4–6) describing creation by the self (“ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt”) and ending with the equation “prajñānaṃ brahma” (3.3).

type:LABEL: text
name: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
summary: A Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad in four chapters, part of the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka, in which kṣatriya teachers instruct brahmins: Citra Gāṅgyāyani teaches Āruṇi, Indra teaches Pratardana, and Ajātaśatru teaches Bālāki.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kena Upaniṣad
summary: A short Upaniṣad of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda school: two verse sections on the unknowable brahman, followed by the prose parable in which Agni, Vāyu and Indra fail to recognise a mysterious being until Umā Haimavatī reveals that it is brahman.

type:LABEL: text
name: Kaṭha Upaniṣad
summary: A verse Upaniṣad in six vallīs framed by the story of the boy Naciketas, who receives three boons from Yama, the third being the teaching about what happens after death and the imperishable self.

type:LABEL: text
name: Īśā Upaniṣad
summary: A brief verse Upaniṣad forming the final chapter (40) of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, opening “īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ” — all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord.

type:LABEL: text
name: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad
summary: A verse Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in three muṇḍakas that distinguishes the “lower” knowledge (the four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas) from the “higher” knowledge of the imperishable, taught by Aṅgiras to Śaunaka.

type:LABEL: text
name: Praśna Upaniṣad
summary: A prose Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in which six students — among them Sukeśā Bhāradvāja, Satyakāma Śaibya and Kausalya Āśvalāyana — put six questions to the sage Pippalāda.

type:LABEL: text
name: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
summary: The shortest principal Upaniṣad (twelve verses), which identifies the syllable Om with all that is, past, present and future, and the self (ātman) with brahman, analysed into four states (waking, dream, deep sleep and the “fourth”).

type:LABEL: text
name: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad
summary: A theistic verse Upaniṣad in six chapters that proclaims one Rudra, called Śiva and Maheśvara, as creator and lord, using Sāṃkhya and Yoga vocabulary; it is the earliest text to make Rudra–Śiva the supreme god and closes with the word bhakti.

type:LABEL: text
name: Aṣṭādhyāyī of Pāṇini
summary: Pāṇini’s grammar of Sanskrit in nearly 4,000 sūtras arranged in eight chapters, describing both the spoken language of his time and Vedic usage; it is an external, datable witness to names and cults of its period, including Vāsudeva and Arjuna (4.3.98).

type:LABEL: text
name: Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali
summary: Patañjali’s “Great Commentary” on Pāṇini and Kātyāyana’s vārttikas (c. mid-2nd c. BCE), whose example sentences incidentally attest the Kṛṣṇa–Kaṃsa story, its performance by actors (śobhikas), devotees of Vāsudeva, and contemporary events.

type:LABEL: text
name: Nirukta of Yāska
summary: Yāska’s explanatory commentary on the Nighaṇṭu word-lists, the oldest surviving work of Vedic exegesis, which records rival schools of interpretation — the etymologists (nairuktas) and the “historians” (aitihāsikas).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Indra
summary: The most frequently praised god of the Ṛgveda (about 250 hymns, roughly a quarter), the soma-drinking warrior who wields the vajra and slays Vṛtra to release the waters; in the Upaniṣads, epics and Purāṇas he remains king of the gods but loses supremacy and is often humbled.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Agni
summary: The sacrificial fire as god — messenger between gods and humans, divine hotṛ and purohita — praised in about 200 Ṛgvedic hymns, including the first (RV 1.1); central to all Vedic ritual and still present in every Hindu rite.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Soma
summary: The pressed ritual drink and its god, praised in about 120 Ṛgvedic hymns, including all 114 hymns of maṇḍala 9 to Soma Pavamāna (“self-purifying”); in later tradition Soma is identified with the Moon and becomes ancestor of the Lunar dynasty.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Varuṇa
summary: The sovereign Āditya of the Ṛgveda who guards cosmic and moral order (ṛta), sees all and binds wrongdoers with his fetters; praised alone in about a dozen hymns and often with Mitra. Later he declines to lord of the waters and guardian of the west.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Mitra
summary: An Āditya personifying alliance and contract, almost always paired with Varuṇa; only one Ṛgvedic hymn (RV 3.59) is addressed to him alone. He is cognate with Iranian Mithra.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Sūrya
summary: The Sun as god, praised in about ten Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.50, 1.115); closely related solar deities include Savitṛ, addressed in the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10). Sūrya later becomes the focus of Saura worship and of great temples such as Konark.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Uṣas
summary: The goddess Dawn, daughter of heaven, celebrated in about twenty of the most admired Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.113); she has little independent cult in later Hinduism.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Rudra
summary: A fierce Ṛgvedic archer-god of storms, disease and healing, addressed in only about three hymns (RV 1.114, 2.33, 7.46), who through the Yajurvedic Śatarudrīya and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad becomes the supreme god Śiva.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Prajāpati
summary: “Lord of creatures”, named as creator in the last verse of RV 10.121 and the central creator-god of the Brāhmaṇas, whose dismembered body is restored in the fire-altar ritual; his role passes to Brahmā in the epics and Purāṇas.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Yama
summary: Son of Vivasvat and, in the Ṛgveda, the first mortal who found the path to the world of the fathers and rules there (RV 10.14); he is the teacher of Naciketas in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad and later the god of death and judge of the dead (Dharmarāja).

type:LABEL: deity
name: Vāyu
summary: The Wind, first to drink the soma, often paired with Indra (Indra–Vāyu); praised in a few Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.134–135, 7.90) and, as Vāta, in RV 10.168. Later he is the father of Hanumān and Bhīma.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Aśvins
summary: Twin horsemen gods of the dawn, healers and rescuers who appear in more than fifty Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.116–120); in the Mahābhārata they are the fathers of Nakula and Sahadeva.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Aditi
summary: “Boundlessness”, mother of the Ādityas (Mitra, Varuṇa and others), who has no Ṛgvedic hymn of her own but is praised as all things (RV 1.89.10); later the wife of Kaśyapa, mother of the gods and of Vāmana.

type:LABEL: deity
name: Sarasvatī
summary: In the Ṛgveda both a mighty river and its goddess, praised in three hymns (RV 6.61, 7.95, 7.96); identified with Vāc (speech) in the Brāhmaṇas, she becomes the goddess of learning, music and speech and consort of Brahmā.
earliest_material: ruined Kashmiri stone temple (8th–10th c., recall)

type:LABEL: character
name: Vasiṣṭha
summary: Ṛgvedic poet-priest to whose family maṇḍala 7 is attributed; priest of the Bharata king Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings, and in the Rāmāyaṇa the family priest of Daśaratha and rival of Viśvāmitra.

type:LABEL: character
name: Viśvāmitra
summary: Ṛgvedic poet of the Kuśika clan to whom maṇḍala 3 — including the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10) — is attributed; he adopts Śunaḥśepa in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and, in the Rāmāyaṇa, takes the young Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to protect his sacrifice.

type:LABEL: character
name: Agastya
summary: Ṛgvedic poet to whom RV 1.165–191 are attributed, husband of Lopāmudrā (RV 1.179), who becomes in the Rāmāyaṇa the forest sage who arms Rāma, and in Tamil tradition (as Akattiyar) the founder of Tamil grammar and a culture-hero of the south.

type:LABEL: character
name: Aṅgiras
summary: Primeval seer and eponym of the Āṅgirasa priestly clan; in the Ṛgveda the Aṅgirases are ancestral “fathers” who with Indra or Bṛhaspati opened the Vala cave and found the cows, and in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad Aṅgiras teaches the higher knowledge to Śaunaka.

type:LABEL: character
name: Bhṛgu
summary: Ancestor of the Bhārgava priestly clan; in the Ṛgveda the Bhṛgus establish Agni among men, and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhṛgu Vāruṇi is the son and pupil of Varuṇa.

type:LABEL: character
name: Atri
summary: Ṛgvedic seer whose family (the Ātreyas) is credited with maṇḍala 5; RV 5.40 tells how Atri found the Sun hidden by Svarbhānu’s darkness. In the Rāmāyaṇa Rāma visits Atri and his wife Anasūyā.

type:LABEL: character
name: Yājñavalkya
summary: The pre-eminent teacher of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and an authority of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, who wins the debate at Janaka’s sacrifice, teaches Janaka and his wife Maitreyī, and to whom the “white” formulas of the Śukla Yajurveda are attributed.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Gārgī Vācaknavī
summary: A woman philosopher who twice questions Yājñavalkya at Janaka’s court (BU 3.6, 3.8), pressing him on what the worlds are “woven upon” until he warns her not to ask too much; her second questioning elicits the teaching of the imperishable (akṣara).
earliest_textual: parts possibly still being composed c. 4th–2nd c. BCE

type:LABEL: character
name: Maitreyī
summary: One of Yājñavalkya’s two wives, described as a discourser on brahman (brahmavādinī), who on his departure asks for the teaching of immortality instead of wealth (BU 2.4; 4.5).
earliest_textual: parts possibly still being composed c. 4th–2nd c. BCE

type:LABEL: character
name: Uddālaka Āruṇi
summary: A leading Kuru-Pañcāla teacher of the early Upaniṣads who instructs his son Śvetaketu with the refrain “tat tvam asi” (CU 6), questions Yājñavalkya at Janaka’s court (BU 3.7) and, by the lineage in BU 6.3.7, was Yājñavalkya’s own teacher.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Śvetaketu
summary: Son and pupil of Uddālaka Āruṇi who returns proud from twelve years of Vedic study and is taught by his father that the self is the subtle essence of all (“tat tvam asi, śvetaketo”, CU 6); in CU 5.3 and BU 6.2 he cannot answer Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s questions on the afterlife.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Satyakāma Jābāla
summary: The boy of the Chāndogya (4.4) who, not knowing his father, truthfully reports his mother Jabālā’s words and is accepted as a pupil by Hāridrumata Gautama for that truthfulness; he later teaches Upakosala (CU 4.10–15).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Janaka of Videha (Upaniṣadic king)
summary: The king of Videha in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad who holds a sacrifice with lavish gifts, sets a prize of a thousand cows for the most learned brahmin, and becomes Yājñavalkya’s student.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Naciketas
summary: The boy of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad whose father, angered by his questioning, gives him to Death; waiting three nights at Yama’s house, he receives three boons and refuses all worldly gifts in favour of the knowledge of what lies beyond death.
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: character
name: Ghora Āṅgirasa
summary: A teacher of the Āṅgirasa clan who, according to Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.17.6, taught Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī a doctrine likening a man’s life to a soma sacrifice, after which Kṛṣṇa “became free from thirst”.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra (Chāndogya)
summary: The pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa named in a single sentence of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.17.6) — “Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī” — the only Vedic occurrence of that name-pair; whether he is the epic and Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa is disputed.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: character
name: Purūravas
summary: A mortal king, called “son of Iḍā” (aiḍa), who loses his apsaras wife Urvaśī; their dialogue is RV 10.95 and the full story ŚB 11.5.1. In Purāṇic genealogy he is the first king of the Lunar dynasty.

type:LABEL: character
name: Urvaśī
summary: An apsaras who lives with the mortal Purūravas on conditions he breaks, then leaves him (RV 10.95; ŚB 11.5.1); RV 7.33.11 also links her with Vasiṣṭha’s birth. She is a celebrated heroine of later literature, notably Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīya.

type:LABEL: character
name: Vṛtra
summary: The serpent (ahi) or “obstruction” who encloses the waters and is slain by Indra (RV 1.32). Yāska records two readings — a cloud (nairuktas) or an asura son of Tvaṣṭṛ (aitihāsikas); later texts make Vṛtra a brahmin-born asura whose killing brings Indra guilt, and the Bhāgavata a devotee of Viṣṇu.

type:LABEL: character
name: Śunaḥśepa
summary: Son of the brahmin Ajīgarta, sold to prince Rohita as a substitute victim for Varuṇa; bound to the stake at Hariścandra’s rājasūya, he is freed by praising the gods and adopted by Viśvāmitra as Devarāta (AB 7.13–18).

type:LABEL: character
name: Saramā
summary: Indra’s messenger who tracks the cows stolen by the Paṇis and demands them back in the dialogue hymn RV 10.108; later tradition makes her the bitch of the gods, mother of Yama’s two dogs (Sārameya, RV 10.14.10).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Brahman
summary: In the Ṛgveda (neuter bráhman) the potent sacred formulation of the poet-priest; in the Upaniṣads the ultimate reality, the ground from which beings arise and into which they return, often identified with the self (ātman).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Ātman
summary: The self — originally the body or breath, then the inner essence of a person — which the early Upaniṣads make the object of liberating knowledge and identify with brahman.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Ṛta
summary: The Ṛgvedic principle of cosmic, ritual and moral order and truth, guarded above all by Varuṇa and Mitra; in later thought its role is largely taken over by dharma.

type:LABEL: concept
name: Yajña
summary: Vedic sacrifice — offerings into the fire with recitation, chant and formula — the central religious act of the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas, which the Brāhmaṇas identify with Prajāpati and with Viṣṇu (“yajño vai viṣṇuḥ”).

type:LABEL: concept
name: Om
summary: The sacred syllable recited at the beginning and end of Vedic recitation; the Upaniṣads make it an object of meditation and a symbol of brahman (CU 1.1.1; Kaṭha 2.15–17; the whole Māṇḍūkya).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Karma
summary: Action — first, in the Brāhmaṇas, ritual action — which the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad makes the determinant of one’s future: “as one acts, so one becomes” (BU 4.4.5); the earliest explicit statements of the doctrine of moral retribution in Indian texts.
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Saṃsāra
summary: The cycle of death and rebirth. The early prose Upaniṣads describe the cycle (the “five fires” and the two paths, BU 6.2; CU 5.3–10) before the word saṃsāra itself appears in the verse Upaniṣads (Kaṭha 3.7; Śvetāśvatara 6.16).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: concept
name: Mokṣa
summary: Liberation from the cycle of rebirth. The early Upaniṣads speak of immortality and of the desireless knower who, being brahman, goes to brahman (BU 4.4.6); the noun mokṣa itself appears in the Śvetāśvatara (6.16).
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Indra slays Vṛtra
summary: The central Ṛgvedic combat myth: fortified with soma and armed with the vajra fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra kills the serpent Vṛtra who lies on the mountain enclosing the waters, and the waters flow to the sea (RV 1.32).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The three strides of Vishnu
summary: Viṣṇu measures out the earthly realms in three wide strides, his highest step holding a spring of honey (RV 1.154; 1.22.16–21); the Brāhmaṇas re-enact the strides in ritual and identify Viṣṇu with the sacrifice. The motif is the Vedic root of the later Vāmana–Bali story.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The sacrifice of Puruṣa
summary: RV 10.90: the gods sacrifice the thousand-headed cosmic Man (Puruṣa), and from his dismembered body come the verses, the animals, the four social classes, the moon, sun, Indra and Agni, and the worlds.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The Nāsadīya creation hymn
summary: RV 10.129, a speculative cosmogony: in the beginning there was neither non-being nor being; the One breathed windlessly; desire (kāma) arose as the first seed of mind — and perhaps even the overseer in the highest heaven does not know how creation came about.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Manu and the fish (the flood)
summary: The earliest Indian flood story (ŚB 1.8.1.1–11): a small fish caught in Manu’s washing water asks for protection, grows, warns of a flood, and tows Manu’s ship by a rope tied to its horn to the northern mountain; alone surviving, Manu sacrifices and obtains a daughter, Iḍā, through whom he generates humankind.
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Purūravas and Urvaśī
summary: The apsaras Urvaśī lives with king Purūravas on condition she never sees him naked; tricked by the gandharvas, she vanishes, and the grieving king finds her among the apsarases, who appear as birds; she foretells their son and the gandharvas’ gift of a fire by which he becomes one of them (RV 10.95; ŚB 11.5.1).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Saramā and the Paṇis
summary: Indra’s messenger Saramā crosses the Rasā river to the Paṇis, who have hidden cows in a cave; she refuses their bribe and warns that Indra, Bṛhaspati, Soma and the Aṅgirases will recover the cows (RV 10.108) — a form of the Vala myth.

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The story of Śunaḥśepa
summary: King Hariścandra, sonless, is advised by Nārada to vow a son to Varuṇa; when Rohita is born the king delays the sacrifice, Varuṇa afflicts him, and Rohita buys Śunaḥśepa from his father Ajīgarta as a substitute; bound to the stake, Śunaḥśepa praises a sequence of gods until his bonds fall away at the verses to Uṣas, and Viśvāmitra adopts him as Devarāta (AB 7.13–18).

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Naciketas and Yama
summary: Vājaśravasa gives away his worthless cows; his son Naciketas asks repeatedly “to whom will you give me?” and is told “to Death”; after three nights unfed at Yama’s house he receives three boons — his father’s calm, the fire-altar that leads to heaven (named after him), and the truth about what happens after death.
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Uddālaka teaches Śvetaketu: “tat tvam asi”
summary: Uddālaka Āruṇi teaches his son Śvetaketu through examples — clay, the banyan seed, salt dissolved in water — that the subtle essence of everything is the self, ending each lesson “tat tvam asi, Śvetaketu” (CU 6.8.7–6.16.3).
earliest_textual: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: Umā Haimavatī reveals Brahman to the gods
summary: After a victory the gods take pride; a mysterious being (yakṣa) appears; Agni cannot burn and Vāyu cannot lift a straw before it; when Indra approaches it vanishes, and in its place he meets a radiant woman, Umā Haimavatī, who tells him it was brahman (Kena 3–4).
earliest_textual: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

type:LABEL: narrative
name: The debates at Janaka’s court
summary: At a sacrifice of king Janaka of Videha attended by brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, a thousand cows with gold on their horns are offered to the most learned; Yājñavalkya drives them off and defeats in turn Aśvala, Ārtabhāga, Bhujyu, Uṣasta, Kahoḍa, Gārgī, Uddālaka Āruṇi and Vidagdha Śākalya (BU 3.1–9).
earliest_textual: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Vedic Śrauta ritual tradition
summary: The tradition of the solemn public Vedic rites performed with three fires by specialist priests (hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahman) according to the Brāhmaṇas and Śrauta Sūtras; it survives in a few lineages, e.g. among Nambudiri brahmins of Kerala.

type:LABEL: tradition
name: Advaita Vedānta
summary: The non-dualist school of Vedānta, systematised by Gauḍapāda and Śaṅkara, which reads the Upaniṣads, the Bhagavad Gītā and the Brahma Sūtra as teaching that the self (ātman) is identical with brahman and that the world of plurality is not ultimately real.

type:LABEL: person
name: Pāṇini
summary: The grammarian of Gandhāra (traditionally of Śalātura) who composed the Aṣṭādhyāyī, the foundational grammar of Sanskrit, probably in the 5th–4th c. BCE (disputed).

type:LABEL: person
name: Patañjali (grammarian)
summary: Author of the Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini and Kātyāyana, generally placed in the mid-2nd c. BCE from his references to Puṣyamitra’s sacrifice and Yavana attacks. Whether he is the same person as the author of the Yoga Sūtra is disputed and not assumed here.

type:LABEL: person
name: Yāska
summary: Author of the Nirukta, the earliest surviving Vedic exegesis and etymology, usually placed before Pāṇini (c. 6th–5th c. BCE; disputed).

type:LABEL: person
name: Sāyaṇa
summary: Fourteenth-century scholar and minister at the Vijayanagara court under Bukka I and Harihara II whose commentaries (Vedārthaprakāśa) on the Ṛgveda and much of the Vedic corpus are the fullest traditional exegesis; he died in 1387.

type:LABEL: person
name: Ādi Śaṅkara
summary: The Advaita Vedānta philosopher whose commentaries on the Brahma Sūtra, the principal Upaniṣads and the Bhagavad Gītā define the school; modern scholarship dates him c. 700–750 CE, though older scholarship gave 788–820 and maṭha traditions much earlier dates.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 1
summary: A later composite book of 191 hymns by many poets (including Agastya’s group 1.165–191 and the riddle hymn 1.164); it and maṇḍala 10 frame the older family books.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 2 (Gṛtsamada family book)
summary: Family book of 43 hymns attributed to the Gṛtsamadas; includes the Rudra hymn 2.33.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 3 (Viśvāmitra family book)
summary: Family book of 62 hymns attributed to Viśvāmitra and the Kuśikas; includes the river dialogue 3.33, the Bharata hymn 3.53 and the Gāyatrī 3.62.10.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 4 (Vāmadeva family book)
summary: Family book of 58 hymns attributed to Vāmadeva Gautama; RV 4.26.1 (“aham manur abhavaṃ sūryaś ca”) is quoted in BU 1.4.10.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 5 (Atri family book)
summary: Family book of 87 hymns attributed to the Ātreyas; RV 5.40 tells how Atri recovered the hidden Sun.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 6 (Bharadvāja family book)
summary: Family book of 75 hymns attributed to the Bhāradvājas; includes the Sarasvatī hymn 6.61 and the Indra–Viṣṇu hymn 6.69.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 7 (Vasiṣṭha family book)
summary: Family book of 104 hymns attributed to Vasiṣṭha and his descendants; includes the Ten Kings hymns 7.18 and 7.33, the Varuṇa hymns 7.86–89 and the Sarasvatī hymns 7.95–96.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 9 (Soma Pavamāna)
summary: All 114 hymns to Soma Pavamāna, gathered from the poet families into one book arranged by metre.

type:LABEL: passage
name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 10
summary: The youngest book (191 hymns), with the cosmogonies (10.90, 10.121, 10.129), funeral and Yama hymns (10.14–18), the river hymn (10.75), Vāc (10.125) and dialogue hymns (10.10, 10.95, 10.108).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.24 (Śunaḥśepa’s plea to Varuṇa)
summary: A hymn attributed to Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti in which the bound Śunaḥśepa calls on King Varuṇa to release him (1.24.12–13).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.32 (Indra slays Vṛtra)
summary: The classic hymn of Indra’s victory over Vṛtra: “I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra …” (1.32.1); the waters released run to the sea.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.154 (Viṣṇu’s three strides)
summary: Hymn to Viṣṇu who measured the earthly realms in three strides; in his highest step is a spring of honey (1.154.5).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.164.46 (“ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti”)
summary: Verse of the riddle hymn 1.164: “They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni … the inspired speak of the one that is in many ways”.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 1.165–191 (hymns of Agastya)
summary: The group of hymns closing maṇḍala 1 that the Anukramaṇī attributes to Agastya Maitrāvaruṇi, including the Indra–Maruts–Agastya dialogue (1.165, 1.170) and the dialogue of Agastya and Lopāmudrā (1.179).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 2.33 (hymn to Rudra)
summary: The longest Ṛgvedic hymn to Rudra, father of the Maruts, asking the fearsome, tawny, many-formed lord to spare and heal; “from Rudra, lord of this world, lordship does not depart” (2.33.9).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 3.53 (Viśvāmitra and the Bharatas)
summary: Hymn of Viśvāmitra in which the great seer conveys king Sudās (3.53.9) and declares that his formulation protects the Bharata people (3.53.12); tradition reads verses 21–24 as imprecations against Vasiṣṭha.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 3.62.10 (the Gāyatrī / Sāvitrī)
summary: The verse to Savitṛ in gāyatrī metre — “tat savitur vareṇyam …” — recited daily by twice-born Hindus and taught at initiation.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 7.18 (the Battle of the Ten Kings)
summary: Vasiṣṭha’s hymn celebrating Indra’s help to king Sudās of the Tṛtsus/Bharatas against a coalition of ten kings on the Paruṣṇī river.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 7.33 (Vasiṣṭha’s birth and the Ten Kings)
summary: Hymn of the Vasiṣṭhas recalling how their prayer won Indra’s aid for Sudās (7.33.3–5) and telling of Vasiṣṭha’s birth from Mitra and Varuṇa, “from the mind of Urvaśī”, and Māna’s (Agastya’s) birth from a jar (7.33.10–13).

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 7.59.12 (the Tryambaka verse)
summary: The verse “tryambakaṃ yajāmahe …” (we worship the three-mothered/three-eyed one … may I be released from death like a cucumber from its stalk), appended to a Marut hymn; recited later as the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra to Śiva.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.14 (Yama, king of the dead)
summary: Funeral hymn honouring Yama Vaivasvata, who first found the path for many, and sending the dead past Yama’s two four-eyed dogs, the Sārameyas.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.75 (Nadīstuti, praise of rivers)
summary: Hymn praising the Sindhu (Indus) and naming the rivers from the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the east to the Kubhā and Gomatī in the west (10.75.5–6); besides this verse the Ṛgveda has only the adjective gāṅgya (RV 6.45.31), so the Gaṅgā is marginal in the oldest text.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.90 (Puruṣasūkta)
summary: The hymn of the cosmic Man sacrificed by the gods, from whose body the world and the four varṇas arise.

type:LABEL: passage
name: RV 10.95 (Purūravas and Urvaśī)
summary: Dialogue hymn in which Purūravas begs the departing Urvaśī to return; she refuses: “Go home again, Purūravas; I am hard to catch, like the wind” (10.95.2).
